FRANK l\IACPHERSON Sl\IITH
Grand Master 1941 - 1942

Frank Macpherson Smith, se.venty-fifth Grand Master of Masons in
California, was born in Rock Island, Illinois, April 1, 1894, of American
parentage. The family removed to California in 1902, and Frank received
his education in the public schools of the City of Los Angeles, and the
University of Southern California. He received the degree of LL.B. from
the· Law School of the University of Southern California in 1917, and was
thereupon admitted to the practice of law.
In 1917 he entered the service of the United States Army and served
with the American Expeditionary Forces. When serving as first sergeant
in Company " B," 364th Infantry, in France, he was seriously wounded in
action, for which meritorious service he was cited and decorated with the
Order of the Purple Heart. He was honorably discharged from the American Army in 1919.
On ' his return to civil life he at once became active in the practice of
law in San Francisco, California, until 1922, when he returl).ed to Los
Angeles and engaged in his profession until his appointment to the Municipal Bench in 1931. In 1933 he was unanimously chosen presiding judge
of that court and in the same year was appointed judge of the Superior
Court, He was elected to that office in 1934 and re-elected in 1940, at the
primaries in each instance. He has served on the Judicial Council from
1931 to date, representing the Municipal Courts of the State of California
from 19'31 to 1933 and the Superior Courts from 1933 to date.
Judge Smith is a member of the American Legion, 91st Division Post;
of Delta Chi, Delta Theta Phi, and Skull and Dagger (U. S. C.) fraternities;
and is a member of the Alumni Association of the University of Southern
California; and for many years a director of the Midnight Mission of
Los Angeles.
Judge Smith was married in 1919 to Miss Eunice Richards, of Seattle,
Washington. They have a daughter, Barbara Jane, who graauated this
year from the University of Southern California, with the degree of A.B.,
and is now continuing her study for her A.M. degree, and a son, Richards
Macpherson Smith , now age 13.

FRANK MACPHERSON SMITH
Grand Master
1941

Freemasonry has had a large claim upon the time and thought of our
retiring Grand Master. He was made a Mason in 1922 in Argonne Lodge
No. 514, at San Francisco, California, demitted to East Gate Lodge No. 290
at Los Angeles in April, 1926, and was its Master in 1933. He served as a
member of the Los Angeles Board of Relief from 1931 to 1938 and was its
chairman in 1937 and 1938. He was president of the Southern California
Past Masters Association in 1938 ; was Secretary of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board in 1934 and 1935, and chairman from 1936 until he was
installed as Grand Master. He received the Scottish Rite degrees in the
class of July 8, 1932, and was honored with the decoration of Knight Com-

mander of the Court of Honor in 1939. He is a member of Al Malaikah
Temple of the Shrine.
The foregoing · record briefly indicates the successful and honorable
career of our brother, so full of outstanding accomplishments. His wonderful exemplification of the true Masonic creed has been an inspiration to
all who have been privileged to work with him. His advice has always been
sound and sage.
May the coming years bring him additional good fortune and may he
long continue to serve in the great cause of Masonry.

The Uses of Adversity
Address by RT. REv. W. BERTRAND STEVENS, Grand Chaplain

My Brethren of Grand Lodge:
To symbolize and to fix our minds upon the thought which I shall discuss this morning 0 I shall picture an incident in the life of the fouµder of
Christianity where He is about to enter the city of Jerusalem in great triumph
and glory, the one time in His life when He was proclaimed .as king. Th~re
was tragedy about it, because as He surveyed the city from ~1s vantage pomt
of the wheat fields and the olive groves, He wept over 1t because there
seemed something definitely lacking in the faith of a city that would reject
the truths of God. When ultimately there was in Jerusalem starvation and
imprisonment, it was a spectaC!e that was a kin~ of foreshadowing ~nd
illustration of what can happen to the world when 1t goes mad, of the kmd
of viciousness that we see today in the world. And as I suppose as He
looked over that city the thought passed through His mind that perhaps
after all it was not worth dying for. Why sacrifice himself for a community
. that did ·not care; why die on the cross for a world that was about to go
mad ? Why not go to some quiet little place and live out His life in comparative security, according to the length of the days of a man's life. W?y pot
give it all up? But He knew that that could not be and He set His face
toward Jerusalem. My subject might be called "Tht! Uses of Adversity,''
or, if I were to give it a somewhat negative title, I might call it "The
Futility of Escapism." We desire to escape the difficulties and sufferings
that come up again and again, anew and anew, and particularly so when
we see about us the kind of bestiality, the kind of brutality that is rife in
the world today.
It is the isolationist spirit. "Well, the difficulties are not mine. ' Why
should we worry? Why not attend to our own affairs? We shall weep
over Jerusalem but it is. not .up to us to do anything about it." The difficulty there is that the isolationist is always caught up with by history,
and whether he likes it or not, he finds himself in the midst of practical
difficulties from which there is no escape.

but our Job IS to adapt ourselves to its changes and t.o do the tasks that

we can t begin to imagine or to visualize the sorrow and pain and bereavement, the sense of loss which will dominate the hearts and minds of men
and women within the next year. We have an inkling of what it will be
~nd it does seem important to me, not only as a minister of religion, but
important to me as a Mason, that in our hearts in our approach to life
there may be that kind of courage, that kind of ~teadfastness that kind of
uprightness that will help not only us, but the people about ds to face life
as it comes, to accept its bitterest cups, to bend our backs to' its heaviest
loads. It is only thus that we can really attain to self-realization.
I have often wondered what kind of a person would be created by a
process of ?urture that :vould protect a child from its very earliest years,
fro~ all pain, from all disappointment, from all suffering, the kind of protect10n that would give ·that child everything that it wants and allow it to
grow up thus to maturity. My guess would be that child would be an
insufferable litle prig, that that child, grown to manhood would not be
fit to live with, because he would have had none of that self-discipline that
com~s thro~gh pai.n, the kin.d of pain. that is symbolized, perhaps, by the

Through pain we grow.

. ~ ha~ a frie.nd .who :was totally. blind and he had a very responsible
position in the city )n which I then hved. He was very much admired and
very much respected. I was up in a neighboring city after I had known
him f<;>r a year or two, and I met his sister quite accidentally. She said,

and think very highly of him but," I said, "what a pity that he lost his

in the family ·never considered it so unfortunate when he became blind
because up to the time he lost his eyesight he was of no use to himself
or anybody else; and the pain of los.ing his sight made a man of him."

11

Now, in some such fashion all of us, by facing the disa;pointments of
Jerusalem, achieve a very mu'ch greater gift of sympathy and understanding. If we have never known the hard things; if we have never known
disappointment, it is very difficult to enter into the sorrows of other
people. ·
I remember how I felt as a very young minister, when I had to visit
people in sorrow. I was aware all of the time that the pain that they were
suffering was not really shared by me, because I never had experienced it
myself. A woman of my acquaintance grew up as the child of a widowed
mother with a very beautiful sister .. This friend of mine was probably just
about as plain as a woman can be. Her mother said to her, "There are two
things that you can do as you grow up. You.can be hard and bitter because
you haven't the beauty of your sister, or you can face the fact that you
aren't beautiful, as one of the things in life that are yours to carry, and you
can develop your gifts of sympathy and understanding. You can develop
your gift of music." And being a very wise girl, she did· just that kind of
thing. Now she is a woman I suppose of 70 who has gone through life
beloved as few people are beloved, because she has faced the bitter things
of life, and through the bitter things of life, she has become a woman
beloved by all.
Then, last of all, I think it is through facing the sadness of life and
all of its pains and disappointments that we arrive at an understanding of
the meaning of religion. I mean first of all, religion in its larger sense, or,
if you choose, religion in its specific aspects, the religion of service, the
religion of sacrifice. "Greater love hath no man ·than this: That a man
lay down his life for his friends." It is the kind of religion which is not
merely doing things in the way of ceremonial or by the use of programs,
but that kind of religion which goes to the heart; it is the willingness of a
man, if necessary, to die for another. Through the hard things we learn
something of the meaning of God. God puts us into this world with a gift
of free will to choose for ourselves. Because we have the gift of choice,
some of us may choose unwisely. There is pain, there is sadness of heart,
there is suffering, but God in His Heaven remains as a God of love; an,d
perhaps it is that, far beyond anything else, that we Masons have to proclaim. Not only that it is necessary to sacrifice a little more, not only that
it is necessary to enlist and to fight the war, but that there is a God above
who knows and who loves and who cares, and when we go down into the
pit of deep suffering, we will know that God is there.
One last illustration, Most Worshipful, and I am done. One of the
great inspirations of this war, to me, has been a little obscure Chinese
clergyman, the Rev. Newton Tsiang, driven out of his home by cruel
Japanese invaders who forced him to walk 300 miles with his wife and
seven small sons up and down hills-hills so high that th.e y were really
mountains-across streams sometimes so wide that they were really rivers,
night and day, sleeping out at night except on those few occasions when
former pupils of Mr. Tsiang would invite them in to spend the night.
Going on and on and on, never complaining, never worrying, never turning
back, facing the hardships as if they were entering the heavenly Jerusalem
itself. As they came to the Yellow Mountain they looked up, and Mr.
Tsiang gathered his wife and his seven small sons around him, and homeless and footsore, together they sang a great hymn to the goodness of
God, that God in His love and goodness had brought them to so beautiful
a place to sing His everlasting praise.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
Breth1·en of the Grand Lodge:
Again the sands of time have run their course, marking the passing
of another Masonic year. Again we are assembled in annual communication, to review our accomplishments as men and Masons during the past
twelve months. Today I return to you the powers, authority and responsibilities with which you entrusted me a year ago. In doing so may I say
to you, with humble heart, that perhaps no individual Grand Master has
had greater opportunity to serve his brethren and mankind generally than
the disturbed conditions of the world have brought to me during my term
of office.
During the early months of this Masonic year, our country was thrown
into a devastating war, which already has brought grief and suffering into
many of our homes. Since that fateful day of Sunday, December 7, 1941,
I have striven sedulously to utilize the influences of our great fraternity
for the common good of our nation and of our brethren who are fightin~
for it and for all it represents. I have sought to bring relief where ·needed,
and courage to those whose hearts have been torn; to impress upon our
membership the obligation to stand firm, to the end that we may be able
to continue as a free and independent people.
·
How successfully I have utilized the golden opportunity that was given
to me, or how ineffectually I have administered your affairs, is for you to
judge. In keeping with our Constitution, I am presenting, for your thoug htful consideration, my written message, in which are set forth my official
acts within the jurisdiction during the past year, together with such recommendations on legislation as appear expedient and necessary for the craft
at this time.
This 93rd Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California
finds our nation in the midst of the most destructive war in history. It is
fitting that, in this message, I discuss some of the implications of this
war, with its threat of violence to our institutions and to Freemasonry.
Fortunate are we that we inherit from the founders of our Republic a
land free from the depravity of dictatorships, the brutalities of feudalism,
the horrors of inquisitorial government, the serfdom of absolutism, the
shame of casteism. Wise, indeed, were the founding fathers in that they
were able properly to appraise the workings of all past and then existing
·governments of the world, and thus could avoid, in their pattern for the
new, the inequalities and prejudices of the old. In calm and deliberate
retrospect they scanned the pages of history, and cast aside as unworthy
those forms of government under which mankind had suffered injustice
and oppression.
Clearly, they saw, a new pattern was necessary, a new relationship
among men, a new design for a new world, a charter that would embody
what was good within the old, with the purpose and vision of the new.
Fortunate it was that the founders were endowed with the fortitude and
courage to fight their way through uncharted seas and to emerge in the
. new land with new hopes and realizations for all peoples. Devoutly
thankful should we be for the divine insight of our fathers who, in carving
out a new rration, also carved out a new pattern of government, a strange,
new pattern that contained the. theory that all men were created equal,
that they were endowed with ci::rtain inalienable rights, that government
should be maintained ·oniy ·with · the consent of the governed. A theory,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA •

13

yes, but a workable one. Workable, because it embodied the principles
and doctrines of, first, the Declaration of Independence and, second, the
Constitution of the United States. Workable, because the immortal document establishing justice, insuring domestic tranquility, promoting the
general welfare, and providing the blessings of liberty was a stepping
stone from the un~ertainties of the past to the broad a nd g lorious vision
of a perfect union of free and independent states inhabite·d by a free and
independent people.
But now again, the ruthless hands of ignorance, treachery and
duplicity, of hordes controlled by murderous gangsters, with their announced aim the utter destruction of the "decayed corpse of democracy,"
are rampant upon the face of the earth. And, again, for the liberation of
mankind, it has become our consecrated duty, as citizens and as Masons,
to give all that is in us to give toward defeat of the sinister forces that
seek to enslave the world. As of this date, 3602 members of the Masonic
fraternity of this Grand Jurisdiction (a list of their names and respective
Lodges you will find attach.e d hereto a nd made a part of this message)
have gone into the armed forces of our beloved country and from those
of us who are denied that opportunity gqes heartfelt. acknowledgment of
their patriotism, with faith in the future and with assurance that the
synonymous principles of democracy and Masonry will surely triumph.
This Grand Jurisdiction is in a peaceful and prosperous condition
but members of the craft realize fully that neither a nation at war, nor
any of its citizens, may wander aimlessly along the highways and byways
of thought and action. War, unfortunately, seems to have become a definite
part of man's life. During the last 3400 years there have been only 227
years of world peace. Yet, after each of 8000 wars, "peace" treaties were
signed. Since 500 B. C. 902 of those 8000 wars were major wars-and
World War I was eight times more devastating than the other 901 combined. Since 1918, which marked the close of World War I, seventeen ·
wars have been waged, with an estimated cost in lives of 2,500,000 and
a money cost of $10,000,000,000.
When, on December 7, 1941. the attack was made which involved the
beautiful outposts of the Pacific, eight of the 582 Lodges of this Grand.
Jurisdiction were and now are located in two Masonic districts of the.
Hawaiian Islands. One of these, the 102nd Masonic district, of which.
Brother Charles A. Sheperd is Inspector, contains the following Lodges:
Kilauea No. 330 at Hilo ; Maui No. 472 at Kahului; Kauai No. 589 at
Lihue, Kauai. The other, the 103rd Masonic district, with Brother Alexander Douglas Potts as Inspector, has these Lodges : Hawaiian No. 21,
le Progres de l' Oceanie N.o. 371, Honolulu No. 409, and Pearl Harbor
No. 598, all located in Honolulu, and Schofield No. 443 at Schofield Barracks, Leilihua.
·
The affair of December 7th occurred while an itinerary for official
visitations and receptions was in course of preparation by me. Realizing
the gravity of the situation, and that it was necessary to continue as usual
so far as the rights of free men were concerned, I issued a proclamation
as of December 16, 1941, addressed to the brethren of the jurisdiction
•
which reads as follows:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

PROCLAMATION
To Be Read in Full at the Stated Meeting Next Following Its Receipt
To the Brethren of the J uFisdiction:
The Axis powers have again acted with the treachery and
duplicity which have characterized their every move-before and
since their unholy alliance.
Beginning with the invasion of China by the war lords of
Japan, and culminating in the infamous attack on Hawaii, honorable practices and customs between nations have been abandoned
for the actions of barbarians.
In between China and Hawaii lie the heel-marks of savage
beasts, implanting on fair and peaceable lands the temporary
imprint of their goose-stepping hordes. The rape of Ethiopia and
the stab-in-the-back of France by Mussolini-enslaved Italy, the
assassination of Czechoslovakia, Poland, The Netherlands, Norway, Greece, J ugoslavia and many others, by the lust and rapacity
of a nation controlled by murderous gangsters.
·
In between China and Hawaii are incalculable deceits and
duplicities-incredible brutalities and cruelties, deliberate obliteration of civilization's cherished outposts, cunning and fraud practiced upon a world-wide scale-all perpetrated and put into force
by the "Master Race" of the Nazis. Their announced aim, the
utter destruction of the "decayed corpse of democracy."

And now that the challenge has been flung-and immediately
accepted-all the energies, all the power of our democracy, so hated
and contemptuously flouted by the "Master Class" and the Samurai
of the world, will be marshaled toward the final victory-certain
and assured.
But between this day and that certain day of the future when
the forces of democracy throw open the gate of liberation for all
mankind, much must be done. It shall be our proud and eager
duty, both as Americans and as Masons, to don the garments of
work, of sacrifice and of iron determination.
Behind our Commander-in-Chief, in the solid ranks of a
united and virile nation, it has become our consecrated duty to
carry out his orders and to allow nothing tu interfere with our
sacred obligations as citizens and as Masons.
In furtherance of these obligations, I urge every craftsman
residing within the jurisdiction to render that service for God and
country, and to rededicate themselves to the high principles and
purposes of our government. In all things, in every action, I
strongly urge that staunchness of spirit, that eagerness to serve,
that has characterized every generation of Americans from the
birth of the Revolution to the present day.

Obey, implicitly, the orders of those in command; pursue
religiously the allotted daily tasks; cheerfully and gratefully accept
the extra hours imposed by, and dedicated to, the war effort;
volunteer; whenever and wherever possible, extra service to the
national cause, and, finally, contribute to the limit of ability and
fortune, to the programs reflecting the national will to complete
victory.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

15

This is my earnest prayer and prediction; that Masons of the
jurisdiction will not be found wanting during the national crisis,
and that they will further prove, as in the years past, their complete realization and appreciation of the sacred privileges of
citizenship.
Our freedom, together with that of the entire civilized world,
depends upon our united efforts. I have every confidence in the
outcome and the patriotic allegiance of my fellow craftsmen of
California.
Fraternally and sincerely,
FRANK M. SMITH, Grand Master.
Dated at San Francisco, California, December 16, 1941.
Attest: Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand Secretary.
This proclamation of December 16, 1941, thoroughly covered the
situation in which we found ourselves at that time and I can say in all
sincerity that the recommendations made in it have been carried out in
their entirety. All of our Lodges have adjusted themselves to the circumstances of the war, even to the extent that their own affairs are being
interrupted. Nevertheless, the Lodges have been able to show an increase
in work accomplished and a gain in membership, as well as attainment
of an even better financial status. All of our 582 Lodges meet as usual
and carry nn the affairs of 'Masonry, as well as perform their part in the
war effort. We must keep in mi'nd that, with the tree of liberty so deeoly
rooted in Freemasonry, and in. the American as an individual, we cannot
fail in all-out support of the war program, so that liberty may be preserved.
Necrology
In the forefront of the struggle for the survival of human freedom,
members of the Masonic fraternity have offered their lives unstintedly.
Deaths among our brethren have been heavy. It is impossible at this time
to state definitely how .many have given the last full measure of devotion
to our country and to preservation o.f its institutions. We shall have to
await further revelations of tlie casualties that have been incurred and
which will continue until the final and inevitable defeat of the forces of
tyranny and aggression.
One of the outstanding losses of our brotherhood was the recent death
in line of duty of the Duke of Kent, Grand Master of the United Grand
Lodge of England. The Grand Lodge of California always has felt particularly close to the United Grand Lodge of England, which has . bestowed
many honors upon officers of our Grand Lodge. In this connection, I was
privileged to send to the Grand Secretary of the United Grand Lodge of
England, on August 24, this cable message:
·
''The brethren, member Lodges and officers of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California,
extend their sincere sympathy to the United Grand Lodge of
England on the death of His Royal Highness the Duke of Kent,
Grand Master.
"Frank M. Smith, Grand Master."

Apart from the victims of war's havoc, the ranks of our fraternity
have suffered deaths from natural causes, inherent in life's uncertainties.
Many of these brethren were capable and efficient officers and members
of our Grand Lodge, whose passing has been not only a personal grief
but a distinct loss to the jurisdiction. To the families of these we tender
all that we have of sincere sympathy. At an appropriate time our Committee on Necrology will make a report giving names and details.

at our Lodges, when they are desirous of and at liberty to avail themselves of it. As for direct relief to brethren in the armed forces, that is
not, in general, an immediate problem, but whenever a nd whatever it is
-as in hospital cases- it must be met.
The· matter of assistance-relief to wives and children-and to those
who may become widows and orphans-may in time become acute. Meanwhile, wherever in these cases there arises a need that is directly attributable
to the war, we must be prepared to give a helping hand until the home
Lodge can be reached and takes over the privilege of serving.

16

· Masonic War Relief Fund
• Realizing, as we all do, that the war that has been forced upon our
nation is an all-out war, that women and children are not escaping its
sufferings, I caused to be issued on February 14, 1942, a proclamation
establishing the Masonic War Relief Fund and appointed a committee to
raise the fund throughout the jurisdiction. Text of this proclamation is
given at the end of this summary of the reasons which prompted it.
Necessity of establishing the fund arose out of the needs of Masons
in the armed forces and the prospective needs of their families-wives and.
children, widows and orphans. During World War I, out of a membership
·of 63,986, there were 5349 California Masons in the uniform of this country:
and 111 of them made the supreme sacrifice. A service fund of $67,610.29
was raised in California at that time . by voluntary contributions to meet
the needs of Masons and their families, from all parts of the world,
attributable directly to the war.
In the present "War for Survival" in which we are engaged, California
Lodges have a Masonic member ship of 126,306-nearly double the membership of 24 years ago. It is reasonable to expect, therefore, that there
will be 10,000 or more California Masons in service before final victory
is achieved. Just what emergendes and causes for service may arise in
the meantime, it is, of course, impossible to forecast, but already many
needs have come into existence, and that these will continue increasingly
is inevitable. To meet them we must be prepared financially, and it is
for this purpose that the fund is being gathered against the day of possible
distress.
·

How Fund Is Being Used
While it is not practicable to specify in advance all the purposes for
which the fund ultimately will be en;iployed its main objectives may be
outlined. In considering these objectives, we must keep in mind various
conditions which affect them and which govern application of the fund
to the various needs. California, being in a "combat zone," is the site of
~cores of Army camps, air fields, Naval stations and general military
establishments, to which thousands of Masons from every state of the
Union are being and will continue to be assigned. These brethren of ours
want fellowship with us in our Lodges and we, on our part, want to know
them and to show them hospitality.. Lodge programs must be expanded
to welcotne them and everything done to make the visiting brethren feel
at home and to have the utmost of enjoyment in their short leaves of
~bsence from the rigors of war-time service.
The expense of such expanded programs is more than many of the
Lodges near to military and naval establishments can reasonably bear.
The fund which we are now engaged ·in raising provides a source of
assistance. Let me emphasize in this connection that there is no duplication whatever of any other service hospitality program, either by U. S. 0.
units or other service centers. Ours is an extra service to our brethren,

Applications for assistance from the War Relief Fund are made to
the Grand Master, with the understanding that the fund is not intended
to be used for regular relief services of our Lodges, but only for what are
designated as "war cases" or "war-connected cases." A com?lete reco:d
of every California Mason in service is in course of preparation and will
be on file in the Grand Lodge office. The cost of printing the record forms,
and keeping the recor d up to date, is a proper charge on the Relief Fund.
Also from this fund there are being provided special "Certificates of
Ser~ice," handsomely printed, signed by the Grand Master and the Gr.and

Secretary, impressed with the seal of the Grand Lodge an d enclose.d m .a
celluloid folder. One of these certificat es is presented to every California
Mason in the nation's service. The certificate serves not only to identify
him but also to commend him to the kind care, love and protection of all
Masons everywhere.
How Fund Is Being Raised
It was and is my earnest desire that the Relief Fund represent the
free-will offering of the brethren. It is believed that voluntary contributions
by individuals give to the contributor a gratifying sense of personal participation in the relief effort. For years we have heard men ask, "What is
Masonry doing in these times? What can I do?" A part of the answer is
made through this fund, for it does provide opportunity for every Mason
in the jurisdiction to do something helpful in a united Masonic effort for
his brother Mason. I ruled that Lodge donations, taken from Lodge funds,
may not be made to the War Relief F und, which must be kept on the
individual, voluntary-contribution basis th at has been outlined.
Lodge secretaries have been urged to report in detail all factual information they may have concerning brethren in the armed forces. Eighteen
Boards of Relief in California have been furnished a bank account in the
form of a revolving fund of $500 each; the two Superintendents of Masonic
Homes in California a like amount, and the brethren in the Hawaiian
Islands and their dependencies a similar revolving fund of $1000. As some
of our brethren are in far distant lands and other jurisdictions, we have
asked Grand Jurisdictions throughout the United States and in many
foreign countries to assist us in this work of brother~y love, r elief and
truth. To date, as a result of this appeal, a like revolving fund has been
placed at the disposal of every Grand J urisdiction in our o"'.n. land, and
also in Western Australia, Eastern Australia, New Zealand, Bnt1sh Columbia, Nova Scotia, North ern Ireland, England and Scotland.

committee will be known as the "Masonic Wa~ Relief Fund Committee."

An appeal is thus made to all craftsmen to assist to the limit of their
abilities in this· worthy cause. Contributions made to this fund will be on
a purely voluntary basis in keeping with the tenets and principles of
Freemasonry.

19

Our fighting forces must be backed and s uppor ted by the sacrifice and
loyalty of all, and I am convinced that this fund, creat ed and maintained
by the good-will and heart of the fraternity, will reflect the determination
of a free peopTe to remain free through the power and might of an aroused
democracy.
I am also convinced that every craftsman will want to add his name
and his offering, whether large or small, to this fund as he r ealizes the
priceless privilege of free and unrestrained giving in a land free of tyrannical control.
All members of the fraternity are urged to make their contributions
through Lodge secretaries for transmission to Grand Lodge, where the
fund may best be administered according to the needs and desires of those
serving us all in the armed forces of our beloved nation.
From time to time I shall address ·the craft further on this subject
and shall enlarge the committee as the expanding work requires.
F raternally and sincerely,
FRANK M. SMITH, Grand Master.
Attest : Lloyd E . W ilson, Grand Secretary.
To the chairman . of this committee, Honorable Earl Warren, Past
Grand Master, and to all the members of the committee on Masonic War
Relief Fund, I give the highest praise for t heir accomplishments in carrying out the purposes for which the committee was formed. As of October 6 the sum of $80,460.92 has been contributed to the War Relief Fl!nd.
This amount has been contributed by approximately 30,500 members of
531 Lodges. There have been 173 Lodges of this number which have sent
in their full quota of $1.00 per member and many of them have gone far
beyond that. There have been but 51 Lodges in the entire jurisdiction
which have made no r esponse whatever and it is hoped and believed that
these will participate in this program before the year is over.
War Service Committee
Allied with and similar in nature to the Masonic War Relief program
is that of the Masonic War Service Committee, which has been functioning
most helpfully under the chairmanship of Brother Mark A. Pierce, P ast
Master of Sunset Lodge No. 352. Objectives of this committee are to
keep our brethren on the battle fronts in touch with their brethren on
the home front; to let them know what we here are doing for the welfare
of their families, so that on their return they may be fully apprised of all
that has happened. while they have been away. Two worth-while and
necessary pieces of service have recently been undertaken by this committee. The first of these is a service to Masons and persons with Masonic
affiliation who arrive in San Francisco from other parts of t he world and
who 'need the service and assistance of their Masonic brethren. The War
Service Committee has arranged to have representatives of this Grand
Lodge meet these ships and to render whatever assistance may be required.
The second program recently inaugurated is to extend our M asonic service
to any Masons who may be in the Army or Naval hospitals in the state,
and this program will soon be expanded.

PROCLAMATION
Masonic War Service Committee

To ALL REGULAR, ANCIENT, FREE

To the Masters of the Several Lodges of This Jurisdiction:
Worshipful Brethren:

AND ACCEPTED MASONS

!T~lh"#:,.tf

Our brethren, in increasing numbers, are Jommg the armed forces of
the nation. They are thus demonstrating readiness to give "the last full
measure of devotion" to the end that "government of the people, by the
people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth," and to preserve
for each of us and for posterity the sacred and inalienable right to life,
liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
On freedom's far-flung battle lines our brothers soon will be__:_in fact
already are-serving in every corner of the globe.
Between them and the "folks at home" it is our duty to maintain
communication, so far as possible and consistent with military requirements; to keep them in touch with Masonry, their families and friends,
and to assure them that we are looking forward to the great day when
their victorious return will be acclaimed.
To this end I hereby appoint a Special Grand Lodge Committee for
this jurisdiction, said committee to be known as "Masonic War Service
Committee." Brother Mark A. Pierce, Past Master of Sunset Lodge No.
352 of Los Angeles, is hereby appointed chairman; Matthew Morton, Jr.,
Past Master of Charter Rock Lodge No. 410 in Berkeley, is hereby
appointed executive vice-chairman; Past Grand Master, and now Grand
Secretary, Lloyd E. Wilson, will serve as secretary of said committee;
said committee will be for this entire jurisdiction, in order completely to
cover the jurisdiction in every respect. Each constituent Lodge is hereby
requested likewise to appoint a Masonic War Service Committee to
cooperate with the general state-wide committee, and for the Grand Lodge
Committee, the Lodge Committees, and their chairmen, I bespeak your
active and energetic cooperation.
Write to our brothers in the service; tell them that the hearts and
prayers of Masons whithersoever dispersed are with them; tell them of
the activities of the Lodge and give them the news about the families and
friends; tell them we are here to serve at their command, and to "keep
the home ·tires burning." All communications concerning this committee
and its activities are to be addressed to the' Grand Secretary, War Service
Committee, and every effort will be made to see that all messages come
through.
From time to time I shall address the craft on this subject and shall
enlarge the committee as the expandin'g work requires.
Fraternally and sincerely,
·FRANK M. SMITH, Grand Master.
Attest: Lloyd E . . Wilson, Grand Secretary.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Certificates to Brethren in Service
One of the items in the distribution of our War Relief Fund, as noted
elsewhere, is the issuance of a certificate (pictured here) to each of our
brethren in the armed forces of the nation of whom the Grand Secretary
has a record. The certificate testifies to the fact that the holder is a member of the craft and commends him to the kind care and consideration
of all Master Masons, wheresoever dispersed. Issuance of these diplomas
was b·e gun in June, 1942, and accompanying each diploma was a letter,
signed by the Grand Master and the Grand Secretary, · which read as
follows:
Dear Sir and Honored Brother:
To you is given the privilege of service in the armed forces
of our beloved country, and from us, denied that opportunity, go
the heartfelt appreciation and acknowledgment of your patriotism.
Masonry is proud of you, and in thaf pride is a deep sense
of its responsibility to you and your comrades. Our duty to our
country is no less imperative than yours and, as we know your
service as citizen and Mason will be honorably rendered, our
efforts will be bent toward the achievement of a service no less
in sacrifice and idealism.
As our official recognition of your service, we are enclosing
herewith a diploma, which we trust you will use often and find
of much value. With it goes our pledge of full support and
cooperation and of our desire to be always of service to those
who serve us all.
With faith in the future and with the assurance that the
synonymous principles of democracy and Masonry will triumph fo~
the benefit of all mankind, and with warmest personal greetings,
Fraternally and sincerely yours,
FRANK M. SMITH, Grand Master.
Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand Secretary.
Of the many letters of appreciation that have been received from
the brethren in the service, to whom the diplomas with accotppanying
letters have been sent, the following is typical:
U. S. Naval Station
My Dear Brothers:
Your warm letter of greetings and pledges of support and
cooperation have brought to me great inspiration for the work on
which I am engaged.
In these times, which involve personal sacrifice and unrelaxed
effort, one realizes great strength {rom expressions such as yours.
Let me extend to you my congratulations for your continued
service to our country and my deepest appreciation of your words
of encouragement.
Fraternally yours,
Lieutenant Commander, U . S. N. R.

Hawaiian Islands' Lodges
Most of our members are familiar with the history and traditions of
le Progres de l'Oceanie Lodge No. 371, at Honolulu, which received its
original charter from France in 1842, and which had planned to celebrate
its lOOth anniversary last April. This celebration, rudely cancelled by war
conditions, would have attracted to it the Grand Masters of most of the
Grand Lodges of the world. One of the outstanding facts about this
Hawaiian Lodge is that its Masters have come from the ranks o.£ rich
and poor alike, from the lowly as well as those in high places, thus
typifying the equality of man, one of the foundation tenets of Freemasonry.
One of the deepest regrets of my past year of stewardship has been
that I was unable to go to the Hawaiian Islands for the annual visit customarily made by the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California.
However, because of the fact that a year or so ago I was privileged to
visit the Islands in the company of your then Grand Master Rollie W.
Miller, I have a personal knowledge of the activities of the Lodges there
and of conditions generally in that area.
Let me mention particularly one of the Lodges-Pearl Harbor Lodge
N o. 598. We of the American mainland, who pride ourselves justly that
we are doing much in carrying out '()ur Masonic principles as a direct
aid to the war effort, might nevertheless we'll take a leaf from the book
of this Lodge at Pearl Harbor. · Here is a Lodge whose Masonic enthusiasm and accomplishment have set a,record which could well be emulated
by every other Lodge in the world. This Lodge, virtually in the front-line
of the global war, has, notwithstanding, collected and remitted several
hundred dollars from its members and remitted the sum of $226-their
share- for our Masonic Relief Fund and would have sent still more w ere
it not that many of its members are in the nation' s armed forces at far
distant places. Here is a Lodge, too, which during the past year has
elected 46 applicants and has conferred 108 degrees on its own members,
as well as several courtesy degrees for Lodges on the mainland. Pearl

88

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Harbor meets at least once a week, sometimes twice, and its membership
is abiding loyally by all regulations and restrictions imposed by the military
authorities. These require that no meetings be held at night, but no request
for day-time meetings has been denied. The spirit of the members of Pearl
Harbor Lodge is expressed by its Secretary, Brother A. Townsend, in a letter dated August 1, 1942, in which he says: "They hold their hopes high,
secure in their faith in themselves and in the knowledge that 'truth is
eternal and unchanging,' and that they are fighting for that which they
believe to be right."
Because of the difficulties under which the Hawaiian Lodges are
operating, I have notified all the Lodges of other Grand Jurisdictions in
the United States that they should not request Hawaiian Lodges to confer
courtesy degrees, and the response to this request has been most
gratifying.
More is said about the work in Hawaii under the caption "Masonic
War Relief Fund" but I cannot close this discussiqn without a passing
tribute to the outstanding accomplishment of Alexander D. Potts, Grand
Standard Bearer of the Grand Lodge of California and Inspector for
Distr-ict 103, in maintaining the high morale of the Hawaiian . Lodges.
No one could have done more than Brother Potts in rendering assistance
where assistance was needed. Brother Charles Shepherd, Inspector for
District 102, which embraces other Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands, also
has established a most creditable record in every way and has worked in
complete harmony with all of the Hawaiian brethren and with Brother
Potts, who has been, in fact, my. personal representative in Hawaii. It is
my hope to make another visit soon to these Islands and to renew acquaintance with the brethren there.
Philippine Jurisdiction
Originally, and until 1910, the Masonic Lodges in the Philippine Islands
were under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California. In 1910,
because of the remoteness of the Islands from the American mainland,
it was c9nsidered desirable that the Philippines have their own jurisdiction,
and this was the condition when the Japanese took over the Islands and
all of the Lodges fell victims to the invader. Many of the brethren escaped •
to other countries, some to the United States, but all found themselves
without a Lodge where they might continue their Masonic activities and
pay their dues.
In this unforeseen development, I assumed emergency authority to
permit individual members of former Philippines Lodges to return to their
parent organization, the Grand Lodge of California, without affiliation, and
devised a plan whereby they could maintain themselves in good standing ·
in their own Grand Jurisdiction by paying dues through the office of our
Grand Secretary. In pursuance of this plan, the Grand Secretary was
authorized to issue necessary credentials to Philippines Lodge members
so that they might enjoy all the benefits afforded to regular paid-up
brethren under normal conditions. The money paid in, $2254.35, has been
set up as a special trust fund and will be turned over intact to the
Philippines Lodges when the invader has been ousted and the Stars and
Stripes again fly over the far-Pacific Islands.
At this time, and pending the inevitable victory, we of the Grand
Lodge of California well may pause momentarily to give thought to what
may be the present fate of many of our brethren so much closer to the
battle fronts. How many may already have made the supreme sacrifice
for the preservation of democracy! How many may be bearing the cruel

89

yoke of the oppressor! How many may be battling with all that they have
to the end that human freedom and decency again be established in the
world! We, _on the less menaced sector, cannot be indifferent to what
they .have given and are giving, to what they have suffered and are
suffering.

Service to Fighting Men
The question of what service should be rendered by the Grand L odge,
by constituent Lodges and by representatives thereof, to Masons in the
armed forces, is without question the most difficult one which confronts us.
I

.

At the last Communication of Grand Lodge, the recommendations of
the then Grand Master were approved and we have been proceeding along
the lines of that program during the current year. When those recommendations were made we were not at war, but the approach to the
problem was so sound that there has been no need to change from the
program during the year.
The Masonic Service Association has been organized and many Grand
Jurisdictions are contributing to its support and pursuing its program
and policy. This association has mapped out an elaborate and extensive
program of War Service. An invitation to the Grand Lodge of California
to join the association was declined because it · was our conviction that

92

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the Grand Lodge of California could give an adequate service through its
own efforts and by the use of its facilities, which wo~ld m?re fully acc~rd
with our policy, intentions and purposes in co?n~cbon. with. War .Reh~f.
We welcome all that the Masonic Service Assoc1at10n will do m Cahforma,
and throughout the world, for the benefit of our service conne.cted brethren,
but the Grand Lodge of California, through its War Rehef Fu.nd and
otherwise will continue its own generous and fraternal War Service program, which has been fully outlined elsewhere in this report.
Conference of Grand Masters
In company with Brother Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand . Secretary.' I
attended the annual conference of Grand Masters of Masons m the Umted
States at Washington, D. C., in February and was present at all ~f the
sessions. As was natural in existing world conditions, much of the discussion centered on the menace of the aggressor nations to human fr~edom
and to Freemasonry. The titles of some of the topies discussed gt~~ an
idea of the range of these deliberations. They include~: "Do Naz1-1sm,
Fascism and Communism Present a Danger That American Freemasonry
Should Meet?" "Freemasonry and the New World Order," and "Welfare
Work of the Masonic Service Association with the Armed Forces of the
United States."
Presentation of the subject matter of these discussions was made in a
most thorough and informative manner by t~e se".eral Gr~nd 1'.fasters
assigned to present them, and the informal d1scuss1ons. which foll~wed
were of great interest. The time consumed in the long tnp. to the nat10nal
capital to attend this annual conference was .well spent m the .valuable
returns derived from it through exchange of views and personal contacts.
your Grand Master was honored by being assigned the first discussion
on the agenda, namely, "What Can Be Don~ Legitimat~ly to !~ter.est
Non-Masons in the Fraternity? Has the Masomc Rule Agamst Sohc1tat10n
Been Construed Too Strictly?" Dividing the question into its two parts,
the answer I gave to the first is "Nothing"; to the second, "No." "Free
will," I contended, "has always been a recognized p~erogati,ve of fre~ men;
freedom to choose to select and to act in accord with ones o~n .will .an~
desire has even been the imprimatur in the human book of mens liberties.
I will not burden you here with further quotations from my address
at the conference, except to give one paragraph in which I spo~~ ?f the
"development of cliques and factions in the Lodge through sohc1ti.ng of
friends, of special groups, and in some case~ _of suppo;ters of on: side or
the other." The rejection of a strongly sohc1ted apphca?t, I po1?-ted o.ut
"would cause reverberations in a Lodge, in a commumty and m social
circles all of which would soon disrupt the Lodge and ruin its usefulness."
This ;ide of the matter is so full of likely evil that, I believe, it condemns
the whole suggestion of relaxing our Masonic rule against solicitation.
George Washington Masonic National Memorial
The 32nd Annual Convention of the George . Washington Masonic
National Memorial Association, held in the auditorium of the Memorial
at Alexandria, Virginia, on February 23, 1942, also was attended by your
Grand Master and by your Grand Secretary. Continuous good progr~ss
was noted not only with respect to the building itself but also in t?e .affairs
of the association. However, the work still is not complete, with much
yet to be done on the great library, the art gallery and the museum. Work

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

93

has been started on the replica room which is to house the George Washington relics and also on the blue Lodge room, which is to be used for
Lodge purposes, .and the 'money is on hand . to complete them. .
As at the Conference of Grand Masters at Washington, California
was honored by having an invited speaker on the program of the convention at the Memorial Association. Your Grand Secretary, Brother
Lloyd E. Wilson, who is a director of the association, was called upon by
the president of the association, Grand Master Elmer R. Arn, of Ohio, to
respond to the address of welcome by the Grand Master of Virginia,
Robert ·S. Barrett. Noting the good work already done on the Memorial,
Brother Wilson pictured the magnificent undertaking as "conceived before
a great war, planned during one, started on its way following one and
which may, I hope, be completed during one."
A statement of the Treasurer showed that California Masons, up to
1942, have contributed to the Memorial a total of $171,467.30, an amount
exceeded in only seven other states.

The Grand Master appreciates more than anyone else that the efficient
functioning of Masonry in this Grand Jurisdiction depends upon our
Inspectors. Through their Officers Association they· make it possible for
each officer to qualify to govern the Lodge over which he may be called
to preside. In addition to that they are required not only to perform the
services required by the Grand Lecturer but also to execute important
commissions as a direct representative of the Grand Master.
This year has been an extremely active one. Co~ditions have required
me to make numerous and heavy demands upon them. They have responded promptly, with the most capable cooperation. The office of
Inspector must continue to grow in' importance as Grand Lodge continues
its expanding program. We cannot overestimate .the services performed
by an efficient Inspector. To each of them I express my sincere appreciation for his unselfish services.
Committee on Masonic Information
As I have traveled over the state I have been gratified to find that
the Lodges were receiving the material furnished by the Committee on
Masonic Information and using it with interest and profit in Lodge meetings and in giving information on Masonic subjects to the applicants for
the degrees during the time they were advancing. I congratulate this
committee on the success of its work and recommend its continuance.

Constitution Month Observance Committee
Under the chairmanship of Past Grand Master Robert B. Gaylord,
the Constitution Month Observance Committee of the Grand Lodge began
to function in January, 1940, and has continued through September of this
year 1942. Because of war conditions that have arisen since formation of
this. committee, it became desirable that its activities be not limited to
Constitution Month Observance, but that its scope be broadened to include
as well the direction of our Masonic Defense Movement. In line with this
need, I issued to the craft, on February 10, 1942, the following proclamation:

PROCLAMATION
National Defense Activities of Lodges
To Masters and Brethren of the Several Lodges of This Jurisdiction:
For the past two years the Lodges of this jurisdiction have observed
Constitution Month in September. However, the critical condition in
national and world affairs is such that if our Lodges are to play a proper
part in efforts to maintain democratic institutions and national and personal liberty in the United States and throughout the world, we cannot
delay action.
I am sure that all Masons in this jurisdiction are not only vitally
interested but are personally concerned in promoting such current activities
as the purchase of defense bonds and war savings stamps, the contribution
of funds to the Red Cross, intelligent understanding of Civilian Defense,
Army and Navy enlistments, and similar war work.· Even mor e important
is the maintenance of public morale, both present and future. The time
will come when the war is over, and it is vitally important that we shall
be prepared to meet . that situation and to preserve for all time personal
liberty and American institutions.
It is therefore ordered:
1. That a perm.a nent committee for. the duration of the war be immediately appointed in each Lodge to present from time to time the part
which should be played by its membership in promoting these war efforts
and such other issues as may arise in the future.
2.. That, as promptly as possible, a meeting be held in each Lpdge
for the presentation of the problems which are before us. T his should be
a closed meeting, and if possible, the presentations should be made not
later than the stated meeting for March. The importance of the subject
justifies the issuance. of a special bulletin to obtain a maxirl).um attendance.
Under our constitution, no Lodge may donate any part of its funds,
however, worthy the cause may be. O n the other hand, I emphasize the.
fact that Lodge fun.ds, whether life members.hip or . otherwise, m,ay be
inve.s~ed in defense bonds and war savings stamps.
.
.
The direct soli.c itation. of funds at a· Lodge meeting is not permissible

98

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

for any of these objects. However, the Lodge should advocate, and the
committee should promote, individual interest and activity on the part of
the mc:mbership in all war defense measures.
·
The conduct of this Masonic defense movement has been referred by
me to the Constitution Month Observance Committee of the Grand Lodge.
A letter from that committee .furnishing detailed information and instructions will accompany this proclamation.
It is ordered that this proclamation be read at the earliest opportunity,
and not later than the next stated meeting in each Lodge of this jurisdiction . .
Dated: February 10, 1942.
Fraternally and sincerely,
FRANK

M. SMITH, Grand Master.

Attest: Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand Secretary. .
Many important functions have been directed by this committee,
among them being the encouraging of Lodges and individual brethren to
buy and buy more and more bonds of this our country. Our records and
the work of this committee now disclose that 438 Lodges have purchased
· and now hold $1,173,436.45 in Defense Bonds. A splendid record worthy
of note and much credit to the committee and its chairman.
Merely to attempt to summarize the committee's work and its splendid
accomplishments would require many pages. After Pearl Harbor I informed your Grand Lecturer that, in order to make it possible for Lodges
to meet as their by-laws designate, and to afford uninterrupted facilities
for the conferring of degrees on applicants, they should not only abide by,
but assist in carrying out, the terms of all proclamations of the Commanding General of the Western Defense Area, and that their temples should
make provision thoroughly to black out their properties whenever a blackout order is given. This, reports show, the temples have done, and it has
been one of the functions of the expanded Constitution Month Observance
Committee to see that compliance was complete.
I likewise recommended that the Masters of the several constituent
Lodges in California at all times comply with civilian defense dim-outs
and with all proclamations concerning lights for illumination, and that this
compliance be made certain by each Master reporting to the Inspector of
his district that each temple building or meeting place of each and every
Lodge has so arranged its lighting facilities as to conform to all requirements prescribed by the authorities, whether civilian or military. General
supervision of these matters has been another function of the Constitution
Month Observance Committee.
Public Schools
Our Masonic organization should continue its close interest in the
public schools of California· along the same general lines as in the past.
Every boy and every girl in every community is entitled to the advantages
of a free education, not merely for their individual benefit but for the
welfare of the state as well. More emphasis, perhaps, especially in these
times, should be placed on the fundamentals of learning, so that the
knowledge gained can be susceptible of practical application. Masonry
needs the schools, and the schools need Masonry. Not only should our
interest in the public school system be kept alive, but our interest as well
in other forms of public life and .action. 9ur elective officials, municipal,

Ross, which is a codification of our laws, is a standard work on the subject,
and if referred 'to will answer any question likely to arise in the mind of
any Masonic official. I suggest to all of our officers that they familiarize
themselves with this work, as doing so will assist in saving the time of
the Grand Master. Five decisions, however, I found necessary to render.
I specifically report the following decisions :
1. I have held that Grand Lodge does not give countenance to and
has no sympathy with a Lodge or its Hall Association raising money to
pay indebtedness on its hall, or for any Masonic purpose by public card
parties or entertainments.
2. In case of a permanent remonl from the jurisdiction of his Lodge,
precluding the performance of the duties of his office by a Master or a.
Warden, the office becomes vacant and the Grand Master may grant a
dispensation for holding an election to fill such vacancy or vacancies
(Ordinances, Sections 35, 34 (2d) ' 181). In case the offices of Master and
both. Wardens become vacant, I have directed th.e Inspector of the district
in my place and stead, to convene the Lodge and preside therein so that
the Lodge might apply for dispensation for an election to fill such vacancy
and after obtaining such dispensation to again convene the Lodge for .
said election. (Sections 34-6th, 117.)
3. I have held that for a member to have been a member in good
standing in this jurisdiction for forty years under Ordinances, Sections 99
and 255, he must have had an unbroken record for forty years in good
standing, or periods in which he was in good standing must add up to
forty years. In computing the forty years, time that he was not in good
standing cannot be counted.
4. I was asked if the English ritualistic degree team may exemplify
the English first degr.ee in a Chapter of Royal Arch Masons. L ruled that
it should not.
This Grand Lodge recognizes no man as a Mason unless he has been
regularly made one in some just Lodge of Masons, acting under charter
or dispensation from some Grand Lodge having proper authority to grant
such charter or dispensation. If the members of this English team prove
themselves eligible to visit our Lodges, they may be admitted and invited
to there exemplify their English first degree.
This Grand Lodge does not recognize any degree except those . of
Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason, nor does it recognize anyone of Masonry not authorized to confer these degrees.
The divulging, use, exemplification or repetition of the ritual, or any
part of it, of the three degrees of Masonry .in a Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons by a Mason rec::ognized by this Grand Lodge is reprehensible and
should subject such Mason responsible therefor or participating therein to
. Masonic discipline.
5. During the year questions arose as to whether an applicant for the
degrees was plii.ysically sufficient to receive the degrees of Masonry. In
each case I ha~e asked the Master inquiring whether or not the applicant
with the defect mentioned could conform substantially or at all to what the
several degrees respectively require of him. In other words, can the applicant in any way or at all meet the requirements as now taught by the
Ritual Committee. In every instance the answer was that he could not.'
I hope I have found the formula to determine these petty questions, the
answer to which every Master knows if he is qualified to be a Master.

Recommendations

ture of freedom every:vhere. Though the shadows of war hang dark over
the world and our nation, and we as citizens and Masons face many sacrifices, w~ can renew our faith and our courage by a clear perception of the
everlastmg truth of Byron's lines:

Jt is my reco.m mendation that ito Lodge in the jurisdiction be given
permission to erect, remodel or repair any temple or other building unless
the project be satisfactorily financed. Ill this connection I favor legislation
by the Grand Lodge that will enlarge the membership of our Building
Committee and give it more power and authority over all such operations.
-During the year l found it advisable to reject all requests for new construction work, as the financial plans submitted for each seemed unsound,
e"s pecially in war-time when we should devote all our efforts to essential
undertakings. I urge strongly that our Lodges make full use of present
facilities, rather than develop new ones, for the duration of the war.
I cannot refrain from urging, also, that we display more warmth,
courtesy and brotherly cordiality toward visiting brethren from other jurisdictions. Let us be unreserved in extending to them the hearty handclasp
of our fraternity and making them feel at all times that they a_re completely at home among us. With this observation I urge that each member
of each examining committee make an effort to satisfy himself that a man
is a Mason rather than to find out how much ritual he actually knows,
and also that at least one of the committee make himself the host for the
visitor for the evening, to be sure that he is not left to wander aimlessly
and alone. Be men, be Masons. Meet and act as such.
Conclusion
With the closing of this communication, as my official duties as your
Grand Master terminate, may I say that I am profoundly grateful for the
high honor that was conferred upon me and that I appreciate deeply the
uniform courtesy and hospitality r eceived by me at the hands of the brethr.en. I would like to bespeak for my worthy successor an equal measure
of consideration and fraternal regard. Whatever of credit, if any, is due
fo my administration is to be shared by all the Grand Lodge officers and
all the brethren of this jurisdiction.
·
I commenced my year's work with the very best intentions-better,
perhaps, than I was able to at all times carry out-for it had been my.
iittention to visit virtually all of the districts of the state. This I found
impossible to do, having regard for my judicial duties and the many pressing matters before the Grand Lodge arising out of the war effort. Nevertheless, I was able to visit a great majority of the districts .and I have
endeavored to meet as many groups of our brethren as was possible.
Several of the Lodges during the year have requested permission to
reduce the fees for degrees. I question the wisdom of this practice, as I
believe the trend for reduction of fees is in the wrong direction. Already
many of the brethren feel that not sufficient care is exercised at times in
the admission of applicants, and a r eduction of fees would accentuate that
situation. There is that in Masonry which attracts men and we should
see to it that our ranks remain always recognizable as composed of men
~f .highest character and honor.
· ln and during these times' I am sure that all of us are deeply impressed
with the responsibilities resting upon us. May the legislatioi:i to be enacted
at ·this session be inspired by wisdom, and our deliberations be conducted
in harmony and brotherly understanding, so that our jurisdiction will con~inue its course of justice and good fortune. Bearing ever in mind that our
tree of Liberty is as deep-roo ted as are the giant Redwoods of our state,
~nd that the principles of our Republic and of .Freemasonry are no less
firml;y grounded, may we direct our energies toward buttressing the struc-

"Freedom's battle once begun,
Bequeath'd from bleeding sire to son,
Though baffled oft, is ever won."
May it be won for all mankind and for all the ages.
FRANK M. S MITH, Grand Master.

The Deputy Grand Master referred the Grand Master's message to the following Committee on Segregation:· John R. Moore,
George Delavan, Jr., and Mark Edson.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRET ARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
The report of the Grand Secretary for the Masonic year just closed

is presented herewith.
The activity and the work of the office has been multiplied many
times over preceding years by the programs which the Grand Master has
inaugurated to meet war conditions. The office staff ·has done an excellent
job and the cooperation of the Grand Master in securing vital equipment
has made possible the accomplishment of a vast amount of work.
In the interest of greater understanding between the office of the
Grand Secretary and the Lodge secretaries on matters of mutual concern,
a series of meetings have been held with Lodge secretaries in various
sections of the state during the past year.
At these meetings either the Grand Secretary or the Assistant Grand
Secretary, and in some cases both, have spent an evening with a group
of secretaries discussing records, forms, procedures and other matters.
More than one-third of the secretaries of the jurisdiction have been present
at these meetings and the discussions have been of great value to all.
It is our judgment that these meetings should be held occasionally
in the future as opportunity affords.
During the year, with the assistance of the printer, we prepared,
bound for ready reference, a complete set of all the forms used by the
Lodges in connection .with their work and in connection with reports and
orders to the Grand Secretary's office. This provided the Lodge secretaries with a ready reference to any form which they might have occasion
to. use and has proved to be most valuable.
One of the questions most frequently asked by any Grand Master
and by others who are interested, is, "How are things going with the
Lodges in relation to applications, etc.?"
Unfortunately, under the system of reporting only once a year, which
is in vogue in this jurisdiction, it is impossible for anyone to answer such
a question until the annual returns are in. There i~ no way of knowing
how many applicants are elected, how many degrees conferred, how many
affiliates are elected,. how many members withdraw, nor how many members have died, and since these reports are made but once a year, it auto-

Comments
As shown in the capital account of Exhibit E, the total of the expenses
and appropriations exceeded the revenue by $3,781.27. Included .in this
excess are the following items : loan to Carpinteria Lodge No. 444, $2500;
Federal Unemployment taxes for prior years, $522.17; and amortization of
ponds for current year, $331.56; total $3353.73.
All dues payable during the year 1941-42, as reported on the 1941
annual returns, have been paid in full. Our Exhibits B-1 and B-2 show proof
of the revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1941 annual
returns and the $25.00 Homes contributions reports for the first three
quarters of the fiscal year 1941-42. The total revenue due, as shown, agrees
with the total cash received from the Lodges by the Grand Secretary.
Cash receipts were accounted for and traced to the proper depositaries.
Disbursements were made by checks and supported by properly approved
vouchers.
All bank balances were verified by correspondence with the depositaries. Certified lists of stocks and bonds belonging to all funds were
received from the Anglo California National Bank which holds the
securities in trust .
In accordance with a resolution adopted by Grand Lodge last year,
the unpaid balance of the loan to Drytown Lodge No. 174, in amount
$440.00, was written off the records of Grand Lodge. A loan was made to
Carpinteria Lodge No. 444, in amount ~2,500.00, as approved by Grand
Lodge last year.
During the year under review, two special funds were set up under
instructions from the Grand Master-the War Relief . Fund and a trust
fund for the . account of the Grand Lodge, F . & A. M., of the Philippine
Islands. A detailed statement of the cash received and disbursed ·for the
account of these funds is shown on our Exhibit C. These funds are not
available for the usual Grand Lodge activities, but are to be used only
for the unusual purposes for which created. · We have not included these
special funds in the total of general assets of Grand Lodge. They are
shown under the caption "Gash in Banks" for the purpose of record.
(Refer. Exhibit E-statement of assets and capital accounts.)
We certify that, in our opinion, subject to the foregoing comments,
the attached statements set forth the financial condition of the Grand
Lodge, F. & A. M. of California, as at July 31, 1942, and the result of its
operations for the fiscal year.
Respectfully submitted,
RUCKSTELL, BURROWS & WEBB,
Certified Public Accountants,
By FLOYD T. WEBB.

Some there are who might question the assertion that this present
generation has made no progress in the realm of art. We admit that
there have been some beautiful paintings produced but is there anything
comparable with ·Sistine Madonna, or with Blue Boy or with Pinkie or
The Angelus or dozens of other old masters now in the de Young Museum
the Huntington Library and other famous galleries of the world which
display . the sheen of the silks and the' satins and the careful technique
em.ployed in painting the laces and the embroideries which you will there
find?
Certain I am that I might be headed for trouble if I were to assert
that this generation has made no progress in the field of government.
But can you produce today a statesman to be compared with Washington,
Adams, Jefferson, Franklin, Hamilton, Webster and other men of their
day? Men who were willing to sacrifice their own opinions and personal
advantage for the good of all. Do you believe that the gigantic task of
framing and adopting our Contsitution could have been accomplished ·
under our pr-esent day political conditions? We have many politicians
today but few statesmen.
Why is it that this generation has made no progress in the realms of
music, arts, and political government? Is it because of the tempo of the
times in which we live or is it because that we have ·given no thought to
those fundamentals upon which progress in these arts and sciences must
of necessity rest? Have we attempted to streamline our ·daily lives and
those things around us which might otherwise be both pleasing, beautiful,
and harmonious and have given no thought as to whither we are traveling?
Every man here has been assured and knows that there is nothing
in Masonry "which will interfere with the duty you owe to God your
country; your neighbor or yourself." Masonry assumed that you' knew

"No debt, no obligation, is fully paid and discharged except we do so
in kind;" ·So, too, no fundamental principle of Masonry can be inculcated
into the individual life save that we ·know and understand it fully. It would,
therefore, seem that the first ·great Masonic duty which we owe to ourselves is that we learn the true meaning of Masonry and the second is
like unto it, that our brethren, too, learn to apply those principles to their
lives, to the end that the life of the community in which we live and of
the nation and of the world will be at peace and happy under· the influence
of Masonic teachings.
. There are many of o~~ brethren who are demanding a militant
Masonry and who would streamline this fraternity; those who advocate
that we condemn this or that religious organization, or this or that political
movem.erit. They insist that we use the influence of our numbers upon
legislative bodies for the passage or defeat of some legislation and that
we espouse the election or defeat of certain candidates for public 'office.
They desire that we commit our fraternity to follow some course and
enter upon some sphere of action wholly foreign to the original purposes
of Masonry. Are not these demands contrary to the fundamentals of
Masonry and the enunciations of this Grand Lodge? Is there any way that
we can exemplify before the world the worth and beauty of Masonry
except by our daily lives, and our conduct in practicing, "out of the Lodge
those great moral duties which are inculcated in it." From no other
examples can those who knock at our portals say that they come, "by a
.
favorable opinion conceived of our institution."
You need not be reminded that our fraternity is subjected to criticism
from without; that non-members . choose to act as judges of us. We may
say that we care not, that they know nothing of Masonry and, therefore,
are not qualified to judge. Deep in our hearts we do care for we desire
that all men conceive a favorable opinion of our institution; we crave for
our fraternity that high esteem and respect of our communities which
rightfully belong to it.
·
Masonry is judged by the individual Mason, by his daily life an·d ·
conduct, be it good or bad. The measure employed by those judges is the
highest standard of the community. Unfortunately, we can not select our
finest, the most upright, the best which we can produce and say to . the
world, "Judge Masonry by him." Masonry is usually judged by its worst,
by those who know .the least of our fundamentals and by those who fail
to practice and maintain our high ideals in their private, as well as their
public lives. Masonry can not lift itself by its own bootstraps. Masonry
rises no higher in its moral and intellectual sphere than the character of
the men who compose its membership.
The whole philosophy and the basic religion of human life is to be
found in the fundamental principles of Masonry, and unlass Masonry
can take these fundamentals, these pure and inspiring moral truths around
which its ritual and its symbolisms .are entwined, and translate them into
the very life and conduct of its membership we can not hope to live as a
fraternity, and I might ask, do we deserve to live?
While we know that perfection will never be attained in this veil of
tears, yet we can and I think must approach the problem of Masonic

123

When Brother ·Robert Gaylord was Grand Master he said, "Proper
Masonic education is a critical question and a crying need." It is still a
critical question and a crying need. I suppose that every Grand Master
since, as well as before Brother Gaylord has found it so.
·
Our first, most excellent Grand Master said to us in his Proverbs
"\Visdom is the principal thing; therefore, get wisdom and with all th;
getting, get understanding." There is a marked difference between wisdom
and understanding. Wisdom is knowledge. Understanding is the ability
to practically apply that knowledge. Do we really help our brethren to
get wisdon;, Masonic wisdom, and with their getting, get also Masonic
understanding?
Thousands have paid their fees, have memorized the required ritualistic
passages, have been enrolled as members and have never and do not now
have any tangible idea as to the meaning and the significance of that
which ·they learned. Those portions of our ritual alone are not intended
to convey any particular wisdom or understanding. As essential as is our
ritual, it is but a means to an end; it is the key of pearl which unlo.c ks
the golden portals of our ancient and beautiful mysteries . . But we must
go beyond the portals, we must enter the sanctuary to know and understand those mysteries. The Masonry that attempts to live within its four
walls can find its only expression in its ritual and in its symbols. As
dramatic as is its ritual and as beautiful and as inspiring as are its symbols
such Masonry has missed the very essence of its life and can not justify
its future existence.
