124

In our Lodges we vote upon an applicant for the degrees and then
about seventy-five days later we tell him that nothing remains to constitute
him a member of the Lodge but to sign its by-laws. In about seventy-five·
days · he becomes one by whom the world may judge our fraternity. Is
this hasty conferring of the three degrees all there is to Masonry? Masonry
is not such a shallow thing as to be mastered in seventy-five days. It possesses the depth which the finest and strongest minds have hardly' sounded
with years of study.
There never was a time in the history of mankind when the teachings
of Masonry should be more emphasized; there never was a time when the
spirit of Masonry was as necessary. Every fundamental of Masonry, every
· virtue sacred to the heart of our fraternity is being singled out for assault
and destruction. These are testing days for Masonry. Evils both social
and political are parading themselves under the banner of good government
and democracy. The very moral fiber of our communities is in peril.
We can and should point out to the novitiate the place which Masonry
must maintain in the social, economical, political and spiritual world of
today. We should impress upon him that brotherly love, relief and truth;
that temperance, fortitude, prudence, and justice mean something more in
Masonry than is recited in th.e ritual. This can ncit be done by reading
stereotyped articles in the Lodge and particularly after a man has reached
the zenith of his desire and has become a Master Mason, nor can it be
done in seventy-five days. We will do well to give more time ·teaching
our candidates more Masonic fundamentals that they may have more
Masonic wisdom and more Masonic understanding.
Masons can not understand Masonry without knowing something of
its history; not only its glorious history in this beautiful state but its
history as a fraternity both ancient and modern. Masons should learn of
the lore of Masonry, of its legends and of its ancient mysteries; learn
how it all started, of its antiquity and of its change from operative to
speculative. We should know of those outstanding men of all generations
who have contributed to Masonic understanding and also of those stalwart
pioneers who gave so much of their time, their talents and their worldly
wealth to make this Grand Jurisdiction what it is today. Is not the
knowledge and understanding of these things as necessary to the individual
Mason as is the knowledge and understanding of American history to
American citizenship?
The work of our Public Schools Week Committee is demonstrating
fundamentals of Masonry. It is essential that our membership be impressed
that Masonry believes in the equality of opportunity for the children of
all, of the high and the low, of the rich and the poor of all creeds anil
religions; and that Masonry believes that certain private schools tend to
create classes and stratify society and as such are un-American. There
must be no stratification of society in America like the rocks in our hills
and mountains where each strata is held in its · place by the one above
and the one below but our stratification should be more like the ocean
where every little drop is free to move as it will and though it come from
the very depths yet it may one day glisten in God's sunlight from the
highest wave. We are lovers of the liberal arts and sciences and . the level

Our novitiates should be taught to know and understand the work of
our Masonic Boards of Relief and of our Masonic Employment Service.
This work is most essential to Masonry and must receive the heartiest
support and cooperation of all Masons. The candidate has little opportunity to learn of our Masonic Homes, of our method of supporting them
and particularly of the Endowment Program, which is one of the outstanding labors of this Grand Lodge. The caring for those elderly men
and women, to whom the world has not been generous or even kind and
whc:i now face the sunset of life with a feeling of peace and security which
is accorded them by our protection; and our responsibility of training the
children committed to our care, · those who will take our places in the
world of tomorrow, burdened with our blunders and our mistakes: These
welcome tasks should be made well known to the members of our fraternity and this knowledge should create in the heart and mind of every true
Mason the desire to carry his share of the burdens. I can look over the
roster of my own Lodge and I see there the names of men now dead.
Men who were well-to-do, men who were really wealthy. I know that by
their wills those men left thousands of dollars to charity. Many of you
might criticize them if you knew what charities were thus remembered,
sufficient to say they left nothing to our Masonic Homes. The fault was
not theirs. They were charitably minded but they did not come to Lodge
very often and the knowledge of our endowment program was not forcefully brought home to them. Part of the fault was with our system of
dispensing this valuable Masonic information. I, too, can not escape my
share of the fault. I knew of our Masonic homes, I knew of our endowment program both as a Master and as a Past Master and I did ·not
enlighten those brethren, with the result that Masonry is poorer and they
were not made richer because of it.
·
The strength of a nation is measured, not by its millions of people,
nor yet by the billions of its wealth. The strength of a nation can only
be measured by the intelligence, the morality and the patriotism of the
whole people. Wealth can and does corrupt the ignorant and this corruption unless opposed by a sturdy morality and by a self-sacrificing and
devoted patriotism will soon sap the foundations of government. Masonry
in this country has always been .foremost among those vital forces contributing to the freedom and the welfare of mankind and has by its
influence and activities created a practical citizenship among its members.
We are justly proud of our righteous claim that Masonry has builded a
great nation, a government "of the pepple, by the people and for the
people" by translating· the teachings and the free principles for which we
stand into the organic laws and high ideals of this government.
The call of Masonry to serve is ·greater today than ever before in its
history. The responsibility resting uppn us is heavier than in years gone
by. Masonry' believes in America and ail that America stands for. Within
our fraternity you will find the gospel 'of democracy more clearly taught
than in any other organi'zation that the world has ever seen. We do not
discuss withi11 our Lodges any of the controversial political issues, nor
the merit; of any candidate for public office, as we owe allegiance to no
political party, nor to any candidate for office, be he a Mason or be he a
profane. Masonry teaches an unfaltering patriotism and a fidelity to the
great principles of American liberty. We, as a fraternity stand here today
pledging ourselves to uphold the principle of education of the masses,
to uphold the citizen's right of free speech, to uphold · man's right to

uphold the doctrine that church and state must forever be separated In

thing we call loyalty? Is it loyalty for me, when able to do so, to refuse
to buy war bonds and stamps when my government needs the money

Our country is now at war. A war not of our choosing; a war not. of
our making; a war which has been thrust upon us; a war to determme
whether we will continue to .live as free men and free Masons under these
principles of government to which we pledge ourselve.s or whether we
must live under a form of government dictated by foreign powers.
I quot~ from a great American and a great Mason, "The time is
now near at hand which probably must determine whether Americans are
to be. free men or slaves. The fate of unborn millions will now depend,
under God, on the courage and conduct of this army. Let us, therefore,
animate and encourage each other and show the whole world that a free
man contending for liberty · is superior." That, my brethren, is not something from this morning's newspaper-that is a part of the general orders
issued by Brother George Washington as Commander-in-Chief of the
American Armies on July 2, 1776, two days before the Declaration of
Independen.ce. How applicable it is to our present day conditions.
This is truly a world war. When the world is at its worst, then
Masonry must be at its best. · Masonry as an organization has not declared
war upon any foreign power yet any malignant influences and any sini.ster
restraints directed. against our government are . also brought ag;unst
Masonry as the two are so closely allied in motives and in purposes.
Masonry stands for peace, has always stood for peace. If our prayers
are heard and answered there never will be another war. But there are
some things which we as .Masons love more than peace. Our forefathers
handed down to us a heritage bought with hardships and suffering, purchased by blood and tears-the heritage of freedom and liberty. We are
willing to sacrifice our peace that freedom and liberty may be guaranteed
to us and to our posterity. · It is only by transmitting thi's heritage to our
children that we can fulfill that obligation, and discharge that duty in
kind received by us from our forefathers. Freedom is the heritage only
of self-disciplined nations; others may deserve it but can not have it.
It is for this generation to determine whether we will be a self-disciplined
nation and whether as such freedom will continue to be a heritage for
future generations to enjoy or become merely "a consummation devoutly
to be wished," a . vague · and an obscure dream of life.
Each of us has a sacred duty which we owe to our country. It was
in your first degree that you were admonished, "As a citizen you are
enjoined to be exemplary in the discharge of your civil duties by never
proposing or countenancing any act which may have a tendency to subvert
the peace and good order of society; by paying due obedience to the laws
under whose protection you live and by never losing sight of the allegiance
due t.o your country.".
·
What is this duty which we owe to our country and with 'which
nothing in Masonry interferes? . What is this allegiance which we are never
to lo:se sight of? What is this thing called loyalty which Masonry teaches?
Is it just .words. which we babble like children or is it something practica1
which we as men must observe?
Can we exp·ect our brethren who now wear the. uniform and are now
in service to be loyal unless we, too, are loyal? Can we expect them to

127.

May I as a leader of a great labor union at this time and in this hour
of need call strikes in vital industrial plants, regardless of the causes which
might in normal times justify such action? May I either slow down or stop
production and refuse to allow others more patriotic to take my place
without regard for the safety of my brethren in service whose lives depend
upon the "stepped up" production. Is that the loyalty of Masonry?
Our Grand Master has seen war as have many of you. He knows the
life of a soldier in the trenches of France, he knows of the mud, the slime,
the filth, the stench, the cooties and other vermin. He knows of the distressing hours by day and night considering the welfare and safety of loved
ones at home. · He has seen buddies to the right and to the left of him
killed in action. He himself knows of the sting of enemy bullets, he knows
of the pain and suffering of wounds filled with blood-poisoning and he is
even now suffering from its after effects. Knowing these things, he has
asked us to give to a fund to relieve our brethren of their distresses
in so far as is humanly possible. He knows that there are many who can
not give and from those he asks only their prayers; but from those .w ho
can give he asks and expects not only your prayers but your money as
well. Is it Masonic lGyalty to refuse?
The Masons of California have made a solemn promise before God
and to our brethren, that, they shall not fight alone. Wherever the battles
of today are being fought in zones of combat there you will find our
brethren. Some passed through the tragedy of Pearl Harbor, some are
with the American Expeditionary forces in foreign lands and some are
with our combat naval units on the high seas. They shall not fight alone.
Some of our brethren were on Wake Island, some were in Bataan
and some were with General Wainwright at Corregidor, hundreds wounded
and killed, thousands captured and are prisoners of war, their fate unknown.
Their sacrifice shall not be in vain. They shall not suffer and die alone.
This is a war against women and children. A war to destroy the
American way of life. A war to take from those whom we love the
necessities of life, the very food which nourishes them. Our enemies desire
to degrade this fair land as they have other lands. According to Red Cross
records, thousands of babies died in the flight from Paris, hundreds of
persons have starved each day in Greece. Children there are who have
never tasted milk, women and old men to whom a loaf of sour, black
bread would be · a luxury. To save us from this and worse our brethren
are now fighting; they are now standing between us and the enemy; they
are baring their breasts to protect us. They shall not fight alone.

"Sacrifice does not mean something offered to appease the gods, but
is the giving, as a proof of love and devotion, of something. t~at is held
more dear and precious to the giver." Our brethren are sacrificing. They
are giving their all for those whom they hold dear. More men will be
called to the colors. More men will be called to sacrifice, to suffer and to
pay the supreme penalty-they and their loved ones must be cared for.
Eighty thousand dollars will not be enough. You will undoubtedly be
asked to give more to this fund and for war bonds and Red Cross and for
other war purposes. Will you give, will you sacrifice, or, must they sacrifice
alone?
This fraternity will meet this challenge, for challenge it is. We will
give because it is patriotic; we will give because it is Masonic; we will
give because it is charitable; we will give because it is sacrificial; we will
give because it is righteous; we will give that our brethren may be assured,
that they may know that we are fighting with them and that we do not
ask, that we do not expect them to fight alone. We will ·give to fulfill our
promise and to redeem our pledge before God, that they shall not tight
alone.
We are in this war and we must of necessity stay in this war until
it is brought to a successful conclusion. This is a war of hate. With the
Axis hate 'is the cardinal virtue. They hate everything and everybody who
opposes their will and wish. We as Masons are in this war because we,
too, hate; ah, but we do not hate as do the Axis powers. We do not hate
peoples or nations or creeds, nor even individuals as such. We hate t~at
for which they stand, we . hate that which they practice. We hate the
tyranny which reduces nations to slavery just because · they want to be
free. We hate the arrogance and intolerance which denies freedom of
worship. We hate the dishonesty and the treachery which attacks peaceloving peoples without warning and even while peace negotiations are
in progress. · We hate the cruelty which leaves men, women and children
to die of want, starvation, and disease to the sound of fiendish laughter.
We hate the cowardice and · injustice which torture and kill . innocent
hostages for fancied wrongs. We hate the murder which destroys men
just because they were Free and Accepted Masons. If we do not hate
these things we, too, will be destroyed.
Hate ordinarily has no part in Masonry. Hate is contrary to our
teachings. The religion of Masonry is based upon kindliness, truth, honesty,
tolerance, justice, love for all men and love for our God.
Masonry is a great brotherhood which springs from a common father.hood. "The supreme motive of Masonry is two-fold, the adoration of God
and the exaltation of man." Masonry has always maintained a most worshipful attitude toward God and a loving ministry toward man. It announces to a doubting, yes, and to an unbelieving world that God is the
God, the giver and judge of all life, the end of all knowledge and one
who is worthy of our adoration 'a nd our praise and one in whom we as
Masons and as a fraternity put our trust. It teaches us to lift the burden
from another's heart, to wipe the tear from an eye of sorrow and that
instead of tryfog to get into some imaginary place beyond the stars to try
to get more of heaven into us while here on earth. Masonry does not
follow the practice pursued by many religious and other organizations
which spend much time in trying to teach a man how to die. Masonry
is life, Masonry is a way of life. Masonry teaches us how to live and
having lived by that standard set · up, we welcome death, "Not as a grim
tyrant but as a kind messenger sent to translate us from this imperfect

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

129

to that all perfect, glorious, and celestial Lodge above where the Supre.me
Grand Master of the universe forever presides."
Many in~eresting .stories have been told of what a man will try to
save when his house 1~ on fire: Some of these stories are amusing, but
most of them a:e tragic. Stones ~f men trying to save things of little
or no :-ralue, t.hings t~at can readily be replaced, but leaving · priceless
possessions, things which can never be replaced to burn. I need not tell
yo.u that even now the world is on fire, that our house is · in . danger of
be.mg consumed
flames~ We have but little time for reflection to deter~mne ':"'hat ?we will save .from the conflagration. Will we save tangibles or
intang1ble.s. Are we going to try to save those conveniences, those comforts. of hfe at the expense of freedom and liberty? Will we cry out in
anguish when our sugar, our tires, our gasoline and other commodities
are t~ken from us. and view with indifference the taking away from us
o~r nght to worship God according to the dictates of the individual conscience, the right to think and the right to speak and the right to vote
~s seems best for the natio~ as a whole?.. Can we insist upon saving our
Jobs, t~e profits of our business, the political power and influence which
we claim ~s. our own and allow the brotherhood of man, the spirit of
sq~are-deah~g, the welfare of humanity to be destroyed? We can find
ne1the; happiness n.or peace. nor satisfaction in life if we save those replace~ble, ~nconsequenttal tangibles and allow those priceless, irreplaceable
intangibles, thos('! things for which Masonry stands to perish in the flames.

?Y

Masonry stands for those things whith are eternal, those things which
are ev~r new, thoug~ as old as the ages. It answers the needs of the human
heart JUS.t a~ eff_ecttvely today as it · did centuries ago and if given an
opportur.u.ty it will ever· grow as a progressive science in the hearts of
our nov1t1ates.
To adhere to Masonry's rigidity of purpose is not stagnation. To
uphold its ancient landmarks is not reactionary. To promote its fundamentals is not failing to keep pace with modern times.
"Finally, brethre~, whatso_ever things are true, whatsoever things are
h~nest, whatsoever things are JUs.t, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever
t~ings are l.ovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if lhere be any

God of peace shall be with you."• For on these things, my' brethren

GRAND LECTURER'S REPORT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
I respectfully submit the following report:
The Grand Lodge of California is in business session, and this Nation
of ours is at war. If, in this report, I omit the encomiums to which so
many of our brethren are entitled under the extraordinary conditions of
all-out war, please understand that it is in the interests of brevity and
business dispatch and not because there has been no meritorious Masonic

service performed during the year.
Some of you may have noted many changes in the officers of the
constituent Lodges occurring since the publication of the Official Roster
in January, 1942. These are substantial evidences of the impact of war
conditions upon our fraternity, but in the reading, few realize the additional
burdens this ftux has thrown upon the Inspectors of the several Masonic
Districts, not only in .the qualifying of the new officers, but also in the
matter of supervision of, and advices to, the newly installed incumbents.
That these changes have been effected without deterioration of ritualistic
proficiency or interruption of Lodge operations, is indeed a glowing tribute
to the zeal, ability and love of fraternity of our District Inspectors an.d
to ·the industry and enthusiasms of the brethren of · our craft.
·
At the commencement of the just past Masonic year, your Ritual
Committee, envisioning a term of ensuing peace, and not foreseeing our
immediate embroilment in this international conflict, entered upon a constructive program looking toward the further improvement of Lodge ;1.dministration in general and to the further increase .i n the number of that
already large · group of California Masons who ,have attained precision
in the ritual of our Order.
Under the presently established system of ritualistic instruction and
supervision, it is not contemplated that, nor is it possible ·for, your Grand
Lecturer to visit the .several Masonic Districts and learn at first hand the
local standards of Masonic activities and endeavors. To supply this
deficiency, a system of uniform reports, to be made pursuant to Section
53 of our Constitution, was devised. These forms served as a guide to
the specific information which your Ritual Committee desired to be covered
in the reports required to be made to the Grand Lecturer. Under ordinary
conditions . the preparation of these reports was, perhaps, burdensome,
but under war conditions it became onerous because of the press of. other
work, both personal and Masonic, which required immediate attention.
Nevertheless, Inspectors of the . Masonic Districts responded to our request and the information thus made available to your Ritual Committee
was found extremely valuable. Some soft spots were discovered, but at
the same time, these reports brought out some very interesting meritorious activities and methods of instruction. This information is being
communicated to all the Inspectors; attention is being given to the deficient
territories and in addition, in all districts, special instruction is being given
in rhetorical delivery and tone quality of speech, as well as placing emphasis on precision of wording. By this means we are raising, and will
further perfect, the general average of ritualistic rendition in this jurisdiction. In this respect, may I here be permitted to express my appreciation for the very fine and meticulous services rendered to the fraternity

as an Officers' Coach and a source of ritualistic aut.hority in the absence
of the Inspector: In the larger Lodges it is suggested ·that three such
brethren be chosen, severally assigned a separate degr.e e and especially
trained in their particular portion of the ritual. This semi-official officer
should be more or less permanent, hold office at the pleasure of the
Inspector of the District, and be regularly invited to attend all Inspectors'
Schools of Instruction. The Master of the Lodge should make use of
this brother's proficiency by holding frequent Schools of Instruction for
the officers of his own Lodge, as well as using this Past Master as the
Coach in preparing the individual officers to qualify for advancement. By
this means persistent and frequently reoccurring errors will be eliminated
in the degree work.
2. We recommend that, where possible, each Inspector hold a separate
School of Instruction for all Lodge candidates' coaches of his District.
meeting jointly, and that the head coach of each Lodge be encouraged
to assemble his own coaches for frequent instruction and discussion of
of the candidates' lectures. By this means, persistent errors in the candidates' work will be eliminated and the instruction made uniform. We
recommend that, so far as possible, coaching by a ''friend of the candidate,"
unless he be a regular coach of the Lodge, should be eliminated.
3. Frequent vacancies in line offices are certain to occur under war
conditions. We suggest that these vacancies be filled by calling Past M'asters
back into the work rather than by advancing the ] unior Officers before
they are prepared for the additional responsibility. Advancement un'<:ler
pressure is apt to result in loss ·of precision in the work. Further, the
individual officer loses, because he fails to perceive the fuller meanings
and beauties of the work and there is also apt to be a lack of his understandings of other Lodge operations due to the difficulties under which he
is laboring. The Past Masters so installed should hold the positions only
until such time as the Junior Officers can qualify in an orderly way and
upon the usual proficiency standards. Pursuing this plan, there will be no
recision of ritualistic proficiency due to war conditions.
4. Many Lodges are, and will continue to be over-burdened with work
during the emergency. All Masters should be cognizant of the fact that
too many degrees and too many long Lodge meetings can be irksome not
only to the officers themselves, but also to the members on the sidelines.
Let us be careful not to have our Lodges degenerate into mere degree mills
during these times. Members her.e tofore listless or dilatory about Lodge
attendance, must be encouraged to come out to replace the attendance of
those who have, entered the armed forces of the United States. Retain the
continuing attendance of these returning brethr.en by a reasonable amount
of ritualistic work handled with precision and dispatch, then plan the
remainder of the meetings so that the Lodge will continue to be a haven of
rest and refreshment, a place of friendships, a source of general enlighten•
ment and, particularly in these times, an inspiration to extra-Masomc
patriotic . endeavor.
·
Finally, and most important of all, hold your Masonic meetings
regularly and without interruption, regardless of what impeding circum.s tances may arise, even though by remote chance it be, though God forbid,
in the very catacombs of destruction. Remember that Free Masonry and
true Democracy are inseparably linked together. One is certain to perish
wher.e the other is cr,ushed. Recall the Lodge attendance of our early
California brethren, riding to meetings through miles of snow and dark-.
n·e ss that the roots of Freedom and ] ustice be firmly implanted in this
new lan'il. Envision the present vigorous activities of our Hawaiian brethren

It is not too early to _prepare for possible disaster. We should not
delay, because even tomorrow may be too late. I will not play upon your
sentiments. The wisdom of completing this job is left solely to your reason.
I trust, then, that the following will be considered but a progress
report and that at the next session of Grand Lodge the vision of the
Grand Master will have been fulfilled and the security of our brethren
better provided for. Until that time, I desire to thank you for your generous response to the solicitation of the committee.
.
The Masonic War Relief Fund Committee presents herewith the report
of its activities and accomplishments.
·
The War Relief Fund was authorized by a proclamation of the Grand
Master on February 14, 1942, and the general committee was appointed at
that time. The proclamation also designated Henry C. Clausen, Past
Grand Orator, as Executive Vice Chairman, William P. Filmer, Past Grand
Master and Grand Treasurer, to be Treasurer of the fund, and Lloyd E.
Wilson, Past Grand Master and Grand Secretary, as Secretary. An Executive Committee was subsequently appointed consisting of the officers
named in this report plus:
Raymond W. Blosser
George V. Rulofson
Alfred F. Breslauer
John W. Shenk
Russell C. Horstmann ·
Edward H. Siems
Francis V. Keesling, P. G. M.
Leon 0. Whitsell, P. G. M.

A number of preliminary discussions -preceded the formal organization
and first meeting of the Executive Committee on March 10, 1942, at which
a plan of campaign was developed, a series of recommendations concerning
the fund were adopted, forwarded to the Grand Ma"Ster and subsequently
approved by him.
.
. Appropriate explanatory letters and one circular were printed and distributed to the Lodges. Official receipts were also prepared and furnished
to the Lodges for use in acknowledging the patriotic contributions of their
members.
·
·
The committee has had the whole-hearted cooperation of all Grand
Lodge officers and of the constituent Lodges and it has been a genuine
pleasure for the committee to serve. The response to the appeal has been
most gratifying. As of this date, approximately 30,500 members qf 531
Lodges have contributed a total sum of $80,460.92. The number of Lodges
in which members have contributed $1.00 or more per capita is 189 and
there is every indication that a great many more will be added to this list.
An appropriately inscribed Certificate of Merit will be presented today to
each of these Lodges which has fully participated in the 1942 fund.
A full accounting of the expenditures properly chargeable to the War
Relief Fund is incorporated in the official audit of Grand Lodge funds.
Attached to this report and made a part of it is the detailed statement
of the participation of every Lodge in the jurisdiction in this fund as well
a.s a list of the Lodges whose members have given their full share for
1942 in the order in which they achieved that goal.
Respe~tfully submitted for the committee,

EARL WARREN, Past Grand Master,
General Chairman.

The report was adopted as presented.
The committee having previously adopted as a part of its
program the issuing of an appropriate certificate of merit to
those Lodges which achieved their goal in the 1942 fund, Past

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns presents herewith an analysis of the consolidated returns of the Lodges in this jurisdiction as filed with the Grand
Secretary.

After eleven long years of depression we have ceased to lose members
and we now are on the upgrade.
During the past year we had:
Gains
Raised ..........................................3570
Affiliated ...................................... 806
Restored ...................................... 544

Losses
Withdrawn ............,............ - ......... 862
Dropped for non-payment dues 1341
Died .............................:. .................2235
Dues remitted ..........- ..................3566
Total net mem!>ership .......................................................................................126,313
A net gain of............................. _................- ....:.........:.,..........:.............'-..
471
During the past eleven years we dropped 29,174 members for nonpayment of dues and restored only 5475, leaving a loss of 23,699 members .
We again remi.nd you of this large group of former. members lost
during the hard years of depression and the slow years of recovery.

Many of those so dropped can be recovered with patient solicitation.
We commend it to your attention. It will be a spirit of brotherly love.
HENRY G. MATHEWSON,
ALBERT F. Ross,
WILLIAM W. McKEE,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS

ALBERT C. W OLLENBERG1

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Accounts herewith submits the following report:
In accordance with the requirements of the constitution of our Grand
Lodge, on the last Saturday of each month, the committee met at the office
of the Grand Secretary tb audit such bills, claims and demands against this
Grand Lodge which had been received, and approved those which were in
order.
Respectfully submitted,

KENNETH S. THOMSON,

]AMES]. YATES,
DWIGHT N. DEANE,

E. ]. KLEINHANS,

Committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BY-LAWS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws reports fifty-five Lodges amended their
by-laws during the year.
Three Lodges increased their fees: Burbank Lodge No. 406 to $75.00,
Guardian Lodge No. 596 to $75.00, and East San Diego Lodge No. 561 to
$75.00.
Four Lodges increased their dues: Yount Lodge No. 12 to $18.00,
Carpinteria Lodge No. 444 to $12.00, Garvanza Lodge No. 492 to $12.00,
and Indian Rock Lodge No. 638 to $15.00.
Ten Lodges decreased their fees: Keith Lodge No. 187 to $30.00,
Santa Barbara Lodge No. 192 to $50.00, Magnolia Lodge No. 242 to $50.00,
Tehachapi Lodge No. 313 to $50.00, Highland Park Lodge No. 382 to
$50.00, Glendora Lodge No. 404 to $30.00, Mount Diablo Lodge No. 448 to
$50.00, Lincoln Lodge No. 470 to $50.00, Beverly Hills Lodge No. 528 to
$75.00, and La Cumbre Lodge No. 642 to $50.00.
One Lodge decreased its dues : Olive Branch Lodge No. 269 to $12.00.
Two Lodges adopted an affiliation fee of $5.00: Burbank Lodge No.
406 and Beverly Hills Lodge No. 528. Maricopa Lodge No. 434 eliminated
its affiliation fee.
Eleven Lodges changed their meeting place: San Diego Lodge No. 35,
Paso Robles Lodge No. 286, Brawley Lodge No. 402, Yerba Buena Lodge
No. 403, Torrance Lodge No. 447, Benjamin Franklin Lodge No. 509,
Signal Lodge No. 543, Lakeshore Lodge No. 551, S. W. Hackett Lodge
No. 574, All States Lodge No. 593 and John Marshall Lodge No. 636.
Fourteen Lodges changed their time of meeting : Hawaiian Lodge No.
21, Alameda Lodge No. 167, Kilauea Lodge No. 330, Fruitvale Lodge
No. 336, Honolulu Lo~ge No. 409, Schofield Lodge No. 443, Maui Lodge
No. 472, Benjamin Franklin Lodge No. 509, Lakeshore Lodge No. ·551,
Kauai Lodge No. 589, Granada Lodge No. 608, La Habra Lodge No. 659,
Signal Lodge No. 543, and Menlo Park Lodge No. 651.
. (The five Lodges in Hawaii are now meeting during daylight hours.)

Seven Lodges amended their by-laws to except holidays as stated
meeting dates: Santa Rosa Lodge No. 57, Humboldt Lodge No. 79,
Dinuba Lodge No. 385, Burbank Lodge No. 406, La Mesa Lodge No. 407,
Cupertino Lodge No. 510, and Arcadia Lodge No. 547.
Two Lodges-Sacramento No. 20 and Mountain View Lodge No. 194
-revised their entire set of by-laws and covered by standing resolutions
provisions for Certificates of Life Membership and the appointment and
jurisdiction of Boards of Trustees. We commend the completeness of their
work and urge that other Lodges review their by-laws and modernize them
where necessary.

in proper form, certified and in accord with Masonic Law and received
the approval of the Grand Master.

REPORT OF SPECIAL TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most W o~ shiPfitl Grand Lodge of California:
This committee has functioned since its appointment pursuant to resolution of the 89th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge in 1938. The
members of the committee for the year 1942 have been:
R. P. Wisecarver, chairman, Thousand Oaks Lodge No. 478.
James E. Hammond, Park Boulevard Lodge No. 508.
Walter Perry Johnson, California Lodge No. 1.
Essentially there has been no change in the tax situation during the
current year and we confirm our recommendations contained in last year's
report of the committee to be found in the 1941 proceedings of Grand
Lodge, page 669.
During the year the committee has held several meetings and we have
been in immediate and constant touch with the office of the Grand Secretary. Many queries from subordinate Lodges have been answered. Generally speaking, the tax status of subordinate Lodges has been stabilized.
Grand Lodge has been making returns and paying the Old Age
Security Tax. The status of Grand Lodge with reference to unemployment reserves has not been so clear. We bave cooperated with the federal
government with respect to federal unemployment taxes during the year
and have paid taxes and penalties in the amount of $522.17, in arrears to
June 30, 1940. This became necessary due to a change in interpretation
of the law by the federal government. The Federal Act was amended
June 30, 1940, and since that date no return or payment has been made
for federal unemployment .taxes. The committee has been investigating
whether a return since June 30, 1940, should not have been made under
the State Employment Act, and the final decision on that question has
not yet been rendered. The questions at issue are whether the Grand Lecturer is an administrative or ritualistic officer, and whether the Grand Tyler
is an employee subject to tax.
Recent additions to the clerical staff make it probable that Grand
Lodge is at the present time under the State Act.
An appropriation should be set aside in the amount of approximately
$1200.00 to cover any possible liability of Grand Lodge for past State
Unemployment Reserves.
Recent revenue enactments by Congress have not yet become available to us. As soon as we have had opportunity to study these enactments
a special report will be made to the Grand Master if any changes affecting
Masonic Lodges are indicated. There are also before Congress many contemplated changes in the revenue laws, but comment should not be made
on those until final action has been taken.
From our contact with the tax situation we are of the opinion that
many technical questions will arise requiring the attention of a special
committee during the coming year, and we therefore recommend the continuance of the committee for the ensuing Masonic year.
Respectfully submitted,
R. P. WISECARV.ER, Chairman,

J.E. HAMMOND,
WALTER PERRY JOHNSON,
Committee.

MORNING SESSION
Wednesday, October 'i4, 1942.
Grand Lodge was called on at 10 :00 a. m., the Grand Master
presiding.

The report was presented by Matthew Morton, Jr., executive
vice chairman of the committee, in the unavoidable absence of
Mark A. Pierce, chairman.
Brother ·Morton prefaced his report with the following
remarks:
·
"Before giving the formal part of this report, I 'would like to say to
the brethren that the report might rightfully be termed 'The Old Army
Sergeants' Report.' Our Most Worshipful Grand Master was a sergeant
in the Army in the First World War, our Very Worshipful Grand Secretary was. also a sergeant in the First World War and I , myself, was a
sergeant m that war. I suppose that this is the only time when two old
Army sergeants have run Grand Lodge and I know that most of you hope
it will be the last time. (Laughter and applause.) I now present the
formal report of the committee."
T o the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Masonic War Service Committee herewith presents its report
for your consideration.
This committee was formed by the Grand Master as set forth in his
proclamation of May 21, 1942, wherein he appointed Mark A. P ierce, Pas t
Master of Sunset Lodge No. 352, chairman; Matthew Morton, Jr., Past
Master of Charter Rock Lodge No. 410, as executive vice chairman and
Lloyd E . Wilson, Past Grand Master, and Grand Secretary as secr~tary
of the committee.
'
The purpose of the committee, as defined by the Grand Master was
to develop a program of service to Masons in the armed forces ;nd a
program of assistance and relief to the members of their families when
and if such assistance became needed.
There are at the present time 3,602 member~ of California Lodges in
the armed forces and there are tens of thousands of Masons in all the
armed ~orces and they range in rank from private to general, from seaman
to admiral. How best to serve these men and at the same time to conserve

162

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the resources of Grand Lodge while carrying out the program adopted at
the last communication is the problem of this committee and the one to
which we have addressed ourselves.
Careful consideration has been given to the Masonic Service Center
program and the Masonic Service Association 'and it is the opinion of this
committee that the same represents a duplication of existing facilities now
offered by other organization s and that the activities of this committee and
of this Grand Lodge should be directed along other lines. What those
activities are, will be set forth in this report.
This committee is of the opinion that Lodges ought to make information available to men in the armed forces wherever possible, relative to
Lodge meetings and Lodge functions of every kind and character. Excellent progress has been made in this direction in Long Beach, San Diego,
Fresno and Oakland and it is recommended that other sections of the
state formulate similar plans where posters and announcements carrying
information concerning Lodge affairs can be displayed in prominent places
for the benefit of those men.
There is also a need in some sections of the state for Masonic Information Bureaus such as are operating in San Diego and in Fresno and we
recommend that this program be expanded where a sound survey of the
situation reveals such need.
It is becoming apparent that Lodges near army camps are alert to the
necessity of expanding their Lodge meetings and Lodge functions to
include service men and it is also apparent that in the case of small Lodges,
they cannot be expected to bear the total expense from their own funds.
We therefore recommend that the Service Committee be given authority
to authorize such expenditures or to reimburse Lodges for such 'expenditures after the same has been approved by the Grand Master. We have
already approved the expenditure of $107.61 for subsidizing entertainment
for service men to Paso Robles Lodge No. 288.
We have been of the opinion that there may arise cases of need in the
families of our California Masons who are in the service and we therefore .
prepared forms and sent them to the Lodges with the request that the
Service Committees of Lodges make· investigations of conditions prevailing
in the families of service men and to report them to this committee. Up to
date there have b een few such cases, but with the extension of the war
program and the calling of now deferred classes in the very near future,
it is entirely possible that as time goes on this will develop into a real
need and if such is the case, it is our opinion that the expenditure of funds
for relief in cases directly attributable to the war is a justified expenditure.
We are at the present time extending relief in one case in the amount
of $25.00 per month to the wife of an out-of-state Mason, internee of a
Japanese prison, and $60.00 per month to the wife and four children of
a member of Manila Lodge No. !',who is interned in the Philippine Islands.
These cases have had thorough investigation and have been approved by
the committee and by the Grand Master.
There have been arriving at San Francisco, San Diego and San Pedro
ships ,b earing sick, wounded and refugee men, women and children. Among
these are Masons and their dependents and as time goes on this is likely
to increase and we should be prepared to render any Masonic service to
them. Your committee has therefore arranged .with the Naval and military
authorities to pass a carefully selected committee of eight men at each
port to act as representatives of this committee on the docks to render this

REPORT ON PHILIPPINE ISLANDS L ODGES
Most .W orshipful Grand Master
and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
The audacious and treacherous attack on Pearl Harbor by the Japanese in the early morning hours of December 7, 1941, changed the
course of history. As an integral part of this movement, and five thousand miles to the southwest, the land forces of the Imperial _Japanese
Government, under the protection of powerful Naval and Air forces,
landed on the north, south and southeast coasts of the Island of Luz~:m,
the largest island of the Philippine Archip~lago. The overwhelmmg
numerical superiority of the enemy enabled him to force the stub?ornly
resisting American-Philippine forces to retire to the Bataan 'Penm~ula.
These troops, with their brothers-in-arms ~n the fortres.s of Cor~egidor,
fought with such courage and valor that 111 defeat their acts w1l~ .ever
remain one of the most glorious chapters in the annals of m1htary
history.
Desiring to protect the city of Manila from unnecessary d.estruction
and aid the civilian population in escaping the . horrors of aerial attack,
General Douglas MacArthur, Commander of the American-Philipp!n.e
forces declared Manila an open city. All military forces and the c1v1l
gover~ment having been removed, the Japanese occupied the city on
January 2, 1942.
The fall of the city of Manila, so Ear as we have been able to learn,
caused the cessation of activities on the part of the Masonic Grand Lodge
of the Philippine Islands, thus adding another chapter to the long and
eventful history of Masonry in the Archipelago.
Prior to the American occupation of the Islands in 1898, the history
of Masonry in that section was one of suspicion, intolerance and persecution. The earliest reference to Masonry is an incident that occurred
in the year 1756. In that year James O'Kenn~dy, a merchant, and . E~­
ward Wigat, a physician, were tried by the Tribunal of the J:loly Inquisition for being members of the Fraternity. They were acquitted.
On September 22, 1762, a British expedition reached M~ni!a Bay,
and on October 5 captured the city. By the Treaty of Pans 111 1763,
Manila was restor~d to Spain. It is believed that the occupational force
established an English Military L odge. This belief is based upon evidence
that the Archbishop of the Diocese of Manila complained of the local
Cathedral being desecrated by the English holding Masonic meetings
there and proposed that "the edifice be burned in order to purify it."
There is no evidence to show, that the Archbishop's proposal was
followed.
A half century passed before another reference to Mason~y is found.
On January 12, 1812, the Council of the Regency of Spam a~d t~~
Indies issued a royal decree placing a bar on the order and ordermg its
members expelled from their positions and .their property con?scated.
On August 1, 1824, King Ferdinand VII, ~ssued . ~ decr~e. agamst the
fraternity, making the penalty of membership, P?httca.l, c1v1l and ~ccle­
siastical excommunication. In the year 1829, a slup arrived at the city of
Manila and in its cargo the port authorities found, among other books,
several' copies of "Preston's Illustrations of Masonry." The books and

The first American Mason in the Islands was George W. Hubbell,
o~ Bridgeport, Connecticut. He was t he American Consul. Following
his death on May 21, 1831, his friends ordered a monument erected to
his memory. The monument was made, but the objection of the Friars
prevented its erection, and it remained in a warehouse from 1831 to 1898
where it was found by the American forces and erected in the Plaz~
~ervantes, in the city of Manila. This monument was standing at the
time of the Japanese occupation.
In 1856 the first chartered Lodge in the Islands was organized. T he
charter was issued by the Grand Lodge of Portugal, and the name
adopted was Logia Primera Luz Filipina. Thirty-five years passed before
~nother Lodge was chartered. January 6, 1891, Nilad Lodge was organized under the jur isdiction of the Grand Orient of Spain. The word
"N'ilad" is from the Tagalog language (the language of the natives of
the Island of Luzon) and means "place where the Nilad p lant is found."
It was from this word that the name " Manila" was derived.
Political conditions becoming increasingly intolerable during the
unrest developed among the people,
and m 1896 a revolutionary plot was discovered. The friars and military
accused Masonry of being entirely responsible for the movement, and
ordered the arrest · of twelve of its leaders. Dr. Jose Rizal, Masonic
leader and writer, was executed December 30, 1896. Twelve days later,
January 11.' 1897, the eleven others were executed, including one who had
to be earned to the place of execution because of broken limbs as the
result of torture.
latte~ part of the nin~teenth centur'y,

The following year, 1898, the United States government was established on the Islan.ds and under its protecting hand religious and political
freedo~ were guaranteed. Suspicion and intolerance rapidly disappeared,
and friendly understanding among the various groups became the established order. Under these happy conditions sixteen brethren of Manila
petitioned the Grand Lodge of California for a charter. July 4, 1901,
Grand Master Foshay issued a di spensation. A chart er was granted
October 10, 1901, and thus came into existence Manila Lodge No. 342 of
the Grand Jurisdiction of California. October 18, 1902, Grand Master
Wells, at the request of the brethren of Cavite, issued a dispensation for
for a Lodge in that city. A chart er was granted October 15 1903 and
Cavite Lodge No. 350 became a part of this Grand Jurisdictlon. Membership increased so rapidly in Manila t hat by 1907 it was apparent that
another Lodge was necessary. Grand Master Hart issued a dispensation
February 19, 1907, and a charter on October 10 the same year for
Corregidor Lodge No. 386.
'
The influx of. Americans into the Islands and the increase of the
popularity of the fr aternity among th e Filipinos caused the Lodges to
g'.o~ and prosper. December 19, 1912, the three Lodges under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California withdrew from our obedience
and established t he Grand Lodge of the Philippine Isla nds . .
Under the leadership and direction of a distinguished line of Grand
Ma_sters, Maso~ry spread to all parts of the Archipelago, and onto the
mamland of Asia. The twenty-ninth a nnual communication of the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands was he ld in the city of Manila January
28, 29 and 30,.1941, at which time th e Grand Jurisdiction had 102 Lodges,

29 in or near Manila, and six in China; one of these in Canton, one in
Nanking, one in Hangchow and two in Shanghai. The jurisdiction had
a membership of 5,656 Master Masons, 2,856 of whom were Filipinos,
_1,988 Americans, 654 Chinese and 158 of other nationalities.

· · Today there are many brethren who hold memberships in the Philippine · jurisdiction who are in the armed forces of the United States,
stationed in California and in the Hawaiian Islands, or domiciled within
the jurisdiction of the. Grand Lodge of California. When their Lodges
and Grand Lodges ceased to function they appealed to the Grand Master
of California on all matters Masonic. .On January 27, 1942, the Most
Worshipful Frank M: Smith, Grand Master of California, directed a
communication to me as representative of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Grand Jurisdiction near the Grand Lodge of California, setting forth
fhe problems confronting these brethren and stating that he was desirous
of extending every Masonic aid, and requesting my views on the subject.
Pnder date of January 28, 1'142, I submitted to the Grand Master a request that the Grand Lodge of California accept dues from these brethren,
issuing its receipt therefor. That these dues, with any other monies that
might be paid to the Grand Lodge of California for the account of the
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, be held in trust by the Grand
Lodge of California until such time as the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
~stands might direct its disposal.
Further, that such receipts as issued by the Grand Lodge of California to members of Lodges of the . Philippine Islands over the signature
of the Grand Secretary and/or the Grand Master, be recognized by the
Lodges of California as bona fide receipts of the Grand Lodge of the
Philippine Islands and entitling the holder thereof to all the rights and
privileges of Masonry.·
· Further, that the Grand Lodge of California keep a record of the
riames and addresses of all members of Philippine Lodges who may pay
dues or receive aid from the Grand Lodge of California.
.··
My views met with the approval of the Grand Master except in the
matter of receipts, in lieu of which he caused certificates to be issued
~o each man paying dues. Certificates have been i&sued to 234 members of
34 Lodges and there are 55 cases pending. There is now $2,254.35 in the
~rust fund. The entire cost of this service is being borne by this Grand
Lodge.
As an evidence of the charity of the Grand Lodge of California
toward members of Island Lodges, I call one case to your attention and
give only a bare outline of that one. This case was handled under the
direction of the Most Worshipful Grand Master, through the Masonic
Board of Relief of Los Angeles. In October 1941 the widow of a Past
Master of a Philippine Lodge was found bedfast and alone . . She was
J?Uffering from cancer of the- spfoe. She had exhausted her savings and
was trying to exist on a small pension from the Federal Government.
.Brother Earl Thaxter, Secretary of the Los Angeles Board of Relief
}:!ad ·the lady moved to a sanitarium and ordered medical attention, advising the Philippine Lodge of his actions. The Lodge instructed him
to make certain expenditures in her behalf, but with the outbreak of war
all aid ceased. The patient died May 8, 1942. Expenditures made in her
d.se by California Masonry totaled $416.40:
Since the fall of Manila all contact with the outside world has been
denied to' the residents of that city. : 'rom sources considered reliable, we

167

have learned that Dr. Harry Eugene Stafford and Mrs. Stafford are now
confined in a Japanese concentration camp near Bagino. Dr. Stafford was
the first Grand Master in the Philippine Islands, serving from 1912 to
1914. From the same source we are now advised that Mr. and Mrs.
Stanton Youngberg are now prisoners of the . Japanese and confined to
the grounds of Santa Tomas University in Manila. Brother Youngberg
was Grand Master in 1933-34. Of our other brethren we have no word.
We pray that the Great Architect of the Universe in His infinit.e
wisdom and mercy will protect and guard our brethren from the cruelties
and inhuman treatment with which an ambitious or rapacious conqueror
has imposed upon others who have been so unfortunate as to fall under
his pow~r. As men and Masons, we pledge to them our devotion, our
unswerving loyalty and every ounce of power we possess to the end that
they may again be free; that Masonry may again go forward with its
great work of charity and tolerance; of its teachings of the Fatherhood
of God and the. brotherhood of man.
· Individually and collectively, we pledge to our government, all we
hold most dear; all we possess and all we are, that the dictators and
tyrants who plunged the world into the greatest catastrophe in all history,
will be destroyed. That through their destruction may come a world in
which good men, gentle women and little children may live, love, work
and play, free from the fear of attack by those without feeling and without conscience.
Respectfully submitted,
RoY C. BRYAN,
Representative of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine ·
Islands near the Grand Lodge of California.

REPORT OF NECROLOGY COMMITTEE
Organ Solo, "Traumerei"
Invocation . . . . .

MacDowell
Past Grand Master Samuel E. Burke

To the M osf .W orshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Once more with a mingling of sadness and sorrow, we take up the
record of the grim messenger, death, and pay a loving tribute to our
departed. Many of our bPethren whom a year ago were apparently in
good health, have gone to their eternal reward. Our records show the
passing of 222 members of this Grand Lodge since our last communication. It is fitting that a eulogy should be delivered for these brethren who
are now in that· Celestial Grand Lodge above. Brother Ellsworth Meyer
will render such eulogy.
The loss of our ' brethren in the ranks of Masonry has been especially
heavy this year. In the interim of our communications 2236 have been
called. A very heavy toll.
A year ago, no one with the most far-sighted or prophetic vision could
have foretold the momentous things that would come to be our lot, individually and nationally. We are now at war with some of the most cruel
and fanatical nations of the world. It is well to take a backward look and
rediscover that our flag, "your flag and my flag," has never been lowered
by any nation or peoples on earth and to resolve, as thousands of our young
men have resolved, that we will never surrender to any nation or people.s
while time shall last. Many of our young Masons, our brethren, have
already made the supreme sacrifice. They have gone out from our homes
to preserve freedom. They have gone in the spirit of that ancient writer
when he said, "'Tis sweet and glorious to die for one's country."
In all the years that record the history of Masonry, we can look with
a justifiable pride at the achievements of Masons in the many wars in
which we have fought for our home's, and for our loved ones. Masons in
this war are no exception, and will continue to acquit themselves with
great valor. The only note of sadness is found in that oft quoted stanza:
"The boast of heraldry, ·the pomp of power,
And all that beauty, all that wealth e'er gave,
A wait alike the inevitable hour,
The paths of glory lead but to the grave."
-Thomas A . Gray.
In the days, weeks, months, and years that we may be spared for
future usefulness, let us highly resolve, "that these dead shall not have
died in vain.'! A fitting tribute to the memory of our heroic dead will be
given by Brother G. Ellsworth Meyer when he delivers the general eulogy.
On August 25, ·1942, the great world-wide fraternity of Masonry was
shocked and saddened by the accidental death of His Royal Highness, the
Duke of Kent, Grand Master of Masons of the United Grand Lodge of
England. When His Royal Highness, the Duke of Kent, was installed
Grand Master, July 19, 1939, it was our happy privilege to be represented
on that occasion by Past Grand Master William Rhodes Hervey, who will
later give us a eulogy honoring the Duke of Kent, Great Master of English
Masonry.

FRANK TADE, Member, Board of Control
On September 3, 1941, Brother Tade was called to the Supreme Grand
Lodge to receive his reward. He had been a member of the Board of
Control for five years.
He was born April 16, ·1876, in Sacramento, California. He was initiated an Entered Apprentice in Sacramento Lodge No. 40, F . & A . M.,
February 4, 1902; passed April 11, 1902; and raised to the Sublime Degree
of. Master Mason, May 30, 1902. He was a member of the Scottish Rite
Bodies of Sacramento, receiving his degrees in Isaac Davis Lodge of
Perfection, February 17, 1903; in the Chapter of Rose Croix; May 26,
1903; Council of Kadosh, February 2, 1905; and the Consistory, February 4,
1905.
'
Very soon after uniting with the Scottish Ride Bodies, he was honored
by his brethren. He was elected to the office of Wise Master in the
Chapter of Rose Croix for four years in succession, 1906, 1907, 1908 and
1909. He was also elected Master of Kadosh for four years, 1910, 1911,
1912 and 1913. His ability, loyalty, and true worth was recognized by the
Supreme Council 33, A. & A. S. R., a nd in October, 1909, he was given the
Knight Commander of the Court of Honor, and December 11, 1915, he ·
received the highest honor in the Supreme Council, the Thirty-third Degree.
He served his own Lodge, Sacramento No. 40, for twenty-two years as
Treasurer. Also was President of the Sacramento Maso nic Temple Association, and President of the Masonic Lawn Cemetery Association. At the
time of his death, he was Venerable Master of Isaac Davis Lodge of
Perfection.
Many centuries ago it was said of the "Man of Galilee," that "He went
about doing good." I can find no higher tribute to pay our Brother Tade
than this, "He went about doing good."

In closing briefly our necrology report, I am sure that those of our
brethren who have gone to their eternal home, would not have us linger·
longer, but would have us bid them a loving farewell and turn again to .
the problems of time. May we look into the difficulties of the future with
the unshakable faith, hop e, and vision, that inspired James Russell Lowell
to pen those matchless words:
"Truth forever on the scaffold
Wrong forever on the Throne,
Yet that scaffold sways the future,
And, behind the dim unknown,
Standeth God, within the shadow,
Keeping watch above His own."

When death laid his inexorable hand on the Grand Master of the
United Grand Lodge of England we had a striking and painful illustration
of the truth that "death loves a shining mark, a signal blqw." Honored
and loved by his brethren and fellow countrymen, eminent for his social
virtues, occupying a high rank in the armed forces of his country, engaged
in an important and dangerous mission in line of military duty, blessed
by a beautiful wife and three young children and holding the highest
station of honor in British Masonry, he did indeed offer a shining mark
to the insatiate archer. The solemn lesson has been brought home to our
hearts that "the paths of glory lead but to the grave," and, as the great
Roman satirist tells us, "pale death with impartial footsteps knocks alike
at the poor man's hut and the palace of kings."

EULOGY ON THE DUKE OF KENT
Grand Master of the Unit~d Grand Lodge of England
By P. G. M. WM. RHODES HERVEY

The United Grand Lodge of England has suffered a great misfortune
by the death of its Grand Master. On his way to Iceland on August 25,
1942, in the course of R. A. F. duties, the airship by which he was traveling
crashed in the north of Scotland and all its occupants, including the Duke
of Kent, the Most Worshipful Grand Master of the United Grand Lodge
of England, were killed.
The Duke of Kent was born at the Cottage, Sandringham, December
20, 1902, and was the youngest surviving brother of King George VI. He
was educated at Dartmouth College for the Royal Navy and served eight
years in it. He joined the Royal Air Force in 1940 and had attained the
rank of Air Commodore.
Prince George, later the Duke of Kent, was made a Mason in April,
1928. He was elected Senior Grand Warden of the United· Grand Lodge
of England in April, 1933, was elected Provincial Grand Master of Wiltshire in 1934 and was elected Grand Master of the Grand Lodge and
installed on July 19, 1939. He had the varied Masonic distinctions of being,
at the time of his death, President of the Royal Masonic Institution for
Girls, the Royal Masonic Institution for Boys, the Royal Masonic Benevolent Institution and the Royal Masonic Hospital. He was a 33° Mason
and a member of the Supreme Council of England.
The Duke of Kent succeeded his great-uncle, the Duke of Connaught,
who had served as Grand Master for thirty-eight years and who, himself,
was the successor of Edward VII, the grandfather of the Duke of Kent
who, in turn, served as Grand Master for about thirty years. At the time
of his installation as Grand Master there were about 17,000 Masons. present

Where today is sorrow in the craft at the untimely death of a
respected, esteemed and beloved brother and Grand Master, it is but a
little time ago that unbounded enthusiasm and overflowing devotion filled
the hearts of thousands of his brethren as he entered the great arena of
Olympia and stood in the West for installation, facing his King in the
East. As the two brothers, the King as Past Grand Master and the Duke
of Kent as Grand Master elect, both in full regalia, stood that hour in their
handsome young manhood, surrounded by thousands of cheering Masons,
it seemed that a spirit of exaltation had seized the multitude and that
fervent loyalty t,o his majesty was matched by high hopes for the prosperity of our brotherhood during all the years of the long life of its young
Grand Master.
After a short time of cruel and devastating war all these hopes were
tragically shattered by the untimely death of him who, "while the dew
was still upon his days and the singing birds in his heart," had given every
promise of a long life and valuable service to Freemasonry.
The Duke of Kent was a lovable, companionable, broad-minded and
benevolent gentleman and had long manifested a deep interest in all the
activities of his Grand Jurisdiction. In these important and critical times
he acted well his part, both in peace and in war, both in society and in
Masonry. On the threshold of grand honors and high authority, in the
service of King and Country, he died at the post of duty.
We weep for Adonais; he is dead.
Tenor Solo, "Recessional"

Kipling-DeKoven

A TRIBUTE TO JOHN WHICHER
By DANA R. WELLER, Past Grand Master

One year ago we paid tribute to the memory of our dear, beloved
friend, John Whicher. In that eulogy there was incorporated a poem of
which John had been very, very fond.
Our brother, Anthony L. Auradou, Past Master, Inspector of the
"Free French" Lodge of San Francisco, has prepared a most beautiful
copy of that poem, changed just a little bit by poetic license to apply to
John Whicher.

182

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A Tribute to Our Late Brother John Whicher, Grand Secretary,
August 25, 1908, to March 31, 1941

life and see time as a stream swiftly flowing from the deep pools of the
past over the turbulent waterfall of the present into the mysterious ocean
of .the future. Here we speak of man's duty, his duty to God, to country,
his neighbor and himself.

"Abou Ben Adhem (may his tribe increase!)
Awoke one night from a deep dream of peace,
And saw, within the moonlight in his room,
Making it rich, and like a lily in bloom,
An Angel writing in a book of gold:
Exceeding peace had made Ben Adhem bold,
And to the presence in the room he said,
'What writest thou?' The Vision raised its head,
And with a look made of all sweet accord
Answered, 'The names of those who love the Lord.'
'And is mine one?' said Abou. 'Nay, not so,'
Replied the Angel. Abou spoke more low,
But cheerily still; and said, 'I pray thee, then,
Write me as one that loves his fellow-men.'
The Angel wrote, and vanished. The next night ·
It came again with a great wakening light,
And showed the names whom love of God has blessed,
And lo! john Whicher's name led all the rest."
"Presented to the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of California, by Anthony L. :Auradou, Past Master, Inspector of
the 113th Masonic District, San Francisco, Calif., October 14, 1942."
Brethren, I wish you could see the beauty of this: Note that the "A"
in Abou Ben Adhem is composed of a square and compass. The script is
beautifully done and it is beautifully colored. It has been at the request
of Brother Auradou that I present this to the Grand Lodge, and having
done so, I would like to move that we accept with gratitude this work
of art and that it be properly framed and hung in the Grand Secretary's
office.
IN MEMORIAM

By G. ELLSWORTH MEYER
"Soft and safe to thee, my brother, be thy earthly bed! Bright
and glorious be thy rising from it! Fragrant be the cassia sprig
that there shall flourish! May the earliest buds of spring unfold
their beauties o'er thy resting place, and there may the sweetness
of summer's last rose linger longest!'"
Time after time during the past year these words have been spoken,
spoken to the accompaniment of sighing redwoods, of pounding surf, the
rustling quiet of the open countryside or the busy hum of a great city as
Freemasons laid to rest a brother.
Now, as is our custom, we dedicate and consecrate . an hour in affec. tionate memory of those members of this Grand Lodge who have slipped
behind the veil which, from mortal eyes, hides eternity. There is no hour
more solemn, .more revealing. Its cadence, soft melody and memories lift
our thoughts until it seems we catch the very music of the stars and our
groping hands gently brush the Infinite as we declare that men who truly
live can never die.
Here we cast aside the mundane. Here we are concerned with ultimate
destiny and eternal values. Here we mark the transitory nature of human

183

Fremasonry takes no note of the worldly possessions .of its applicants
and members. It evidences no interest in the store of goods left behind.
Just as it is the internal and not the external qualifications which recommend a man when he knocks at our door, so it is the warp and woof of
character with which we are concerned as he silently slips into the twilight
shadows.· We remember his many virtues that we may the better be
enabled to· emulate exemplary conduct and weave our everlasting raiment
of purest gold.
These were our brethren. Short days ago we felt their warm handclasp, were cheered by their friendly words, comforted by their deeds of
kindness and encouraged by their faith in our ability to discharge duty on
every occasion. Now they have filed past the grand tiler into the Celestial
Lodge to view the trestle board upon which the Supreme Architect, who
does all things well, has drawn that life eternal in which they had abounding faith.
These were our brethren and in essential features the pattern of their
lives was very like our own. They found in life the same little joys, the
same sorrows, the same stumbling blocks, as well as the same opportunities
for service. They, too, found duty with them always; it rose with them
in the morning, walked with them by day and stood by their pillows at
night.
There on our final roll is the name of one who toiled in the fields,
occasionally mimicking the birds overhead as he viewed his tender shoots
pushing aside the clods. He found duty in his prospect of feeding men
and peace in its discharge. The discharge of duty another found in making
available those same crops. There, too, is the name of the school teacher
who heard the call of duty emanating from the class room where he
inspired youth to become evangels in the cause of good government,
champions of the oppressed and stewards of our fathers' faith in free
institutions. Is there not also the name of a man of the cloth? His duty
was to quicken conscience, raise the fallen and bring to men that peace
which passeth understanding. There, also, is the name of one who sought
to hold the scales of justice in equipose, unafraid to champion the poor
against the rich, the lowly against those in high places or to sit as the
arbiter between contending men. There we read the name of one who with
medical skill ushered in new life, made its final hours easy and between
that alpha and omega of mortality responded to the call of duty through
driving rains and across the weary miles of night.
Varied indeed were the roads down which our brethren traveled.
Varied were the tasks to which they brought their services, not as austere
performances but with lofty purposes and deep sympathies. Masonry has
been strengthened by their interaction and cooperation and while their
humility may have caused them to think of themselves as pupils, we
recognize them as builders each of whom carried a few bricks and some
mortar to be builded into· the temple of man. We affirm that they could
"walk with the crowd and keep virtue, talk with kings nor lose the common
touch." Nor is it mere fraternal pride, when we declare that they found
in Masonry inspiration and a design by which they could work out their
own goodness amid the difficulties of life.

184

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We note these many vacant chairs with mixed emotions. Our fraternity has lost a host of dependable workmen and each of us many a
generous friend of pleasing personality and engaging charm whom we
were proud to call brother. We know not what power caused their spirits
to take up the tools of human life lest it was a call to duty whispered
by Divine Providence, and they have laid those tools aside in response to
a call to higher duty. Perhaps some sorrowful heart, knowing that there
was yet so much work to do, may have cried out, "Why, Father? Why
this one?" We can only answer by asking, why does the red rose drop
its petals? Is it to toll perfume on some purer air? Does not the tree
discard its autumn-tinted leaves that it may lift new leafy arms to God
in prayer? Does not the sun abandon its setting glories to the shades of
night that it may shine upon some other shore? Even so, these our brethren who came from out the boundless deep have turned again home to
hear their Pilot's benediction, "Well done, thou good and faithful Servant."
As we speak of duty and those we know have crossed the bar, we
are not unmindful of the possibility that there may be others, at present
unknown to us, from among our brethren in uniform. If so, there will be
yet others before we again assemble in annual communication. This. is not
a pleasant thought but grim reality, for violent death walks the highways
and the byways of the world; it is no respecter of fraternal allegiance. .
May it not be said of ,these that they have held in proper order the
call of duty, to God, to country, to neighbor, before themselves? Can it
not be said of these that they were truly zealous in behalf of human rights,
national integrity and justice ? To these the Masonic concepts of fortitude,
liberty and equality are no mere abstractions of the Lodge room, nor matters for fraternal mummery but heritages beyond the value of life itself.
We may never know humanity's true loss, for this war's shells like
those of the last may forever silence the lips of another Kilmer singing,
"Poems are made by fools like me; but only God can make a tree." There
may be winging steel at some new Gallipoli to claim a youth of twenty'
whose discoveries revolutionized scientific thinking. Perhaps, but even if
such minds be spared, still the cup of agony will be pressed to the lips
of countless widows and orphans. There will still be placed upon our
shoulders a responsibility which we cannot discharge at present by life
as usual or by turning the other way when the guns at last cease firing.
It is not enough to speak in glowing patriotic terms. It is not enough
to build monuments of words. Posterity "will little note, nor long remember what we say," but it will never forget our duty ·to furl the battle flags
of the nations in the parliament of man, to make manifest our avowed
doctrines of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, to make
certain that these dead shall not have died in vain. This henceforth is our
imperative duty.
Permit me to express that solemn charge by putting my words on
silent lips:

185

'Neath many a foreign field we lie,
Men who were not afraid to die.
O'er us no crosses rise in ordered row
Nor yet do crimsoned poppies grow. '
We. lie beneath embattled country sod,
Beside the dark jungle trails we trod,
Along the tropic island coral strands
And in the north ice bound lands. '
Scattered mounds mark where ~e fell
These our last resting places tell;
'
We who carried freedom's torch on high,
To these strange lands in which we lie.
We ask no spiring monuments of stone
Here leave us sleep eternally alone,
'
Only teach youth not hate but to laugh
And make a new, free world our cenotaph.
-Original.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
To your Committee on Grievances there has been referred a total
number of twenty trial records. Four of these are petitions for restoration
and will be presented to you under separate reports. In three others, we
have found ourselv:es unable to agree with the findings or the recommendations of the Trial Commissions, and these likewise will be presented to
you under separate reports. Th.e remaining thirteen records, in which .
your committee has agreed with the disposition of the case in the Trial
Lodge, and as to which we therefore recommend to Grand Lodge that
they be affirmed, will be covered by this report.
Before taking up these particular records, there are three matters
which we feel should be called to the attention of those in attendance
upon Grand L odge.
Each year we have a number of matters arising under Section 332
of the Ordinances, which section deals with the matter of automatic
expulsion following conviction of a crime clasified as a felony, and which
has been followed by imprisonment. As you know, the accused in these
matters is advised by a form notice that he will stand expelled unless
within a period of sixty days he demands a trial in the Lodge. There
seems to be some misapprehension as to the nature of the trial where such
a demand has been made. It has come to the attention of the committee
that some Lodge officers have expressed the view that the only question
to be tried is whether the accused was in fact convicted of a crime classified
as a felony and imprisoned pursuant thereto. This is a false impression.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

187

In the event the accused demands a trial in his Lodge he is tried as to
his guilt or innocence on the charge which is brought a~ainst him. While
a conviction m~y be accepted as prima facie evidence of his guilt, circums~an.ces may anse, and frequently do, in which the accused may establish
his mnocence of the charge of which he was convicted in the courts. The
matter of inquiry is his guilt or innocence of the crime, and not merely
whether he has been convicted thereon.
The second matter to which we desire to refer arises as a result of
one of the rcords covered by this report. We found in one case that the
Mas~er. ~~esiding over the. trial relinquished his right to pass upon the
adm1ss1b1hty of offered ev1det;1ce to the counsel for the accuser. In this
particular case we. found that the counsel for the accuser ruled much more
liberally in his own favor than for the accused. Masters whose duty it
may be to preside over trials should exercise the full .functions of their
position, and should not relinquish them to either of the parti~s or the
representatives of either party. Likewise, we feel that those who act as
counsel for the accuser should be cautioned that their role is not that of
a persecutor. It is rather the role of a prosecutor, whose . duty it should
be to see that every right of the accused is protected and that he should
be given every opportunity to· present facts redoundi~g to his benefit.
The third matter relates to permitting nominations to be made at the
time of the selection of Trial Commissioners. This committee has several
· t~mes._ expressed to Grand Lodge its feeling that the making of nominations 1s out of harmony with the spirit of our laws governing the selection
of Trial Commissioners. However, Grand Lodge has heretofore ruled that
this alone will not constitute ground for a reversal where there has been
no miscarriage of justice. In one case covered by this report when the
Lodge was selecting its Trial Commissioners, the number of which had
been fixed at seven, one of the members of the Lodge arose and placed
seven names in nomination. The seven so nominated were selected as
Trial Commissioners. You may well imagine our surprise when on reading
the transcript of the trial itself we found that the brother who had made
the· seven nominations of Trial Commissioners was counsel for the accuser.
We would have been inclined to take cog nizance of this situation were it
not for the fact that this particular case involved a long series of e~bezzle­
ments from ~ Lodge ext~nding over a number of years, the proof of which
was conclusive, and which was also supported by a detailed confession
by the accused.
Your committee has carefully reviewed and considered the trial records
hereafter enumerated. We find in them no errors which have affected the
substantial rights of the accused, and in each of them we . feel that substantial justice has been accomplished. We may further add that a number
of these are matters involving automatic expulsion under Section 332 of
the Ordinances.
