Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred the application
for reinstatement of petitioner, Trial Records No. 616 and 703, begs leave
to report as follows:
In 1929 petitioner was expelled from Alamo Lodge No. 122; when.
the matter was reviewed by Grand Lodge under Trial Record No. 616,
the finding of guilty by the Trial Commission was reversed and the matter
remanded for a new trial with directions that the specifications upon which

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Trial Record No. 910 involves a petition for restoration by one D. L . S.
In 1936 the petitioner was convicted of a felony and imprisoned pursuant to such conviction. He was thereafter expelled under the automatic
expulsion provi.sions of our Section 332 of Ordinances.
Following the incarceration, a great mass of material, including affidavits from various people who testified at the time of his trial, and others
who should have been witnesses but were not available at the time, was
collected and laid before the governor of this state. This material is rather
convincing to the effect that the conviction of this brother was a miscarriage of justice. As a result of these activities, the governor issued a full
and complete pardon to the petitioner, who now seeks to be reinstated.
Your committee has carefully examined this record, and in addition has
received evidence relating to the activities of the petitioner since the time
of his incarceration. Even though we might assume that his original conviction was justified, and of this we have grave doubt, the evidence is now
overwhelming to the effect that there has been a complete rehabilitation
from any· moral lapses from 'which he m;iy have been guilty.
We are therefore of the opinion that he now merits restoration, and
consequently offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Be it re5olved that D. L. S., referred to in Record No. 910, be, and he
hereby is, restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
F RANK B. BELCHER,

In this matter the accused was charged with unmasonic conduct predicated on a single specification which alleges, in substance, that for m~re
than a month last past the accused has been engaged in the saloon business
;i.nd employed as a barkeeper in a public drinking house which serves
intoxicating liquors and which is not an eating place serving meals or
food to the puqlic.
·
An officer of the Lodge testified that he had visited the cocktail lounge
and observed the accused serving hard liquor to patrons; that he did not
go into the back part of the place to see if there were stoves there or any. thing like that; that only drinks were being served; that he saw no sandwiches-Just corn and pretzels; that he talked with the accused who said
they didn't want to serve food; that he explained to the accused the danger
of expulsion; that accused said he had been rejected by the shipyards and
that this was the oniy job he could get-that he had to stick to it to make
a living.
The accused was not present but the Trial Commissioners had before
them a letter from him reading as follows:
"November 12, 1941.
"To Richard B. Mortimer, Worshipful Master
"Sequoia Lodge No. 349, F. & A. M.
"Worshipfu'I Sir and Brother:
" Your summons received; however the date and time of the
trial makes it an impossibility for me to be present as Friday
evening is one of the largest evenings of the week in the• bar
business and my services are depended upon by my employer.
"This letter I desire to enter as my plea with the assistance of
someone whom I ask to be appointed as counsel for the defense.
"Guilty-yes, I'm guilty-guilty of being in a profession that
has given me an honest livelihood for more than a month past
and promises to give me a profitable income for months to come.
"Were there not men like myself who respect their job and
consider themselves to be professional hosts, catering to ladies and
gentlemen that, perhaps like yourself, enjoy an occasional drink or
. two, the bar business would be left to drop again into the hands of
thieves, liars, and cut-throats as it did during the period of time in
which the eighteenth amendment was in effect.
"Why is the bartender and bar owner to be selected as those
alone responsible for the present liquor conditions-why not the
man who owns a fleet of trucks engaged in transporting liquor,
or the man who advertises the product in his newspaper or magazine, or the man who works for the government in supervising
every phase of the liquor industry from its distillation to its ultimate consumption, are they not guilty too in support of the bar
business.
"The Til-Two does not serve food, other · than that which is
demanded by law. We do not operate on. a scale large enough to
serve meals" in the accepted sense, but our business is operated on
a far higher plane than many places that serve both food and
drink. We operate a place where you may bring your wife, <laugh-

192

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ter or sweetheart and know that she will not be insulted or
annoyed. Many places serving meals cannot make this . same
statement.
"The question that I ask you to consider is this: Are we to
judge a man by what he is or what his job is, by his morals or
his money, by his work life or by his home life. Are we to condemn a sober and industrious man, a man who has never been
arrested or convicted of a crime, who maintains a .home for himself
and mother, a man who is respected by those he serves, works
with and lives near as an unfit associate· of Masons and other
gentlemen simply because his work is serving liquor when serving
liquor is legal in California.
"Section 210, to which I am guilty, is in my opinion more
guilty than I because 210 discriminates between two men performing the same task in two different places of business; it is also
guilty of prejudice and narrow-min4edness.
"I ask in closing that you investigate my character, my home,
which I am providing for myself and mother. Investigate also
my personal habits, my credit standing, and the amount of respect
I receive from those whom I serve, those whom I work with and
those whom I live near. Co~pare your findings with like findings
of those who serve drink as an incidental to the serving of food
and decide are they less guilty of unmasonic conduct than I.
"Sincerely and fraternally,
" W . G.H."
No other evidence was presented. The Trial Commission found the
accused -guilty and fixed his penalty at suspension.
Section 210 of our Ordinances, so far as the pertinent provisions are
concerned, provides, in part as follows: "* * * and any Mason who may
hereafter enter upon and engage in the saloon business, either as owner,
agent or employe, except in connection with and as a part of the operation
of a bona fide hotel or restaurant, or who shall become a barkeeper, shall
be deemed guilty of unmasonic conduct, and shall, upon due trial and
conviction of said offense, forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges, including membership in any Lodge/'
The Constitution of the State of California authorizes licenses for the
sale of liquor where it is to be consumed on the premises only to a bona fide
hotel, restaurant or other public eating place. There is a presumption
that official duty has been properly performed and that an unqualified
place will not be licensed. This, however, is a rebuttable presumption and
while the Trial Commission might have found in accordance with such
presumption we feel that they were justified by the evidence in finding to
the contrary and in determining ~hat the accused was guilty of the charge.
You will recall, however, that our Section 210 provides that one guilty
of a violation thereof shall "* * * forfeit all Masonic rights and privileges,
including membership in any Lodge."
Your committee feels that this language does not permit of suspension.
The word "forfeit" is so comprehensive as, in our minds, to preclurle any
penalty other than expulsion.

193

We, therefore, offer the following resolution and move its adoption :
Resolved that the finding of guilty as made by the Trial Commission
be affirmed but that the penalty lie and the same hereby is fixed at
expulsion.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK B. BELCHER,

Your committee to which was referred Trial Record No. 1009 respectfully reports as follows:
Accused was charged with unmasonic conduct contained in one specification to the effect that he had fraudulently embezzled the sum of
$1,000.00 or more belonging to the Citizen's Commercial & Savings Bank
of Soquel, California. At the trial before the commissioners there was
introduced a copy of an indictment signed by the United States Attorney
to the effect that accused had been a cashier of said bank and had embezzled more than $3,500.00. He was placed on probation for three years
and, so far as the record shows, had never been imprisoned. At the conclusion of the trial the commissioners voted as follows: Guilty, 7; Not
Guilty, 0. The vote on unmasonic conduct was Guilty, 7, Not Guilty, 0.
By a vote of 3 to 4 accused was not expelled but by unanimous vote
he was suspended.
This committee is of the opinion that the penalty for such an offense
should be increased from suspension to expulsion and, accordingly, offers
the following resolution: That the action of Santa Cruz Lodge No. 38
in finding accused guilty of unmasonic conduct be and the same is hereby
affirmed but that the penalty imposed is hereby raised from suspension to
expulsion.

semester, plus $1.00 for initiation fee, in one case, and in the other of
$3.00 for each semester, plus $1.00 for initiation fee, that there are no further assessments and all of these ·sums are received by the students and
are spent by them for their own activitie~. No part of this money accrues
to the Trustees, nor is the expenditure thereof supervised by the Trustees,
other than through the guidance of the hostess of the club house. The
building itself is furnished and serviced entirely free for the students. You
will note also that regardless of membership in these two clubs, all persons
whether eligible for membership or not are invited to the building and
that all Masons and ·all those having Matcinic affiliations are at liberty to
visit and use the club house from time to time.
. The trustees continue to look to these organized bodies of students to
maintain the activities of the club house and to assume responsibility for
the protection of the property and the good name· of the institution. This
policy has existed from the start. It is an exemplification of the university
doctrine of student control and is a manifestation of that honor spirit
which was first instilled at the university by its late and great president,
Benjamin I. Wheeler.
I am happy to say that ·during the twenty years that I have had some
responsibility in this regard, I have found that by trusting students and
empowering them to conduct their own affairs, the club house has best
been able to engender a fine social and spiritual atmosphere. Only such
a policy is consistent with the ideals which govern a free democracy.
(b) Conditions of the Property. The past year, as heretofore, efforts
of the Trustees have been directed to the proper maintenance and preservation of the properties. The building and its furnishings are in good
shape. Repairs to the roof have been made and some foundation work
renewed. In compliance with fire and block wardens' suggestions considerable sums have been expended for black-out facilities, sand, shovels, fire
extinguishers, etc. All of this expense has been charged against our
reserves.
The certified public accountant, in his report dated October 5, 1942,
which has been submitted to your Finance Committee, shows total income
of $7,572.00; total maintenance expense of $6,828.36, plus a transfer to
reserve funds of $971.34. Leaving a net loss carried to capital and surplus
of $121.81. On the capital sheet, our assets amount to $167,549.85. These
consist in part of cash on hand, $913.46 and of reserves of $4,136.35. Bills
payable · amounted to $76.00. There are no other liabilities. All reasonable
insurance is carried on our properties.
'
(c) Old Age Insurance. Upon application 'by the Trustees, the treasury has determined that" the club house is subject to old age insurance
taxes and compliance therewith is now being made. The advantage to the
club therefrom is that some pension assurance will be given to our employees. Of these, our hostess, has served the club faithfully and with
much distinction tl)ese many years. It is my hope that she will not be
obliged to retire during this war period but the vicissitudes of life prompt
us to make provision for that hazard. The officers of the club have th.e
matter under consideration with the Finance Committee of the Grand
Lodge. I trust that no final conclusion will be necessary at this session.
Fraternally yours,

is a large modern building, very well furnished and incorporating a spaci~us
lounge, ballroom, library, game rooms and study rooms all for the exclus.1ve
use of the members. Activities include informal afternoon and evening

ANNUAL REPORT OF TRUSTEES · OF THE
MASONIC HOMES

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Trustees of the Masonic Homes ·of California herewith present the
fiftieth annual report for the year ending' July 31, 1942, together with the
reports of the Superintendents of our Homes, and the financial reports of
the Secretary and Treasurer.
The Board of Trustees met on ·October 17, 1941, after the adjournment
of Grand Lodge with the· following members present.:
Charles M. Wollenberg (term expires 1942).
James B. Gist (term expires 1943) .
Samuel E. Burke (term expires 1944).
Chari~ Albert Adams (term expires 1945).
Leslie E. Wood, Deputy Grand Master.
Claude H. Morrison, Senior ,Grand Warden.
Gilbert C. DeForest, Junior Grand Warden.
The reappointment of Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams to
the Board of Trustees for a four-year term commencing October 17, 1941,
and the election of Leslie E. Wood, Deputy Grand Master; Claude H. Morrison, Senior Grand Warden; Gilbert C. DeForest, Junior Grand Warden,
were formally reported to the board.
The board then organized for the ensuing year by electing the following
officers:
Charles M. Wollenberg, President.
James B. Gist, Vice President.
By virtue of his re-election as Treasurer of the Grand Lodge, F . & A. M.
of 'California, William P. Filmer remains Treasurer of the Masonic Homes
of California.
By virtue of his election as Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge, F. &
A. M. of California, Lloyd E . Wilson became Secretary of the Ma~onic
Homes of California Board of Trustees.
Population
The various governmental assistance programs continues to have a
marked effect on the population of our Homes. As of our last annual report,
the population of the Home at Decato was 300, today we have 305 aged
residents at the Home. We can expect an increased demand for admission
as members of the Craft are drawn into the armed services and ask assistance in caring for an aged mother, and again due to the high cost of living,
those on Old Age Assistance find that $40.00 will not meet their requirements and ask for the security of the Home.
At Covina our population has decreased .from 114 reported in 1941 to
95 reported herewith. Here also it might be that, as the war services take
the younger men, we will be requested to provide the security of the Home
for their children.

War Activities
Since Pearl Harber we have, like all America, had to meet war conditions. · The Civil Defense Councils of both Los Angeles and Alameda
Counties designated our hospital units .as Casualty Stations and we at once
prepared to serve our communities in case of disaster. We have provided
all equipment necessary to safeguard our properties and under our efficient
Superintendents have trained and instructed our personnel and residents.
We have set up a plan whereby if dariger threatens we will cover our
holdings with war risk insuranc.

A Civilian Hero
Ben Helwig, 1934-1936, Orange Grove Lodge No. 293.
. In this time when heroic deeds are so much in our minds, I should
like to ~peak of one o~ ~mr former children, not in uniform, whose heroism
under disastrous cond1t1ons should be an inspiration to us all.
Ben Helwig entered the Home in 1927 from Orange Grove Lodge
No. 293. He was then eight years old. W hen he was sixteen years old
he suffer~d an acciden~al eye injury on the playground. In spite of the
b~st .~ed1cal and surgical care, the injury resulted in complete loss of
his VIS!On.

We !>laced him in the California School for the Blind at Berkeley,
where he remained until he graduated at the age of twenty. Following

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this he attended the Oakland Technical High School, where, despite his
handicap, he was able to complete with credit a course in mechanical
work in June, 1941. He then returned to his moth~r's h01_ne in Lo.s Angel.es.
By means of our Scholarship Fund he was provided with a trained gmde
dog, which enabled him to find his way about Los Angeles.
With the development of the national defense program h.e desi;ed to
obtain some mechanical equipment, particularly a lathe and its adjuncts.
Through the generosity of interested donors he was provide? ~ith_ what
he asked for. With these he went to work in a small out-bmlding in the
rear of his mother.' s home. At the same time he applied for a job in a
machine shop located in the neighborhood. Th~ ma~hine sho~ yropriet~r
visited him in his work shop and discovered his skill and ab1hty. He is
now working in this machine shop as an inspector. of alu~inum alloy
cable drums for aileron controls in Douglas warplanes. His pluck and
determination have attracted considerable public attention and have been
made the subject of illustrated stories in the Los Angeles Times and in
the Flying Aces Magazine.

204

Jack Cooksey, who graduated from the home in . 1939. So~n. after
graduation he enlisted in the Army and went to March Field, for training as
a bombardier.
His mother, in a recent letter to us, says:
"He is a bombardier on one of the 93rd Bombing Squadron
flying fortresses. When last heard from he was stationed at Melbourne, Australia. He has the rank of master sergeant. He was in
Manila when war broke out; and his pal, who went through bombing school with him, was killed not ten feet from Jack.
"He has been all over and has seen so much. . . . He and
six other boys were awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for
their flight from the Philippines to Australia (via Java).
"We are very proud of him and all the boys from the Home.
I think you did a wonderful job with them all, and especially our
boy. I know he would be very much pleased to hear from you."
Jack's mother includes also a letter which he wrote her under date of
January 6, 1942. This letter was written from Java:
"Well folks, here's your darling son still alive and kicking.
Have been through a lot of experiences. Have been bombed, shot
at, and have been on eight bombing missions. I have seen some
of my best friends killed before my eyes, but it has taught me a
lot that I will never forget. I have been through about four different countries in about two· weeks:
"We pulled a raid a couple of days ago and caught the Jap
fleet sleeping, sunk about three ships and disabled two; one of them ·
was a battleship and we made three direct hits on it, two on deck
and one at the waterline. We are using six hundred pounders.
Sure was fun.
"Don't know how long I'll last in this war but have made out
an allowance to you of fifty dollars a month; save it until you hear
that I am gone, then do what you want with it. Don't worry about
me as I am really not taking any more risk than if I was driving

205

"Don't believe all you hear over the radio about the great Jap
arrr:y, as they really aren't doing so good considering the small
resistance they are meeting. If we had more planes we would whip
them right quick, no fooling."
Employees
Both Ho~es have experienced a shortage of labor occasioned by
employees leaving for other employment and the impossibility of replacements due to war demands. With the children at Covina the situation is
not as acute as at the Home for our Aged, as it is possible to assign the
youngsters to meet the emergency and theirs is a willing response. At
Decato the situation is more serious; three hundred and five residents, all
aged, some bedfast and others suffering from various crippling ailments
must be cared for in hospital, dining room and quarters. N evei:theless,
there are many of our residents who are physically able to assist in this
emergency and many do. All on admission have signed an agreement to
perform such work as he or she might be physically able to undertake.
Your Trustees are going to hold our Home group to this agreement and
insist that all able to render such service to their home as conditions demand.
It is not only their obligation but a war service.
Finances
The report of our financial condition indicates a surplus for the year
of $37, 100.00. This in spite of increased cost of labor and commodities;
largely due to an increase of fees from initiates and increased income from
securities, and enforced savings by sugar rationing and shortage of other
commodities.

Securities, Real Estate, Etc.:
All of the securities, etc., listed under Schedule B-1 have been received
by donation. The book value represents the market value at the time of
donation. A nominal value of $1.00 is used for purpose of record when the
actual value is unknown.
Notes and contracts receivable are listed at the unpaid balance as at
July 31, 1942.
Life insurance policies, received mainly from residents of the Homes,
have been recorded at the amount recoverable at the death of the insured,
if determinable; otherwise at a nominal value of $1.00.
Real estate has been recorded at the assessed value as taken from the
tax bills up until the past year. Due to the constant fluctuation in real
estate values, and to avoid reporting book losses resulting from such fluct uation when as a fact no actual loss had occurred, all real estate donated
during the past year has been recorded on the books for record purposes
at a nominal value of $1.00.
The stocks and bonds and some of the notes are held by the Anglo
California National Bank for safekeeping. These we~e verified by certificat ion from the bank. The,.remainder of the notes and the iilsurance policies
are held at the office of the Homes Secretary and were inspected by us.

Every effort is being made by me and our Matron, Mr s. Virginia Loni,
to promote harmony and contentment among our members, and to develop
a home-like atmosphere in the Home, and in a large measure we feel 01.1r
efforts are not entirely in vain.
It shall always be our aim to operate the Home as economically and
efficiently as possible, remembering that economy should never be effected
at th e expense of our residents. To have the buildings and grounds present
a neat and attractive appearance; and to provide every comfort possible for
the residents of the Home.
At the beginning of the year, there were 305 residents; 46 were
admitted during the year, at an average age of 73.90; 37 passed away, the
average age being 80.62 ; there were 3 departures. O f the 305 in the Home,
150 are women and 155 are men, including 19 married couples. There are:
2 residents between the ages of 50 to 60.
30 residents between the ages of 60 to 70.
49 residents between the ages of 70 to 80.
3 residents between the ages of 90 to 100.
The average age at this time is 76.00 years for men and 74.70 for women.
The health condition has been excellent, with the exception of those who
are infirm and feeble o"."ing to advancing years.
There are 49 of our members being cared for in our hospital at the
present time. T his department is equipped with sanitary and electrical
devices, which enable us to give to those who are ill, every care and attention for their comfort and .well-being.
Miss Esther G. Payne, who has served the hospital department faith,
fully and well for the past twenty years, and who is well and favorab ly
known by the members of the Fraternity for her kind and sincere efforts
in behalf of our members who find it ·necessary to be hospitalized, is in
charge of the hospital. Dr. W. L . McWhirter; who is the medical director.,
is also our X-Ray technician and is rendering a very valuable service in
both departments.
The members are encouraged to inter est themselves in the daily
routine work; and a large number of residents have contributed t o the
welfare of the ·Home, by their services.
Following are few of the departments where you will fi nd some of
our guests going about their duties with a smile on their faces and song
in their hearts: Engine room, laundry, carpenter, paint, and barber shops,
garage, mail, passenger, freight and express automobile service, kitchen,
pantry, dining room, vegetable and store rooms, office work, library, telephone, information desk, flower gardens, vegetable gar den, poultry yards,
and many other light duties. The assistance by our members in these various departments is more necessary now than ever before, due to the
shortage of help, and greatly assists in maintaining the high standard
which has always been maintained in the Home. Mrs. Lord and I wartt
to assure our members that we fu lly appreciate their f:OOperation and
assistance.
During the year, we have continued our paint campaign. Since our last
report, we have painted the kitchen, dining room, and all the halls, club
rooms, card room, and member s' room on the first floor North and East.
A new fr eight elevator has been installed to lift articles from the
commissary department to the kitchen. All the main departments: Kitchen,
dining room, laundry and heating plant have been operating during· t he
year economically and efficiently.

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
To the Board of Trustees,
Masonic Homes of California:
.
.
It is my p~ivilege and pleasure, as well as my dut:l'.', to submit this m_y
second annual report of the management an_d operation of the Masonic
Home at Decoto California, for the year ending August 31, 1942.
During the ;ear there have been a few changes go~erning the policies
of the Home, which we hope will be helpful and beneficial to all concerned.

227

228

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Most of the farm land is leased; the portion we have retained has
furnished an abundance of fruit, berries, eggs and vegetables.
In another part of the report, you will find listed the entertainments
which have been provided by various Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, and
friends for the entertainment of the Home folk. The East Bay Past
Matrons' Association, I believe, is entitled to special mention. Their program was excellent, and enjoyed immensely by our guests. We also had
an opportunity of meeting the Grand Officers of the 0. E. S., and in their
usual graceful way presented the Horne with quilts, table-covers, pajamas,
and an abundance of jams, jellies and preserves for which we want to
extend to these good ladies our grateful thanks and appreciation. I also
feel that special mention should be made of the ' Masters and Wardens
program, which was excellent and enjoyed very much by the Home family.
Many magazines, books, periodicals and papers have been presented to
the Home during the year, by friends and members of the Fraternity.
These contributions are very much appreciated by the family.
.\ Ve are unable to express adequately our deep appreciation to the San
Francisco Film Distributing Company for their splendid contribution of
fine movie films; however, we want to assure this fine organization that
their generosity in providing the films is fully appreciated and we want
to extend to them our grateful thanks.
·
Dr. W. A. Pankey, who for many years arranged the devotional services for the Horne was called into the United States Service. Since his
departure, Dr. Winkley -of Hayward, has taken charge, and through his
efforts a minister is assigned and services are held in the Auditorium every
Sunday. We want to assure Dr. Winkley, and the kind gentlemen who
assist him, that their efforts are very much appreciated by the residents of
the Home.
Due to the "present labor shortage, we are having some difficulty in
keeping a full staff, which necessarily means that we must curtail our
service in many respects; however, we are hopeful that no one will suffer
as a result.
In conclusion, Mrs. Lord and I wish to extend our appreciation of the
service rendered by our employes throughout the year, in their respective
departments, and to express to the members of the Board of Truste.e s our
sincere gratitude for the counsel and advice given when meeting problems
in connection with the management of the Home.
J. R. EUBANKS, Superintendent.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina Home
To the Truste es of the Masonic Homes of California:

The last year in the Covina Home has been marked by decreasing
enrollment, many changes in the personnel of our employed staff necessity to increase salaries, rise ii} prices of all commodities inevit;ble increase in our per capita cost of operation.
'
Of the list of employees as of December 7 1941 half were no longer
wi~h us at the end of July. Some of these h'ad g~ne into more highly
paid war work. We are finding it increasingly difficult to obtain satisfactory persons for various types of service required to be done in the
Home.
e are having serious trouble in getting dental service, since
our dentist for the past fifteen years, Dr. Donald H. Wilkins entered
the . ~rmy. Under these . circumstances, it is difficult to pre;erve the
stability and settled condition of operation to be desired for the best
rearing of children.

"!"

Admissions and Discharges-During the past year there were nine
admissions of children and twenty-nine discharges. Of the twenty-nine
discharges, causes of discharge were:
Graduated from high school............................:...............................15
Returnecl to parents at their request, account remarriage ...... 9
Returned to father at his request .................... ~ ............................. 1
Joined CCC at age of 18..........:.............•.......................:..........:...... 1
Unsatisfactory conduct.:............................... ,...................................~ 3
"Unsatisfactory conduct" means conduct and attitude which would
damage other children of the Home more than continued residence would
benefit the child concerned. In such cases, occasionally the greatest good
t~ the gre~test number dictates the removal of the out-of-step boy or
girl from the Home group. Of those thus discharged during the past
year all three are now doing. well. Two of them were placed in other

246

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

environment under our supervision and were assisted financially by the
Hoine until they graduated from high school; in the third case it was
possible to put the burden of responsibility upon the boy's parent, whose
circumstances had improved since the boy's placement in the Home. We
are in cordial relationship with all three of these young people, and they
all say that the shock of their dismissal was the one thing necessary to
wake them up.

keep their contact with the Home and with each other through our
Alumni Newsletter will be a useful and stabilizing inf! uence in their lives.

Our class of .high school graduates of 1942 are occupied as follows:
In colleges or vocational training schools ....................................6
In defense indus tries ....~·-·----····················--·---·····--·'·····-········--···········-·4
In clerical or business employment....,...............·----·····················.4
In Armed Services of the United States...................................... !
Safety P recautions-\Var conditions so far have touched the children
in the Home but little. Our inland location gives us a feeling of relative
security. Those who were responsible for the construction of our buildings fortunately provided that all of them in which children live should
be of Class A construction; walls, floors and roofs are of reinforced concrete, fire-proof and shock-resistant.
Although it seems unlikely that any enemy action will come to our
neighborhood, we have taken precautions to meet it should it occur. A
number of our staff members have had instruction in air raid warden's
work, including first aid ; several of them hold air raid warden's certificates; the Home is an air raid warden's post. We have increased our
fire protection, and have our older boys trained for their duties as auxiliary firemen.
The civil authorities of Los Angeles have designated our hospital
as an emergency evacuee hospital, which in case of necessity would care
for convalescent cases. We are prepared also to receive, in case of emergency need, as many as fifty evacuee children.
No Summer Cam~We felt that it was wise this year to forego the
summer camp at Balboa Island, which, during many years past, has
been a feature of our annual program. A special recreation program was
set up at Covina, with a te.mporarily employed recreational leader; and we
were thus enabled to carry on a vacation program which was much enjoyed by the children.
Reduced Transportation-A limitation on our freedom of movement
has been imposed by the change in transportation facilities between the
Home and Los Angeles. Electric cars servicing this area were taken off
in November, replaced by buses whose nearest approach to the Home is
a mile and a half away. This has been .a great inconvenience not only to
children, but to employees of the Home, and to relatives of the children
who must depend tipon this transportation when visiting the Home. It
has put an extra demand upon the Home's bus and station wagon at the
very time when the rubber shortage makes it imperative to conserve
the use of these vehicles.
Alumni in the Service-We have information concerning forty-nine
alumni of the Home who are in the armed services of the United States.
At this time we are particularly g lad that it has been our custom through
past years to keep in touch with our graduates; now when so .many of
them are having to sever home ties, we believe that every opportunity to

247

ln the main hallway of our Administration Building has been placed
a panel bearing the name and rank of each former Masonic Home boy
or girl serving in the armed forces. As the military effort of the nation
develops, other names and. data will be added.
A . Civilian Hero-In thi"s time when heroic deeds ate so much in our
minds 0 I should like to speak of one of our former · children, not in uniform, whose heroism under disastrous conditions should be an inspiration
to us all.
Ben Helwig entered the Home in 1927 from Orange Grove Lodge
No. 293. He was then eight years old. When he was sixteen years old
he suffered an accidental eye injury on the playground. In spite of the
best medical and surgical care, the injury resulted in complete loss of
his vision.
We placed him in the California School for the Blind at Berkeley,
where he "remained until he graduated at the age of twenty. Following
this he attended the Oakland Technical High School, where, despite his
handicap, he was able to complete with credit a course in mechanical
work in June, 1941. He then returned to his mather's home in Los Angeles. By means of our Scholarship Fund he was provided with a
trained guide dog, which enabled him to find his way about Los Angeles.
With the developme.nt of the national defense program he desired to
obtain some mechanical equipment, particularly a lathe and its adjuncts.
Through the generosity of interested donors he was provided with what
he asked for. With these he went to work in a small out-building in the
rear of his mother's home. At the same time he applied for a job in a
machine shop located in the neighborhood. The machine shop proprietor
visited him in his work shop and discovered his skill and ability. He is
now "working in this machine shop as an inspector of aluminum alloy
cable drums for aileron controls in Douglas warplanes. His pluck and
determination have attracted considerable public attention and have been
made the subject of illustrated stories in the Los Angeles Times and in
the Flying Aces Magazine.
Training Boys for War-Th.e present feverish prosperity of the defense industries and the strong demand for every type of human service
in connection with the war have had an unfavorable effect upon the
thinking and behavior of our older children, especially the boys. As they
reach the age of seventeen or eighteen, they find that they are in great
demand for various employments, at wages which are out of proportion
to their real value as employees; and this tends to give them a distorted
idea of their own maturity and competence. These ideas percolate downward to those who are only fourteen to sixteen years old.
It seems probable that these boys will be called to some form of
military service as soon as they arrive at the age of eighteen. Having
in mind the requirements which will then be made of them, we believe
it to be tC> their interest that we require from them a more serious
application to their tasks and studies than was thought necessaty in
times of peace. They will have to meet enemies who have been subjected
to drill and discipline" from the beginning of their adolescence; something
akin to this must go into the training of young Americans who are to
meet and overcome such foes. In these times it is not sufficient to excuse

248

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

them by saying "boys will be boys"; we must keep in mind that these
boys will soon be men, and must bear men's burdens in a war-torn
world. The best we can do is to train them, and make them sufficiently
hard and tough to meet the severe tests which are ahead.
JOHN M. DOWNEN,

Superintendent.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCING
BUILDING PROJECTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Financing Building Projects reports the following
as a short outline of its activities for the year ending September 30, 1942.
Due to the exigencies of life and the demands of the nation for officers to
carry to a successful conclusion the war in which we now find ourselves
involved, this report is being presented by the only member of. the committee that is present at this session; the chairman of the com_m1ttee, ~ast
Grand Master Filmer, having not sufficiently recovered from his long siege
of illness to 'warrant his presence at this communication, and the other
member of the committee, Worshipful Brother Herbert C. Goldman, being
now in training at Miami Beach, FJorida, having been commissioned as a
captain in the Army.
•
It is thought that a review of the circumstances under which the
committee was originally organized would be of interest and would conduce to a better understanding of the activities of the committee, and
therefore, the indulgence of Grand Lodge and of the Grand Master is
asked, that .the following brief outline may be given:
The committee was originally authorized by Grand Lodge in 1928.
For a number of years prior to this date it had been recognized by a
number in Grand Lodge, and .particularly by members of the Committee
on Finance due to the number of Temple problems being presented each
year to th~t committee, that there was a genuine need for a co~mittee
to properly supervise the building of new Temples, but no action had
previously been taken by Grand Lodge, owing to a fear that it might
seem Grand Lodge was usurping some of the prerogatives of the constituent Lodges. However, the pressure on the . Committee on Finance to
advise on Temples that were in trouble throughout the st~te became so
great, that in 1928 the chairman of the Committee on Finance at that time,
\Vorshipful Brother Wm. P. Jeffries, concluded that he would have presented to Grand Lodge legislation authorizing such a committee and after
consultation with the chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, Past
Grand Master Weller; and the chairman of the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes, Past Grand Master Hervey, legislation was prepared,
prese.nted and adopted, setting up a committee of t?ree, composed of, ~s
ex-officio members, the Grand Treasurer and the chairman of the Comrn1ttee on Finance and one other member to be selected by the Grand Master.
This made Past Grand Master Filmer (as Grand Treasurer) and Brother
Jeffries (as chairman of the Committee on Finance), members of the committee, and Brother Robert Greig of Berkeley was appointed by the Gr.and
Master as the third member.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

.·263

Brother Jeffries was selected as chairman and in such capacity acted
up to the time of his death in 1935. Due to Brother Jeffries' devotion to
Masonry and outstanding ability as a financier and also as one who was
thoroughly acquainted with building problems, the work of the committee
was given a high standing from its very beginning and was at the time
and has been since of inestimable benefit .to Masonry.
In 1933 Brother Herbert C. Goldman of Long Beach, due to the outstanding work which he had done on behalf of Grand Lodge 'in surveying
and reporting on the damage done to Masonic Temples in and near Long
Beach in an earthquake earlier in the year, was recommended by Brother
Jeffries to the Grand Master for appointment on the committee and has
served in such capacity up to the present time.
Upon the death of Brother Jeffries in 1935, the compiler of this report
was selected as chairman of the Committee on Finance and thereby became,
ex-officio, a member of the Committee on Financing Building Projects. Past
Grand Master Filmer was selected to succeed Brother Jeffries as chairman,
has been continued as such and holds the chairmanship at the present
time. However, due to Most Worshipful Brother Filmer contracting pneumonia in the early part of March, 1941, and his need to be relieved of all
work, the brother who now stands before you was requested by Brother
Filmer to carry on the activities of the committee until he was again able
to assume the responsibility. It was hoped at the time that the need for
any other hand at the helm of the committee, other than that of the ablt:
hand of Brother Filmer, would be of very brief duration. Unfortunately,
to many the heart has been made sick with anguish because· of the hope
so long deferred.
While Brother Filmer has been, a number of times, well on the road
to recovery and yet, true to the oft repeated saying that "disasters come
not singly," he has time and again suffered relapses. His courage and
fortitude through it all have been remarkable indeed, but his recovery has
not yet been sufficienly complete to warrant attempting to be present at
this session. I am very sure, however, that he is with us in spirit and that
his interest in and devotion to the Grand Lodge of California have not
been dimmed. I am sure I express the sentiment of not only this Grand
Lodge, but of all Masons throughout California, when I say the he.art of
Masonry goes out to our beloved brother in his trial and our earnest
prayers are tllat his full recovery will not be much longer deferred.
The other member of the committee, Brother H. C. Goldman, has
shown a great devotion to his duty and is indeed entitled to the thanks
of this Grand Lodge for the work he has done on this committee. At all
times he has been ready to travel to any part of the state, at his own
expense, to do whatever might be required of him to properly attend to
the problems presented to the committee and at each session of Grand
Lodge heretofore has been present and without receiving travel pay, as
the Committee on Financing Building Projects being a special committee
the members thereof are not entitled thereto. Herb wa.s always proud that
he had the opportunity to do this service for Masonry, without receiving
any reimbursement of expenses. From the year 1935 up to this year he
always compiled and presented the report of this committee. On August
31st he was notified he had been commissioned as a captain in our Armed
Forces. Never have I seen anyone so overjoyed as Herb was when he
received this news. As previously expressed, he is at the present time at
Miami Beach attending a school of instruction.
Other members of the Committee on Financing Building Projects
have traveled on business of the committee. It is to be noted that no

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

request for return of any expense has ever been asked by any member
and that the· entire activity of the committee has been carried on without
any expense to Grand Lodge.
While the work of the committee this past year has not been as extensive as it has been in other preceding years and yet it has been considerable, as probably can be understood by the file of correspondence which I
have in my hand. The work has been tremendously interesting. The closer
touch one has with the various problems of the Temples throughout the
state the more it is borne in upon one what a splendid opportunity is presented for real service to the ·craft by suitable and able handling of these
problems. Nor need there be any fear that the subordinate Lodges bear
any resentment or harbor any feeling that Grand Lodge is usurping prerogatives in attempting to review and supervise Masonic building activities.
In every instance the help of the committee has been eagerly sought and
gladly followed.
It has always been the purpose of the committee to review the problem from the Lodge standpoint and attempt to be helpful in an every day
practical "feet on the ground" attitude. Personally, I am very thankful
the opportunity has come my way to be of some service to Masc:mry in
this particular.

rials are becoming scarcer with indications that some items will soon be
impossible to obtain. There is a general demand throughout the nation to
postpone any development that can be deferred without material loss, and
that there will come a time when there will be a genuine demand for
employment by those who are now engaged in defense activities, and that
by waiting until that time Welcome Lodge will not only be serving a
national need but will actually save considerable money for the Lodge.
In the meantime the Lodge can take advantage of the present situation
and strengthen its financial condition; thus it will be better prepared to
realize its present ambition."

The following is a brief outline of the activities of the committee:
Beverly Hills Lodge No. 528 and Beverly Hills Masonic
Building Association
Report by this committee last year was made upon the wish of· the
brethren at Beverly Hills to provide for themselves a new Temple. The
wish was revived again ·this year and plans and specifications for a new
building prepared and also a plan of financing tentatively agreed upon.
The financing plan contemplated the raising of funds without having
recourse to any funds of the Lodge. It also proposed the · complete
financing without the. necessity of a loan. However, due to the fact that
the Lodge could get by without the Temple and that in the construction
of the Temple there would be used some, although a limited amount, of
vital war material, and that the committee had, the previous year, adopted
a policy of discouraging the building of Temples for the duration, the
application was not approved.
·
Two members of this committee met with the officers of . the Lodge
and of the Building Association and the request of the Lodge, together
with the attitude of the committee, was thoroughly gone over.
The brethren of Beverly Hills Lodge very graciously acceded ·to the
decision of the committee and ceased active effort toward the building of
a new Temple and are now waiting (and probably with a good deal of
impatience) for the time to come when they can again consider providing
themselves with an adequate home.
For the information of all present, the committee is desirous of stating
the position previously assumed by this committee on the building of new
Temples and reported in the 1941 proceedings, in its rejection of the application of Welcome Lodge No. 255 at Lemoore, in which its position was
stated as follows:
"Your committee has given this matter thorough study and has concluded that the project should be deferred until a more appropriate time.
We do not attempt to thwart the ambition and desire of any Lodge to
own its own home, but considering the present high cost of building, the
probability that costs will further materially increase, that building mate-

265

site.
The consent of this committee, for the using of Lodge funds for this
purpose, was not obtained at the time of the purchase. Upon being
apprized, by the Inspector of the district, Brother Clark H. Shaw, of the
need of securing the consent of the Committee on Finan'cing Building
Projects for the use of Lodge funds for such an investment, application
was made to this committee this year, for the approval of the action taken
previously. Such approval was given. No building activities at the present
time are contemplated nor authorized.
Carpinteria Lodge No. 444
In this committee's report at last year's session of Grand Lodge, it
reported on the need of the above Lodge for $2500.00, for the purpose of
restoring damage done to its Temple by an earthquake and that it had
certified all the facts surrounding the Temple problem to Grand Master
Wilson.
The earthquake damage was severe and in order to prevent further
damage the need for action was immediate. The holder of the mortgages
also gave notice of intent to foreclose unless this damage was repaired.
The loan on the Temple at that time was $12,000.00. The then mortgage
holder made the proposition to the Lodge, that if immediate payment
could be arranged it would accept $5,000.00 in full settlement of the debt,
or in other words, it would grant the Lodge a discount of $7,000.
Before the Lodge could negotiate a new loan it, of course, was necessary to have the earthquake damage repaired. Tentative arrangements had
been made for a lo;in sufficient not only to pay the $5,000.00 required to
settle the old loan, but also an additional $2,500.00 to pay the amount
which was needed for restoration. Upon the recommendation of this committee, together with that of the Committee on Finance, the Grand Master
made the $2,500.00 advance. The Lodge was able to completely, restore
the Temple and was enabled to secure the $5,000.00 necessary to pay off
the old mortgage, but it was not able to secure sufficient to reimburse
the Grand Lodge for the $2,500.00 advanced.

Projects; that it should be determined what, if any, additional r epairs
were · needed on the Temple; what amount would be left remaining in

advance were to be considered as such, and therefore, it probably would
be advisable at this time to determine what, if any, amount the Lodge
should return to Grand Lodge and in this manner entirely dispose of the
transaction.

Such a report was made to the Grand Master and he has directed
the Committee on F inance to look into the matter. and make a repoct
to Grand Lodge of its conclusions.

REPORT O F COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE
MASONRY
T o the Most Worshipf"l Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows :
In last year's report the committee outlined its policy concerning
Clandestine Masonry and stated that it should not be given existence even
to the extent of naming its Lodges in our reports. In conformity with this
policy we believe that our work should be largely educational, but always
contacting these spurious bodies and their activity to the end of preventing
. fraud and imposition.
As an example of the wisdom of this say-nothing policy as opposed
to that of publishing all the statistics, we desire to cite the following :
There has come to the attention of this committee a copy of the July
number of "Square & Compass," a magazine published in Denver by regular Masons, containing an article entitled "Filipino Masons in California."
The article dealt entirely with Clandestine Filipino Masons and their
Lodges in California and treated the entire subject as an activity of regular
Masonry. The material in this article was taken entirely frorn previous
Grand Lodge reports of this committee. The article was unwittingly reproduced in a Masonic magazine published in San Diego by one of our own
good brothers. Such unfortunate occurrences are the result of putting all
the information in our printed reports and the elimination and correction
of them is one of the objects of this committee.
During the past this committee has reported upon 21 so-called Grand
Lodges of Clandestine Masonry having an existence at some time or other
in California. Some of the constituent Lodges noted in these reports have
existed under as many as three different Grand Lodges. However, of the
21 Grand Lodges reported on, five have been heretofore reported as having
a mere paper existence, and inactive. Six of those reported, having a total
of thirty-seven constituent so-called Lodges, have either passed out of
existence entirely or nothing has been heard of them since 1936.
Of those remaining in existence, one is purely patriotic in character
and concerns itself with labor issues and cannot be considered essentially
Masonic in character. Of the others, three are Filipino Grand Lodges
with a total of 51 constituent Lodges; four are Mexican or Spanish speaking Grand Lodges with 52 constituent Lodges; and two are Negro Grand
Lodges having a total of 46 constituent Lodges. Two Lodges seem to be
working under no Grand Lodge authorization, but independently as individual Lodges.
Concerning these Clandestine Lodges, those operating among the
colored race are of no particular concern to regular Masonry. They do
not operate outside of their own race and seem to be doing a good work
within their own numbers. One of these Grand bodies is very sick in its
structure and Lodges and may eventually eliminate itself, while the other
is going on with its work, proudly imitating the Grand Lodge of California
as far as it can.
Of the three Filipino Grand Lodges, there is considerable activity at
the present time and you have had a particular report up.on them from
Brother Potts in so far as they concern the Hawaiian Islands. Our Grand_

270

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Master did Masonry a real service in this connection by hi"s action reported
in his annual report. This action of the Grand Master in requiring the
payment of dues by members of regular Philippine Lodges and the issuing
of certificates by the Grand Secretary, effectually separated the regular
Masons of the recognized Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands from
the members of the three Clandestine Grand Lodges operating in our
jurisdiction. We appreciate and praise the work of our Grand Master in
this connection.
The real concern of this committee is with the four active Grand
Lodges operating in the Spanish language and having 52 constituent
Lodges in this jurisdiction. At first we were concerned only with Grand
Lodges of this variety, having their headquarters at some place in Mexico.
Later, however, a Grand Lodge having its headquarters in Laredo, Texas,
came to the front and became the most active. The activity of this so-called
Grand body seems to have been considerably if not effectually curtailed
by the action of the Grand Lodge of Texas in curbing its activities there
and its Lodges in this state have largely transferred their allegiance t6 a
Grand Lodge organized later with headquarters in New York · state. This
New York Grand Lodge seems now to be the most active and is at present
organizing another new Lodge.
Heretofore the material with which Mexican and Filipino Clandestine
Lodges dealt was not of a class or type that would ordinarily disturb
the individual Lodges of this jurisdiction in their wo~k in the field .o f
Masonry. It was only when the activities of these Clandestine .Lodges
involved fraud or imposition that regular Masonry concerned · itself, and
then only for the sake of helping the individual imposed upon. With the
changing economic conditions and with the war conditions as they affect
the Filipino race, this status may change and we may find ourselves confronted with a problem of major importance. It is therefore essential that
the work of this committee be continued with greater intensity so far a~
a close surveillance of the activities of these Clandestine Lodges is concerned. It may well be that with a changing economic world the attainments of those who have heretofore been content with this spurious brand
of Masonry might be improved to the extent that they may become proper
material for regular Masonic Lodges. Before that time actually arrives,
this (';.rand Lodge should be in possession of the information and the data
which would enable it to act intelligently and wisely in the interests of
Masonry.
In the case of the Spanish speaking race, if it becomes a question of
a lack of acquaintance with the English language that is inducing these
men to affiliate themselves with Clandestine Lodges, then it may be the
work of this Grand Lodge to authorize in certain communities the chartering of Spanish speaking Lodges ·under rules covering the operation of
the present French Lodges and German Lodge now operating in San
Francisco and Los Angeles under charters from this Grand Lodge. . Or if
these men desire rather to become members of regular Mexican Lodges
in various communities with which they may be identified, it may be a
question of California ·Lodges granting . waivers of jurisdiction to enable
them to acquire such membership. This, then, may be further followed
with the organization of Mexican Masonic Clubs through which these men
could attain their social objectives, and at the same time allowing them
to visit the California Lodges to obtain their Masonic inspiration and
teaching. The approach to the· solution of this problem must be studied
and the action determined upon only when the facts are thoroughly known
to the committee and the full information can be given to Grand Lodge.

. The outcome of war on the other hand, may itself formulate our
a.ction with respect to Filipino Clandestine Masons and their organizations. In this connection it is to be noted that at least at present the
member~hip of these organizations is not of the calibre of regular Filipino
Lodges m the Islands. The Lodges in the Philippine Islands are composed
of Anglo-_Saxons and Filipinos, the latter constituting the majority of
membership. However, these Filipinos are the business men, officials and
others responsibly identified with their respective communities and the
activities in the Islands, whereas the membership of the Clandestine
Lodges in California is upon the average of a much lower grade. For the
P.resent, at least, th·e· great number of these are not even acceptable Masonic
t~mber. War conditions may, however, change this and anyway, the solut10n of this problem must be left to the future.

Grand body for its consideration some of the factors involved in the
probl~m. an.cl ~o~e of the possible solutions. It remains for regular Masons
of this Jun~d1ct10n to e.ducate themselves to their duties with regard to
~ontacts with Clandestine Masonry and to keep this committee fully
informed as to what is going on with regard to it in the various communities where it has become active. The committee reiterates that no
regular Masonic Lodge should admit to its meetings a Clandestine Mason
nor .should an individual Mason visit or fraternize in any way with a Clandestine Lodge. The committee has this year investigated several activities
reported to it and has assisted in the suppression of the issuance of Masonic
certificates by one of our former brothers.
During the coming year this committee will gather more specific data
as. to the extent and character of Clandestine Masonry in California and
will endeavc;ir. to f~rmulate and suggest methods which will eventually
stop the activity at its sources. It must be ·borne in mind that this cannot
effectually be done by prosecution without developing a persecution sym?at~".· Hence the necessity. of solving the problem through the study of
~nd~v~dual cases and suggesting the remedy which will apply and heal the
md1v1dual case.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
HIST ORY
To the Most .Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report of its activities during the past year, together with its recommendations.
· In compliance with the written request of the Grand Master, that the
length cf oral reports be reduced to a reasonable minimum, we will content
ourselves in this report with a very brief recital of some of the many
interesting, new items which have come to our attention during the past
year.
.

Members of the committee have responded to requests from Lodges

~n all parts of the state to deliver addresses on Masonic history. The travel-

ing and other expenses incident to their visitations have been borne by
the individual members and, as in past years, no part of the committee's
appropriation has been used fo~ personal expenses.
You~ committee ~ms recently come into possession of interesting and
.
informative data relative to the following California Masons:
·
William Watt, a member of Madison Lodge No. 23, who owned the
rich quartz claim into which the famous Brennen ledge at Gra.s s Valley
dipped.

William T . Coleman, chairman of the San Francisco Vigilante Committee of 1856.
Leland Stanford, War Governor of California and member of Michigan
City Lodge No. 47.
John W. Geary, the last Alcalde and first mayor of San Francisco
and member of California Lodge No. 1.
Jacob Leese, whose daughter was the first white child born in' Y erba
Buena.
John Bigler, Governor ~f California and member of Washington Lodge
No. 20 of Sacramento.
Ruel Colt_ Gridley, a ~ember ~f several Nevada and California Lodges,
who won !~sting fame dun.ng the Civil War by personally raising $150,000
for ~he .Sanitary ~und. This sum was raised by Gridley through the public
auctioning of a smgle sack of flour in the western states.
John Chilton Burch, · California congressman and Past Master of Trinity Lodge No. 27 at Weaverville.
J ~hn' Goller, a member of the ill-starred J ayhawker Party of emigrants
who, in 1849, all but perished in their trip through Death Valley. Goller
was a member of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42.
David D. Colton, friend of Charles Crocker and business associate of

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the so-called Big Four in the Central Pacific Railroad Company. He was
a member of St. John Lodge No. 37, at Yreka.
We have also found some additional and interesting stories of the
activities of 'Paschal Taylor, popularly known as "Jock" Taylor. A member and at one time Tyler of Lassen Lodge No. 149 at Susanville. Taylor
appears to have been the champion practical joker of the Honey Lake
Valley.
We have completed the history of that pioneer Mason, John Paty, a
s hip captain who lived in Honolulu. He was mentioned by Carter M.
Carew in a letter written in 1843 to his brother in Philadelphia. Carew
states that Paty was the leader of the Masons at Yerba Buena who were
considering the advisability of applying for a dispensation to form a Lodge
in California.
After over eight months of research, your committee has completed
its study into the life of Lansford Warren Hastings. He was a mem_ber of
Tehama No. 3. He was beyond question one of the most energetic and
spectacular characters of the pre~gold rush period. He was self-centered
and ambitious and had a rather exaggerated ego. However, he possessed
a dynamic personality; was a plausible and convincing Speake;; ve;satile
and not easily discouraged and had the happy faculty of adap~mg hupself
to all and any circumstances. He was a born adventurer ~nd filibusterer.
In the spring of 1842, he had passed the bar in the state of Ohio and
joined the Elizah White party bound for Oregon. He was soon elected
captain of the party which arrived safely in Oregon several months later.
He laid out Oregon City, the first officially plotted . townsite on the
Pacific Coast.
In 1844 with John Bidwell, he laid out the town site of Sutterville for.
Captain Sutter.
In 1845, he returned to Ohio via Mexico and Texas and while east
wrote and published a book entitled "Emigrant Guide to Oregon and
California." He lectured throughout the east on the future of the Pacific
Coast. He painted the future in glowing terms and urged those seeking
health, wealth and adventure to investigate the potentialities of the land
of sunshine and flowers.
On' August 15, 1845, a party of ten men left Independence, Missouri~
headed for California. Experienced plainsmen advised that it was too late
in the season to start on so long and perilous a trip across the desert
and mountains. To these warnings, the adventurous ten paid no attention.
They were mounted on horses and mules and led by . the one man .who .
had no.t as yet learned the meaning of failure, Lansford Warren Hastings.
They rode full speed ahead to the very limit of the endurance _of both men
and beasts and arrived at Sutter's Fort on December 24th, Just one day
ahead of th e snow storm which closed the Donner Pass to travel that year.
Hastings was a member of the Constitutional Convention of 1849 and
took an active part in all debates on major questions before the convention. As chairman of the committee on boundaries, he was responsible
for outlining the present boundaries of the state.
In 1846, he returned east over the trail and was instrumental in
inducing emigrants to take the so-called Hastings' cut-off, a much sh?rter
route in point of miles to California than the Fort Hall route. H~ enlisted
under Fremont during the California war in 1846 and was placed m charge
of enlistments.
Upon the outbreak of the Civil War, he espoused the southern cause
and became a major in the Confederate Army. He worked out an elaborate

and somewhat fantastic plan for the capture of Southern California, Arizona and New Mexico and incorporating this vast expanse of territory
into the Confederacy. Lack of funds on the part of the Confederacy was
in the main responsible for the failure of this plan.
Following the war, he visited Brazil in search of land to colonize with
southerners who desired to be free from Yankee rule. He received a grant
of 600,000 acres 500 miles up the Amazon. Through his effort several ship
loads of southern home-seekers reached Brazil. Hastings died in 1870
enroute to Brazil. Today a mere handful of the descendants of the settlers
remain in Brazil.
We have also collected all available information on the life and activities of that distinguished and heroic flyer, General James H . Doolittle,
whose bombing of Tokio thrilled the entire allied world. He is a member
of Hollenbeck Lodge No. 319.
The life story of Homer Lea, the crippled dwarf, reads more like a
scenario born in the fertile brain of a Hollywood script writer who gives
full rein to his overwrought imagination, than it does to the modern
realistic history of a person in flesh and blood.
In 1896, Lea graduated from a Los Angeles high school and later
attended Occidental College and Stanford University. He was a born
soldier and a military genius. He devoted most of his time to the study
of military history, tactics
and strategy..
.
At the age of 23, with no military record, he offered his services to
the Revolutionary army in China and was appointed lieutenant general
and chief of staff. He successfully carried on the fight for the overthrow
of the Manchu Dynasty. He was present at the establishment of the
Chinese Republic and the inauguration of Sun Yet Sen, China's first
president.
Lea was the author of two books which startled the military world
by their bold and daring revelations. His factual and philosophic discussion of the causes of war and the downfall of nations has been characterized as the most lucid, searching and convincing analysis of those subjects
contained in English literature.
Lea died shortly after the establishment of the Chinese Republic. He
was a member of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202, Past Grand Master James B.
Gist having conferred the second and third Degrees on him in 1905.
Your committee has in its files magazine and newspaper articles
depicting his unique career and also several special papers prepared by
those who were his life-long friends.
We wish to acknowledge our indebtedness to Past Grand Masters
Gist and Weller and to Brothers Marshal Stimson and Marko Newmark,
all of Los Angeles, for articles and facts .pertaining to Homer Lea's colorful
history.
At our annual communication in 1940, a member of our committee
related the history of Walter Wilcox, the Masonic orphan sent by the
Masons of New Orleans from that city to California in 1877. In Walter
Wilcox, we have the Masonic orphan sent from . the east to the west.
Recently we learned of a Masonic orphan sent from the west to the east
a few years later. Our attention was calltd to this by the following item
which appeared in a newspaper published in Truckee, California, at the
time.

Many of these will in all probability distinguish themselves and write their
names high in the military annals of th eir country. These brethren have
been, are now, and will be living history. The full record of 'their valiant
and heroic deeds should be preserved for posterity. Your committee feels
that the most convenient agency to properly follow and record the war
career of the members of each California Lodge would be some willing
and competent member of that Lodge. Therefore, your committee respectfully recommends that each Lodge appoint some brother to keep a fu ll
and complete record of each member of his Lodge who has been is now
or will be in the armed forces of the United States during th~ presen~
world war a~d we suggest ,that a scrap book be kept in which may be
pasted all articles published relative to said inducted members.

This boy's father, Charles Sympson, had been a member of Madison
Lodge No. 23 at Grass Valley and died in 1879. Through correspondence
with the Illinois Lodge we learned that Eddie arrived safely in that state
and was raised by his relatives, but shortly after reaching his majority
he died. There is no evidence of his having become a Mason.
Olivet Lodge No. 205 at Corning had a member who demitt~d to
Western Star No. 2. His was a rather significant name. It was B. A.
Mason.
In the early mining days there was a bar on the Klamath River
called Masonic Bar and there was on file in Siskiyou County Recorder's
Office the record of a mine named "The Masonic Bar Mine.'' We have not
been able as yet to identify the owners thereof as Masons.

Your committee recently learned that The Masonic Monthly, a publication in the City of San Francisco, contained articles purporting to portray
the real history of Western Star No. 2. The articles in question were published in 1879 and are alleged to contain much source material relating to
the transactions of that Lodge from its first meeting up to and includi,ng
the year 1877. We have located a copy in an eastern library and will soon
have the information for our files. We hope these articles may throw some
light on the history of that historic Lodge from its inception and including
the year 1852. The minutes of the first two years are not now in existence.
This magazine also published a letter written by Past Grand Master Hyam
"giving some additional light" on the history of Western Star.
Brother Miles McK. Anderson, Past Master of San Mateo Lodge No.
226 and a member of this committee, has written, directed and presented
a 1fasonic play depicting the formation of the Grand Lodge of California
in 1850. One scene re-enacts the election of Benjamin D. Hyam as Grand
Master in 1852 and the special session of Grand L odge called that year
by the Deputy Grand Master to consider charges against the Grand Master. In another scene Brother Anderson gives his interpretation of the
events which transpired on the evening of June 3, 1852, when Grand Master Hyam was a visitor to California Lodge. Also the visit of the Grand
Master to Downieville on the occasion of his making Dr. C. D. Aiken a
Mason after he was rejected by Mountain Shade Lodge No. 18 is
graphically portrayed. The play ends with the defense of Hyam as contained . in his "Narrative,'' a reprint of which is included in the pamphlet
entitled "Years Past and Minutes Gone" by Brother Mark A. Sawrie.
Before this war is concluded, there will have been many thousands
of California Masons inducted into the armed forces of the United States.

277

At the last annual communication of Grand Lodge the sum of $250.00
was appropriated for the use of this committee. Our actual expenditures
only amounted to $103.38. Therefore·, in keeping with our experience this
past year and th e economy program necessitated by the present emergncy,
your committee feels that it will be ab le to adequately function with an
appropriation of $150.00.
We hereby submit the following recommendations and move their
adoption.
·
(1) That the Committee on Masonic History be continued for the
ensuing Masonic year.
(2) That the sum of $150.00 be appropriated and set aside for the use
of said committee.

REPORT OF MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT
BOARD
To .the Most Worshipfi'l Grand Lodge of California:
Your Endowment Board herewith presents its tenth annual report for
the period commencing September 23, 1941, and ending September 23, 1942:
The board is now constituted as follows:
1942

Robert B. Gaylord, Vice Chairman
Wm. P . Filmer, Treasurer
Reynold E. Blight, Secretary
An earnest effort has been made this year by your board fully to perform its duty to Grand Lodge and it reports a record of successes and
failures. We have striven to stimulate interest in, and a deeper consideration for, our two splendid homes on the part of Lodges and the membership,
and to secure voluntary contributions to the Endowment Fund.
·•
As heretofore, we have pursued the program of disseminating information to the craft through the Lodges relative to the great benevolent work
of Masonry in this jurisdiction by establishing and maintaining two adequate and useful homes, the loving parental care given our orphans at
Covina and the solicitous interest in the welfare of our elderly Masons and
women at D ecoto, the need of an Endowment Fund to protect and safeguard the homes and our guests therein, the continuing policy of Grand
Lodge to augment the principal of the Endowment Fund by voluntary
gifts until it attains adequate proportions, the opportunity offered to members of the craft to give out of their store a donation to a noble cause--a
donation that will not be ephemeral, but will continue its beneficence for
many generations of men, and to impress the membership with the present
duty of observing the great tenet of relief.
. The impact of the war with its dislocations, disturbances, uncertainties
and griefs seriously affects th e disposition and ability of many Masons to
cooperate financially in our efforts. The important task of providing an
ample War Relief Fund was commenced in the Endow:ment Fun.d . m~nth
of May and solicitations for that fund ran concurrently with our sohc1tahons
for the Endowment Fund. Many demands from many quarters have had
to be met by all patriotic and charitable men. Your board is grateful for
the success it has attained under adverse circumstances, but feels that it
has failed to carry its message to the members and to impress the officers
of more than one hundred Lodges which could not, or would not, assist in
the work assigned to us by Grand Lodge. The fault is doubtless ours, and
we confess it in all humility.

Report of Auditors

To the Endowment Fund Committee, Masonic Homes of California:
We have audited the accounts and records of the Permanent Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes of California for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1942, and present herewith the following statements:
Exhibit A: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements (other than
Luckenbach Fund, Exhibit C), for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1942.
Exhibit B: Summary statement of Endowment Fund ·assets, as at July
31, 1942.
Schedule B-1: List of regular Endowment Fund securities on hand,
acquired prior to July 31, 1941.
Schedule B-2: List of regular Endowment Fund securities on hand,
additions to fund fiscal year 1941-42.
Schedule B-3: Statement of securities redeemed and sold.
Exhibit C: Statement of John and Lena Luckenbach Fund as at July
31, 1942.
Exhibit D: Statements of Endowment Fund income and capital ac. counts.
Securities (Schedules B-1 and · B-2) : ·
All of the corporation stocks and the irrigation district bonds were
received by donation or bequest; other bonds so received are designated by
the letter "D." All donated securities are listed at market value at the time
of donation, with the exception that where the value is uncertain because
of its being an unlisted or a closely held security, then in that case a nominal
value of $1.00 is listed for the purpose of record. Insurance policies are
listed at a nominal value of $1.00 for conservative purposes.
Bonds purchased are recorded at cost. As most bonds carry a heavy
premium, an amortization schedule is provided in order to reduce to a minimum any loss to the Endowment Fund when the bonds are redeemed.
