To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During the year 1.941-42 this committee issued four quiz programs on
the subjects, (1) Masonry in California; (2) Famous Masons; (3) Masonic
Law and Custom; (4) Famous Masons Who Have Fought for the United
States. These programs were largely an experiment, to see whether the
brethren approve by use the proposed method of imparting information on
the question and answer basis. We are happy to say that, from all accounts,
the experiment proved a great success. Lodges in all parts of the grand
jurisdiction used the programs and scores of letters have been received
from Worshipful Masters expressing appreciation and commending the
venture. It would seem well to go on upon these lines and the committee
asks authorization to issue this coming year seven programs.
The committee reports progress in the preparation of a series of pamphlets designed to be used by coaches while instructing candidates in the
lectures of the three degrees. It did not seem wise to hurry the preparation
of these pamphlets, so as not to repeat the mistakes of other years. We are
gathering most valuable data from other Grand Lodges and we hope to
complete this commission during the coming year, subject to advice and
approval of the Grand Master and other Grand Lodge officers. A reprint
of the little booklet entitled Masonic Law and .Custom was had this past
year and many thousands have been sold through the Lodges. We believe
the wide dissemination of the information in this brochure is most salutary.
In these days of gas rationing and the necessary conservation of tires,
it did not seem worthwhile to issue the roster of available speakers,
authorized at the last communication of Grand Lodge. When traveling
conditions become more normal the roster will be prepared.
Of the appropriation of $500 made by Grand Lodge for the use of
this committee $415.70 has been disbursed, leaving $84.30 balance on hand.
In order to carry out the proposed program for the coming year, the committee asks Grand Lodge to appropriate $650 to cover expenses of printing,
postage and stenographer's services.
Respectfully submitted,
N. PERRY MoERDYKE,
DELEERT BERRY,
RICHARD H. CHAMBERLAIN,
GEORGE

c. JENSEN,

RUDOLPH JENNY,·
REYNOLD

E. BLIGHT,

Thursday, October 15, 1942.

presiding ..

The Grand Master then presented to the brethren assembled Brother Alexander Douglas Potts, Grand Standard Bearer
of the Grand Lodge and Inspector of the 103rd Mas_onic District, with the request that Brother Potts take such time. as he
wished to report on the situation r_ela.tive to. M_aso.nry m the
Hawaiian Islands. Brother Potts, w1thm the hm1tat10ns placed
upon him by military regulations, gave. a full and complete picture of the situation in ·all our Lodges m the Islands. A resume
of the remarks of Brother Potts is presented herewith.

REPORT ON MASONRY IN THE HAWAIIAN ISLANDS
Presented at the 93rd Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California by Alexander Douglas Potts, Grand Standard Bearer.
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren:
Yesterday afternoon when one of our Grand Masters said you had
heard from the last foreigner, he made a mistake, brethren! because I
bring the alohas from the brethren in the Hawaiian Islands. It 1s a pleasure
and a privilege for me to address you this morning. I am here only throu~h
the efforts of your Most Worshipful Grand Master ~nd our Very Worshipful Grand Secretary· and the courtesy of the Umted States that I was
privileged to visit this Grand Jurisdiction this year.
.
.
In doing so I had to make certain promises. I had to promise that if
the United Stat~s Navy brought me here,_ I would not di~~uss wi.th a?yon_e,
or with this Grand Body, anything concerning the m1.htary s1tuat10n m
the Islands that I would keep my conversation concermng Masonry only.
I made th;t promise, brethren, an~ I intend. ~o stan_d wi~h i!, so I am not
going to tell you anything concermng the m1htary s1tuat10n m the Islands.
"i hope you will not be disappointed when I say I can't tell you.
All I bring you, brethren, is a very brief messa~e concerni~g the conditions of your Lodges in the Hawaiian Area. Had 1t been yoss1ble for me
to assure your Grand Lodge that I would b~ presen~ at this Annual Co?1munication and providing censorship permitted, this report would have
been prepared previously to my leaving Honolulu.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

305

In the Hawaiian Islands we have been getting a lot of reports concerning the attitude of the people here on the Mainland, and particularly in the
West Coast Area. While I have not been with you long enough to ascertain the correctness of these reports, it would seem to me that this is true
to a great extent. No one really realizes the horrors of war until they,
themselves have witnessed the devastating effects such as we in Honolulu
did on the morning of December 7, 1941, and so I s"a y to you, brethren,
make no mistake about it. This country is at war and our institutions are
being endangered from its effects.
On the morning of December 7, 1941, at 7:55, we were viciously
attacked by a ruthless enemy and at 11 :00 a. m. the Honorable Joseph B.
Poindexter declared martial law. We then became under the control of the
military authorities and virtually all institutions, including the eight
Masonic Lodges in the Islands, were ordered closed. Our first official act
in conformity with the request of the military governor was to publish a
notice to the effect that all Masonic Lodges in the Islands would be closed
until further notice. This situation, however, could not continue and shortly
after we contacted the military governor and explained the situation to
him. He received us very courteously and explained that under martial
law and for the protection of the people of the Territory, he had asked
that no meetings of any description be held due to the threatened situation,
and while he was very much in favor of having Masonic Lodges function
in their usual manner, he felt that it was his duty to restrict the number
in attendance at such meetings and then only should such meetings be held
after permission had been obtained from him, which he would grant provided the military situation permitted.
We were confronted with the situation of electing new officers and
holding installations for the ensuing Masonic year: Due to the fact that
we could not hold meetings in the evenings, it made it necessary for us
to secure Special Dispensation from our Grand Master for a change in the
hour. All Lodges in the Islands changed their by-laws so that they now
meet at 4 :30 p. m. instead of 7 :30. This change was necessary due to the
fact that we were not only subjected to total black-out, but also civilians
had to be off the streets by 7 :00 p. m. Hence the mere fact of blacking
out the temple would not solve the problem which confronted us. As time
went on, we found it very difficult to hold these meetings as scheduled,
due to the fact that many of the officers of the Lodges were either called
into the Service or employed on defense projects which necessitated their
securing permission to be absent from their jobs on days that meetings
were called. This same condition affected the candidates and on many
occasions we found it necessary to postpone meetings that had already
been scheduled, due to the fact that we were unable to obtain a full quorum
of officers, and on many occasions when we did secure the officers necessary
to exemplify the degrees, we found the candidates could not be located.
This situation became very discouraging and some of the Lodges felt that
we should discontinue accepting applications. This, of course, could not be
done and it had . to be made quite clear to those officers who were either
in the Service or on defense projects that it would be necessary for us to
elect new officers and fill the vacancies. This was done in a number of
cases, as we were determined to carry on, regardless of the effects that
disaster had brought upon us.
Strange as it may seem, new applications became very numerous, and
as a striking example of this, we are now confronted with one of our
Lodges, namely Pearl Harbor No. 1598, having on hand at the present time
sufficient applications to keep that Lodge working continually .one day

306

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

each week for the next two years before it can handle all of the applicants
that have been elected. This situation is also true concerning Lodge
le Progres de l'Oceanie No. 371, which has at the present time 38 new
applications on hand, in additfon to 20 firsts and seconds they are working on.
As a striking example of the effects of the war on this particular
Lodge, I might say that at the outbreak of hostilities, the Junior Warden
was an officer in the United States Navy. Immediately after the disaster,
the Senior Warden left the Territory and joined the British Navy; the
Worshipful Master, being a Reserve Officer in the United States Army,
was immediately called into service and the Senior Deacon, who is a
captain in the Army, was likewise called into service. For a time the
situation looked very discouraging. However, through the kind cooperation
which was and is being granted us by the military authorities, the Worshipful Master was permitted to continue with his Masonic activities in
addition to his military duties there. This, of course, made it necessary
for us to secure Special Dispensation to hold an election and installation
of officers. This was accomplished during the middle of the year and it
was felt at that time that the Lodge would then be able to function
properly during the remainder of the Masonic year. Since my arrival in
San Francisco, however, I have just learned that both the Worshipful
Master and the newly elected and installed Junior Warden have been
called to active duty elsewhere and we are now confronted with another
problem .which will necessitate the coaching and installing of new officers.
While the officer situation may seem to be a problem, it is not quite
as bad as the condition which confronts us relati~e to the coaching of
candidates. We find it. very difficult to be able to contact many of these
candidates who are in the armed forces and only able to secure liberty on
occasional days during the month. Hence it has made it very difficult for
us to carry on in a normal manner.
Immediately following the disaster, we were confronted with an
unu~ual number of requests for courtesy degrees. These have proved very
burdensome to the Lodges, not only due to the manner in which the
address of the candidate is furnished us, but due to the fact that practically
all of them are defense workers who have been sent to the Islands on a
one year's contract and are now endeavoring to get the degrees of Masonry
while in the Hawaiian Islands. While it has always been a great pleasure
to the Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands to conform to these requests, we
found it necessary to present the situation to your Grand Master and
asked him to explain the conditions under which we were operating here
in the Islands and that it was practically impossible for these Lodges to
even take care of their own candidates without being burdened by courtesy
degrees. This situation, of course, is not true in the ~utlying Islands, but
the fact is that the most of the courtesy degrees are all centered in and
around Honolulu.
Since the disaster of December 7, we have had other problems,
especially coming to us from the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, these
requests being furnished to us in a manner which makes it practically
impossible for us to give the service we should, due to the addresses of
these visiting . brethren and due to the military restrictions prohibi.ting
civilians from entering military posts, we have been unable to cooperate
with them to the fullest extent. The mere fact that these requests continue
to be sent -to us, immediately leads us to believe that many of these Grand
Jurisdictions have not the slightest idea of the conditions under which we
are op.erating. To date we have received 187 such requests, _most of them

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

307

stating that Brother Jones, a member of a certain Lodge in this. Grand
Jurisdiction, has a son or a cousin, either in the Army or the Navy,
stationed somewhere in the Hawaiian Islands and they would deeply
appreciate it if we would make immediate contact with him and so advise
his Lodge. The mere fact that such requests come to us daily is very
evident that these jurisdictions have never lived under or witnessed the
effects of martial law. We merely give these examples so that you will
have some idea as to the uselessness of making such requests.
From time to time many apparently foolish requests are being made
of us by a number of these Lodge officers, which are being made in all
sincerity and with a full knowledge of our Masonic law in California and
we are inclined to believe that they are making these requests at the' sug. gestion of a number · of sojourning Masons from other jurisdictions. For
example, requests will be made for permission to initiate and pass more
than five candidates in one day, give part of the degree one day and the
lecture the next, waive coaching of candidates, make Masons on sight,
hold meetings on Sunday and conduct meetings without the presence of
either a Master or Warden', only a Past Master being present. We have
ruled that this cannot be done, and war or no war, Masonry must carry
on without any deviation from our ancient rules and custom.
While we are having our difficulties there in the Islands, we feel that
we cannot praise the military and the naval authorities too highly for the
splendid cooperation and assistance that they have given our fraternity.
They have expressed their desire to cooperate with us in every way
possible in order that we may continue our Lodge meetings and other
Masonic activity in as normal a manner as possible. We also feel that a
great deal of credit should be given to the National Sojourners, whose
officers of the three chapters now in the Hawaiian Islands have stepped
forward and volunteered to assist us in any way they possibly can. ·It is
our intention to maintain close cooperation and friendship with these
organizations and work with them in every way possible in order that
this conflict may be brought to an end as quickly as possible and we feel
that this will be accomplished in the not too far distant future.
War Relief
I might say we haven't done just as well as we would like to in the
Hawaiian Islands. Some of our Lodges have made a success; others have
not. But I think these Lodges who have not done much in the War
Relief have gone over the top in the Masonic Homes. But it is going
over. Last year, when I visited Canada I was surprised to find that they
already had a war relief fund such as we have here. In the Province of
Alberta they have a little over ten thousand Masons and in the year 1941
these ten thousand Masons in the Province of Alberta raised $50,000.00
and sent it to the Grand Lodge of England. It makes me a little ashamed,
brethren, in this wonderful jurisdiction, with 126,000 Masons and we
have not raised over $80,000.00." We have lost sight of the priviiege given
us to serve these brethren who are now serving us in the front line of
defense and this war isn't going to last very long either, and it is our duty
to support them when that time comes. Sometimes you ask why we are
carrying on as we are in the Hawaiian Islands. I will tell you: The thing
we love dearest is Masonry. Why, take some of these men in some of our
Lodges, and I mention Pearl Harbor Lodge in particular, where the
officers and especially the Master, sacrifices one day of his time each week
that he can devote it to Masonry. He loses $15.00 every week, one day's
pay, in order that he may continue the activities of P earl Harbor Lodge.

Yet some of us feel it a burden if we are asked to pay one dollar to the
War Relief Fund. Just think that over and see what that one Master has
done for Masonry. They are taking their Masonry seriously, because the
thing they loved most was just about taken away from them. Sometimes
I think we can appreciate things only when they are taken away from us.
These brothers in Pearl Harbor on December 7 saw their brethren killed.
Yes brothers fighting waist deep in the waters of Pearl Harbor, stained by
the blood of their brothers, fighting for their brothers, for something they
held dear-liberty and freedom. And they, brethren, are fighting today as
they did on December 7, not only on the ocean and in the Army. They are
fighting in the Lodges, fighting for truth and justice, that ·you and every
Mason in California may go on enjoying the liberties which you hold· so
dear.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TWENTY -THIRD
ANNUAL OBSERVANCE OF PUBLIC
SCHOOLS WEEK
To the M ost W orshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
During the week commencing Monday, April 27, 1942, California had
sugar rationing, air-raid warnings, "black-outs," first aid classes, and
courses in the training of air-raid wardens, auxiliary police and auxiliary
firemen; together with rain, measles and chickenpox and (in at least one
community) a campaign of vaccination and immunization. It was also
Public Schools Week; and its twenty-third annual observance was an
extraordinarily good one-not merely relatively speaking, having in mind
the condition which seemed to militate against its success-but considered
by itself. There were several reports with such comment as "best ever,"
"auditorium entirely too small for the crowd," "program best in years"
and "our schools never had so many visitors." As indicative of the situation throughout the state generally, we quote· from two newspaper clippings
-one attached to the report from a Lodge in one of the smaller communities, and the other accompanying the report of an observance in a
very large city.
"Aside from the general excellence of the program material, it appears
that the Twenty-third Observance of California's Public Schools Week
must be judged to have had a more general participation than any such
observance in the county in recent years."
"Despite the growing pressure of war-time duties upon all of us,
despite the swing"over of American energy from peacetime functions and
enterprises to the urgent business of war, Public Schools Week was
observed with even greater than normal attention and appreciation this
year."

It seems incredible that there were those who believed that because
of the difficulties that would be encountered we should not attempt to
hold an observance this year. Fortunately our Grand Master was not of
their number; and it was largely due to his wise counsel that there was
no interruption in any of the activities which reflect credit upon Masonry
in California. He realized that if a more just and orderly world is · to
emerge from the terrible conflict now being waged, it will be because our
schools will have instilled in t.h e minds and consciences of our youth the
passion for justice and knowledge that will bring that world into existence ;
and he pointed out to the timid souls that in continuing to give their public
schools that support which is now especially needed, the Craft would
rededicate themselves to the high principles and purposes of our government.
As indicative of the response which must have been exceedingly
gratifying to the Grand Master, we quote from a communication received
by our committee from five of our Island Lodges giving an entirely
unnecessary explanation of why they felt it would be inadvisable to attempt
to promote an observance in Honolulu this year:
"Our schools are now operating under very tryi~g circumstances ;
some having been taken over for purposes for which they can well be used
in connection with our defense program. Some are working on a part time

310

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

schedule and in others two different school organizations are using the
same b~ilding. Furthermore, under martial law which prevails in the
Territory large gatherings are prohibited, motor traffic is forbidden after
7 :30 and ~ll pedestriarts must be off the streets before 9 p. m."
This communication was personally s.i gned by each of the five Masters;
and it was a fine and very greatly appreciated, gesture from our brethren
in the only place 'in the jurisdiction where the observance of Public Schools
vVeek this year could not be reasonably expected.
Viewed in its entirety, our latest observance was not greatly different
from those of preceding years, and no less successfol. Such differences as
there were consisted of changes in the form of the observance. in certain
communities made necessary by war-time regulations and restrictions. For
the most part, however, the change made was the adoption of a type of
program which had long prevailed elsewhere. And curi~usly enough, there
were many instances reported where the change met with such favor that
the program provided as only a temporary substitute made ·necessary by
the conditions will probably be continued as a permanent feature of the
observance.
As illustrative of what occurred in more than one instance, mention
may be made of a community which until this year had observed Pub.lie
Schools Week by evening programs in the auditoriums of the schools with
exhibits of school work displayed in the halls, and where practically no
attention had been given to encouraging visits to !he schools during school
hours. This year the school buildings in that community were closed at
.night; and unable to observe the week in the customary manner, the committee according to the report from the Lodge, "worked out a program
by wh,ich certain schools held 'open house' from 8:30 in the morning until
3 :30 in the afternoon with gratifying results. Visitors crowded the school
rooms and were glad to avail themselves of this opportunity to see teaching
in its practical aspect ... Everyone was so pleased with the 'open house'
idea that we will probably continue to make use of it."

In passing it should be noted that what is termed the "open house"
program is suscep'tible of many variations. In some instances it consists
of little, if anything, more than an entertainment in the school auditorium
with perfunctory visits to some of the classrooms either before or after
the presentation of t.h e program in the auditorium; and in this connection
we believe it will be well worth while to quote, in its entirety, an extremely
interesting description of a program arranged by a school principal, and
which was attached to a report from one of our Lodges:
"For s'o me time we have felt that our Open House was not
. functioning in the manner we had hoped it would. True, it did
provide us with an opportunity to 'dress up' and 'show off' and it
did succeed in bringing large numbers of mothers and fathers to
the building. But merely dressing ~P and bringing. parents to the
building we feel is insufficient for the consummation of our purpose
in holding open house at all.
"To be functional open house should allow the parents to visit
the school at a normal time--to see the school operation in a normal, natural manner, observing the children at work in a situation
where they themselves feel ··at home.' Observing the printing of a
newspaper is much more effective than visiting when the presses
are not 'in action.'

"We have, therefore, adopted a different plan for our open house
this year. We are replacing one large formal open house night with
a series of room teas sponsored jointly by the children and the
teacher on the one hand, and the room mother, chairman of room
mothers and chairman of education of the Parent Teacher Association on the other. This joint sponsorship assists .us in reaching all
of the parents in a given room and 'insures a wider interest than
would be the case were we to plan the tea alone.
"The teacher plans a brief but normal unrehearsed demonstration of regular work for a period of about one-half hour. The last
one-half hour of the day is chosen. The children are then dismissed and a group conference on the evaluation of the work is
held. General discussion may follow and finally tea is served by
the room mothers. These ladies also arrange to care for the
children whose mothers are at the demonstration. These demonstrations will, of course, vary in kind and technique, but each will
be a part of the normal, natural day. They will occur throughout
the entire building one or more times in each room, the parents
being specifically and particularly invited each time. Dates will be
selected that will bring in as many fathers as possible. We shall
plan to schedule dates in order to avoid conflicts in the use of the
tea facilities.

the tremendous effort involved in open house. We will give parents a much better opportunity to meet and know the teacher.''

This year there were, of course, the usual exhibits of school work;
but everywhere, and especially in the larger school systems, emphasis was
on the war effort being made in the schools. This was particularly noticeable in the . displays in the show windows made available by the large stores.
In one city there was an exhibit of work being done in the courses which have
been introduced into the schools to prepare students for military service;
and in another there were several window displays depicting various phases
of the national defense or war effort. There was also one entitled "All
Fronts Ready," showing a Red Cross nurse, R. 0. T. C. cadet, and a welder
at work And in a third city, in an invitation issued by the superintendent
of schools to the public, particular attention was called to the courses in
air mechanics, acetylene welding, arc welding and burning, and air craft
fabrication; and to the air craft motor school and radio school. Apparently
everywhere, even where no special courses had been intro.duced, particular
stress was laid on regular classroom work in mathematics, science,
English, history and foreign languages; as well as on physical education
and the work of the 'vocational shops.
The custom of holding what may be termed "pre-week" gatherings
to stimulate interest in the observance is growing. For many years the
officers of three Masonic Lodges in one of our cities have entertained the
superintendent of schools and the principals together with the mayor and
the members of the Board of Education· at a dinner held the week before
the opening of Public Schools Week At this meeting there are "pep"
talks and each of the principals outlines the school's program. This year,
among other gatherings of a similar nature, there was an entertainment
given in its Lodge room by a Lodge which has thirty-six of its members
engaged in the educational work of the community.
· Fine publicity was obtained for the observance in one of the smaller
communities by a poster contest in which a prize was given for the poster
which best depicted in spirit and handwork "The Real Purpose of Public
Schools Week" There were also three groups of prizes (for the senior
high school, junior high school and elementary school pupils') for the best
essays on these three subjects: "I Own a Part of America," "What the
School Can Do to Help National Defense" and "How an American Girl
or Boy Can Help Win the War."
It will be perhaps remembered that in these reports to Grand Lodge,
and in bulletins sent to the Lodges, it has been repeatedly, and as forcefully
as possible, pointed out to Masters and committees arranging programs
that the aims and purposes of Public Schools Week could be best effectuated through visits to the schools; but apparently it took the war with

about general acceptance of the idea. Never before were visits to the
schools the dominant feat_µre of so many local observances. And never

This reference to spelling warrants mention here of a school-wide
informal testing program at a Union High School conducted in advisory
groups. It showed that spelling, while not mastered by all students, is not,
as some people insist, the forgotten child of the school curriculum. The
five tests of 20 words each were selected from Buckingham Extension of
Ayre's Spelling Scale. The group average on the test varied from 85%
to 95% with a school average of 91 %. Of 2086 papers submitted 963 were
perfect. Two-thirds of the papers showed not more than one error. Three
papers were submitted in which none of the words was correctly spelledbut this doesn't prove that "the fundamentals are being neglected" and
that "the children can't spell the simplest words.''

There were many pupil programs in the way of entertainment which
either through tableaux or playlets stressed patriotism and loyalty. The
theme of a very ambitious one centered on the relation between our
country and Latin America. I\ stemmed from the work of the Spanish
classes in the high school and was developed in cooperation with other
interested persons in the community to emphasize the importance of PanAmerican relations. Approximately 100 students participated in a pageant
which depicted an imaginary tour through Mexico, Panama, Peru, Chile,
Argentina, Brazil and Cuba. With characteristic music, a narrator introduced the representatives of these countries, all garbed in authentic costumes, and who presented the flags of their respective nations; and then
representatives of the United States presented a musical review of America.
An especially noteworthy event was what was termed a "Victory
Program" presented in the auditorium of a high school and which was
dedicated to three former students of the school who had lost their lives
in the war, and to other students. who are now in the service of their
country.
A bit of unconscious humor (or perhaps it may hav~ been satire)

and the singing of the Star Spangled Banner; and in the footnote there

No less extraordinary than the number of visitors to the schools, was
the amount of newspaper and radio publicity received. Just as in spite of

found time to learn by a personal visit just what the schools are doing,
so apparently did the broadcasting stations and the newspapers, in spite
of the war-time demands upon them, find-or make-time and space to
very generously and lavishly publicize the observance. Among the clippings attached to a report was a column under the head "Citizenship in

The development of such knowledges, skills and loyalty has
always been a constant first concern in our schools. The current
emergency has only served to quicken an interest which has always
motivated the work of our teachers and administrators . . . .

The schools offer students on all levels many opportunities
to practice being a good citizen. A goo~ citizen respects our laws,
public property, the rights and personalities of other people,
cooperates for the general welfare, abides by majority decisions,
respects the minority, keeps informed, is a good leader when
selected, is a good follower . . . .
Older students practice these virtues in class work, home
room duties, student government, and club activities. Our schools
are a true picture of democracy in action. . . .
Finally, it is not enough that education in the present emergency should revolve around our country alone. After victory we
and our children face the necessity of creating a lasting world
peace. Our schools are contributing toward this job. Students
study world history and world problems. They study the ways in
which the people of the various countries live, the way in which
they can help u·s , and we can help them. . . .
The courageous study .by students of today of the world
problems that will have to be solved should aid the solutions of
tomorrow.
This has b een a critical year- but no less so will be those in the
immediate future. Special effort is now being made in our public schools
to train our youth to meet the demands war has laid upon them. But with
peace will come other demands and duties and responsibilities; for these,
too, our young people must be trained.
Our first and ever present thought must be concerned with the winning of the war. But no matter how decisive may be the victory, the war
will not have been won unless it results in the kind of peace for which we
fought that other war-"a peace that will keep the future safe against
war." That peace was lost because we were not willing to join in a concert of power to enforce it. In the words of Woodrow Wilson "the free

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M:. W:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Control is pleased to submit the following report of
the activities coming under its supervision during the past Masonic year.
In doing so it desires first to express to the Grand Master, also the Gran'd
Secretary and his assistants its appreciation for the information and assistance given to the board.
It is the belief of the board that all justified relief has been freely
extended.
.
The Board of Control further feels that notwithstanding the scarcity
of labor at the present time, that in this period of great stress and uncertainty as to future conditions, great pillars of Masonic strength are vested
in our Boards of Relief and Employment Services; that they represent
organized power, which when needed and called upon will be ready in
key positions to immediately serve to the utmost in every capacity required,
to benefit the Masonic fraternity; that their need will be greater in the
future than in the past.
The complete harmony and cooperation between the Board of Control
and the Boards of Relief and individual Lodges continues to be conducive
of gratifying resu Its.
'
The personnel of our Boards of Relief and Employment Servic~s
are entitled to our sincere commendation.
The continued progress and success of our Bo;i.rds of Relief and
Employment Service will be indicated by the following report.
Meetings
·The board held one meeting on January 31, 1942, in Los Angeles. It
had several conferences by mail during the year and a special meeting
with secretaries of Boards of Relief and managers of Employment Bureaus,
October 13, 1942 (during Grand Lodge).
Members of the Board of Control also attended annual Board of Relie.f
and Employment Bureau breakfasts at Long Beach, San Diego, Los
Angeles, Fresno, Sacramento, and Oakland.
Reimbursements
We have recommended to the Finance Committee that the following
requests for reimbursements be granted:
San Francisco ........................................................................ ;.............$19.00
Los Angeles .................................................................................... ,... 35.00
Total ..............................................................................................$54.00
This amount of $54.00 represents the entire reimbursement asked of
the Grand Lodge after all Boards of Relief have finished an entire year
of service in helping our sojourning brethren and their dependents in the
usual manner.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

319

Special ·Reimbursements
Case No. 1:
The Grand Lodge is requested to make reimbursement to the San
Francisco Board of Relief of $850.00, which is purely an advancement
made to the wife of a member of the Grand Lodge of Scotland. A very
large part of this amount has already been deposited by her husband with
the Grand Lodge of Scotland. The Grand Lodge of Scotland has authorized
us to continue the advancement of funds, which is being done at the rate
of $50.00 per month.
The Board of Control has approved of this reimbursement and the
Finance Committee will favorably report same to Grand Lodge.
The Board of Control now asks for approval by the Grand Lodge of
the continuation of further advancement of $50.00 per month, subject to
the discretion of the San Francisco Board of Relief.
The Finance Committee and also the chairman of the Policy and
General Purposes Committee concur with the Board of Control in referring
this matter to th~ Grand Lodge for action.
Case No. 2:
Reimbursement is asked by the Los Angeles Board of Relief for a
net amount of $416.40, which has been recommended by the Board of
Control and approved by. the Finance Committee. This money was advanced after careful .consideration and consultation with Brother Lawrence
Benton, Past Master, Manila Lodge No. 1, and advancement was approved
by correspondence with Manila Lodge No. 1, of the Philippine Islands,
and by Roy C. Bryan, representative of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge
of the Philippine Islands. This case is closed.
The Board of Control and the Finance Committee believe that the
above two amounts, namely $850.00 and $416.40, should be set up on the
Grand Lodge books as amounts due the Grand Lodge.
Employment Service
A year ago, we reported that "the upswing in many lines of business
and industry occasioned by the preparedness program has had great influence in reducing unemployment." That was written before December 7,
1941. What occurred on that day, with the resultant declaration of war,
has rea,lly had great influence in further redudng unemployment.
Notwithstanding this fact, our seven employment services received
24,681 applications from our unemployed brethren and dependents, which
was a slight increase over the previous year. There were 17,541 jobs
secured, and we could have filled many more jobs if we had qualified applicants available. Reports show there was an increase of 4.4 per cent in the
number of permanent jobs secured over the previous year.
One bureau found jobs for 2714 applicants between the ages of 40-50;
and also found jobs for 1366 of 50 years and over.
Employers' requests for help reached an all-time high, 30,303 as compared to 24,194 in 1941 and 14,836 in 1940.
The expense for the year was $33,376.77, of which Grand Lodge
appropriated $18,800.00, or 56.3 per cent. The a;verage cost per job was
$1.90, and had our brethren secured these jobs through private fee-charging
agencies, they would have paid out more than $300,000.00.

REPORT OF CONSTITUTION MONTH
OBSERVANCE COMMITTEE
T 0 the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Calif ornia:
Your Committee on Constitution Month Observance _rep?rts in confirmation of oral reports presented at the current communicat10n: . .
This committee has two functions: ( 1) the observan_c~ ?f Constitution
Month in September, and (2) the promotion of war acttv1t1es on the part
of California Masonry.
These functions will be segregated in this report.
A t the outset we wish to express appreciation. to the members of the
speakers panel to Lodge committees and to others who have so ge~erously
and effective!; contributed to the prosecution of the wo~k. ?f this committee. A single speakers panel has been used for _all acttv1ttes; response
has been prompt and satisfactory whenever assistance was requested
from the panel.

' 33,l

This committee originally was appointed in 1940 by Grand Master
Whitsell for the purpose of fostering the observance by Lodges of
"Constitution Day." The period of observance was extended to the entire
month of September due to the impracticability of use of a specific concurrent day by all Lodges. The work of the committee to date of the 1941
Communication is embodied in the report presented at that communication.
On December 7, 1941, there occurred the attack on Pearl Harbor
with the subsequen~ declaration of war. ·
Following the tragedy of Pearl Harbor and the declaration of war,
Grand Master Smith advised this committee that in his judgment proper
action should be taken to foster war activities on the part of the membership of the Lodges in this jurisdiction and delegated to this committee
the responsibility for that effort.
On January 11, 1942, a meeting was held at San Francisco for the
consideration of this extended activity of the committee. There were in
attendance at this meeting the Grand Master and the Deputy Grand
Master; also the General Chairman, Vice Chairmen and other members of
the committee, together with Brother James B. Blum, Secretary of the
Oakland Scottish Rite bodies. Brother Blum originated a suggestion for
Masonic war activities contemplating primarily activity on the part of the
Scottish Rite bodies in this vicinity. As a result of that suggestion, active
work on the part of this Grand Lodge was initiated.
The <:;rand Master, on February 10, 1942, issued a proclamation to
the Masons of this jurisdiction calling upon them to play their part in
war activities and authorizing this committee to promote that movement.
This order is embodied in his own report.
Blacl~-outs, dim-outs and Army regulations have restricted the attendance at meetings. Necessarily these regulations have also interfered with
joint meetings, both public and closed. However, we feel that the brethren
of this jurisdiction have creditably acquitted themselves in this emergency.
The report of the committee is segregated as to its concurrent duties.
War Activities
Pursuant to the proclamation of the Grand Master, this committee,
on February 10, 1942, issued a letter to the brethren of the jurisdiction
embodying suggestions for the effectuation of the purposes of the order
of the Grand Master. A copy of that letter is attached to this report as
Exhibit A.
It was the desire of the Grand Master tha.t the initial meetings in all
Lodges be tiled: Subsequent meetings were open to the public in a desire
to promote war activities on the part of the general citizenship of Caliornia. Although a speakers panel was maintained, the Lodges were
requested· to use local speakers so far as practical.
On March 17, 1942, the committee issued a further letter to the
brethren. This letter speaks for itself and is attached to this report as
Exhibit B.
On May 25, 1942, a third letter was issued by the committee and
which also speaks ·for itself and is attached to this report as Exhibit C.
Accompanying this letter was a copy of the regulations issued under
authority of the War Department r egulating public meetings. It is unnecessary to embody these regulations in the report; their cohtents are well
known and for the present their purpose has been served.

Statistics
By reason of the nature of the activities, the presentation of detailed
statistics is impractical. The only definite statistical details available cover
purchase of bonds by the Lodges themselves. They do not even include
individual purchases which may have been inspired by Lodge activities,
· nor do they cover other war activities which were inspired or accelerated
by the work which has been done un der the proclamation of the Grand
Master as conducted by this committee. Merely by way of illustration,
we suggest the following:
a. One Lodge reported that prior to the May letter issued by this
committee 30 per cent of its members had contributed to the Blood Bank.
b. Another Lodge reported that members of the Lodge familiar with
the various war activities, including those suggested by this committee,
directed the attention of Lodge membership to the respective activities
and addressed the Lodge at regular intervals upon the various lines of
work to be accomplished.
c. Another Lodge arranged for presentation of the work by duly
qualified speakers at each stated meeting.
d. In an.o ther Lodge a check at a meeting held as early as June
showed that 100 per cent of those present were engaged in some form of
war work and that practically all of the items listed in the committee's
letter were represented in the work of the membership.
e. In another Lodge one of the members was a postoffice employee
who brought stamps and defense bonds to the Lodge. He made sales in
the ante room resulting in defense stamp sales of approximately $175 and
· defense bonds aggregating some $5000. This Lodge has a membership
of 220.
f. In another Lodge dinners were held at which the brethren in
attendance paid 25c each toward the expense but received in return a 25c
defense stamp.
g. As early as May 1st the children at the Covina Home from their
· own small savings purchased $4375 in bonds and stamps.
· h. A report from the superintendent of the Covina Home shows in
detail a very substantial number of Covina boys who are in active service,
all of whom have acquitted themselves creditably, and most of whom are
. commissioned officers.
i. A recent report from Honolulu shows that the island Lodges have
purchased $55,300 of defense bonds and are "still going strong."
It is interesting to note that the most encouraging reports have come
from relatively small Lodges. Whether this is due to closer contact among
the brethren or because of greater . activity where a smaller membership
· is involved is a question as to which differences of opinion doubtless wo1,1ld
exist.
·
Reports have been requested as to the purchase of war bonds. 'As
above stated, these reports necessarily are limited to purchases by Lodges
themselves and do not include purchases by individual members which
have been inspired by Lodge meetings or Lodge committees. From these
reports we furnish the following compilation :
One hundred forty-five lodges report holdings of war bonds on January 1, 1942, amounting to $513,095.50.
Fifty Lodges have made no report whatever. This indicates either a
lack of interest on .the part of the Lodges or such ineffectiveness on the
part of the officers .that no attempt has been made to render a report of
any kind.

Constitution Month

In war or in peace, the first privilege and function of citizenship is
to vote. In the letter of May 25, 1942, we mentioned the fact that in 1896
80 per cent of the qualified electorate voted for a President of the United
States, and that this shrank progressively during a period of less than
thirty years to 49 per cent. Later statistics were not then available. At
primary and special elections the percentage is far below these figures.
We are fortunate if 25 per cent of the electors vote at the primary; The
voters at the primary determine the candidates for office and the selection
of candidates too frequently is decided by a minority vote with the result
that less than 25 per cent of the qualified electors determine the officers
who shall exercise governmental powers. Masonry is not a political institution, but Masonry is an institution designed to perpetuate individual liberty
and the exercise by the man on the street of the functions of government.
It was hoped by the committee that it would be possible to promote
among the Masons of California a plan whereby they and those whom they
might be able to influence would participate in the electoral franchise to
the extent of voting at the last primary election in this state. It is the
belief of this committee that if this plan had been promulgated, some of
the candidates for office in California in whom a large number of Masons
believe, would have been elected at the primary instead of being compelled
to go through a second campaign at the general election. This does not
involve the endorsement of any candidate or political activity on the part
of any Lodge other than to urge that every American citizen exercise his
electoral franchise for whomsoever or whatsoever he may choose to vote.
Your committee was requested to refrain from a specific attempt to
increase the vote at the primary and therefore refrained from that effort.
However, we rcommend to our successor members on this committee that
well in advance of every primary election the electorate represented by or
who can be influenced by the Masons of California be urged to participate
in every primary election and that similar efforts be made in connection
with general elections.
In several instances it has been suggested that a constitutional talk
wholly divorced from Masonry may be presented in our public schools in
the same manner as that in which Public Schools meetings are conducted.
These suggestions deserve consideration by subsequent committees.
Present-day conditions necessarily result in limited attendance and
fewer meetings. This situation emphasizes the importance of an active
committee in each Lodge composed of men who will take their responsibilities seriously and who will .reach the members of the Lodge. ·
We do not list any ' Lodge in the jurisdiction for either praise or
blame, nor do we list any Lodge which has failed to definitely participate
in war activities or which has lacked even the interest to present the
requested reports. We give full credit to those Lodges and their officers
whose patriotism has inspired results for our country in the greatest war
in its history and which represents a crisis in world civilization. Those
Lodges and those officers who have failed to participate are aware of the
fact without the listing of names in this report; it is not for this committee
to pass judgment upon them.
This report is largely historical and statistical, but your committee
feels that the subject is of sufficient importance to make the matters above
recited a part of the permanent record of Grand Lodge.
Notwithstanding the other war activities of Grand Lodge, including
War Relief and Masonic Service, and particularly in view of the duty of

this committee to endeavor through Grand Lodge membership to perpetuate the principles, duties and privileges which are exemplified in the
Constitution of the United States, we believe that this committee is a
useful instrumentality of Grand Lodge. The expense of its work is small.
We therefore recommend:
·
1. That this committee be continued for the coming year and thereafter subject to discontinuance by order of Grand Lodge, and
2. That a reasonable appropriation, either in the discretion of the
Grand Master or as determined by Grand Lodge, be made for the work
of the committee during the coming .Grand Lodge year.

EXHIBIT A
February 10, 1942.

To the Masters of the Several Lodges of This J11risdiction:
Worshipful Brethren:
We are at war!
The Grand Master has issued a proclamation calling upon our Lodges
to actively promote the various movements which are necessary to the
prosecution of the present war. From his proclamation, it will be seen that
he is interested not only in the demands which are made upon us at this
time, but also in the preservation of normal American morale, both during
the war, as well as during the critical period, which will follow the termination of the war. He has delegated to the Constitution Month Committee
of Grand Lodge the responsibility for informing the Lodges of his desires
and aspirations in this connection. The following categorically details the
general purpose of the Grand Master. This letter is issued with his
approval, and for all purposes is to be deemed authoritative concurrently
with the proclamation which he has issued to the Lodges.
1. The only spec'ific general patriotic observance by the Masons of
California heretofore has been Constitution Month in September. The
Grand Master's proclamation voices the sentiment of the jurisdiction that
we cannot delay for months in bringing to our brethren the importance of
the crisis which confronts us, and the traditional part which Masons may
play in meeting that crisis.
2. Each Master receives two copies of the proclamation and two
copies of this communication. One copy is intended for the use of the
Lodge. The other copy should be delivered for information and instruction
to the speaker at your Lodge meeting.
3. It is the order of the Grand Master that a closed meeting of the
Lodge for the presentation of this subject matter be held at once-preferably at the March stated meeting.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF. CALIFORNIA

4. The proclamation calls attention to the fact that this meeting is
· of sufficient importance to justify, and in fact to require, the issuance of a
special notice to each member of the Lodge for the purpose of obtaining
adequate attendance.
5. Each Master is required to appoint a committee to promote patriotic
activities on the part of each Lodge collectively and its members as individuals, to act throughout the duration of the war. Appoint a committee
which means business and which will discharge its responsibility. There
will be future meetings and expanding efforts on the part of California
Masonry.
6. Each Lodge is expected to obtain its own speaker. There is no
Lodge in this jurisdiction which does not have upon its rolls a member
who is competent and willing to present so yital a suggestion. Each Lodge
is expected to consider the matter as a separate unit in the same manner
that any other important business of the particular Lodge is given personal
attention at a stated meeting. Because Constitution Month is designed to
ultimately com_m and the attention of communities in general, this committee advocated the holding of joint meetings open to the public. The
present situation is one in which we must as individual Lodges and individual Masons put our shoulders to the wheel to protect our institutions
and our freedom. This committee has a panel of speakers mainly confined
to the larger centers of population. If necessary, recourse may be had to
that panel. If such necessity arises, apply to the Grand Secretary, Masonic
Temple, San Francisco, or to the various members of the committee in
their respective localities, at the addresses appearing upon this letterhead.
In connection with the observance of Constitution Month, several
typical addresses were prepared for reference by local speakers, or, if
necessary, for presentation verbatim at a Lodge meeting. The scope of
the present subject is so broad and the approach so varied that it is
impractical to prepare typical addresses. Therefore, this letter will merely
suggest the points to be covered and indicate sources of reference if the
· speaker is not already informed. The speaker, however, should bear in
mind that at the conclusion of his remarks an opportunity will be afforded
for questions by the membership, and he should be fully informed as to
details of the various war activities so that he may intelligently answer
these questions even though he does not cover details in his own remarks.
Do not fail to furnish each speaker with a copy of the Grand Master's
proclamation and this letter.
Information may be obtained as follows:
(a) Defense bonds and war savings stamps; at any postoffice or bank.
(b) Civilian defense; consult the local. Defense Committee. The defense
plans vary so much throughout the state that any general detailed presentation is impractical; conform to loca'l usage. The Attorney-General has a
suggested form for a local ordinance covering this subject, but it has not
been universally followed. Pamphlet No. 1 has been issued by the State
Council of Defense upon the general subject matter of Civilian Defense.
For copies of the ordinance form, write the Attorney-General of California,
addressed to his office at State Building, Civic Center, San Francisco,
California. Pamphlet No. I is instructive; for copies write State Council
·of Defense, Sacramento, California.
(c) Army and Navy recruiting; consult the nearest Recruiting Office.
(d) Red Cross; consult the Red Cross Committee.
( e) First Aid; consult local agencies or the Red Cross.
7. Lodges are not permitted to subscribe funds handled by other
organizations such as the Red Cross, however worthy they may be. How-

ever, ~odges may invest their funds., whether life membership, or other
funds, tn defense bonds and war savings stamps.
8. :t-lo solicitations for bond purchases, contributions, or other purposes, shall be made in the Lodges. It is the function of the Lodge to
promote interest and urge participation in all war activities, but the Grand
Master's proclamation prohibits direct .solicitation as such. lt is a function
of the Lodge committee, however, to a.dopt such means as suggest themselves, either through communications to the members, or otherwise, for
the purpose of inspiring the members to discharge the duty which rests
upon them at this time as American citizens.
9. All of the foregoing matters should be emphasized by each speaker,
but in addition to the emphasis upon these movements and a general appeal
for preservation of our institutions and liberties, it is urged by the Grand
Master and this committee as his representative that special emphasis be
placed upon:
(a) The maintenance of public morale. The events at Pearl Harbor
and the inadequate supply of war equipment, with the prospects of war
taxes and restrictions upon civilian use of various commodities, tend to
create an atmosphere of depression. We must learn the lesson which
England learned in the early days of the war-that we must face the
future with courage and determination.
.
(b) Anticipate the maintenance of morale following the close of the
war. When the battle is over and victory is won, the fruits of victory
must be carried through the years so that we may reap the full harvest
of institutions and freedom which have been adequately defended and
which must . be passed unimpaired as a heritage to the generations which
succeed our own.
Masons have ever upheld the banners of truth and Justice and liberty.
In what is perhaps the most critical period of human history, we must not
fail. If we cannot worthily maintain the traditions of those who have gone
before and play an outstanding part and take an advance position in maintaining national freedom and individual liberty, we may as well close the
Lodge in fear and trembling at the distant prospect of a conquering tyrant.
If we do not rise to the full stature of manhood and Masonry, our high
sounding phrases within the Lodge are no more than sounding brass and .
tinkling cymbal.

EXHIBIT B
To the Masters of This Jurisdiction :
Worshipful Brethren:

March 17, 1942.

Reports indicate that all Lodges in the jurisdiction desire to use every
effort to promote the defense work which the Grand Master has delegated
to Constitution Month Committee, and many of them seek suggestions as
to the most efficient procedure.
The following quotations are taken from a letter forwarded by the
Master of Indian Rock Lodge of Berkeley. They afford food for thought,
and the Grand Master feels that they are of sufficient value to justify
authority to our committee to distribute this letter among the Lodges.
We commend the extracts to the Master and the committee of each
Lodge, and suggest that this letter be read to the Lodge at" a convenient
time when a substantial membership is in attendance. It will also be of
valu.e to speakers who present defense activities to the Lodge from time
to time.
.
"As you will notice from the enclosed report, we had an official
attendance of fifty-two of our members and also a handful of visit~
ing brethren whom we were glad to have present. Our Lodge's
membership at the present time is one hundred and twenty-five.
. "Our defense program has barely been launched, but it is the
wish of the members that we hold such a meeting at least once a
month, and it is my hope that I will be able to do so. I analyzed
the letter from the Constitutional Observance Committee and tried
to buil~ mine around the plan therein stated. Brother John McKee,
P . M., 1s my chairman, and chose "Morale" as his particular field.
It is putting it mildly when I say that he jarred everyone present
out of his complacency and sent him home thinking.
"I am fortunate enough to have one of the city's leading doctors for a member. He was more than glad to accept a place and
handle .all Red Cross and First Aid work. His talk was probably
the high-light of the evening. In addition to these two brethren
I have appointed a man who is well-known among us in civi~
affairs, to handle civilian defense. A newspaper man who is the
local head of a national organization, and one brother who has
campaigned throughout the East Bay on Defense Bonds and
Stamps, make up the rest of the committee.
"On the day following the meeting my chairman telephoned
me and informed me that the committee had been working all
afternoon on one activity which was mentioned by the doctor. He
laid particular stress at the time on the desperate need for blood
donors to our blood bank. His taik left a tremendous impression.
A number of the brethren already have taken this matter to heart
personally in a short few days. Brother McKee is so enthusiastic
ov.er this ~ne particular angle that he has asked me to write you
this letter in the hope that you will accept it in · the spirit in which
it is offered. We have no desire to tell our Grand Master or Grand
Lodge how ~at~ers should be done, yet we feel that you will acceptour suggestion m the same way that our Lodge accepted it from ·
our doctor. We did not know how desperately our help is needed
or how important it is. Realizing this now, and also how relative!;
small our group is, we see the vast possibilities of presenting this
matter to every Mason in California. If they could only see the

need and benefit that would derive from their donations of blood
to the blood bank, we feel sure they would make deposits as soon
and as often as physically possible. If our fraternity were to do
only this one thing, we feel that our war effort would be very, very
worth while."
The Grand Master confirms the understanding of the committee that
it is not mandatory that meetings for defense purposes be closed, although
he hopes that the initial meeting will be closed. In the discretion of the
Lodges, subsequent meetings may be open to the families of mem~ers
or to the general public. If open meetings are held, care should be exercised
that their scope falls within the lines defined in the proclamation and the
original committee letter; that there be no violation of the laws of our
institution, either as to the taking of subscriptions at the meeting, concurrent entertainment, or other interference with the dignity of the occasion ;
and (to quote the language of the Grand Master) "no compulsion shall be
allowed on anyone." The Grand Master also feels that no discussion shall
be permitted at any meeting, whether public or private, except as it is
constructive and not critical.
Fraternally yours,
ROBERT B. GAYLORD,
General Chairman.

EXHIBIT C
May 25, 1942.
To the Masters, Officers and Brethren of This Jurisdiction:
The results among the Lodges under the proclamation of the .Grand
Master covering war activities has been gratifying,. but our effort must
not relax until peace has been declared. It is impossible to present an
adequate statistical report other than the number of Lodge meetings which
have been held and the results in purchase of war securities.
More than two-thirds of the Lodges have reported at least one meeting. We urge that the remaining Lodges forward a report of meetings
which have been held or are held in the immediate future. The attendance
has been excellent.
At the last tabulation of reports of war bonds and war stamps purchases, returns ·were made by 402 Lodges, showing purchases since January
1, 1942, aggregating $499,110.70. This represents purchases by Lodges
themselves, and does not include purchases by members or purchases
which were inspired by Lodge activities. Prior to January 1, 1942, 324
Lodges held no government bonds other than war bonds. Two hundred
twenty-four Lodges held no government securities .Prior to January 1,
1942. One hundred fifty-seven Lodges have failed to make a report regarding bond purchases. One hundred eighty Lodges have failed to make a
report regarding the amount of bonds purchased since January 1, 1942.
The reported holdings of war securities prior to January 1, 1942, is
$489,120. Therefore, since the prosecution of this work through the Lodges
in the jurisdiction, the holdings of war securities have more than doubled.
General MacArthur is quoted as stating that during the siege of
Bataan the defense troops each assigned one month's pay for the purchase
of war securities.
From their pennies the children at the Covina Home purchased, prior
to May 1, 1942, $4,375.00 in defense bonds.
Instances such as these should inspire us to renewed efforts to sustain
our country during the war.

The committee is informed that some of the Lodges hesitate to invest
in war bonds because of possible insecurity of the investment. This fear
is sufficiently answered by stating that 50 per cent of the entire issue of
government securities is held by the commercial and savings banks of the
country and that these investments represent probably 40 per cent of the
entire assets of the banks. If government bonds are insecure, it is difficult
to conceive of any investment which under these circumstances possesses
a value.

Constitution Month-September
The efforts which Grand Lodge is promoting under the head of war
activities interfere in no way with the observance of Constitution Month.
All current efforts are designed to promote th e prosecution of the war.
The observance of Constitution Month is designed to foster .the perpetuation of hum~n liberty and individual action which are a heritage through

342

PROCEEDI.NGS OF THE

_the centuries from the sacrifice, the str~ggles and the blood of those who
have gone before and which are defined, at least in part, in the Constitution
of the United States and in its Bill of Rights. Some hundred years ago
Lord Tennyson said:
"For I dipt into the future, far as human eye could see,
Saw the Vision of the world, and all the wonder that would be;
Saw the heavens fill with commerce, argosies of magic sails,
Pilots of the purple twilight, dropping down with costly bales;
Heard the heavens fill with shouting, and there rain'd a ghastly dew
From the nations' airy navies grappling in the central blue;
Far along the world-wide whisper of the south-wind rushing warm,
With the standards of the peoples plunging thro' the thunder-storm;
Till the war-drum throbb'd. no longer, and the battle-flags were furl 'd
In the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world."
Since the days of Lord Tennyson the heavens have been filled with
corpmerce, there have fallen from them the ghastly dew created by grappling navies, and we have seen the plunge of standards through the thunder
storm ; sooner or later the war drums will throb no longer and the battle
flags will be furled. When that time arrives, inevitably we must face a
new alignment of nations and a probable reconstruction of A~erican
society. We hope and believe that in that realignment of nations our
country will play a dominant part. \Vhether, however, there be victory or
defeat, the restoration of the constitutional relationships in our own land
as we have known them through the years rests with us. The necessities
of war disturb the normal conduct of our society and it is for free men
to firmly determine that when the war is over individual American freedom .s hall be restored to its pristine character. To that principle Masonry
is consecrated and for its accomplishment we must strive. Constitution
Month is dedicated not to war, but to peace ; it is dedicated to the constitutional freedom of the individual.
It is not too early to prepare plans for the proper observance of
Con~titution Month. It is hoped that so far as practical arrangements will
be made for a public meeting at which an appropriate address will be made
by a competent speaker. The details of his remarks are in his discretion
provided he emphasizes the value and the perpetuation of the principle~
of the Constitution of the United States.
Nor is it too early to emphasize to our citizens the value of the
electoral franchise. Recent statistics are not immediately available, but
we find that in 1896 80 per cent of the qualified electorate voted for a
President of the United States.· In 1900 this percentage shrank to 73 per
cent; in 1908 to 66 per cent, and in 1924 it fell to 49 per cent. At primary
elections and special proceedings for bonds or similar issues, the percentage
is far below these figures. We are fortunate if 25 per cent of the electors
vote at a primary election. The voters at the primary election determine
the candidates for office, · and the selection among the candidates for office
is too frequently decided by a minority vote. The net result of such a
situation is that less than 25 per cent of the electors of the country determine the officers who shall exercise governmental powers. · It is a far cry
from this situation to the pioneers of the Declaration of Independence and
the War of 1776. If our citizens line themselves as consistently for the
exercise of the election franchise as they take their place for a sugar ration,
there need be no fear for the future of our land or for the perpetuation
of American institutions.

EXHIBIT D
August 24, 1942.
To the Masters; Inspectors, Speakers Panel, and Brethren
of This Jurisdiction :
Constitution Month Observance
September is Constitution Month in this jurisdiction. Advance notice
was issued in May. In the interests of economy this letter is addressed
to and will be received by Masters, Inspectors and Speakers Panel instead
of separate communications, and it is hoped that each addressee will regard
this as a personal communication.
Lodges already have received several commu·nications upon the subject
of war activities. As previously suggested, Constitution Month is definitely
distinct from meetings to promote war activities. When the war is over
we face a period of reconstruction more vital than the problems of the
Sixties and more difficult of solution. War necessarily involves autocratic
powers, but even if a successful war be waged that success is valueless
if it fails to preserve and perpetuate for ourselves as well as for the world
at large the institutions which are declared in the Constitution of the
United States. Constitution Month is devoted not to war activities but to
that human liberty and right of individual initiative which is our heritage
from centuries of sacrifice and blood-the priceless heritage of freedomthat we shall have government by law and not of men.
Without repetition, we request that each brother to whom this letter
is addressed re-read that portion of the May letter..which refers to Constitution Month.
·
Meetings-We repeat prior suggestions that so far as possible meetings be public, conforming to similar custom for Public Schools Week.
It is the purpose of September meetings to promote' general conception
of and regard for the privileges of Americ;an citizenship. In May, copies
of existing regulations for public meetings were f6rwarded to all Lodges.

State .Election-There will be an election in this state in November.
The normal apathy in voting occurs on the part of the better class of

be no activity for any Constitution Month Committee more important
than promoting an attendance for five minutes at the polls on the part of
every member whose name appears upon the roster.

REPORT OF THE FINANCE COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipfitl Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Finance begs leave to submit the following
report :
Audit of Accounts
Your committee has again employed Brother Floyd F. Webb of the
firm of Ruckstell, Burrows and Webb, certified public accountants, to
examine the books and records of the Grand Treasurer, the Gran i Secretary, the Masonic Homes of California and the Endowment Fund. The
reports of Brother Webb's examination of these records have been filed
with your . committee and have had its consideration. These reports are
now on file with the records of Grand Lodge and will be published in the
annual proceedings in the report of the Grand Secretary. They indicate
that all records are correct and in proper shape and all receipts properly
accounted. for and all expenditures properly made.
Your committee is again mindful of the debt it owes Brother Webb
for the personal interest he has shown in making the various audits because
of his membership in the fraternity and his interest is more than usual in
this work. He has given the fraternity an unusual service for the fee
allowed.
The total amount paid for the audit this year is $700.00, of which sum
the Homes has paid $550.00 and the balance of $150.00 has been paid out
of Grand Lodge funds.
.
This committee wishes to refer to the comment of the auditors on
the first page of the report, in which mention is made that "The total of
the expenses and appropriations exceedeq the revenue by $3,781.27," and
particularly to the second part of this comment which fully accounts for
this excess; that the item, "Loaned to Carpinteria Lodge No. 444-$2500.00," is not an expense but actually a capital investment and that this
particular item, while paid out of the current year, yet was an actual allowance made the previous year and therefore not properly chargeable to the
present year; and further, the item of Federal Unemployment Taxes for
other years, $522.17, is an item that has been in controversy between
Grand Lodge and the Federal Government for some time and adjusted
during the current·year and, therefore, is another item not properl;v <:harge-

Your Committee on Finance has analyzed the relJorts of the Trustees

The funds furnished by Grand Lodge for the maintenance of the

students attending these universities that cannot be measured by dollar

Committe~ on Correspondence
It has been the practice of this Grand Lodge for most of its existence
to have a Committee on Correspondence, the duties of the committee being
the reviewing of the proceedings of other Grand Lodges throughout the
world and making a resume of the important activities and happenings in
such jurisdictions and reporting the same to Grand Lodge, which report
has. always been printed in the annual proceedings .
For this purpose this committee for a number of years has appropriated $500.00, covering the expenses of compiling this report.
This past year, under the chairmanship of Worshipful Brother Henry
Clauson, this reviewing was partialed out among the membership of the
committee and all the reviewing and compiling was done without expense
to Grand Lodge. For this work and compiling, and it is very considerable
and without expense to this Grand Lodge, the Committee on Finance
wishes to express its gratitude.
This committee is of the opinion that the reviewing of annual proceedings is a valuable work and should be encouraged. After all. whatever
Masonry is doing, wherever it may exist, is something in which we are
all interested. Such information is made available through the good work
of the Committee on Correspondence. The report of this committee should
have much more consideration than is ordinarily given it. We commend to
all, and particularly to the Masters of Lodges, the reading of the report
compiled by this Committee on Correspondence.
Your Committee on Finance believes that an appropriation not to
exceed $500.00 should be made available for the use of this committee,
providing it is needed, and therefore offer the following resolution · and
recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $500,00, or as muclf thereof as may be
required, be appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge for the
purpose of defraying the expenses of a Committee on Correspondence,
said bills to be paid in the usual manner on approval of the Committee
on Accounts.

Adopted.

Report of Grand Treasurer
Your Committee on Finance has reviewed with care the repor.t of the
Most Worshipful William P . Filmer, Grand Treasurer. The report fully
sets forth the financial condition of Grand 'Lodge, of the Endowment Fund
and of the various Trust Funds, including a list of securities held and of
securities bought and sold during the year, as well as all financial transactions. The report again indicates the great care given and the efficiency
displayed by our Grand Treasurer in handling. the financial affairs of
Grand Lodge. The responsibility which the Grand Treasurer has is very
great. The praise and appreciation of this committee is unbounded for
the work which this worthy officer is performing for Grand Lodge.
As has· already been reported on the Audit of Accounts, all items
of receipts and disbursements have been properly accounted for and all
records are in perfect shape.
Last year this committee called attention to the difficulties under
which our Grand Treasurer had performed his duties for a large share
of that year. His duties this year have been performed under even more
trying circumstances, in that the illness which struck him down in March
of that. year has pursued him for this entire year.
Time .after time it seemed that Brother Filmer was well on the road
to recovery, but somehow unkind fate seemed to follow him and again
and again he suffered a setback. His courage and fortitude have been
remarkable indeed. Again we express the fervent hopes, not only of this
committee, but of the entire fraternity of the State of California, that this
time there will be no setback and that time will not be long delayed when
he will again be with us.
His duties this year have necessarily been p'e rformed at home and
altogether too frequently when Brother Filmer was in bed, yet at no time
and in no way have the duties of his office been neglected.
We know the entire fraternity joins with this committee in expressing
thanks to the Omnipotent that we still have the firm hand of our Most
Worshipful Brother Filmer, Grand Treasurer, at the helm of the finances
of Grand Lodge.
Traveling Expenses of Grand Master
Your committee has discussed with the incoming Grand Master his
plans for the year and particularly as to the extent of his visitations. This

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

354

committee has been greatly impressed with the understanding which the
new Grand Master has of the responsibilities before him and of his hopo
to travel extensively and meet the craft in every part of the jurisdic·
tion, and thus be better able to judge the needs throughout the entire
jurisdiction.
It is obvious that our incoming Grand Master is assuming his respon·
sibilities with great earnestness and with a sincere devotion to duty and
with a determination that, not only will gains which have been made this
past year be fully maintained, but additional advancements made.
Due to many conditions which cannot now be determined, such as
the amount of travel that may be permitted by the Federal Government,
the means of travel, the continued increased cost thereof and emergencies
that are almost sure to arise, but cannot now be foreseen, it is equally
impossible for the incoming Grand Master, or this committ~e, to deter·
mine, even approximately, the amount the Grand Master may require
for his traveling expenses.
This committee has previously gone on record, and remains of the
same opinion., that extensive visitations by the Grand Master are both
desirable and helpful and that the craft as a whole derives more benefit
from the money expended in this way than from nearly any other source.
We are also of the opinion that the Grand Master should have
returned to him all expenses he is out in attending to his duties as Grand
Master. The committee therefore wishes to go on record that if the
amount appropriated for the purpose of paying these expenses is not
found sufficient, the Grand Master should not circumscribe his activities,
and that whatever amount he finds necessary should be paid to him out
of the treasury of Grand Lodge. The committee, however, is setting up
the same amount as last year, that is, the sum of $4,500.00, and therefore
offers the following resolution and recotnmends its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $4,500.00 be appropriated from the funds
of Grand Lodge for the purpose of defraying the traveling expenses of
the Grand Master.

Adopted.
