Reimbursement of Expenses of Inspectors
Up to two years ago it had been the policy of this Grand Lodge that
~he expe?ses of_ the Inspectors, in performing their various duties in visiting and mspectmg Lodges within their district, should be returned by the
Lodges. For t~e _past two years, however, this policy has been changed
and an appropriation has been made by this committee of $3 000 each year
for . the purp~se. of r eimbursing the Inspectors for the expe~ses incurred.
This appropriation was made to cover the amount that would be required
should a_ll the Inspectors ask for the return of the reasonable expenses
actually incurred.

It is to be noted, and with great satisfaction, that · while this money
has been made available for these expenses, only a small portion of it has
been asked for. This important body of Masonic workers are performing
a real service for Masonry and could, in complete propriety, ask for the
retu,rn cif expenses and yet, a large share of the work is being done for
the pure joy of the services rendered and without the willingness to accept
any return for any money out. This is the spirit that makes Masonry
what it is. This 'Grand Jurisdiction is indeed fortunate to have such a
body of faithful workers.
While it is the wish of this committee that all expenses incurred by
Inspectors should be reimbursed, and it is recognized that should all ask
for the amount to which they are justly entitled, it would require at least
$3 ,000 and yet, as less than one-third of this amount has ever been asked
for and as it is the ·belief of the committee that the actual expenses that
will be asked for should be set up as nearly as possible, it is making an
appropriation of $2,000 and setting this amount up in the budget. However,
the committee wishes it understood that should an additional amount be
required it will approve the payment thereof. It, therefore, offers the
following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $2,000.00 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lodge for the purpose of defraying expenses of Inspectors in performing their official duties, such repayment to be made upon bills duly
presemed to the Grand Secretary, which said bills shall first be approved
by the Grand Lecturer.

Adopted.
Carpinteria Lodge
Last year this committee recommended the approval of a loan to' the
above Lodge in the sum of $2,500.00, for the· purpose of rehabilitating
damage done by an earthquake and also to enable the Lodge to refinance
a previous loan in a much reduced amount. At the time it was hoped by
the Lodge and by this committee that a sufficient sum could be borrowed
so that the old loan could be not only entirely refinanced, but the amount
advanced by Grand Lodge could be returned. The understanding was that
the Lodge was to borrow $5,000.00 for the purpose of refinancing an old
loan of $12,000.00, $7,000.00 being allowed as a discount for immediate
pajrnent, and an additional sum of $2,500.00 or, in all, a total of $7,500.00
for the repayment to Grand Lodge.
Negotiations finally resulted in \he Lodge being able to borrow only
$4,000.00, which was accepted by the previous lender in full for the
$12,000.00 obligation. This $4,000.00 loan is returnable at $75.00 monthly,
which included both principle and interest, at the rate of five per cent
per annum. These payments are being made regularly and approximately
$500.00 has been repaid.
The hope of the brethren in Carpinteria to secure additional rent
from the building has not been realized and because of this the Lodge has
not found it possible to repay any part of the $2,500.00 loan to Grand
Lodge.
To show its good faith the Lodge has increased its dues from $9.00
· to $12.00 and is carrying along in a full Masonic way and taking care
of all its running expenses and necessary charity.
It expresses a wish to repay the advance by Grand Lodge in full as
soon as possible and will secure a further loan for this purpose whenever
it can be done. The attitude of the brethren is commendable.

REPORTS OF THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND
GENERAL PURPOSES
I

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes herewith submits
its reports and recommendations with respect to the various matters contained in the annual message of the Grand Master and the resolutions
introduced into the Grand Lodge which have been referred to it by Grand
Lodge for consideration.
Grand Secretary's Staff
The Grand Master directed the attention of Grand Lodge to the necessity of increasing the staff in the Grand Secretary's office in order to
efficiently and promptly handle the necessary work for this Grand Jurisdiction and recommended that the matter of the increased staff be given
consideration. Your committee is of the opinion that the office of the
Grand Secretary should be efficiently administered and to that end that he
should have such clerical and accounting assistance as may be required to
promptly, efficiently and accurately perform the important duties of his
office and approves the recommendation of the Grand Master.

Adopted.
San Francisco Office
The Grand Master during the past year assumed the responsibility
for ordering needed additional equipment for the office of the Grand Secretary in San Francisco and asks that Grand Lodge approve his action.
Your committee is of the opinion that the office of the Grand Secretary
should be furnished and equipped in a manner creditable to this Grand
Lodge. It not only is a place for the transaction of a vast volume of business and administrative detail but it is the resort during the year of many
Masons of this and other jurisdictions. Its physical equipment and general
atmosphere should comport with the dignity of this Grand Lodge. Additions to the improvements already made could and should be made to make

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the office conform to these requirements. Your ·committee therefore recommends that the action of the Grand Master in this matter be approved.

by the secretaries of the subordinate Lodges to the Grand Secretary be
required and that the matter be referred to the Committee on ] urisprudence,
to report at the next annual communication.

362

Adopted.
Building Committee
The Grand Master recommended that no Lodge in the jurisdiction be
given permission to erect, remodel or repair any temple unless the project
be satisfactorily financed and he expressed his opinion that the committee
be enlarged and given specific power and authority. Your committee has
given . consideration to the recommendations of the Grand Master and
finds that Grand Lodge, by Ordinance 78, provided for a special committee
consisting of three members on financing building projects, but did not
prescribe the duties or authority of the committee. The committee was
brought into existence by reason of unfortunate and inadvisable financial
ventures entered upon by some of the subordinate Lodges which, in the
course of time, brought disgrace upon the Lodge and more or kss odium
on Masonry. In order to guard against the recurrence of such misfortunes,
the committee was set up so that plans for the expenditure of money for
a building by a Lodge might have a disinterested and fraternal examination of an outside, protecting influence. The work of the committee has
been salutary and it has approved many projects which were sound and
disapproved those few that were palpably unsound. Because of the vast
extent of the territorial jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, it appears wise
to increase the committee so that different sections of the state may be
represented in its membership, and the attention to building projects be
closer and less burdensome. Your committee is further of the opinion
that the duties and powers of the committee should be expressly defined in
such manner as to yield the greatest assistance to the Lodge undertaking
a project and to give a full protection . to this Grand Lodge and Masonry
against future criticism which may arise from the defaults or omissions
of a Lodge which has assumed unfortunate obligations. That said committee should not approve of building projects and their financing, but
shou Id consent to or disapprove the same. Your committee recommends
that Section 78 of the Ordinances be amended by providing a Building
Committee of five members of which the Grand Treasurer would be
ex-officio a member and chairman, the chairman of the Finance Committee
a member ex-officio and three members appointed by the Grand Master
and that this report be adopted and the subject matter referred to the
Committee on Jurisprudence for the formulation and presentation of an
appropriate amendment to the · Ordinances of Grand Lodge.

Adopted.
Reports to · Grand Lodge
The Grand Secretary has directed the attention of Grand Lodge to
delays which occur in the office of the Grand Secretary respectin~ degrees
conferred, dimits granted, affiliates elected, Master Masons raised, and
deaths. The returns are received once a year and must be collated so
that the records are from twelve to fifteen months in arrears. To correct
the situation and to secure accuracy, the Grand Secretary recommended
that a Monthly Membership Return be required of the Lodges and asked
for permission to try out the plan during the present fiscal year. Your
committee is in full accord with the recommendation of the Grand Secretary but is of the opinion that' the law should be amended to require
monthly returns. If the need exists, there is no reason for a trial period.
Your committee therefore recommends that Monthly Membership Returns

Territory of Hawaii
The Grand Lecturer made certain recommendations with regard to
the Inspectoral District of Hawaii and the prompt dispatch of the business
of this Grand Lodge in that Territory during these adverse war conditions.
Your committee is of the opinion that the subject matter should not be
disposed of at this communication but the same should be carried over as
unfinished business to the next Annual Communication of this Grand
Lodge and so recommends.
Masonic War Service Committee
The excellent and inspiring report of the War Service Committee has
been referred to this committee. We find much to applaud and nothing to
alter in the report and therefore have no recommendations with respect
thereto.
Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands
The report of Brother Roy C. Ryan, representative of the Grand
Lodge of the Philippine Islands near the Grand Lodge of California has
been referred to your committee and it appears therefrom and also from
the message of the Grand Master that the Grand Lodge of California,
under proper conditions and restrictions, is receiving dues from members
of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands and issuing certificates
showing such receipt and . is impounding and holding for the credit and
subject to the order of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine Islands, all
monies paid in by members of the subordinate Lodges of that Grand
] urisdiction. · Your committee is of the opinion that the service of this
Grand Lodge to a sister Grand Lodge, which has ceased to exist by reason
of political and military oppression, is timely and meritorious and, therefore, we recommend· that the courtesy and trusteeship instituted by the
Grand Master and the Grand Secretary on behalf of this Grand Lodge be
approved and continued.

Adopted.
History Committee
Your committee is informed of the valuable and extensive work which
has been done and is being done by the History Committee and recommends that such committee be continued.

Adopted.
U. S. Merchant Marine
RESOLUTION
1W hereas, it is the present policy and custom of the Grand Lodge of Masons
in the jurisdiction of California to acquire certain data relative to members
of constituent Lodges within this jurisdiction when such members enter
the Armed Forces of the United States of America and to reward such
entrants with a certain certificate acknowledging said entrant's membership
in such constituent Lodge, and
Whereas, such "Armed Forces of the United States of America" are designated by the Government of the United States as members· of the "Army,"
"Navy" and " Marine Corps," and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

364

Whereas, there is in existence and employed by the Government of the
United States a branch of maritime service known as the United States
Merchant Marine, which service includes the transport of war supplies
and materials, and
Whereas, such ships and their crews are subject to all the exigencies and
dangers of war if, and when, intercepted by enemy vessels or submarines,
and
Whereas, the Grand Lodge of the jurisdiction of California has not included Masons employed as members of the United States Merchant
Marine as the recipients of the same courtesy and favor as is bestowed
upon Masons in the aforesaid "Armed ·Forces of the United States of
America/'
Be it resolved, that, at the communication of the Grand Lodge of the
jurisdiction of California held October 13-17, A. L . 5942, in the city of
San Francisco, California, it is and shall be declared the purpose of said
Grand Lodge of California to include in its category of Masons employed
in the Armed F orces of the United States any and all such Masons in
good standing as are now, or hereafter may be, employed in the service of
the United States Merchant Marine, provided such Mason has joined the
United States Merchant Marine since December 7, 1941, and
Be it further resolved, that the Grand Secretary shall be so informed and
instructed to issue to such mei:nbers of the United States Merchant Marine
all and every emolument as is now, or is to be, issued to members of the
Armed Forces of the United States.
The r esolution has been introduced by Brother Benjamin J. Moss,
Past Master of Ionic Lodge No. 520, proposing that the members of the
U . S. Merchant Marine shall be included in the category of Masons employed in the Armed Forces of the United States and be recipients of the
same courtesies· and favors as are bestowed by this Grand Lo.dge upon
Masons in the Armed Forces of the United States. Your committee is of
the opinion that the members of the U. S. Merchant Marine are rendering
a patriotic service of a hazardous nature and are fully entitled to the
suggested consideration and therefore recommends th at in connection with
our War R elief activities that they be classed with the Armed Forces.

Adopted.

"Section 12. The Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand
Wardens, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, and Grand Lecturer

The Grand Master at the 92nd Annual Communication recommended
the enactment of legislation which would give a committee of Grand Lodge
"general supervision over the financing of new temples, the refinancing of
old temples, and the financing of remodeling and construction wherever
such operations assume major proportions" and the same having been
referred to this committee it has had our consideration. A similar recommendation has been made by the Grand Master at this communication
and referred to this committee.
Such a committee has functioned for a number of years with wholly
beneficial results; the work of the committee has not only had a restraining
influence where such was needed, but the aid of the committee in working
out plans in financing has been of no little assistance to some of out
Lodges.
By Section 78 of the Ordinances such a committee consisting of two
ex-officio members and a third member appointed by the Grand Master
annually was created but its powers and duties have never · been specified;
the reference to the committee in Section 152 is a limitation on the use of
Lodge funds and not a grant of general powers. This condition should
be remedied.

as here set forth
Section 298. At the end of this section the following words be added,
"by mail." The last line of this section reads as follows: "It shall be leit
. at the residence or usual place of business of such brother (by mail) ."
Section 308. In the fourth sentence of this section starting with the
words: "or it shall be left at his ordinary residence or place of business

recommended that in as much as there were other sections which
would be affected, the matter be postponed until the next annual
communication, at which time it would be taken up as a matter
of unfinished business and the recommendation wa~ adopted.

MORNING SESSION
Friday, October 16, 1942.
Grand Lodge was called on at 10 :00 a. m., the Grand Master
presiding.
At the invitation of the Grand Master, Past Grand Master
Samuel E. Burke invoked the blessing of God.
The Minutes of the sessions of Thursday were read and
approved.
By unanimous consent of Grand Lodge the Grand Lecturer,
Very Worshipful Chester H. Warlow, was permitted to present
a matter relative to an action on Thursday. The Grand Lecturer requested that Grand Lodge reconsider its action in classifying $6(X).00 appropriated to the Grand Lecturer as expense
and reclassify it as salary. Past Grand Master Crites, chairman
of the Finance Committee, made the motion transferring that
item from expense to salary and leaving the item of $200.00
for the Grand Tiler and $100.00 for the Grand Organist as
expenses, for which they would not be required to submit itemized statements, and the motion, duly seconded, was unanimously
carried.
To conform with the action on Thursday on the recommendation of the Committee 011 Policy and General Purposes recommending that the Grand Secretary attend the Conference of
Grand Secretaries, the Finance Committee recommended an
appropriation of .$500.00 to cover the expenses, the same to be
paid from the miscellaneous item of the budget, and the motion,
duly ·seconded, was carried.

The annual election of officers was held, with the. following result:
The R.". W.". Leslie E. Wood, Provide~t Lodge No. 609,
wa:s elected Grand Master.
The R.~. W.". Claude H. Morrison, San Diego Lodge No.
35, was elected Deputy Grand Master.
The R.". W.". Gilbert C. DeForest, Reading Lodge No. 254,
was elected Senior Grand Warden.
The W.". Lawrence C. Kelley, Pentalpha Lodge No. 202,
was elected Junior Grand \Varden.
The M.". W.". William P. Filmer, Past Grand Master, King
Solomon's Lodge No. 260, was re-elected Grand Treasurer.
The M.". W.". Lloyd E. Wilson, Past Grand Master, Ingleside Lodge No. 630, was re-elected Grand Secretary.
The V.". W.". Chester H. Warlow, Fresno Lodge No. 247,
was re-elected Grand Lecturer.

He also announced the appointment of Chas. M. Wollenberg
to be a member of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes

The M.". W.". Dana R. vVeller, Past Grand Master, was
appointed Master of Ceremonies and the officers elected and
appointed were installed by the retiring Grand Master in due
and ancient form.
The newly-installed Grand Master then invested his predecessor with a Past Grand Master's lapel button, in which was
set a beautiful diamond.
The Chas. Albert Adams insignia was transferred from the
retiring to the incumbent Grand Master and the other chair
officers exchanged the Arthur S. Crites lapel pins.
The V. ·. W. ·. Grand Secretary invested the retiring Grand
Master with the apron of a Past Grand Master.
Past Grand Master John Stewart Ross, on behalf of Grand
Lodge, presented to the retiring Grand Master a beautiful silver
tray and silver coffee urn, which he was instructed to present
to Mrs. Smith.
George H. Raddy, the Master of Tehama Lodge No. 3, on
behalf of the members of that Lodge, presented the newly installed Grand Master with a handsome and useful leather travelmg case.
Inspector Alexander Douglas Potts in a beautiful ceremony
presented, on behalf of the Lodges of the Hawaiian Islands,
a gorgeous silk lei to each of the following: M.". W.". Leslie E.
Wood, Grand Master; M.". W.". Frank M. Smith, Past Grand
Master, and M.". W.". Lloyd E. Wilson, Past Grand Master
and Grand Secretary.
At 2 :10 p. m., all business being completed, Grand Lodge
was closed fn Ample Form.

Grand Secretary.

Most Worshipful William Parker Filmer, Past Grand Master,
and Grand Treasurer since October 17, 1913, died at his home in
San Francisco Sunday afternoon, November 22_, 1942. Funeral
services were conducted by M. W. Leslie E. Wood, Grand Master,
on Tuesday afternoon, November 24, 1942, Grand Lodge being
opened in special communication. M. W. Francis W. Keesling,
P. G. M., was appointed by the Grand Master to fill the vacancy
in office thus created.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most W~rshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In this, our first report, your committee first pays tribute to Brother
Jesse M. Whited. During his long, faithful and successful career as
chairman of · t.he Committee on Correspondence, he ·has earned the warm
affection and unusual admiration of th-e Masonic-speaking world. Would
that we were as gifted as he in reporting the top stories and singling out
reviews for special comment.
As we approached our task it seemed as though . we heard the sound
of a startling note. Contemporary reviewers spoke with alarm of the
growing tendency toward minimizing the importance of correspondence
reports. The cause may have been uninteresting selections or dull methods
of presentation. In any event, we were faced with the question : Why
correspondence reports?
·
The answer is bound up, literally, in the some hundred volumes received
annually in the office of our Grand Secretary. Each represents the activities of a sister jurisdiction comparable to that of California. Every Blue
Lodge and Grand Lodge officer and committee member should direct a
most searching interest into these reflections of things Masonic-what
Masonry is doing throughout the nation and the world. It would be impossible for each brother to study all these volumes.
Convinced, therefore, that a correspondence report. can be of great
value and interest, your committee inaugurated several innovations. Each
member was an active participant. From our. several compilations we
have stripped that which was considered superfluous and concentrated on
culling the best from each Grand Master's Message, each Grand Oration,
each Grand Lodge activity. We present, therefore, what is intended as a
time saving guide or index to the current Masonic thought.
You may be interested in what we found to be the synthesis of that
thought in this time of war. It could be summarized in a question. How
can we sit in our Lodge rooms and talk of universal brotherly love when
the men of this world are killing each other in the greatest human slaughter
of history?
·
The answer though is quickly found in the realization that this is also
Masonry's war. The enemy would destroy our existence would force a
rejection of that which we may call our divine insight: 'that man is of
equal cosmic importance. There is nothing soft about our idea of the
universal brotherhood of man. It is worth working for , worth fighting
for, worth dying for. On that central war theme do our Masonic Grand
Jurisdictions unite in saying: "The die is cast; there shall be no .regrets."
Respectfully submitted,
HENRY

c. CLAUSEN,

OSCAR OLSON,
FREDERICK 0. EATON,
FRANK HOBERG,

PERTINENT PASSAGES FROM THE MOUTHS
OF GRAND MASTERS
Washington, 1941
A year ago I said to you, and I say to you again today, that I have no
program of legislative reform, and no changes to suggest in the standard
· work. That is neither because I regard either the code or the standard work
as perfect, but because it has seemed to me that we have too often spent the
all too short· period of our annual communication hotly debating the
minutiae and detail of Masonry to the neglect of matters of greater concern.
For example, we could spend a day debating whether some change should
be made in the code which would make available as material forty or fifty
men not now eligible to petition for the degrees, when our time might much
better be employed in trying to solve the problem of why more than 10,000
brothers, who have petitioned for the degrees and received 'them, haven't
found enough of interest in what Masonry has to give them to attend Lodge
at .any time during the past year. That is to me a much more emergent
problem, ·and it isn't going to be solved by legislation, but rather by giving
to our Masonry the vitality and the power that influences the lives and
character of men.
New Mexico, 1941
He worships God in the fashion of his choice. He belongs to such
fraternal orders of his choice with the privilege of thinking, speaking as his
conscience dictates.
He has his troubles, but his principal struggle should be to preserve
this Nation, with its priceless privile'ges. He is a most fortunate man-he
is an American.
We as Masons should weigh these statements and determine the full
value of all of them.
Each Masonic Lodge is a cross section of the best there is in its
respective jurisdiction. In each Lodge I have visited in the several jurisdictions, as well as our own, similar keen visaged brethren look down upon
us with apparent satisfaction. In each Lodge, workmen, my brethren, do
their share and· the similarity is again striking. Our landmarks make them
thus. · Our laws, rules and regulations, coupled with that resulting 'harmony
and good fellowship garnered from nature's own garden reveals that
priceless untrammeled reward of "this friendship of his fellowmen." Let
us preserve that great heritage that cost our forebears so many hardships
that we may enjoy a better life. Our Masonic temples are naught if
Masonry is not at work within.
Nevada, 1941
The fate of the Fraternity in Spain, Italy and Gennany, where the Craft

440

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

has been ruthlessly proscribed and its members impri~oned, and in some
cases murdered, gives rise to the thought that Freemasonry may not survive
the storm of unrest that is agitating the world today.
Masonry will survive as long as democracy survives. If ever democracy
is banished from the world then the death knell of Masonrv will sound also.
Our Craf~ is the child of democracy; it teaches brothe~hood, fraternity,
freedom; 1t advocates the gentler virtues. That being so, it is abhorred of
dictators; whose suprem·acy is based upon the virtual enslavement of the
peoples whom they rule with iron hands. Masonry was banished in
· Germany and Italy because the dictator regime will not allow, dare not
allow, those who writhe under its regulations any allegiance with or interest
in any organization that is not directly headed by the dictator, and whose
activities are inspired by the species of tin God that presides over the
national destiny. ·Dictators realize only too well the insecurity of their
position. Loud though they may beat their drums, rattle their sabres, voice
their threats, they invariably sit upon powder magazines of suppressed
public opinion. They maintain their positions only through intimidation and
fear; they survive only as long as they succeed in cowing 'the sullen millions
beneath their sway.
So the grim dictum of his own infallibility; his own supremacy,· must
be enforced by the dictator if he is to continue to exist. There must be one
will-his, one objective--his, one master--him. There the pre'ss, the pulpit,
the thoughts of the masses must be chained. Fraternity, Fraternalism, freedom of thought, are as noxious to him, and as dangerous to his continued
existence, as anarchy is to a king.
. Though the Frat~rnity has then, of necessity, been banished from
dictator-ridden countries, it is strong, and growing stronger, in the two great
strohgholds of democracy, America and England. In these coO.ntries, where
freedom of thought and action have been preserved, Masonry thrives and
will continue to thrive.
Texas, 1941
Hist~ry is replete with the story of the world's long, bitter and slow
p_rogress m the constant battle against ignorance, superstition and oppression. Hundreds of years lie behind the destruction of a complete despotism
and of the establishing of democracy and a republican form of government.
Behind this story lies an untold number of inspiring acts of courage faith
and s~cri?ce. in connt;ction with the lives of those men who fou~ht to
establish Justice, equality and freedom for all, more particularly in our own
great Nation. And in this Nation this glorious accomplishment was realized
to a great extent through the sacrifices, courage and influence of our own
early Masonic ancestors. For these things that Freemasons have always
placed even abo-v~ life its~lf, and are now seriously and boldly challenged,
I feel that Horatius has given us the answer, as well as the inspiration for
the future: "How can a man die better than when facing fearful odds for
the ashes of his fathers and the temples of his gods?"

Utah, 1941
My. ~x?erience and observations throughout the year have deepened
~y conviction that. Freemasonry is too precious and its mission to vitally
~mportant to mankmd to be neglected. In the chaotic world of today there
is more. need .t~an ever for greater devotion to its principles and the earnest
promot10n of its welfare. Freemasonry is urriversal in its character and

s~mndly based ?Po.n the natural rights of man: the right to be free, the

to the dictates of our own conscience. These Masonic principles and ideals
are also the cornerstones in the foundation of our blessed republic, and I
am sure that we as Americans and as Masons fully appreciate, in these
trying times wheh tyranny and despotism are seriously t11.reatening our
every ideal in practically every quarter of the world, the importance and
necessity of carrying on our work with more patience and perseverance
than ever before, to the end that our ideals and our principles shall be

and to our country to cherish and protect the name of Freemasonry.
Missouri, 1941
We are living in a period of the world's history which makes those of
us who believe in morality and free government thankful that we live in
the United States of America. The Masonic Fraternity on the European
Continent has been suppressed. It has been suppressed because it stands
for freedom of thought, and freedom of expression; for government of the
people, for the people, by the people, and for freedom of worship. These
great principles were established in the United States at Philadelphia in
1787, when the Constitution of the United States was written. The Constitution, and its Bill of Rights, has been a model for free governments the
world over since that time. A large number of the framers of the Constitution of the United States were members of this great Fraternity of ours.
We are facing a solemn and serious period in our history; in fact, the
most serious emergency we have ever faced. As Freemasons we must
continually endeavor to instill appreciation of free government, and free
expression; freedom of thought and freedom of worship.
I thank God every day that I am a citizen of the greatest and freeest
country on earth, ·and that I have the privilege of worshiping as I please,
of acting with complete liberty, so long as I do not infringe upon the
rights of others, and of having the right to belong to any organization or
Fraternity I choose, so long as it does not foster treason against the
Government. We cannot really appreciate these privileges because we have
always had them. But, our Brethren in Denmark, Holland, Norway, and
all those other countries which have come under the heel of totalitarian
dictators, are either in concentration camps, or have foresworn their liberties
and their fraternal obligations.
Arizona, 1941
With the world so torn with strife let us ever remember that Craftsmen
down through the ages have endeavored to improve the lot and mode of
life of mankind, and let us re-consecrate ourselves on the Altar of Freemasonry, and ·re-dedicate our lives to the re-establishment throughout the
world of that peace and harmony which is no small part of the great purpose
and design of Masonry.
"Do not live to make a living,·
Rather live to make a life,
For the measure of succeeding
Is your service in the strife;
All that you may leave behind you,
When your soul has crossed the bay,
Is the good you've done to others
As you tarried by this way."

West Virginia, 1941
Masonic Lodges, as' such, can do few things in public. Masons as
individuals are usually in the front ranks of all patriotic, civic and moral
movements, whether it be the sale of defense bonds or the entertainment of
soldiers and sailors, the raising of the levies of the American Red Cross
or those of the United Service Organization-two organizations which,
we under-stand are recognized by the War and Navy departments, while
other welfare organizations are not. Young Masons who are in the military
and naval services are, we know, good men and true. They do not need
especial coddling· to protect them from immorality and home-sickness.
Indeed, they ought to be exemplars of good conduct and steadfastness to
their comrades who have not had the advantages of the teachings they have
received in their Lodges.
As individuals, and as men who have learned in the assembly of Freemasons something of the dignity and duty of manhood, we spurn the
approach of the invading dictator as we would strike the head of the
venomous viper. Strange indeed is the soul that does not quiver in rage at
the depravities of the war across the seas. But our Lodges are places of
refuge from this fury, places for the nourishing of the sinews of moral
strength. No controversial subject can enter here, however much as individuals we may feel there can be no controversy about it. But, without
doing violence to that tradition, and in the fullest possible confidence I
declare in your presence in the most solemn manner that the Freemas~ns
of this jurisdiction will not fail God or country in this or any other crisis.
Mississippi, 1941
The vital essence of Freemasonry is that it is a brotherhood a fellowship, of free and enlightened men having its roots in the rich soil ~f intimate
acquaintanceship and association. Long before constitutions were written
or regulations were framed for the government of the craft, our ancient
brethren with uncanny wisdom rested the welfare and perpetuity of their
society upon the firm foundation of their mutual understanding and love
for one another, and across the succeeding centuries this has continued to
be the enduring basis of our fraternity. These brethren of former years
were wont to describe this relationship as the "mystic tie"-a very happy
and fascinating expression and we should continue to give it currency in our
modern Masonic language.

MEMBERSHIP-REQUIREMENTS, ACTIVITIES,
INTERESTS, AND DUTIES
Indiana, 1941 (Grand Master):
Prior to our last Federal Election, I observed a notice in a newspaper
that a ladies' organization of one of our political parties was to hold a
meeting in one of our Masonic Temples at which a speaker was to be heard
on political subjects. I immediately called the Worshipful Master of the
Lodge and ordered this meeting cancelled. I was given every assurance
that my order would be obeyed and was afterwards advised by him , that
the meeting had not been held.
West Virginia, 1941 (Grand Master) :
Since Freemasonry is an unfettered organization, dedicated to freedom
of thought, word and deed, and opposed to any infraction of these liberties,
we need to grow in strength, both in numbers and in spirit, that we may
better serve our brotherhood, and, serving it; so serve humanity. There is
no ideal, no dream of true democracy, that does not embody the ideals and
purposes of our Fraternity. In the future, as in the past, "!"e will be persecuted and survive. An institution founded, as ours is, upon universal truths,
can never cease to exist, because its fundamental principles are carried and
cultivated in the heart of every true thinking man who would say, "All
men are brothers."
West Virginia, 1941 (Grand Orator) :
The great need of the day is in the field of human conduct, and
especially in the relationships between man and man and group and group.
We believe that in the long run conduct springs from internal desire rather
than external compulsion. Our task, then, is to create right desires as the
motive power for right conduct. Freemasonry has always builded in the
realm of human relationships and in the field of right desires. Freemasonry
and other groups of people of similar objectives are therefore at the very
heart of the most crucial problem in the greatest of human crises. We seek
to build upright men of sound character, industrious, self-reliant, and motivated by a self-interest that believes in trying to practice the Golden Rule.
As one of the most potent factors let us keep alive our Freemasonry.
Let us keep it strong and true and its light shining clear for, like the candle
and the lighthouse, its beam goes farther than we know.
Utah, 1941 (Grand Master):
I am happy to report that generally the condition of Freemasonry in
Utah is good. Wherever I have been on my official visitations whether in
the smaller lodges in the country or the larger lodges in the cities, I have
been greatly impressed with the fine character of the men who compose
the membership of our lodges. I can say to you with all sincerity that we
have a right to be proud of our fraternity in this state. At every visitation
we have made but one there has been a good attendance of the membership

New Mexico, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
In the Grand Master's address he reports that an outdoor Masonic
meeting was held in the open hills of Gage, New Mexico. The lodge was
opened under a special dispensation and the third degree conferred. After
the degree work was completed, several short talks were given by the
brethren. There were 130 members registered and many lodges were represented from coast to coast, especially numerous were the brethren from
jurisdictions in Texas and Arizona. A similar open air meeting was staged
in California by Canby Cross Lodge No. 679, where the third degree in
Masonry was conferred atop Prisoners Rock near Tulelake at sundown on
the evening of July 13, 1940. Thus Masonry uses some of these unusual
stunts to endeavor to create more interest in the Fraternity.
Utah, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
Although we are not as strait-laced as are some brethren on the matter
of physicai qualification, we would commend Grand Master Ogden on his
handling of the one case of discipline reported, and we very much like his
position as indicated in the words:
"As long as our law on physical qualifications remains as it is, wilful
disregard of its provisions cannot b.e ignored."
That is sound doctrine and is susceptible of application far beyond
Masonic boundaries and if executed, would be productive of highly beneficial results.
Texas, 1941 (Correspondence Committee) :
On recommendation of Grand Master (California) Grand Lodge now
declares:
" ... that the Secretary of a Lodge should be permitted to make a
statement to a proper officer of any organization, the prerequisite for
membership therein being that a man be a Master Mason, concerning the

organization."
Some departure from the one time secrecy of Lodge records! Time
was, when engaged in character building, the supporting arm of Lodge discipline was thrown around a "falling brother," not infrequent_ly with reclaiming effect. What now, since all such procedure is to be heralded to
the vast number of such organizations composed most largely of women,
boys and girls, together with "chums" with no sort of Masonic relationship?

So often the average Mason looks upon his Lodge ;tS a club or as a

place primarily intended for brotherly companionship. Masonry is, of

· A few months ago, as individual citizens and Freemasons, we could
differ on questions of international policy. Now the debate is over. The
government under whose protection we live is engaged in a titanic struggle
that cannot cease until it ends in victory for the principles of democracy

We cannot all bear arms, and we cannot all share the hardships and

Washington, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
Under the head, "Conference of Grand Masters," the Grand Master
(Indiana) sets forth his carefully prepared paper on the question of who
should be the final judge of a candidate's physical qualifications-the local
Lodge, the Grand Lodge or the Grand Master. He took the position that
lndiana's rule where the final decision is up to the Grand Master was the
best. Our jurisdiction's rule reads as follows:
"The Lodge shall itself determine the petitioner's physical qualifications, by the sole test of whether any maim or defect in his body renders
him incapable of conforming literally to what the several degrees require
of him."
Wyoming, 1941 (Grand Master):
Question: We have an application for membership from a good man
who is physically disabled, permanently. He has no use whatever of his
right arm other than with the help of the other arm. Of course, it is possible for him to place himself in position to take the work, but would not
be possible to give the signs properly. Is there anything in our laws to
prohibit him of becoming a Mason? He has all the other qualifications and
I feel he wculd be a good member and will get a lot of good out of Masonry.
Answer: I refer you to Section 435, Paragraph ( d), of the code, but by
the decision of the Jurisprudence Committee in 1935, I think they give the
Master of the Lodge a great deal of room to admit those who are not in
absolute physical condition, therefore, I would raise no objection if you
were to receive this petition and act favorabl~ thereon. But you know that
the Worshipful Master of the Lodge is the final person to decide these
matters. (Approved.)
Calgary, 1941 (Grand Master):
A Masonic Lodge can and shquld be a factor in the ·life of its community, not through any concerted action on the part of the Lod~e itself,
but rather through the exemplary conduct of its members. The Institution
as a whole is often judged by the actions of an individual, and when we
assume the obligations of a Mason, we are responsible not to ourselves
alone, but to those Brethren with whom we are associated.
Our greatest need is not more Masons, but better Masons-Masons
who will take their vows seriously, who are willing to work for Masonry and
ask no reward save the satisfaction which comes from the consciousness in
having done their part towards making this world of ours a better and
a happier place in which to live.
Kansas, 1941 (Grand Master):
During the dark days of the Civil War, M. W. Jacob Saqui, in his
address as Grand Master, said : "Obedience to the government is, and ever ·
has been , the duty of Masons, and it should be our pleasure1 as it
undoubtedly is to our interest, to comply with the injunctions of this
cardinal principle." These words are as true today as they were when they
were spoken eighty years ago.

. To Confer Two or More Degrees on Same · Candidate at One and the
Same Communication: Since a precedent has been set by the Grand
Masters who served during the first World War of 1917-18, and since we
have been at war, I have granted dispensations to confer E. A., F. C., and
M. M. Degrees at one and the same communication .in cases where the
petitioner had left, or was about to leave, to enter the service of his country;
all three degrees to be conferred only after the candidate's petition had taken
its regular course, that is-investigating committee appointed and petition
lay over its regular four weeks.
Louisiana, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
The United Grand Lodge of England is now the largest in the world
with 5,184 Lodges and more than 400,000 members. There has been an
increase in the number of Lodges every year since 1930. In that year, there
were 4,622 and in 1940 5,184 Lodges.
The great growth in recent years of Masonry in England has been due
to the policy of encouraging a large number of Lodges with a limited
membership of from 70 to 100.
This policy has been found very effective in building up the Lodges by
placing many in the larger cities within a comparatively small territory.
As a result, the members know each other and a spirit of acquaintance
and ·friendship has been easily built up.
In Lodges of this siZe there is good scope for promotion and ambitious
members have a chance of getting through the chairs.
Another reason for the large increase in numbers is the fact that the
United Grand Lodge of England discourages the formation of other socalled Masonic bodies-that is, above the Mark and Royal Arch-and, in
consequence members do not have their interest divided or face an accumulated financial obligation, but give their full attention and zeal to the
Craft.
South Carolina, 1941 (Grand Master):
I have given a number of dispensations mainly to permit more than
five candidates to receive Degrees on one evening. These are on record in
the office of the Gr.and Secretary. A number were also given to shorten the
time, statutory, between degrees. Most of these two types were given
to allow the candidates to enter the armed forces of the U. S. as Master
Masons. I considere<l it was far better for them to enter as such rather
than to enter only having one or two degrees.

who, in turn, create strong Lodges? Is it genius or work? Do we need

WASHINGTON MEMORIAL
Utah, 1941 (Grand Master):

Masonic National Memorial meeting held in the George Washington Memorial building at Alexandria. It was most impressive and "touching," for that
is the place where they take the checks on per capita tax for the erection and
completion of that wonderful building· which will ere long be finished. We
were told that the next room to be finished is what they call the Blue Room,
where many of the relics now in the lodge room at Alexandria wm be

After lunch, we went to Mt. Vernon where a wreath of flowers was
placed on Washington's tomb. A very befitting address for the occasion
was delivered by the Grand Master of California.

WAR ACTIVITIES
Massachusetts, 1941 (Grand Master):
Since December 27th last I have attended some sixty odd Masonic
gatherings. To me these opportunities to meet and mingle with the
Brethren have been particularly pleasing. Especially have they enabled me
to learn first hand the thoughts and desires Masonically of the officers and
Brethren in all parts of our Jurisdiction. Foremost in the minds of all are
the problems arising out of the present world conditions. Wherever I
have gone I, have found a genuine effort to determine what assistance may
be needed and a laudable desire to render such assistance within the capabilities of the Craft generally. There has been not so much a necessity to
arouse enthusiasm as to direct contemplated efforts in the right direction.
In the first World War fifty per cent or more of the officers and ten
per cent or more of the enlisted men or draftees were Masons. In addition,
their blood relatives constituted another ten to fifteen per cent of the armed
forces. Approximately twenty-four per cent of all the men engaged in one
way or another in the World War were members of the Craft. Whether
that percentage will hold today it is impossible to say, but we do know
that numerically there are about thirty per cent more Masons in Massachusetts at the present time than in 1916, and our national population has
not grown as fast.
Much adverse criticism was heaped upon the Craft generally in the
last war because of the failure to render Masonic service to the enlisted
and drafted men. I am not sure that such . criticism was always deserved or
that the failure, i{ such it was, was in fact as harmful to the Fraternity as
is currently assumed. Surely the tremendous growth during the war years
and directly thereafter would not indicate that the Fraternity had lost
prestige. Nevertheless it is everywhere agreed, first, that there is a real
need for services which shall sustain morale within and without the borders
of the camps, forts and other training areas, and second, that Freemasonry
can satisfy that need to an appreciab.Je extent. There is not, however, the
same unanimity of opinion as to the exact type of service which may be
needed.
Mississippi, 1941 (Grand Master):
I have given a great deal of thought to the question of how the Masons
may best serve their brethren in our military establishments. Events of
the past two years have pressed this problem upon the attention of the
leaders of the Craft. It was brought home to me and to the Masons of
Hattiesburg in a very forceful manner with the location of Camp Shelby
near Hattiesburg about 18 months ago. This was one of the first camps
to be put in condition for the reception of soldiers and they began to come
in large numbers, particularly from the state of Ohio in the fall of 1940.
We organized a. committee and went out to the camp soon after the 37th
(Ohio) Division came in and began to inquire as to who were Masons and
to our very pleasant surprise we found that the Commanding General and
practically every member of his staff and a large number of officers and
a goodly company of men belonged to our fraternity. These initial meetings
resulted in these brethren accepting our invitation to come to our Masonic
Temple in Hattiesburg, first to a supper, and then to other meetings and
to the conferring of Degrees. We soon formed a warm attachment for
these brethren from Ohio and our fellowship with them has been very
delightful. We have arranged during the subsequent months several affairs
for these brethren and also for others who came in from other ~tates,

particularly from Indiana, Kentucky, West Virginia, Pennsylvania apd
New York.
Utah, 1941 (Grand Master):
We all recall our feeling of dissatisfaction during and after the last
World War with Masonry's part in the organ.i zed activities carried on for
the benefit of our soldiers and sailors both at home and abroad; and the
only way to avoid a repetition of this experience during the present
emergency is to act now whil!! the opportunity is here. As already stated,
the Masonic Service Association, of which this Grand Lodge is a member,
has set up organizations for and is now actively engaged in maintaining
Masonic centers near a number of the larger camps in the 'eastern and
southern States, and we have been invited to support this work by a contribution of at least ten cents per capita, which would amount to about
$450.00.
I cannot feel, however, that this alone is all we should attempt, nor
do I feel that we can or should meet the requirements of a reasonable
program in this direction by appropriations from either o ur individual lodge
treasuries or the treasury of the Grand Lodge which can ill afford further
depletion than our annual operating deficits have made necessary. This is
a program that appeals both to our patriotism and to our feeling of
Masonic brotherhood, and I feel that every Mason in Utah will want and
should have an opportunity to contribute to this cause as freely and as much
as he may desire or as his circumstances will permit. Furthermore, in view
of our limited numbers, if we are to do anything here at home, which I
most definitely feel should come before anything is sent out to support
activities elsewhere, we· must ·ask all who can give, not to limit themselves
to a fixed per capita amount but to give as much more as the worth of
the cause may move them to do. I; therefore suggest that we take action
at this time to raise a fund by .voluntary subscription open to all Masons
of Utah and to be called to their attention by means of uniform notices
sent out by the lodge Secretaries, which fund will be held in the treasury
of the Grand Lodge and expended under direction of the Grand Master both
in direct activities in this State along the lines indicated and in contributing
to the activities in this direction of the Masonic Service Assocation to such
extent as may be decided upon at this session of Grand Lodge.
Kentucky, 1941 (Grand Master):
Much discussion has come on welfare work by Masons in the camps
of our country. The Grand Lodge of Kentucky was, I think, just as much
interested as is any other Grand Jurisdiction, in this ·work. But, when,
in March, 1941, Brother Orton and I were guests of the National
Sojourners' Club, Fort Knox, Kentucky, we talked extensively with Captain
Halstead and several other officers. They stated that the men did not need
welfare work and recreation-that the Federal Government furnished that.
They indicated that what the Masons in the armed forces wanted most
was the privilege of attending our lodges occasionally, and I assured them
that they had that now.

New Mexico, 1941 (Proceedings):
Perhaps .the world today faces a cns1s such as has never confronted
it before. Mankind has ever suffered from the mental, moral, and physical
devastations of wars caused by the greed of rapacious rulers, but during
those years, despite adversity, tire' peoples of the earth were slo~ly progressing in their building of a better and happier world where man might
live. Now, however, we see all 1nations welding together the skill and labor
of their peoples into an awful· effort directed solely toward the destruction
of each other.
Such chaotic conditions naturally produce unrest, impatience, and
intolerance. Institutions that once were sacred, are no longer respected, and
soon may not be tolerated. Only such organizations that definitely contribute some valuable service will survive. Churches as well as fraternal
organizations have sensed this trend and are redoubling their efforts to be
of active service.
Freemasonry· cannot be offered as a substitute for religion, but it is a
solid rock of fundamental truth where all men may meet and work with
common understanding and sympathy. It has been the hope of this committee tha,t it might help Lodges bring Freemasonry into the every-day
lives of their members. Too often it seems that our Masonic teachings are
folded away with the aprons when the Master's gavel sounds the closing of
Lodge, not to be used, nor thought of, until the next regular meeting.

Washington, 1941 (Proceedings):
A very interesting and informative paper on "The Genealogy of the
Grand Lodge of Washington," by Brother Howard A. Hanson, Worshipful
Master of Research Lodge No. 281, and Grand Historian of Grand Lodge
of Washington, was presented for inclusion in the record. This paper is
well prepared and will well repay any student . of Masonry for the time
expended in studying same. The following are excerpts:
The California Line of Ancestry. We have traced the genealogy of
the Grand Lodge of Washington through the Missouri line of ancestry back
to the Grand Lodge of England. We shall now consider the California
line. The Lodges participating in the formation of the Grand Lodge of
California held charters or dispensations from the Grand Lodges of the
District of Columbia, Missouri, Connecticut, New Jersey and Louisiana.
Thus, the California line, since it traces through Missouri, in reality
includes the Missouri line as well. But, in addition to the Grand Lodges
in the Missouri line, the California line traces through the Grand Lodges
of California, the District of Columbia, Connecticut, New Jersey, Louisiana,
Mississippi, Kentucky, Maryland, Virginia, Massachusetts, New York, South
Carolina, Pennsylvania and to all five of the Mother Grand Lodges: The
Grand Lodge of Washington, therefore, enjoys the distinction of being
directly related to seventeen American . Grand Jurisdictions and five
European Mother Grand Lodges.
Peter Lassen and the Second Pacific Coast Charter. The second
Pacific Coast charter was granted, May 10, 1848, by the Grand Lodge of
Missouri, for Western Star Lodge, No. 98, at Benton City, California. Its
first Junior Warden was Peter Lassen, whose name is perpetuated in Mount
Lassen, Mount Lassen National Park and Lassen County, California. The
Lodge is now known as Western Star Lodge, No. 2, and is located at Shasta.
The Grand Lodge of California apparently considered seniority of
Lodges on the basis of their first meetings, rather than the dates of their
charters, as appears from the following letter from the late Brother John
Whicher, Grand Secretary:
"The first recorded meeting of a Lodge of Masons in California was
that of California Lodge, No. 13, of the District of Columbia (now No. I)
which met in San Francisco, Thursday evening, October 7, 1849. The
charter was dated November 9, 1848."
Maryland, 1941 (Proceedings):
Exact history, of necessity, must be based upon facts supported by
reasonably accurate evidence; nevertheless, without violating any of the
rules of exact history, we are now justified in expressing the belief that
there were Masonic Lodges in Maryland as early as 1729, so long as we
express it as a belief and not as a proven fact.
On September 18 of this year, while we were examining the records and
returns of .the old Baltimore Union Lodge No. 21, now on file in the Grand
Lodge archives at Richmond, we discovered a doc.ument.
At the top of this document appears the following heading: "A true
Copy of the Warrant of the Lodge No. 15 held upon Fells Point."

456

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Then follows an exact hand-written copy of the original Charter,
issued June 28, 1770, by the Provincial Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, for
old Lodge No. 15-now Washington Lodge No. 3.
On the reverse side of this document is an endorsement of a most
unusual and revealing nature. It is no less than a Dispensation issued by
the officers and Past Masters of Lodge No. 15, to Robert Stewart, Thomas
Constable, and Hugh Stewart, "with any other Officers and Brethren ~hat
they may approve of, to Hold a Lodge of Free and Accepted Ancient
York Masons" in Baltimore, "under the Title of a Branch of No. 15,"
until they could "obtain a Warrant properly Authenticated and duly
Authorized."
Manitoba, 1941 (Proceedings):
The Origin and Growth of Freemasonry. Many have been the questions that have been asked regarding the origin of Freemasonry, particularly by the younger members of our Masonic Lodges. . . . It seems
to me that all possible questions with reference to our Masonry have been
asked and "it is about time" the leaders of the order provided answers to
some of them, if Freemasonry is to survive the test which now confr<;mts it
with other institutions.
With reference to the questions that have been asked regarding the
origin of Freem.asonry-many fantastic answers have been offered, not
only by well tried and tested Freemasons, but actually in Masonic literature.
For instance, it has been suggested that Noah and his two sons were three
of the major officer·s of a Lodge. Such a claim ranks with that of a friendly
Society, that Adam was an Oddfellow. That may be true, for he was
"odd" but to lay claim that Noah and his two sons were senior officers
of a Masonic Lodge is going a little too far.
In order to emphasize its antiquity, attempts have been made to prove
that the first Masonic Lodge was formed by the first Christian British
martyr, St. Alban, in 287 A. D. Those are claims no historian would
support, knowing Masonry as you and I know it.
I repeat. that Freemasonry can stand on its own merits and needs no
false bolstering. Its origin may probably be found in the procedure and
ceremonies of the Operative Guilds of "free masons" which were organized
bodies of skilled men who worked in the various countries during the great
cathedraf~building period of the Middle Ages.
Those· old guilds were closely associated with the Christian Church,
and their a\legiance to the Church was one of their articles of faith. A great
deal of what we have become acquainted with in our Masonry is derived
from such a source. In the 17th century we find that besides operatives,
persons of aristocratic birth and social standing were admitted into those
guilds.
With the incoming of the 18th century, the movement for the centralization of the order began. Lodges were springing up here and there without
authority as there existed no Grand Lodge to grant a Charter or warrant.
So in 1717 the Grand Lodge of England came into being and that marked
the beginning of Freemasonry as you and I know it. Our rituals and
ceremonies were compiled round about the year 1700 and the genesis of
modern Masonry may be traced to the medieval building guilds.
After the creation of the Grand Lodge, Freemasonry began to expand
very rapidly. The Grand Lodge of Scotland and also the Grand Lodge of
Ireland shared in the activities which led to expansion. The first overseas
Lodge was formed.

It is fitting that we here today, Masons and friends, pledge anew our

Man does not make Masonry any more than a people make a democracy, nor any more than we made America great. We did not make our

have made us great, and I trust, grateful as individuals and that we will

Arkansas, 1941 (Grand Orator):
"We live in a most extraordinary age. Events so varied and so
important that they might crowd and distinguish centuries, are, in our times,
compressed within the compass of a single life." This was the utterance
of the most eloquent statesman of his day, Daniel Webster, when more
than a hundred years ago he officiated at the dedication of the Bunker Hill
monument, to review the career of the then infant republic. With how much
more justification could we emphasize at this particular instant that there
transpire so many occurrences of such cataclysmic import and of such
unpredictable consequences that we reel and stagger under the impact with
the swirling currents that rage about us. In the sphere of government, in the
realm of ·sociology, in the province of economics and industry, old land-marks
have been uprooted, traditions have been defied and defiled, viewpoints
become distorted, and the entire perspective of human beings is blurred
and obscured in the consciousness of our limitations, our frailty and our
weakness. We are in the stage where we blindly grasp for anchorage,
trusting to secure a hold on something rigid and stable, at the same time
the extended hand clutches at phantoms and wills-of-the-wisp.
It is, perhaps, accurate, if a bit discouraging, to say that those who
think profoundly to conclusions, and act on convictions, constitute but an
infinitesimal segment of the human race. A vast majority, credulous and
easily satisfied, are content to accept whatever doctrine may be hurled at
them. With the easy surrender of their responsibilities they have promptly
delivered up their inherent rights and privileges, have relinquished liberties
wrested from tyrants after generations have suffered in anguish to obtain
them. They have become ready prey for the false leaders, the opportunists
always prowling about to victimize the unthinking mobs. These same
leaders know only too well that the law of inertia applies as much to humans
as to inanimate bodies; that people float with the current with the greatest
facility.

FOREIGN MASONRY
Washington, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
The Grand Lodge of Nicaragua requests that fraternal relations be
established with our Grand Lodge.
Upon investigation we find that this Lodge is recognized by eleven
American Grand Lodges, namely: California, Iowa, Louisiana, Nevada,
North Carolina, Ohio, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Missouri, Arizona
and Massachusetts, and that it conforms in all respects to our Code requirements. It is an independent, self-governing organization incorporated under
the laws of Nicaragua.
I, therefore, recommend that recognition be granted and that repre-.
sentatives be exchanged.
Colorado, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
·Your Committee feels now, as it has in the past, that Masonry is one
of the most powerful agencies for the development of good will between
nations. We therefore see no good reason for nonrecognition of those
foreign Grand Lodges which merit recognition, and believe the general
lack of recognition between North American Grand Bodies and South and
Central American Grand Bodies to be largely due to carelessness and lack
of attention to a matter which seems at this time to be of mounting
importance. Language differences and customs are hard to overcome, it is
true, but what is still more difficult to overcome is inertia. Since our own
North American Grand Lodges are not in need of outside support, they
are quite prone to be unmindful of the great service they may be able to
render less fortunate and less powerful Grand Bodies in less favored
localities. Yet it is these latter that are the very ones we should endeavor
to aid and support. The older and more powerful Grand Bodies .do not need
our recognition-but all of them have it. A small, struggling South or
Central American Grand Lodge, however, battling against local political
and religious antagonisms. and present day European (Nazi) propaganda,
may be much strengthened by recognition from one of the big brothers
up to the North.

CYPHERS .
West Virginia, 1941 (Grand Master):
The trust of preserving Ancient Craft .ritual, as it has been handed
down in America ever since the days of Thomas Smith Webb, is a continuing and exacting labor. Constant vigilance must be observed from year
to year among the lodges as the officers change, and from generation to
generation as .the faithful die.
We recognize the right of independent sovereignty of a Grand Lodge
in selecting whatever system it may choose to propagate Freemasonry
within its own territorial jurisdiction, and are aware that in some jurisdictions keys and cyphers are authorized or winked at. However, when a
Grand Lodge, after many generations, discards the indispensable landmark
of "Secrecy" in the preservation of its ritual, that action must, of necessity,
become the cause of grave concern and anxiety to those of us engaged in
the important work of teaching Masonic ritual. Dr. Albert Mackey, the
great American Masonic scholar, said: "Freemasonry, as a secret association, has lived unchanged for centuries-as an open society it would not
last for as many years." With that statement, I think, we can all agree.
There are no short cuts or primrose pathw;cys leading to the mastery
of the Masonic ritual; but I have yet to hear anyone complain of the time
consumed or effort expended in the pursuit of this worthy and commendable
enterprise.
If Freemasonry is to endure, I insist that we must guard well its ritual
-that is basic and fundamental. To do less is to invite ultimate disaster.

Louisiana, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
A topic which is receiving attention in many jurisdictions is the question of the ritual or what we call the esoteric work. The dissemination of
the esoteric work has become such a financial burden on the craft that
many jurisdictions are resorting to many ways to relieve the fraternity of
this burden. P. G. M. Ray V . Denslow, correspondent of the Grand Lodge
of Missouri, reports some ·interesting facts in this connection which we
quote for the information of the brethren of our jurisdiction:
"Since the Masonic ritual is the framework or skeleton on which the
Masonic fraternity has been builded, a study of trends is appropriate. There
is a decided movement through the country to establish a cipher ritual.
In fact, many Grand Lodges have had these cyphers for many years. In
several jurisdictions a study of ritual is being encouraged by the granting
of proficiency certificates which, to our mind, constitutes the best of all
proposed plans. In one jurisdiction the bars have been let down by not
requiring an examination on the third degree.
"The Grand Master of Arizona believed that much of the time now
consumed in learning the ritual could be spent more constructively in
making stated meetings more enjoyable, and that 'the adoption and distribution of an initial-letter key would not only materially shorten the time
now devoted to memorization, but would result in much more uniform and
correct ritualistic work.' "

Ohio, 1941 (Grand Master):
The written ritual, received from Past Grand Master, M. W. Brother
Dillon Crist, has been used on various occasions.
The wisdo!T\ of the Grand Lodge in preparing the written ritual becomes
more evident as time goes on. It insures absolute uniformity in the work
throughout the state as well as the generations, and by consulting it, one
effectively guards against inaccuracies through the lapse of memory or time.
The ritual should have a more general use.
There is a growing tendency to form clubs by Masons employed by
firms or corporations. They organize for fellowship but specialize in conferring the Master Mason degree on fellow employees receiving the degrees.
While they show marked proficiency in the ritual; the occasion is frequently
marred by additions which are not permissible.
Section 92, Note 6, page 142 of the Code states, "Any addition to, as
well as any omissions from .the work as prescribed in the ritual by this
Grand Lodge is in violation of the resolution which enjoins conformity to
said ritual." Masters of Lodges should understand that the Grand Lodge
holds them responsible for the observance of · a strict conformity to the
ritual.. It is with that understanding that they may confer the degrees.

CORNERSTONES
Texas, 1941 (Grand Master):
Among the ancients, the cornerstones of important edifices were laid
with impressive ceremonies. These are well described by Tacitus in the
history of the rebuilding of the Roman capitol. After detailing the preliminary ceremonies, which consisted in a procession of vestals, who with
chaplets of flowers encompassed the ground and consecrated it by libations
of living water, he adds that, after solemn prayer, Helvidius, to whom the
care of rebuilding the Capitol had been committed, laid his hand upon the
fillets that adorned the foundation stone, and also the cords by which it
\Vas to be drawn to its place. In that instant the magistrates, the priests,
the senators, the Roman knights, and a number of citizens, all acting with
one effort and general demonstrations of joy, laid hold of the ropes and
dragged the ponder·ous load to its destined spot. They then threw in ingots
of gold and silver, and other metals which had never been melted in the
furnace but still retained, untouched by human art, their first formation in
the bowels of the earth!

WAR RELIEF
Washington, 1941 (Proceedings):
M. W. Brother Walter F. Meier's last Masonic contribution was his
research paper on Masonic Relief-a Right or a Gratuity. His investi'gations
embraced the Grand Lodges of the United States, Canada and England.
In his summary he observed that:
"The whole problem of relief falls into two categories, current help and
old age security. Masonry, which has dealt with the problem for more
than two centuries, has adhered to the philosophy that in each category the
recipient has no legally. enforcible right, while the institution cheerfully
assumes as heavy a burden as it can. There is and must be, a relation to
the need on the one hand and the ability to afford relief on the other. The
Masonic philosophy has been developed in recognition. of. both .factors." .
Pennsylvania, 1941 (Proceedings):
The trustees of the War Relief fund of Pennsylvania, in their report
for. the fiscal year ending November 15, 1941, show investments as follows:
Mortgage bonds, $139,071.20; first mortgages, $61,837.50; bonds, $9,750.00;

Indiana, 1941 (Grand Master):
In conformity to ancient custom in all Regular and well governed
Masonic jurisdictions, June 24th is celebrated in observance of the Festival
of St. John the Baptist. ·
St. John the Baptist, a Patron Saint of Masonry, gave his life in the
service· of humanity, endeavoring by Divine direction to call attention to
the great philosophy of the "Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of
Man." This is the basic philosophy of Masonry.
By action of the Grand Lodge in 19!6, June 24th was set apart .and
designated as Masonic Home Day.
It is fitting that my first official communication to the Craft in our
jurisdiction call attention to the opportunity afforded each Master Mason
of putting into practical effect one of the immutable laws of Freemasonry
"the greatest of these is charity."
Our Masonic Home deserves our earnest consideration and we as true
Masons cannot disregard its needs. It is the monument in our Commonwealth which is visible evidence to all beholders of what Masonry stands
for. Let our contributions be in proportion to our blessings received in
Masonry.
Indiana, 1941 (Jurisprudence Committee):
The recommendation of the Grand Master that the incoming Grand
Master be authorized by this Grand Lodge to appoint a committee whose
duty it shall be to have a motion picture made of oµr Masonic Home, such
picture to contain scenes of our grounds, buildings, school, farm and
equipment as well as the activities engaged in by our members, has been
referred to the Jurisprudence Committee.
After careful consideration and conference with the Ways and Means
Committee, the Jurisprudence Committee are of the opinion, that, in the
first place, this proposition would entail a considerable amotmt of money
in excess of $600.00 as has been suggested by the Grand Master.
Furthermore, the members of the Jurisprudence Committee are unanimo'us in the opinion that nothing should be done to disturb the sanctity
of the Masonic Home which has prevailed from the very beginning, that
the Home and its members should continue to be kept as sacred as possible
and that the old folks and the children should continue to remain dear to us.
It is our belief that a proposition of this kind, showing the members in
moving pictures throughout the State, would hurt the pride and the feelings
of our old folks considerably and would perhaps cause some unrest among
them. We believe that this proposition would not be a good thing for the
children in the Home and that later on in life this might cause some element
of embarrassment to them. This, of course, we do not desire to do. The
Masonic Home has always been sold to the members of the fraternity
throughout the State by personal visitation. We believe that this method
should continue and we do not believe that our members should be used
in moving pictures to accomplish this result.
Your Jurisprudence Committee, therefore, .recommend that this recommendation of the Grand Master be not adopted. (Concurred in by Ways
and Means Committee.)

Kentucky, 1941 (Grand Master):
I. My opinion is that the brother on the committee, who reported
unfavorably was acting thoroughly within his rights. The Book of Constitutions of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky reads: "Manufacture and Sale
of Liquors. No lodge shall receive the petition of any one who is engaged
in the manufacture or sale of spirituous, vinous or malt liquors as a
beverage. Any lodge guilty of violating this provision shall be dealt with."
(Book of Constitutions, 1940, p. 36, section 108.) One who sells whiskev
for medical purposes is not rendered ineligible by this section.

II. . Preston Lodge itself was culpable, if it knew that this petitioner

III. No matter what the business of the petitioner is, if he sells
