This opinion is constitutional; and I believe it is clear.

SUGGESTIONS FROM THE GRAND LECTURERS
West Virginia, 1941 (Proceedings):
Then, occasionally we hear the statement that the Grand Lodge has
"changed" the work. That statement is made in error. It is true that
sometimes the Grand Lodge through the Grand Lecturer and Committee
on Work is obliged to correct errors that have crept into the practices of
the Lodges, b~t these corrections are always made to preserve the work,
not to change 1t.
The Grand Lecturer and Deputy Grand Lecturers are the custodians of
our ritual. Their .instructions should be followed strictly by every Lodge.
Washington, 1941 (Grand Lecturer):
From personal observation and from reports reaching me, it appears
that placing four copies of the standard work in the hands of officers of
Lodges has not proved to be the expected panacea for ritualistic ills. There
is no question that possession of the work has been a boon for many. But
that it has materially raised the general standard of rendition and knowledge
of the work is subject to grave doubt. In the light of experience I now
believe no Lodge should have been supplied with the work except on direct
request and then with not more than two copies. Complaint is heard that
the many little details not specifically described or directed in the work are
being omitted or altered until, in some r espects, there is developing a lack of
uniformity.
Arizona, 1941 (Grand Lecturer):
I would most sincerely recommend that the officers of all the Lodges
put forth the utmost effort to keep up attendance in their Lodges. I am
firmly convinced that one of the best ways in which to do this is to excel
in ritualistic work, to make your Lodge a friendly Lodge, to afford to the
members and visitors frequent opportunities to get real basic Masonic
education, and in every way strive to keep before the members the ideals
a~d principles. inculcated in Masonry which are the same ideals and princ1ptes for which free men fight and upon which the American way of
life is based.
Arizona, 1941 (Grand Lecturer) :
With our g:eat ~ation in t?e midst of a terrible and bloody war, with
plow shares again being beaten into swords, with men of all nations tearing
at each other's throats, with brother fighting against brother, let us here
resolve to do our full. patriotic duty and, as Masons let us put forth an
"all out" effort, side by side with our government,' to see to it that a
government of free men, by free men, shall not perish from the earth.
Indiana, 1941 (Grand Lecturer):
Many of our Lodges in the last few years have been lenient with their
members in the collection of dues. No criticism is made in those cases
where members were temporarily unable to pay. However, in being lenient

471

with this class of members, many Lodges have neglected to enforce payment · from those who were able to pay. In some Lodges enforcement of
the law in this respect practically has been nullified. It is a fact that
hundreds of members in our Grand Jurisdiction, who for the last several
years have not paid any dues to their Lodges, are still in good standing,
-enjoying all the privileges and rights of Masons. Should any of these
members or t heir dependents make application to their Lodges for relief
it would be the duty of those Lodges to take care of them. A lso, we should
not lose sight of the fact that members and their dependent s, whether or
not they pay dues, are eligible to our Masonic Home, thereby adding to
our already great burden of rendering relief to those who deserve it. To fill
up our Masonic Home, which always has a waiting list, with this class of
members and their dependents would be unjust to those who are more
worthy and more deserving of our Masonic Charity.
The safe and Masonic way is to square every account each year. If a
member is unable to pay, the Lodge should remit his dues. If he is able
to pay, make him do so or suspend him.
A Lodge managed on sound business principles always .will be in a
healthy condition, both financially and numerically.

CO-ORDINATE MASONRY
Connecticut, 1941 (Grand Master):
The original structure of American Masonry has during the years
undergone a large expansion, not only through the development of additional degrees and ceremonies, but also by means of the establishment of
numerous correlative orders, membership in which is dependent either on
membership in a Masonic Lodge or relationship to a member. While this
expansion of the Masonic ideals is valuable, it must never be forgotten
that any organization which bases its membership on Masonic relationship
thereby accepts a definite responsibility to avoid any act ion or conduct
which might derogate against th e honor and integrity of Ancient Craft
Masonry. The world at large does not recognize the distinction that we
maintain, but criticizes thoughtless action on the part of any correlative
body as though it were a Masonic misdemeanor.
Oklahoma, 1941 (Grand Secretary):
"Can or should Lodge Secretaries co-operate with Secretaries of other
Masonic Bodies by furnishing them with information regarding suspensions,
dimits, etc.?" The object of this discussion was an endeavor to arrive at
some conclusion as to what would be the remedy for the evil of brethren
maintaining their membership in the higher Bodies and allowing themselves
to be suspended in their Blue Lodge. .It was agreed by all that close
co-operation between the various Bodies should be had and it was a problem
that each Grand Jurisdiction should look out for themselves.
New Mexico, 1941 (Correspondence Committee):
England's membership has shown a substantial gain. The. small lodges
which are encouraged there and the disapproval of the so-called "higher"
bodies of the Grand- Lodge are said by Englishmen to be strong con.tributing factors in this growth. It also finds that Masonry stands before
the world confident that right will again prevail no matter how many lodges
and lodge rooms be destroyed nor how many Masons may b e persecuted.
Masonry will "march on"-when dictators are no more. This sentiment
is universal.

PATRIOTISM-WHAT WE ARE FIGHTING FOR
Louisiana, 1941 (Grand Master):
Freemasonry has always done its full part in every great crisis of our
American history. It was by no acc.ident that into the cause of the American
Colonies Freemasonry lent its influence, and when they gained their inde-•
pendence it was no accident that this government was built upon those
principles for which Freemasonry has always stood; and we, as. Masons of
today, are going to justify that great heritage. We a r e united in every
respect and dedicated to the defense of the ideals and principles of America.
The world today is sharply divided into two camps: one, the totalitarian ruled by Dictators; the other, the government of the people, ·by the
people, for the people, under representatives elected by the free and untrammeled citizens at regular intervals and for a definite term of office.
Mississippi, 1941 (Grand Master) :
Freemasonry is a representative Democracy which stands for the
absolute equality before the law of every human being regardless of race,
creed, or preferment.
Masons, individually and collectively, believe in freedom of assembly,
which is not permitted by dictators, free speech, except libel and treason,
and liberty to do anything that does not injure himself or some other person
or property. Masons, not only in this Grand Jurisdiction, but throughout
the world have always been willing and are now ready and willing to give
their time, their property, yea, their lives to defend this Masonic representative Dem0 cracy.
Masons hate the aggressive wars of the totalitarian Dictator, but are
willing and ready to wage an aggressive war in defense of the fundamental
principles of our ancient and honorable fraternity and "the flag of the
United States of America and the Republic for which it stands."
Masonry is vitally interested in the outcome of this struggle. Masonry
cannot function in a country governed by a Dictator. Let us wholeheartedly cooperate with our Government i'n its struggle for the things that
are vital to the existence of Freemasonry and our form of Government. L et
us take Cooperation for our motto.

Wisconsin, 1941 (Proceedings):
To be an American is to desire, deserve and enjoy a privilege; one of the
priceless gifts bestowed upon the human race when appeared the Star of
Bethlehem.
Americanism partakes of the Glory of the Son .of Man ; of the mother's
love for her offspring; of the father's pride in a dearly beloved son, coupled
with a deathless affection for the land of one's birth or adoption, together
with boundless gratitude to .the source of one's sustenance, prosperity and
happiness.
In an American's heart there is no room for jealousy of a brother's
well-being-no envy of the deserved prosperity of another.
The American mind moves not in circles. It pierces through and beyond "issues"! I t is undismayed by obstacles! It darts straight at the mark !
It is an American's delight to always unselfish ly serve his Country,
uphold its laws, and keep unsullied its Flag. His loyalty is ex~mplified by
his daily life; his devotion by his g lad offer to sacrifice on its Altar of
Liberty and Justice I
He knows, though dynasties may rise and fall, other forms of government come and go, that our "Government of the People, by the People,
for the People, shall not perish from the Earth," and so, each. ~ay, my
brethren, he gives t hanks to Almighty God for the blessed privilege of
being an American.
Kansas, 1941 (Grand Master):
"The lapse of time, the ruthless hand of ignorance, and the devastations
of war have laid waste and destroyed many valuable monuments of antiquity
on which th e utmost exertions of human genius have been employed. . . . .
Freemasonry, notwithstanding, ha6 still survived."
As we assemble in this Eighty-sixth Annual Communication of our
Grand Lodge, we may find just cause for pride and rejoicing in the fac t
that after centuries of travail, Freemasonry still s urvives, and maintains its
potency and prestige among the free peoples of th e world. Nay, more, my
brethren, even in those lands where dictators have decreed that lodges
should disband, we are confident that th e spirit of Freemasonry still lives.
Although the g lorious history of our institution may entitle tis to a
comfortable feeling of pride, it would be fatal for us to rest upon the record
of past achievements. Masonry today is being tested as never before. A
world in torment has issued a challenge that we cannot ignore. Where

475

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

people who have been taught the principles of self-government are being
herded and driven like beasts of the field, there is the irrepressible cry for
the brotherhood of free men. Where greed and avarice are encroaching
upon human lives and human rights, there must be re-awakened a spii;it
of altruism. Where cynical brutality is dominant, there is an unquenchable
longing for lofty idealism. Where solemn covenants and promises have
been contemptuously broken, there must be fostered the principles of
fidelity and integrity. Where hatred and violence prevail, there is need for
the mystic trowel. Where pride and arrogance reign, there must be nurtured the spirit of humility that recognizes a Divine Source of strength
and wisdom. Where atheism has produced spirittial lethargy, there must
be re-kindled a-consciousness of the abiding presence of God. Where people
have sunk to the depths of despair, they must be given that solace which
can revive in their hearts the spirit of hope.
'
Masonry is founded upon the principles that are needed. Never were
they more sorely needed than today. A mere cessation of warfare will
not cure the ills of the world. We must highly resolve that out of this
holocaust will come a peace founded upon the ideals that are contained
within the teachings of our institution.
Can Masonry meet the challenge? It cannot do so by pretendin·g to
be a substitute for the Church. It cannot by trying to follow the pattern
of a chamber of commerce. It cannot by becoming a political faction. The
universality of Masonry must be maintained.
Can we meet the challenge. We can hope to do so if we have sufficient
patience and wisdom; if we live the principles of Masonry in our relations
with ourselves, our neighbors, our country and our God; if we steadfastly
uphold and promulgate those principles in our private and public affairs,
to the end that the world at large may be convinced of their good effects.
Time, patience and perseverance can accomplish a world-wide recognition
of the Brotherhood of Man and the Fatherhood of God.

in ultimate victory, putting our faith and trust, as we know our Sovereign
and Brother does, in the Most High.

INVESTIGATING COMMITTEES
New Mexico, 1941 (Grand Master):
The importance of the investigating committee, its functions and the
need of secrecy brought out a great deal of discussion. The consens-us of
opinion seems to be that investigating committees are prone to b\! lax in
their vital and extremely important duties. Brother F. Homer Newton, of
Michigan, who delivered the paper on this subject, stated:
"As far back as the year 1560 the Landsdowne Manuscript set forth
certain commandments as to the conduct of Masons. They provided, among
other things, th,;tt a Mason must be true to God, his country, and to his
brother Masons; that he must do unto others as he would be done by; that
he keep the counsel of his Lodge; be no thief and slander not another, that
he respect and protect the chastity of a brother Mason's wife, his widow,
his 'daughter, mother or servant; that he do no unlawful thing w~ereby
the craft might be dishonored; that he undertake no work for which he
knew himself incompetent or unfitted; and that. he give honest work for
his pay."
Careless investigation of a candidate who is to live up to its qualifications can be the source of a great deal of trouble for a Lodge. This point
was stressed strongly and a number of reports from Grand Secretaries
were read on this very important subject.
Indiana, 1941 (Grand Master):
There is no doubt that the duty performed by a Committee appointed
to investigate the qualifications of a petitioner is the most important of any
committee now functioning within our several Lodges. Various means
have been provided and distributed to serve as a guide for members of these
committees, but in my opinion it should be the recognized responsibility
of the committee to inform the petitioner that, should he become a member
through initiation, that he will be required not only to conform to the
various forms and ceremonies of the several Degrees, but also to pay
annually to his Lodge a certain amount of money for dues. I am convinced
after many inquiries that some members of our Fraternity, who have become
delinquent, were never informed that it was required that annual dues be
collected by the Lodge, and, consequently, having had no previous advice
of this requirement, these members became delinquent due to their not
being advised of this requirement.

476

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

I believe it would be proper for candidates to be fully advised on this
matter.

FEES
Washington, 1941 (Grand Master ) :
Of twenty-eight amendments to •by-laws presented for approval, ten
were reducing the fees for the degrees; eight of these reduced the fees ·to the
minimum prescribed by the Code, i. e., $30.00, which make 65 out of our 268
Lodges with their fees reduced to that amount. Exclusive of Research
Lodge No. 281, which has a prohibitive fee to discourage petitioners, our
maximum is $120.00. The average is about $50.00, and 90 of our Lodges
charge that fee.
The reason givert for these reductions, in every instance, is the desire to
attract more petitioners. Some local situations may make this the wise and
proper thing to do. Personally, I am convinced that in most cases, if more
consideration were given by the officers, and the Master particularly, to the
development of a program that would increase the value of the Lodge to its
members, it would not be necessary to reduce fees to secure petitioners.
Sometimes even at $30.00, I question whether the candidate gets his money's
worth; and yet I know that we can, if we will, give our candidates a conception of Masonry and its purposes, that will make the amount of the
fee, n'ot matter how large, seem insignificant.
I am not saying that conditions may not sometimes warrant a reduction
of our fees to the minimum. I am saying that before a Lodge reduces fees
it should make a survey of just what it is giving the candidate for his money,
and see whether the answer is not in increasing what they give, rather than
in lowering what they take.

DE MOLAY
W ashington, 1941 (Jurisprudence Committee):
Investigation of the records disclosed that for the last ten years at least,
this Grand Lodge has upheld the Grand Master in refusing permission for
any of our Lodges to sponsor DeMolay. We can find no place where this
Grand Lodge has in any way recognized this organization. Apparently,
disagreeable features and situations have arisen but we do not deem it
advisable to recognize an order that has no connection with us-even to
the extent of investigating it.
· However, we feel that it would be advisable, if it meets the pleasure
of our Grand Master, that he investigate what lodges are sponsoring such
bodies and facts concerning such supervision, making such recommendations and taking such action as he deeins advisable.

LESLIE EARL WOOD
Grand Master 1942 - 1943

Our seventy-sixth Grand Master is a native son of California,
having first seen the light of day in the city of San Diego on April 2nd,
1896. He is the youngest of four children born to Rosslyn A. Wood and
Clara Keyes Wood. In 1925 he was united in marriage to Miss Edith
Marie Anderson, and a daughter, Barbara Lou, was born to them in
1927.
Masonry has played an important part in his life and his efforts
have added to the welfare of the Craft in the jurisdiction. He is recognized
as an eloquent, forceful speaker 'and is admired for the straightforward
manner in which he deals with any given subject. It has often been said
of him "that he is not afraid to say what he thinks."
He was raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason in Sequoia
Lodge No. 349 of Oakland, California, in September, 1919. Three years
later he moved to Sacramento, where he became identified with the Sojourners Club of that city. He first served as its secretary and was then
elected president. In 1925 he became the leader in a movement to organize Provident Lodge No. 609 and served as the charter Master. In
1930 his outstanding ability was recognized by the Grand Lodg-e and he
was appointed Inspector of the 22nd District.
After the death of Grand Lecturer Thomas Baker in 1934 he was
appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer for the Northern District and at the
conununication in October of that year was elected Grand Lecturer.
His first real contribution to Grand Lodge was the perfection of the
present system of teaching the Ritual.
He was furth~r honored in October, 1939, by his election to the
office of Ju,nior Grand Warden. He was elected Senior Grand Warden
in 1940; Deputy Grand Master in 1941, and served with distinction as
Grand Master from October 15th, 1942, to October 16th, 1943.
He is a member of the Sacramento Bodies of the Scottish Rite;
Ben Ali Temple, A. A. 0. N. M. S.; Pyramid No. 3, A. E. 0. S.; Past
Patron of Temple Chapter No. 513, 0. E. S. He has the distinction of
being an honorary member of Bethel No. 74, Order of Job's Daughters.
Since 1923 he has been successfu1ly engaged in the printing business
in Sacramento. He has always taken a active interest in the affairs of
his city and state.
He will long be remembered by his coi,mtless number of friends as
one who is never too busy to help another in time of trouble. His
friendly counsel and advice have smoothed the pathway for many of his
brethren and his 'kind and sympathetic understanding of the other man's
problems have endeared him in the hearts of his friends.

LESLIE EARL WOOD
Grand Master

1942

It can be truly said that he has earned all the honors that Masonry
has conferred upon him and has never failed to justify the many confidences reposed in him.

Devotional Services
The V. Reverend Grand Chaplain, Byrl F. Babcock, then conducted a most inspiring and uplifting devotional service, using as
his theme "Faith for These Times."
My Brethren. of Grand Lodge:
In this wonderful opportunity to claim your attention as this great
94th Annual Communication opens, I have but one wish. It is that
something which I may say will help Masonry and you as individual
Masons. As Handel said that afternoon in April 1742, when his
"Messiah" was first sung and Lord Kimond came to congratulate him:
"My Lord, I should be sorry if I only entertained them. I strove to
make them better."
We have come together today at a time when men's souls are being
tested; hearts and homes torn asunder; sacrifice and chaos crowded into
each hour of every day, yes, a time in which our thinking and our actions
are being distorted and our philosophy of life being driven into new
avenues of experience so different from the past.
1
We are living in an age of sterling adventure. Man is conquering
time and space, and producing things in quantities never before known.
A new application of science and invention has taken place in which
wonderful machines are being built the like of which have never been
dreamed of by prior generations, and these new processes now dominate
the stage of action. Tremendous research laboratories, the last word in
equipment, manned by thousands of technically trained men, backed by
millions of money, working out each day more effective methods and
creating new deviees. Our world is being transformed and the end
is not yet.
Tremendous wealth has been created in our United States as indicated by 'the approximate 50 million savings bank depositors having
billions of dollars to their credit.
Our manufactured products have increased to staggering amounts.
We talk and plan bigger and better machines; more and more goods.
War, of necessity, gears our thinking toward the material and the
secular. We become top-heavy with the load and our normal, well
rounded-out equilibrium is endangered. O'ur wealth and material resources
should give to us a feeling of pride but we must see to it that these
things alone shall not be the only considered factor as we seek a triumphant victory in this great struggle for a continuance of a freedom
and a way of life which we have so ricl;ily enjoyed.
There are other things in life besides kilowatts and horsepowers.
Our moral idealism must be kept alive. We must not allow our technique
to outstrip our morals. We must not permit our machines to devefop
faster than our manhood. The humanizing aspect of life must be developed along with the machine itself. We need and must have modern
inventions and products of the research laboratories. W e need and must
have the most highly improved processes of manufacture yet it is vital
indeed that we build th e manhood of our country in equal proportions
so as to direct this machinery and properly use these instruments.
Progress in science makes progress in morals necessary; and when we
increase the power of man we must at the same time increase the strength
of the check r ein. The materialistic emphasis alone spells disaster.
Do y ou think, A merica, that you are going . to live .because you can
build your buildings so high tha t. they seem to part the stars ?

498

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Do you think, America, that you are going to live because of the
sense of security. which you have in the money that is in your vaults?
Do you think, America, tllp.t you are going to survive because of
the length of your railroads and because of the great physical sense
of security which you possess? If you do, then you don't know history.
Call the roll of the nations :-Assyria, Phoenecia, Chaldea, Babylonia,
Egypt, Greece and Rome. Let civilization pass by in its unimpeachable
verdict. And what is that verdict? No nation has ever lived, and no
nation can live in the future of civilization that does not use its physical
and material power as the opportunity for conserving and maintaining
spiritual and moral ideality.
Just what does live in civilization? Tell me, if you will, the name
of a single banking house of Ancient Rome. Give me the name of a
single ship that carried the commerce of Greece. Their ribs are bleaching
white today, buried under the sands of the sea these many centuries, and
no one knows their names and no one cares. But Plato lives; Aristotle lives;
Socrates lives; Livy live&; Tacitus lives; Hippocrates lives ;-arnd why?
Because they touched humanity with a spiritual and an intellectual inspiration that permanently maintains itself in the ceaseless struggle of the
human heart to lift upward and to love life. As tested thro.u gh the
experiences of the nations of old, the supreme product of civilization is
man himself and I know that Martin was right when he said:
"Men lack vision unless they see
That in the human plan
Nothing is worth the making
That does not make the man.
Why build these cities glorious
If man unbuilded goes?
In vain we build the world
Unless the builder also grows."
We must have mass production in these days of global war. It is
necessary to have a quantity of life and things. But we want also life
in its quality, and things for their real value. We not only want to
make life longer, but also more useful and productive.
It is a great thing to ' have· an hour when the best stirs you. I am
sorry for the man who never had such an hour; who never climbs a
peak; who never feels an ecstasy; who never has a thrill; who never
scents the fragrance blowing in from flowers which blossom in fields.
A man who is always mediocre, and who trudges on with his head down;
his pulses dull, and his senses stale. This hour is for tall men; suncrowned, who dwell above the clouds in public du~y and in private
thinking. This hour is for men and Masons who will take hold of a
Great Faith-a courageous, believing and buoyant faith in God-in Country-and in Victory. Emerson has well said, "Do not leave the sky out
of your landscape." And just as the sky brings the bounty of the
harvest, the exquisite beauty of the flowers, and the glory of the landscape, so faith in God brings the fulfillment of man's high destiny.
Masonry was builded on high idealism, and it has thriven upon it
for centuries. We have made idealisms of various sorts real. Now we
are called upon to evaluate an idealism that will create a mighty faith
in our cause, in our future, and in the victory that we are determined,
.with American tenacity, to win. Victory is the word that epitomizes
the thoughts of men everywhere on this earth this day. And as one

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

499

seeks for the way that men have most successfully gained the goal of
victory, he will jlnd nowhere a more satisfying guide than in a letter
that a man wrote whose name was John. He wrote: "There is a victory
that overcomes the world-our Faith." Robert Louis Stevenson said:
"In the harsh face of life, Faith can read a bracing gospel." I firmly
believe that the p·eople whom you and I represent here today need a
bracing gospel in their hearts.
The days have not always been fair, the news has not always been
good, and there are dark days, perhaps, ahead; but it has always quit
raining and it will again. My faith tells me so. Right may be crucified
today upon a cross, it may lie in a new tomb tomorrow; but on the
third day it rises again-rises in Poland, in Norway, in Belgium, yes,
in France, rises to lead its captors captive, and to fling again its free
banner to the breeze.
·
We are ndt the first people in this New World, this Western Hemisphere, to face danger and desperate times. From Greenland to Cape
Horn, these continents were won with blood and battle, defended by
the sword and preserved by the greatness of heroes. We, too, must
live greatly, it has been well said, or fail and perish miserably. We must
rise to this great destiny with a mighty faith in our ultimate victory,
or we must sink into a slough of everlasting despond.
We are not a people who will ever willingly accept totalitarianism
for our democratic way of life. We are not a people who will ever
willingly exchange s,lav.e ry for the freedom we have known. We are
not a people who will , ever worship a sun-god instead of Jehovah, or
place in our hearts and our shrines the picture of a mad paperhanger
instead of the Man of Galilee.
I believe that with all my heart. Do you? I say it so convincingly,
perhaps, because of a story I was told the other day. A man was talking
with a little girl who had come from England to spend a time in America
where she might be safe from the death that rained from the skies. This
man asked her how she thought it would all come out and she said,
"Oh, sir, everything will be all right. Qur King has told us sol" It is
written that unless our faith be as that of a little child, we shall not
enter into the promises. We need that faith to ride out this storm,
my brethren.
An old French letter says of Louis the Sixteenth, "He was a goodly
man, and if there had been rto confusion he would ha~e likely made a
wise king; but destiny bequeathed to him a revolution, and he was
not equal to it." You and I and this generation have inherited a world
revolution, and I covet for us the faith and the courage to be true to
our traditional greatness and meet this destiny unafraid.
All Cal varies look like defeats, all Crosses appear to be catastrophes;
but they do . not prove so in the end. Cannons belch thunder and death
today, and tomorrow the birds build nests in the mouths of them ~nd
the cannoneers are forgotten. Firm in the faith of a just cause, fearmg
no ~dds oblivious of temporary disaster, we are one with men like Sir
Colin C~mpbell, who said to his Highlanders at Balaclava, "We die,
lads, where we stand." They stood and died, but England lived. Grenville, sailing the tiny "Revenge" out of Flores Harbor that the Spaniard
might not butcher his men, and dying in battle against the fleet of the
enemy; Cambronne at Waterloo, leading the Old Guard against an army;
Pickett with his line of grey warriors at Gettysburg-they all knew a
brief moment of defeat and glory, but men have gained courage and
greatness by drinking at the fountain of their faith.

500

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Keep that faith, my brethren, and we shall triumph; for Right may·
lose a battlc--a score of battles-but Right does not lose a war. As
Anne of Austria said to Richelieu, "My Lord Cardinal, God does not
pay at the end of each week; but in the end, God pays!"
There was once a beautiful maiden, and she found favor with the
king, and he made her his favorite queen. But a time came when her
people were oppressed and there came an old patriarch of her family
and besought her to speak to the king and intercede with him. She
hesitated, lest she lose favor, but the old patriarch reminded her of her
duty. "Who knoweth, Esther," he said, "but that it was for such a time
as .this thou ·hast come to the kingdom?"
Fly high your flag upon the hill,

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
One year ago you honored me by placing in my hands the insignia
and the title of Grand Master, the greatest gift in the power ·of Masonry
to bestow. Today I am reminded that soon that honor and the authority
that goes with _it, will pass to other hands, probably more capable than
mine. But before a Grand Master relinquishes the oriental chair to his
successor it becomes his duty to make a report of all his official acts
during his tenure of office and to make such recommendations as may
seem to him expedient and for the best interests of the craft. In keeping
with that requirement of the law I present this written message for
your consideration.
·
Whether or not I have u sed the authority with which ·you invested
me, wisely and in accordance with Masonic principles and customs is
for you to decide. I am aware that the goal of accomplishment which
I set for myself at the beginning of the year was not attained and many
things w hich I desired and fully expected to do, have been left undone.
Because of the many restrictions imposed by reas~n of the war, the
lack of help in my business and a desire to preserve my health, it was not
possible for me to visit all the districts of the jurisdiction, much to my
regret. I have, however, attended all the annual breakfast meetings held
by the several Boards of Relief and Employment Services throughout the
jurisdiction and have visited as many· of the districts as time, health and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

501

general conditions would permit. In all I made more than 120 visitations
and traveled between twenty-five and thirty thousand miles.
State of the Craft
_I ~m. ple~se~ to report that, in my judgment the craft throughout the
1s m a healthy condition. During my travels I have been
pnv1leged to meet and observe the officers of many of our Lodges and
~ene~ally speakin~, h~ve found them to be .men of more than average
mtelhgence, conscientious, and sincere in their desires to serve the best
interests of Masonry.
.

JU~1~d1chon

However, in some of the Lodges this is not the ' case and too often

! ~a~~ f?und men ser_v_ing as Masters who appear to be utterly lacking

m 1mhahve or the ab1hty to properly guide the destinies of a Lodge.

I unh~sitatingly make the statement that, in my opinion the custom
followed m many of the Lodges of appointing a brother to the office of
Junio_r Steward and allowing him to believe that, in seven or eight years
he will be elected Master, is to blame for this condition.
I fully realize and appreciate that, in Masonry we meet upon the
level and that distinctions among brethren should not exist. I know
that every member of a Lodge, whose dues are paid and against whom
no charges. are pending, is eligible to hold any office in the Lodge; but
I also realize that the conferring of this honor should depend upon the
ability as well as the eligibility of the individual.
Too often we find men who have been appointed to one of the lower
offices, because of friendship on the part of the Master or as a reward
for some service to the Lodge. Neither the Master nor the brethren have
had any previous opportunity to observe the brother in office and do not
know whether or not he will be successful as an officer, but because of the
custom now in vogue, he is allowed to continue and each succeeding
Master appoints him to a higher station, whether ·he is qualified or not.
No Master should presume to speak for his successors and allow an
appointee to believe that he is being started through the chairs. He
should be informed that the appointment is for ihe current year only and
that the next Master may exercise his right to appoint whomsoever he
pleases to serve with him in the chairs. I feel that it should be made perfectly clear that the appointive officers serve at the will and pleasure of
the Master and that the offices up to and including that of Senior Deacon
are proving grounds upon which to try out future Masters. Under this
system it would not mean that because a brother served in one of the
appointive offices, he would be denied the honor of becoming Master,
but on the contrary it would be an added incentive for him to give his
best efforts to the Lodge, with the realization that the Mastership is
something to strive for and an honor given only to those who have
earned it and have proven their ability to discharge the important duties
of that office.
We find altogether too many Masters ~ho believe that the ritual is
the alpha and omega of Masonry. In their opinion the only qualification
necessary is near perfection in the ritualistic ceremonies of the degrees
and that the larger the class of candidates, the greater the success of the
year.
One who has spent as many years as I in teaching the ritual of our
order, could not help . but have a true appreciation of its beauty and im-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

portance to Masonry. It cannot be denied that, when properly and impressively rendered, it is inspiring and enlightening to all who witness it
and that by it we are enabled to im~art many valuable truths concerning
the fraternity and inform the novitiate of those underlying principles upon
which Masonry is erected. To the candidate, during the time of his initiation, passing and raising, it is the most important function of the Lodge
-for him it is a vehicle by means of which he attains an ambition-that
of becoming a member of the fraternity. Rightly does he consider it the
means to an end-the mearts to enter the fraternity that he might be
taught more about those divine principles, the practice of which has
made Masonry lead the way through the ages and become a powerful
force for good in practically every civilized community of the world. But,
to his disappointment he often finds thM the ritual is not only the beginning but the end so far as instruction is concerned. He is invested with
the secrets of a Master Mason and then forgotten while the Lodge turns
its attention to the next candidate. He comes to Lodge a few times to
enjoy the beauties of the degrees and, tiring of .t he same performance,
soon becomes one of the absent members--only a name upon the books
of the Lodge.

Grand Master in 1912. He presided over this Grand Lodge at the sixtyfourth annual communication in 1913.

502

The average man petitions for the degrees in earnest search for light
and knowledge, of which he thinks we are possessed and he has a perfect
right to expect that this information will be imparted to him. He expects
to find fellowship and the opportunity to ·mingle with his brethren. Where
a Lodge does nothing but confer degrees to the exclusion of all else, ~he
regularity alone becomes monotonous and there you find the reason for
the oft repeated complaint "we can't get the members to attend Lodge."
I do not think that a Lodge should be a one-man affair. No man is
big enough to put over a show in which he is the only actor. I have
suggested to many Masters that they appoint an advisory committee to
assist in planning the meetings and activities of the Lodge. This committee should consist of the officers, in order that they may have first
hand knowledge of what is going on and it might well include several
members from the side lines who, if given the opportunity, will usually
be found willing and anxious to serve the Lodge. It has been proven
over and over again that members will attend if they are given something
worthwhile in addition to degrees.
Necrology
It is with sincere sorrow that I report to you that again the hand of
death has removed from our midst many old friends and brothers. The
Committee on Necrology will conduct an appropriate service in memory
of those who will meet with us no more and it is not my intention to
eulogize any of those brethren here except to call your attention to .the
loss of three officers of Grand Lodge who have laid aside the working
tools of the craft.
Hardly had the new Masonic year gotten under way, when the news
reached me of the .death of Most Worshipful William Parker Filmer,
Grand Treasurer. Although "Billy" as he was affectionately called by his
many friends, had been in . poor health for some time, nevertheless . the
news of his passing came as a great shock. He was a tower of strength
in this Grand Lodge and in the Southern Jurisdiction of the Ancient &
Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, where he held the high office of
Lieutenant Grand Commander and Inspector General for California. He
was third in seniority among the .P ast Grand. Masters, having been elected

During his year as Grand Master, the jurisdiction suffered the loss

unanimously elected Grand Treasurer, in which position he served with
distinction for thirty years, until · death drew the curtain on a long and
faithful Masonic career.
I convened the Grand Lodge in the Temple in San Francisco for the
purpose of conducting the funeral services of this much beloved man and
Mason. The esteem in which lre was held ·and the affection with which
he was regarded, not alone by his brethren of the craft, but by all who
knew him, was shown by the attendance of more than five hundred
persons from all walks and stations of life.

Consolidation of Lodges
During the latter part of the year I approved the consolidation of two
of our Lodges; Welcome Lodge No. 255 at L emoore, and Riverdale
Lodge No. 496 at Riverdale. The Lodge is now known as Welco~e
Lodge No. 255, having chosen the name and number of the older I,,.odge.
I heartily favor consolidation where Lodges are situated close to each
other and where the membership in either one or both is not large enough
to make for a strong, effective organization. I feel that it is preferable
to have a smaller number of strong Lodges than a larger number of
weak ones. There are several Lodges in the jurisdiction that should
seriously consider consolidation.
Transfer of Trial
Charges were preferred against a Past Master of La Parfaite Union
Lodge No. 17 by the Junior Warden of the Lodge. Because of the
nature of the charges and the possibility that prejudice against the accused
might prevent a fair trial, the Master requested a transfer to some other
Lodge. I granted the request and transferred the trial to Starr King
Lodge No. 344.
Institution of New Lodge in China

In the late summer of 1942 Grand Master Frank M. Smith received
a· request from a group of Masons in the south of China to grant a dispensation to form and open a Lodge of Masons, under the Jurisdiction of
the Grand Lodge of California. The request was made by cable and did
not contain sufficient information to justify the Grand Master in granting
the request.
In Janu~ry of this year the request was again made, stating the
matter had firs t been taken up with the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands and that they had been assured by that Grand Lodge that the
request was being considered favorably. Before action could be taken,
Pearl Harbor had been attacked and immediately thereafter, cpmmunica-

The Grand Secretary and I had the opportunity of talking with
Worshipful George A. Fitch, Past Master and the Master-elect of the
proposed Lodge. After going into the matter thoroughly with Brother
Fitch, we were both convinced that a real need for a Masonic Lodge
existed and under date of Ma.rch 27, 1943, I caused to be issued a dispensation to form and open a Lodge in the city of Chungking, China, to
be known as Fortitude Lodge, U. D.
Under the dispensation I named Worshipful Brother George A.
Fitch, Past Master, as the first Master; Brother David Kiang, to be the
first Senior Warden and Brother Peter Kiang to be the first Junior
Warden. Brother Colonel M. B. DePass, Jr., military attache of the
United States Embassy at Chungking. and a Past Master was commissioned Inspector of the new district, to be known as the I 18th Masonic
District.
'
At my request the Lodge was duly instituted and the officers installed
i>Y the Inspector.

Shortly after the outbreak of the war, this Grand Lodge instituted a
plan to accept the dues of members of the Philippine Island Lodges, thereby keeping them in good standing and assuring the Grand Lodge of that
jurisdiction a new start, both in members and money, upon which to rebuild what the war has destroyed. ·As the formation of this new Lodge
in China was considered favorably by that Grand Lodge, I granted the
dispensation from California as a further service to them.
It is ~y· recommendation that the Lodge be continued under dispensation for the duration of the war and that no charter be granted by this
Grand Lodge, but that, when the Philippine Grand Lodge again becomes
active, we surrender to them all claims upon the new Lodge and let
them determine its future.

Contributions from the War Relief Fund
A request was made by the brethren of Fortitude Lodge, U . D., in
. Chungking, China, for the sum of twenty-five hundred dollars to feed
and care for the starving and unfortunate Masons in the south of China.
I requested the Gran'd Secretary to forward that amount to them, through
the San Francisco Branch of the Bank of Canton.
I also requested that a contribution of twenty-five hundred dollars be
made to the American R,ed Cross and that five thousand dollars be contributed to the United Service Organization on behalf of the Lodges
and brethren of the jurisdiction of California.
I feel that these contributions are in perfect keeping with the war
relief effort of this Grand Lodge, and the purposes for which this money
is being used is certainly for needs or emergencies brought about by the
war.
There can be no question about the starving Masons in China. These
men and their families have been driven from pillar to post by the ruthless invaders of that country and have lost th eir homes, their businesses
and their fortunes. Surely, money from this fund or the general funds of
Grand Lodge could not serve a greater need.

office of the Grand Secretary, the names of nearly nine thousand Cali-

Sotoyome Lodge No. 123
Several years ago, a Brother Bush, Past Master of Sotoyome Lodge
offered to deed the Temple, which he owned, to the Lodge, provided the
Lodge would pay him $250 per month, for life and in the event of his
death, the payment to be made to his . widow, as long as she should live.
The Lodge agreed to this arrangement and a contract was duly
executed. Payments were made to Brother Bush, as agreed and since
his death have been made regularly to his widow.
At the time the agreement was made the building was in good condition and the lower floor was bringing in a substantial rental. Since that
time, however, the tenants have moved and the building is now in need
of repairs, which the Lodge is not financially able to make.
·
Mrs. Bush, being informed of the financial condition of the Lodge,
agreed to accept a reduced payment of $125.00 per month. This payment
was continued until the Lodge had practically exhausted its funds, when
it appealed to the Grand Master for assistance.
I enlisted the aid of the Grand Treasurer and after a thorough investigation on his part, he recommended that Grand Lodge come to the
assistance of this Lodge financially. He ascertained from Mrs. Bush, now
in her eighty-third year, that she was dependent upon the payments from
the Lodge .for her livelihood, ·but that she would be willing to accept
$150.00 per month, if she could be assured that the payments would
continue. She felt that this amount would cover her actual expenses.

Hawaiian Island Lodges

Although the agreement was not made by the present members of
the Lodge, it is nonetheless binding upon them and constitutes, not only
a financial responsibility, but a moral obligation . as well. If Sotoyome
Lodge should fail to satisfy this just claim, it would reflect not, upon
the Lodge alone, but would be held against the entire fraternity by the
residents of Healdsburg. I feel that the brethren of the Lodge are to
be commended for the fine spirit they have shown and to Mrs. Bush, we
are indebted for her generous cooperation.

California Masonry has reason to be proud of the eight Lodges in
the Hawaiian Islands. Though situated in the theatre of war, they have
continued to function without interruption and have carried high the
banner of Masonry. They have taken part in all the. war activities of
this Grand Lodge and were among the first to go "over the top."

I authorized the. Grand Secretary to forward the sum of $150.00 each
month to Sotoyome Lodge, with the understanding that the Lodge would
repay Grand Lodge at the rate of $50.00 per month as long as Mrs. Bush
shall live and thereafter until the entire amount has been repaid, I now
ask the Grand Lodge to approve this action.

Realizing that these Lodges are working under military rule 'a nd must
obey immediately any order issued to them, I felt the necessity of having
a representative to whom all 'matters, requiring immediate action, could
be referred. In many cases time would not permit the Lodges to communicate with the Grand Master or Grand Secretary.
I appointed Worshipful Alexander Douglas Potts, Inspector of the
103rd district and Grand Standard Bearer of the Grand Lodge as the
special representative of the Grand Master, with power to issue dispensations and keep a watchful eye over the affairs of the_ Lodges.
This authority in no way affected the authority of Worshipful Charles
A. Shepherd, Inspector of the 102nd District, except in matters that
would ordinarily require the attention or approval of the Grand Master.
To both these brethren I express my deep appreciation for their

War Relief Fund
At this ti.m e this message was written the War Relief Fund had
reached a total of $127,573.00, a truly magnificent accomplishment and
surpassing the goal which was set at the time the fund was started. You
will recall that the goal was one dollar per member and at that time
our membership was 125;843. Our membership July. 31, 1942, was 126,313
and that has been passed. Our membership today is 129,509 and we are
within striking distance of that goal.
This is an accomplishment of which the members and the Lodges may
well be proud and those few Lodges which have declined to participate
will regret in future years that their names were not included with the
·Lodges providing so helpful a service during this war.

A part of this fund is on deposit with the eighteen Boards of Relief
of this jurisdiction and with practically every Grand Lodge of the world,
to be made available to any California Mason with the armed forces of
the country, any place in the world, who may be in need and to t)1e

It is impossible to say how much of the fund has been used to date in

been possible, but we can be proud of the fact that Masonry in this jurisdiction has suffered no Mason in uniform or the members of his family to
want for anything in our power to give. The service we are rendering is
purely M asonic and is not a duplication of the efforts of any other organization. Its effect will be lasting in the minds of those whom we are
privileged to help and will redound to the credit of the fraternity through

I feel that the time of greatest need has not yet come, but as the
war continues and wounded men are returned to our shores in ever increasing numbers, our service to them will nat~rally increase.
When the war is finally won and our boys return to peaceful pursuits,
Masonry must lend a helpful hand to reestablish our own and to assist in
the rehabilitation of thousands of our members who may find it extremely
difficult fo adjust themselves to the sudden transition from war to peace.
Apart from contributions to organizations from this fund, and the
money used for relief, the fund has been drawn upon for administrative
expenses. It has been necessary from the beginning to inform the Lodges
what the program was and to get that information to the individual members in order to raise the fund.
In this connection I caused four Grand Lodge Bulletins and other
promotional materials to be issued to · the entire membership during the
course of the year. The volume of records, clerical work and correspondence necessary to successfully conduct a fund raising ~ camP,aign of
this proportion, and the war program which it supports, obviously required
the employment of additional people in the Grand Lodge office.
The total cost of all promotion, all administrative expenses including
equipment, typewriters, filing cabinets, etc., for the period since the war
began has been but $15,423.19. The essential thing to remember in this
connection is that without taking one cent from the reserves of Grand
Lodge a satisfactory fund has been raised, a satisfactory program has
been carried forward, every call upon this Grand Lodge has been met
and there is of this date in excess of $100,000 new money on hand available to meet such demands as may be made upon us.
I am sure that no one can consider this cost disproportionate when
they realize that the program is now set-up so that the entire fund can
be used for the purposes for which it was . raised, with little additional
expense.
Appeal to Limit Delegates
Due to the congestion on the railroads and bus lines of the country
and the request, by the government and military authorities, that civilian
travel be limited, I issued the following letter to the Lodges of the
jurisdiction.

509
August 16, 1943.

To My Brethren, Greetings:
We all appreciate the fine job that the railroads of the country are
doing in the transporting of troops and needed supplies; we realize the
importance of getting these supplies and men to the places :where they
will do the most good in the shortest possible time; we know that thousands of men in uniform are using every means of travel to return home
for a brief visit before going " over there" and that other thousands cif
mothers and wives are traveling over the country to be with their sons
?r husbands, maybe for the last time . .
We know these things and we heartily approve. We realize that the
man in uniform must come first and civilian travel must be limited.
The successful conduct of the war is the first consideration of all of
us and must take precedence. The part which we have had in the war
effort has been a large one and we must meet to plan for a greater participation during the coming year. This and other business considerations
make the holding of our annual business meeting imperative.
I would like to see every Master, Warden and Past Master at Grand
Lodge this year, but I know that is neither possible nor advisable.
Transportation facilities are already strained to the limit. Because of
this condition I ask the Lodges of the jurisdiction to send only one
.representative to Grand Lodge this year. This will not only show that
we are cooperating with the government, but will make. it possible for
all Lodges to be represented at the annual communication.
The presence of Grand Lodge officers, Past Grand Masters, Inspectors
and Grand Lodge committeemen is necessary for the proper conduct of
Grand Lodge and their presence is requested in addition to the Lodge
representative.
I ruggest that all who expect to attend the coming communication,
within the limits as outlined above, secure their travel and hotel reservations as soon as possible.
Remember, if your Lodge sends more than one representative, it may
mean that some other Lodge will not be represented.

Attest:

Cordially and sincerely,
LESLIE E. Woon, Grand Master.
LLOYD E. WILSON, Grand Secretary.

I now express my appreciation to the Lodges for their splendid response to this appeal.
Vacanies in O ffice
With approximately nine thousand of our members in the armed forces
of the country, it is only natural that many Lodge officers should pe
among them. In the majority of cases, the vacancies thus created have
been filled by appointment or s pecial elections, held under dispensation.
In some instances, however, the · offices· have been Jeff vacant so that the
regular officers might step .back into the line when :they return. This is
being done as a compliment to those men who are ·serving their country
and to assure them of the opportunity to continue in their travels toward
the East.
I fully appreciate the sacrifices being made by these brethren and
would not suggest anything that would deprive them of the pleasure and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

honor of ultimately serving their Lodges as Masters, but the can of
country must come first and for a time, they have exchanged the tools
of Masonry for the implements of war. We do not know how long the
war will last or when they will return to us, but we may be reasonably
, assured that some of them never will come back. ·

"We do not make Masons. We can only confer the degrees. Granting
that the teachings of Masonry will make a good man better, it quite
naturally fonows that men must come to us with a desire for the knowledge we have to impart and a sincere desire to be helpful to their fellow
creatures or the mere rendition of the ritual will have no effect and they
will no more be Masons than they were before receiving the degrees.

510

Mason~y has undertaken a great responsibility in its wa; program and
success depends upon the cooperation of every Lodge as wen as each
individual member. Unity and strength are needed now more than ever
before and Lodges must be manned by a fun corps of officers, if they
are to carry their share of the load.
Cases have been reported to me where the Master and both Wardens
have been inducted into the service. It does not require much imagination
to foresee what would happen to these Lodges if the stations were not
properly fined.
Masonry and what it stands for are among those things for which
our brethren are fighting and dying. It is a part of our job to carry on at
home-to preserve those ideals and principles which we hold so dearto keep Masonry strong and our Lodges active and alive to the needs of
the hour. These things our brethren expect of us and have a right to
ask. We cannot fail.
I do not believe that service to one's country will deprive any brotl;ier
of the privilege of serving Masonry. I feel that the right time to show
our appreciation is when they return. They have a prior claim on the
offices they vacated to serve their country and humanity and I cannot
believe that any Lodge would fail to put them back in the line. In the
meantime I strongly urge the Lodges to keep an stations fined.
Dispensations
When I assumed the office of Grand Master; one year ago, I realized
that I had many things to do, but that two jobs of major importan.ce
could not be overlooked or neglected. Masonry must be kept in line with
the war effort and the hysteria, which always sweeps through a nation
in · time of war, must not be anowed to take hold of our fraternity.
We have approved requests for approximately fifteen hundred
courtesy degrees for other jurisdictions. This is a service we are glad to
perform for our sister jurisdictions and their members who find themselves within our borders. In a few instances other jurisdictions have
elected men to membership who have become residents of California and
these requests for courtesy degrees have been denied.
I have granted only three dispensations to waive the investigation on
candidates in the service or about to enter the service and these requests
were approved only because the candidates were personally known by
all the members of the Lodge.
A surprising number of requests have been made to waive investigation on service men who have been in California only a short time and
could not possibly be known by the members of the Lodges. In one
instance I was asked to waive the residential requirements and the investigatibn on· a soldier from the eastern part of the country who had
been in the jurisdiction of the Lodge less than two months. The Master
of the Lodge admitted that the request was made because the candidate
was a soldier.
I dealt with this matter in the March issue of the Grand Lodge bunetin
and it might be wen to repeat my statement at this time.

511

"While we all have. the greatest respect and admiration for the uniforms of the fighting forces of -the nation, we must realize that we are
not electing uniforms to membership. We must investigate the men who
wear them and make sure that they are worthy of the privileges they
seek. This is also true of the many men now working in defense industries. Let us not consider their p·resent occupations or the size of
their pay checks as qualifications for admission.
"Masonry has gone through many wars. It will survive this one. Let
us guard our portals so that, when sanity and justice again return to
the world we will have strengthened rather than weakened our beloved
order."
If we, the Masons of today do not keep our eyes on the doors of
our Lodges and our feet solidly on the ground, then may almighty God
pity the Masonry of tomorrow.

Decisions·
I was asked if it were possible for a man to present a petition to a
Lodge when he was not personally known to any of the members.
I answered that it is not the intention of our laws to make it impossible for one to petition for the degrees because he is not known
by the members. I felt that it would be no violation of the law for any
member· of the Lodge to sign his p.etition as a recommendor, after first
having made a careful investigation to ascertain if the petitioner was
worthy of the privilege he sought.

II
At the last communication of the Grand Lodge the following resolution was adopted.
"Be it resolved that, at the communication of the Grand Lodge of
California, held October 13-17, A. L. 5942 in the City of San Francisco,
California, it is and shall be declared the purpose of said Grand Lodge
of California to include in its category of Masons employed in the armed
forces of the United States, any and all such Masons in good standing
as are now, or hereafter may be, employed in the service of the United
States Merchant Marine, provided such Mason has joined the United
States Merchant Marine since December 7, 1941."
"Be it further resolved that the Grand Secretary shall be so informed
and instructed to issue to such members of the United States Merchant
Marine all and· every emolument as is now, or is to be, issued to members
of the armed forces of the United States."
I was asked, if under the provisions of this resolution, a Lodge could
receive a dispensation to act upon the petition of a member of the Merchant Marine, who does not possess the necessary qualifications of residence.
I gave as my ·interpretation of the resolution, that members of the
United States Merchant Marine were to be considered in the same category

512

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

as members of the armed forces of the United States so far as any
remuneration or relief is concerned. That they would be entitled to
receive from the Grand Secretary the same certificate of membership
issued to members of the armed forces and could properly receive the
benefits of the War Relief Fund of Grand Lodge, but that the resolution
did not, in any way, abrogate the provisions of the constitution and that,
under Sections 213 and 216 of the ordinances, the Grand Master has no
authority to issue such dispensation.

III
An application for membership was received from one who had lived
in California for seven years but had resided in the jurisdiction of the
Lodge less than six months. He being a member of the armed forces
of the United States, the Lodge, by appropriate action, requested a dispensation to waive the residence requirements, which request was granted
and the application was received by the Lodge.
Later the applicant wrote the Lodge that it would be impossible for
him to receive the degrees and asked that the application be withdrawn
and the fees returned.
·
An argument was advanced that, because of a technicality it might
be possible to withdraw the application. That the fact that a dispensation
was requested and granted would, on the face of it indicate that the applicant was disqualified because of the lack of residence before the dispensation was granted. The technical question was whether or not the
dispensation gave him the qualifications of residence or whether it merely
set the requirement aside. That if the latter was the case, it might be
construed to mean that he never had residence qualifications and on
such grounds the · application could be withdrawn.
I held that it was true that the applicant did not possess the necessary
qualifications of residence and that the dispensation did not give him
that qualification, but certain powers are vested in the Grand Master,
among them the authority to grant dispensations to receive the applications of members of the armed forces of the United States, who do not
possess the qualifications of residence and that such dispensation rendered
the qualification unnecessary. That, by virtue of the dispensation, the.
application had been regularly received by the Lodge and could not be
withdrawn, except in accordance with Section 227.
IV
A Lodge submitted for approval a resolution to change its meeting
night. The resolution provided that, when the meeting fell on a holiday
it would be held the following Tuesday or Wednesday, according to the
night they could get the Lodge Hall. It ·further provided that the amendment would be effective only during the year 1943.
·
I answered that the resolution could not be approved because it did
not provide a specific day for the stated meetings of the Lodge and secondly, a provision in the by-laws could not be made pperative for a limited
time only. That a Lodge could, at any time, by appropriate action,
amend its by-laws, but once an amendment had been made and approved by the Grand Lodge or the Grand Master, it was effective from
then on unless again amended by the Lodge.

case. He was finally removed to a hospital where it was discovered that

A Lodge asked approval of a proposed change in their by-laws to
lower the fees from twelve dollars to nine dollars per year. The amendment also provided that dues should be paid annually in advance instead
of .q uarterly, as provided in the Uniform Code of By-Laws Section

VII
The Grand Secretary requested a ruling as to whether or not it is
proper for a Lodge to request a proficiency diploma and for the Grand
Secretary to issue it to a member of a California Lodge who has been
examined in a Lodge in another jurisdiction and has been declared proficient by that Lodge.
·
I held that if the member was examined by the Lodge of another jurisdiction at the request of the California Lodge to which he belongs, it
wnuld be perfectly proper to issue the certificate. When a Lodge of
another jurisdiction confers the degrees on a candidate as a courtesy to
one of our Lodges we do not question the fact that he has been regularly
made a Mason. Neither should we refuse to accept their statement that
he has shown the necessary proficiency in the lecture of the third degree.

VIII
It was reported to me that last year one of our Lodges . held a dinner
and entertainment, where there appeared various radio and vaudeville
stars. Tickets were sold for $1.25 each upon the representation that the
proceeds were to be turned over to the Masonic Home for Children at
Covina. Approximately $85.00 or $90.00 was taken in which was subsequently turned over to ·the Home.
This year they proposed to hold a similar event in the Shrine Auditorium and to ask the other Lodges of the city to join with them. They
planned to have not only radio and vaudeville stars but movie stars and
the Philharmonic Orchestra and to sell tickets in sufficient numbers to
fill the auditorium, which seats approximately 10,000 persons, advertising
to the public that the profits would go to the Masonic Homes of California.
I wrote that it is not proper for a Masonic Lodge to sell tickets to
the public for any function and certainly would nQt be in keeping with
the dignity of Masonry to advertise a show to raise funds for a Masonic
charity. .That Masonic charity begins and ends with its members and
I sincerely hoped the time would never come when the fraternity must
ask non-members to assist in our benevolent work.

During my absence from. the jurisdiction, the following letter was
referred to the Deputy Grand Master.
"Does the request for restoration after being suspended more than two
years have to be referred to a committee? . . . How are we to know
that during the time of his suspension he had not served time in ·prison
or had committeed some other Masonic offense?"
"We find nothing to obligate the Lodge to have an investigating
committee."
The Deputy Grand Master gave the following answer in which I
concur:
"I have gone over Section 260 of the Ordinances and must agree with
you that there is no provision for the appointment of a committee to
investigate the application of a brother who has been suspended for
more than two years.
"I do not feel, however, that the fact that there is no constitutional
provision for the appointment of a committee relieves the Master from
considering very carefully such an application. The very fact that you
are required to hold over an application until the next stated meeting,
indicates very clearly that time is ptovided for investigation or consideration.
"In most cases where the applicant is a resident of the community in
which the Lodge is located, he is undoubtedly well known and the members can very readily make up their minds as to whether or not they
wish to restore him. In other cases where the applicant has not been
a resident of the jurisdiction of the Lodge for some time, it might be
somewhat difficult to find out about the conduct of the member during
the time of his suspension.
"I feel that it is definitely the responsibility of the Master to protect
his Lodge · by instituting such an investigation as may be practical. He
may either appoint a committee to investigate and report or he may
request a Lodge where the suspended brother now resides to investigate,
or he may require the bro~her to make a statement as to what he has
been doing during the period of suspension, which statement may be
supported by references to persons who can support the statement.
"I feel that it is entirely proper for you to raise this question, but I
do believe that the mere absence of constitutional requirement does not
relieve either the Master or the Lodge from satisfying themselves fully
before voting on such application."

seventy years.
There is no question but that the men in the armed forces are rendering a spe.cial service not only to their Lodges but to all humanity, but I

XIV
There have been presented to me so many questions relative to <limits
that it has seemed wise to group the various situations and the rulings
which I have made on them. The questions concerned the requirement
that dues be paid three months in advance and interpretations of this
part of the law have most frequently been requested.
Case 1. I was asked if the three months in advance dates from the
date the application for affiliation accompanied by the .REQUEST FOR
DIMIT is signed by the applicant, or from the date of the stated meetihg

517

I held that dues must be paid at least three months in advance from
the date of the stated meeting at which the application for affiliation,
accompanied by the REQUEST FOR DIMIT, is presented to the
Lodge.
Case 2. I was asked if three months in advance sfiould be construed literally to mean from the first day of the first month in the
quarter, or from the date of the stated meeting of that month.
I held that it must be construed literally to mean the first day of the
first month of the quarter.
Case 3. A member of Lodge "A" whose dues were paid to December 1, 1942, applied for affiliation in Lodge "B" at the October stated
meeting, and signed a REQUEST FOR DIMIT.
I held that his dues were not paid three months in advance.
In this connection I was asked if°it was necessary that the REQUEST
FOR DTMIT be read at a stated meeting before it could be issued, and
I held that it must be so read.
I was also asked what the situation would be if Lodge "B" was
dilatory in the matter and did not forward the REQUEST FOR DIMIT
to Lodge "A" in time for them to take action. I held that if at the time
Lodge "A" received the REQUEST FOR DIMIT in January the member was not in good standing, the DIMIT could not be issued. I further
held that he must pay dues for the next quarter in order to be in standing
at their stated meeting in January.
·
Case 4. A member of Lodge "A" whose dues were paid to December 1, 1942, applied for affiliation in Lodge "B" subsequent to the
stated meeting of October, and prior to the November stated meeting,
and signed a REQUEST FOR DIMIT.
I held that his dues were not paid three months in advance.
I was asked if he might pay for one additional month in order to
have his dues paid three months in advance, and I held that under our
law dues must be paid quarterly in advance, and that the applicant would
have to pay for the first quarter of 1943, or until March 31st.
Case 5. In case 4 it was pointed out that the applicant whose dues
were paid to March 31, 1943, might be elected at the December stated
meeting and become a member of Lodge "B" either in December or
January. I was asked when his dues would become payable in Lodge "B".
There are two situations to be considered in answering.
Member "X" elected at the December stated meeting filed his DIMIT
with his application for affiliation , and his dues commenced January 1st.
Member "Y" filed a REQUEST FOR DIMIT with his application
for affiliation and the DIMIT was received at the January stated meeting,
and his dues commenced February 1st.

In answer to the statement that he would then be paying in two
Lodges at the same time, one of which he was not a member, I held
that his obligation was to Lodge "B" and that that Lodge was not concerned with any settlement he might, or might not be able to make with
Lodge "A" for the return of dues paid in advance.

It is somewhat surpnsmg and certainly gratifying to look back over

"I quote from the last paragraph of a decision by Grand Master Ross,

Recommendations
With practically the entire world at war to determine whether men
shall remain free or become the slaves of dictators, having the power of
life ·and death, it is gratifying_ to know that the principles and teachings
of Masonry are still commending themselves to men. But with the unprecedented number of petitions being presented to 01;1r Lodges it might
be well for us to pause and take stock.
Many men are applying for the privileges of Masonry who have no
conception of what it is or what it stands for. They only know that it
is the largest as well as the oldest and most honorable of fraternal organizations and that a certain prestige is attached to membership therein.
Their petitions are presented, not with the thought that they may be
useful to the craft and their fellow-men, but are prompted by selfish
desires to get what they can out of ·it without giving anything in return.
Many of these men are gaining admission because the investigation was
slip-shod or incomplete or some brother did not possess the fortitude to
refuse to sign their petitions or for the reason that the Lodge is overly
anxious to build up a large membership. The reasons are many and
varied but regardless of the cause, the effect is always the same; the
lowering of our standards of membership.
Masonry has been handed down to· us through the ages, not as our
exclusive property, to do with as we see fit, but ours only for the short
span of our lives; to practice and enjoy and then to pass on to succeeding
generations in all its beauty; in possession of all its strength and splendor.
It should be our determination to so live our lives, that Masonry shall
not suffer because of our membership but, on the contrary that our
efforts in its behalf may add something beneficial to it. This is the rule

.b.y which a sincere Mason measures himself. Surely, then,· he has the
. ;1ght to a~p.ly that same rule to any other man who seeks a participation
m our privileges and if he does not measure up to that standard, he
should not be elected to membership. If Masonry is to continue to play

m all ages past, 1t will be becau·se this and future generations of Masons
