'
I requested the Grand Secretary to send a questionnaire to all Lodges
in the jurisdiction to ascertain how many Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts are being carried on the rolls of the Lodges, who have been stopped
by Lodge action. As of September first, with approximately three-fourths
of the reports returned, there were more than eight hundred.
I call your attention to the laws of this Grand Lodge. That before
initiation, a candidate can be rejected by any member of the Lodg; merely
by making an objection to the Master. After a candidate has been
initiated, this is not the case. The objection must be stated to the
Master and if the cause seems insufficient to him, he shall state the
matter to the Lodge at the next stated meeting and the Lodge shall then
decide, whether or not further investigation shall be made. After the
investigation, the matter is again presented to the Lodge and the Lodge
decides whether or not the candidate shall be permitted to advan.ce. ·
I can understand how one man might make an invalid objection, but
when the matter has been reviewed by a Lodge and after careful investigation it is decided that the candidate shall not proceed, it must be admitted that the objection is valid and the candidate is unworthy to become
a Mason. In the case of the more than eight hundred Entered Apprentices
and Fellowcrafts now being carried on the rolls of our Lodges, perhaps
some of them did not desire to proceed further, and stopped of their
own volition, but they form a very small percentage of the total. In the
great majority of cases they have been stopped becau'se some brother has
entered an objection and the qbjection has been sustained by the Lodge.
Then we must admit that, if they were found unworthy of advancement,.
they must have been unworthy at the time they were elected and initiated
or passed, but no objection was made because the membership generally
did not know that their applications had been received.
It has often been said that, if a member desires to know what is going
on in his Lodge, he should attend its meetings. It is even pointed out
that it is his duty to do so. It has been further argued that the membe.rs
should know who is applying for the degrees. During this year it has
been necessary for me to be away from my home a large part of the time.
I have not attended the meetings of my Lodge with any degree of
regularity, because I have not be~n at home on the nights they have been
held. Can it be said that I have no right to know what is going on in
my Lodge; that it is none of my business who have presented applications
to my Lodge, because I was not present to hear them read by the Secretary? I contend that any member, whether he attends his Lodge or not,
so long as he keeps himself in good standing, is entitled to know who is
asking for admission, and he certainly has the right to pass on the eligibility of applicants and to object to the admission of those, who in his
opinion have no place in our fraternity.
When an application is presented to a Lodge it is read by the Secretary
to perhaps . twenty per cent of the members, who happen to be present
at the time. It is then referred to a committee of three men for investigation. Let us assume that the committee conscientiously and carefully

522

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

investigated to the best of its ability, and finding · nothing detrimental to
the character of the applicant, renders a full and favorable report to the
Master. This fact is then reported to the Lodge and the brethren cast
their ballots and the appl~cant is elected solely on the report of the threeman committee. At least seventy-five or eighty per cent of the _members
know nothi~g of the application. Later, one of the absentee brothers discovers that the candidate has been elected, initiated and perhaps passed
to the degree of Fellowcraft. Knowing something against the candidate
• that the committee of investigation failed to discover, which would make
him unworthy to become a Mason, the brother objects to his further
advancement. The objection is upheld by the Lodge and the candidate
is stopped. If the objector had known of the reception of the application or
had heard about it before initiation, he would doubtless have made the
objection at that time and the candidate would have been rejected. But
because this fact is not made known to the entire membership we are
carrying the names of hundreds of men upon our rolls who are n"o t
worthy of the. honors we have conferred upon them. Masonry can mean
nothing to them and their membership in the fraternity can mean nothing
to us, except as an object lesson, that we are too lax in our investigation
of candidates. If the time ever comes when Masonry ceases to be 'attractive to good men, it will be because we have allowed too many men of
questionable character. and integrity to affiliate with us. We have made
it too ea'sy to become members and we have admitted too many members
who will never become Masons.
I recommend that our Lodges be required to notify their member.s of
all applications for the degrees or for affiliation, within ten days after their
reception by the Lodge. That the notice shall carry the full names, residence and business addresses and the age and occupations of the
applicants.
·
This may be new to California Masonry, but it is not an innovation,
as this practice has been followed by several of the largest jurisdictions
of the United States, inch:1ding New York,. Massachussetts and Pennsylvania, together with every Grand Lodge in the Dominion of Canada and
many of the G'r and Lodges of the world. If a candidate is passed upon
by every member of the Lodge and is elected, we may feel assured that
·he is worthy and well qualified. If he cannot pass this test, Masonry will
be better off without him.
Section 100 of the constitution provides for a contribution of $25.00 for
the use and benefit of the Masonic Homes of California. Said amount to
be paid by each applicant for the degrees and by each applicant for
affiliation, unless such contribution has ·previously been made upon a
former application either for the degrees or affiliation, to a Lodge in this
jurisdiction. This section further provides that contributions collected
by the Lodges shall be transmitted to the Grand Secretary on the first
day of November, February, May and August, subsequent to the initiation
of applicants for degrees or the election of applicants for affiliation.
Provision is made for the return of the unused portion of fees for the
degrees in cases where the applicant dies after reciving the first degree
or the first and second degrees and al~o for the ·unused portion of the
fees where an objection has been made and sustained by the Lodge to
the passing or raising of th.e candidate. In cases such as these no provision
is made for the return of the contribution to the Masonic Homes.
·
A d~cision fo'u nd on p·a ge -215 of the R~ss Digest, approved by Grand
Lodge, specifically states that the contribution to the Masonic Homes:

cannot be returned after death of an initiate. The word "initiate" has
been defined as one who has received the first degree.

.Wh~re the fees for the degrees are $75.00, the Lodge collects $100 0 00
wh1c? incl~des ~he contribution to the Homes. It is presumed that th~
cand1dat: is. advised of the fact that he is making this contribution but
I have inqmred of many newly initiated Masons and find that the~ do
not know of the contribution but were told that the fees were $100.00 and
they naturally understood that the entire amount was for the degrees.
I do nc;>t claim that a Lodge enters into a co~tract with an applicant
when he 1.s el~cted to receive the degrees, but I do contend that an
understanding 1s had _by the. candidate that he will receive all three
de~~ees for the sum paid by him and will be entitled to all the rights and
privileges of a Master Mason.
_ Wh~re a candid~te refuses to present himself for the degrees, the Lodge
has a nght to retain the fees, but where a candidate dies before receiving
all the d~gre~s or has been stopped by action of the Lodge, I feel that
the contnbutton. to the Masonic Homes should be returned along with
the unused portion of th~ fees for t~e degrees. We have no right to
acc.e pt money fro!11 a candidate for which we give him nothing in return.
Neither he nor his dependents can be admitted to the Homes or receive
any of the benefits of Masonic charity in case of need.
It i~ c?mparable to one ordering a bill of merchandise, for which he
has paid ~n advance a~d then having the merchant inform him that he
does not intend to deliver the merchandise but that he is going to keep
the money. If. that shoul~ happen to anyone in this Grand Lodge, I am
sure a law suit would qmckly follow. Yet, in substance that is exactly
what we say to the candidate who does not receive all the degrees.
· I recornmend that the contribution to the Masonic Homes be paid
to. the Grand Secretary by the Lodges, after the applicant has been
raised to th~. degree of Master Mason and that, "in the event he dies before
he .has received that degree or has been prevented .' from receiving it by'
action of the Lodge, that it be returned.
Conclusion
. I realiz~ that it wou!d be. impossible for any Grand Master to accomplish anything wo~th:whtle without the splendid cooperation of the several

year by thes~ brethren has been of inestimable value to me and to the

I am appreciative of the many courtesies and acts of kindness shown
me by Lodge officers throughout the entire jurisdiction. The many manifestations of brotherly love have made very pleasant, what would otherwise have been a trying and difficult year.
-If the efforts of the year are deserving of any praise or commendation,
I would like it to be given to those who have earned it-my brethren of
California. A Grand Master can do nothing by himself and he cannot lead
unless the brethren are willing to follow. One of the finest things I hay_e
received this year is the friendship of so many of my brethren. I shall
keep and preserve that long after I have laid down the gavel of authority.
I have discharged the duties of this office to best of my ability, with
a full realization of my limitations. If I have made mistakes along the
way, they have been of the head and not the heart. The sweetness of the
year wilr live long in my memory and any discordant note that may
have been sounded will be forgotten. For the great honor you have
accorded me, I thank you from the depths of a grateful heart. As I pass
the gavel over to one so worthy of receiving it may I say that I do not
return to the ranks, because I never left them.
And now, my brethren, may God, in his infinite mercy watch over
you and keep you always.
Respectfully submitted,
U:sLIE E. Woon, Grand Master.

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipf1'l Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
I have the honor to present to you herewith my second annual report as
your Grand Secretary.
Last year I reported that the war had caused a vast increase in the amount
of work required of ithe office and I now report that there has been an additional increase in the year just closed.
In spite of a number of staff changes due to war conditions, we have been
able to maintain an adequate staff most of the time. It has done an excellent
job in the various duties which have arisen, both with the regular work of the
office, and with the work occasioned by the war program.
We have continued our practice of meeting with groups of secretaries
throughout the jurisdiction whenever possible and these meetings have proved
to be of great value.
During ithe year a new secretaries' association was formed in San Diego
and a meeting was held with the San Gabriel Valley secretaries, looking toward
the organization of that group. In this connection I am pleased to report that,
with buit: a few exceptions, the co-operation of the secretaries throughout the
State in all matters relating to the Grand Lodge office has been excellent and
there is a general disposition on their part to perform their work efficiently
and promptly.
War Program
One phase of war work which creates a tremendous volume of correspondence and record work is in relation to the requests for courtesy degrees.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

525

Since the war started we have received from other grand jurisdictions requests
for courtesy degrees totaling 2,274. During the same period we ourselves have
requested 823 degrees by courtesy.
We have received approximately one thousand requests per month during
the past year from other grand jurisdictions to contact their members in California in the armed forces and we have been able to follow all of these requests promptly because of the co-operation of the lodges and the inspectors.
. A~ outstanding war program of this grand jurisdiction, and again one:.
which. involves much correspondence and detailed records, is the acceptance of
dues m trust .of members of lodges in the Philippine Islands. Thus far we
have carried on correspondence with 529 different individuals and of these we
have been able to complete 466 cas~s. The remainder are pending and will no
· doubt be satisfactorily completed in due time. As shown by the audit there
was, as of July 31, 1943, $7,065.99 in the trust fund for the Grand· Lodge of
the Phillippine Islands, and as of September 28, 1943, the total is $7,502.35.
.
The. War Registration Service is another part of the war program entailmg considerable correspondence, records, and the preparation of many forms.
As of September 28, 1943, 8,866 war service certificates have been issued to
members of our lodges in the armed forces.
The preparation and distribution of the Grand Lodge Bulletin, of necessary
promotional ma~erials, the transmitting of Certificates of Merit, the receiving
of and accounting for funds, and the correspondence entailed in these functions, all essential to the successful prosecution of the Masonic War
Reli~f Fund, have been performed in the Grand Lodge office.
Lodges
One dispensation to form a new lodge was issued during the year to
Fortitude Lodge U. D., Chungking, China. The membership and financial
status of this lodge under dispensation are not included in any of the reports
herein set ·forth. Under the circumstances it has 'seemed wise to keep their
reports entirely separate, whenever they are received, since the ultimate plan
qf, the Grand Master in granting the dispensation_ was to hold the lodge and
all of its funds for final disposition by the Grand Lodge of the Philippine
Islands.
During the year there has been one consolidation, thus reducing the total
number of lodges to 581. The consolidation was between Welcome Lodge
No. 255 at Lemoore and Riverdale Lodge No. 496 at Riverdale and became
official on May 18, .1943, with the new lodge being known as Welcome Lodge
No. 255 at Lemoore.
Unfinished B usiness
The following items of unfinished business are brought forward from the
last communication:
1. Monthly membership return system, referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence for report at this communication. (Page 362-1942 Proc.)
2. The Grand Lecturer's recommendation relative to inspectoral districts in
Hawaii, referred for disposition to this communication. (Page 363-1942 Proc.)
3. Re:solution introduced by John Johnston, Past .Master and Secretary of
George Washington Lodge No. 525, to amend Sections 298 and 308 of the
Ordinances and postponed to this communication. (Page 368-1942 Proc.)
Legislation
Last year we repor~ed the inauguration of a new monthly membership
return system. At that time we did not ask for legislation because we wanted
to thoroughly test the plan out. The plan has been in operation for one full

year and iii our judgment has been highly successful. We, therefore, ask that
legisla1ion be presented officially establishing the monthly membership return
system, and in this connection we also recommend that appropriate action be
taken relative to Section 204, since special forms for restorations and suspensions will no longer be required, they being reported on the monthly membership re1urn.

Audits
Immediately following the death of the Most Worshipful William P.
Filmer, Grand Treasurer, at the direction of the Grand Master, I caused an
audit to be made of all of our accounts covering the period of August 1, 1942,
to December 31, 1942. This audit will be found elsewhere in the reports.
Under the prevailing system of auditing, the annual returns due August
15th of each year are not audited until the following August. The fw1ds
received with the annual returns this year approximated $290,000 and it seemed
to me that a supplementary audit would be in order certifying rt:o the fact that
the moneys due the Grand Lodge had been collected by the Grand Secretary
and had been properly paid over by him to the Grand Treasurer. I accordingly
made such a recommendation to the Grand Master and with his approval
caused such supplementary audit to be made, which appears elsewhere in the
records.

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & 4. M. of California:
Your Grand Treasurer succeeded the revered late Brother, Past Grand
Master and Grand Treasurer, William Parker Filmer, by appointment
of the Grand Master, November 22, 1942. Due consideration of the
interests of Grand Lodge and the responsibility of the appointed Grand
Treasurer prompted an immediate audit of the accounts and records of
the Grand Treasurer. In due course, the auditors, Ruckstell, Burrows &
Webb, submitted their reports for the five months' period from August 1
to December 31, 1942, and, as anticipated, the affairs of the office were
found to be in order.

The funds of the Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes, Endowment, War
Relief, Philippine Island dues and various trusts in custody of the Grand
Treasurer, as such, and as Treasurer of the Masonic Homes, had been
deposited in savings and commercial accounts in banks selected by my
predecessor. These depositaries have been continued. Securities in custody
of the Grand Treasurer, as such, and as Treasurer of Masonic Homes,
had been deposited under an agency account with the Anglo California
National Bank. This arrangement has been continued.
There are some clianges in the law essential to orderly and careful
transactions respecting securities and funds. Consideration of procedure
has resulted in some suggested amendment. The Grand Treasurer is a
constitutional officer of Grand Lodge and his duties are prescribed by
ordinance. Procedure related thereto was designed at a time when the
financial operations of Grand Lodge were much simpler. It would not
be possible for the Grand Treasurer to conform technically without substantial expense, particularly relating to deposit and withdrawal of funds
and payment of authorized accounts and statements. The essential mechanics of disbursement of funds may be performed in a large measure in
the office of the Grand Secretary without disturbing the practical requirements of security. There should be authority to unquestionably legalize
such practical and safe methods.
In March, 1943, a survey of the securities in the Endowment and
Luckenbach Funds was made by· the statistical department of Wells

532

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Fargo Bank & Union Trust Co. That survey developed an interesting
classification of the securities in those Funds and was accompanied by
recommendations which should have the careful consideration of an investment ·committee. A casual consideration of tlie mounting value of
securities belonging to Grand Lodge ·prompts emphasis on the necessity
of a continuing survey of the portfolio. Securities, whether stocks or bonds,
are in a constant state of flux. The unquestionable duty of making such
a survey should be imposed upon a qualified committee. That committee
should be authorized to make such adjustment and rearrangement of in.vested funds, including diversification, as may be required for protection,
and should have authority to dispose of securities for the benefit of the
portfolio but not for trading purposes.
There is now a Committee on Investment of Endowment Funds which
seems to be properly set up to discharge these enlarged functions.
Careful forethought and administration with respect to investment of
funds have been productive of well selected po_rtfolios, which is indicated
by the excess of market value over book value with respect to investments made ·for the account of Grand Lodge. Included in the securities
of Grand Lodge are stocks and bonds of questionable or unknown value,
some worthless. These have been acquired almost eQtirely by donation.
In this respect, however, attention is invited ·to the substantial donations
of prime securities.
\Vith respect to investments, Grand Lodge should give consideration
to the provisions of Section 655 under Edicts and · Resolutions, entitled
"Regulation as to handling Grand Lodge funds." In view of the fiduciary
character of funds of Grand Lodge, the entire investment . should be
limited to such securities as are authorized for the ~ndowment Fund,
namely, federal, state, county or municipal bonds legal for savings banks.
With respect to receipt and disbursement of funds, and securities in
custody of the Grand Treasurer, reference is made to the _auditors'
report.
An important item in the portfolio to which attention is invited is the
total of government bonds acquired. Treasury bonds, all acquired prior.
to July 31, 1942, total $293,000.00. United States War Bonds acquired
prior to July 31, 1942, total $64,000.00, and United States War Bonds
acquired since July 31, 1942, total $95,100.00. Otherwise the changes that
have occurred are unimportant and due to redemption and sale of securities of nominal value.
Between the closing of the fiscal year of Grand Lodge, July 31st, and
the date of the annual communii;:ation, a substantial amount of the income
of Grand Lodge by way of per capita becomes due and payable. With
regard to this, the Grand Secretary made an important recommendation
that there should be a supplementary audit. The Grand Treasurer unhesitatingly concurred in this recommendation and a supplementary report
of the auditors, of receipts from the closing of the fiscal year, July 31,
1943 to October 1, 1943, wjll be · presented to Grand Lodge for its
information.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANCIS V. KEESLING, Grand Treas1weY.

· REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M. W. Grand Lodge of California:

This day finds the peoples of our United Nations still at war, but the
crescendo of our battle song has risen to a theme of triumph and we can now
certainly see, in the discernible future, our flags floating gracefully in the
peaceful breeze of full and complete victory. The devastations of this greatest
of all conflicts have not reached the shores of our own United States mainland, though our outposts have been seared in the blue flame of destruction and
our hearts are heavy with the sacrifices made and being made by our sons and
brethren on the far-flung battle lines. On land, at sea and in the air, through
swamp and jungle, across desert sands, over oceans' waves, this maelstrom is
swiftly and surely encomp_assing our enemies, but its edged tides and winds are
'affecting the lives and searing the souls of every man, woman and child. Its
outer ripples and breezes are reaching even into the heart of Masonry and
presenting problems of policy and operations that must be solved. It is my
duty here to report to the brethren of the Grand Lodge of California how our
lodges are riding this storm, to recount what, in relation to the storm itself,
are insignificant triumphs over adversities and to narrate some of the problems that seem to be all but engulfing a few of these, our con.s titutent lodges.
Some of our lodges have prospered even beyond the vision of the most
imaginative, conferring more than 300 degrees in a single Masonic year, doing
this work creditably and efficiently, while other lodges, which in normal times
would be doing a normal year's work, have not had a single application within
the period. A few of our lodges have not lost a line officer during the past
year and are functioning smoothly and efficiently even in these times .of stress.
The majority of them, however, have suffered the loss of one or more such
officers, while several of our lodges now have not a line officer, either elective
or appointive, who was officially at work in his lodge when this great conflict
started. That haven of permanency, the secretary's office, has not been by"
. passed by this storm, and here we also find many new names among the list
of the brethren holding these· irrip6rtant bffices.
This situation has been caused by the flux of society during war times.
Most of the brethren who have been compelled to vacate their stations have
entered the armed forces of the United States, yet many have moved from
the jurisdiction of their lodge to enter civilian war work at other places. The
inspectoral districts have not been immune, an unusual .number of new inspectors having been appointed during this year. One di-strict has even had
two new inspectors since the previous meeting of this Grand Lodge.
These numerous changes of both officers and inspectors have naturally
affected lodge operations and the rendition of the ritualistic work of the several
degrees. There have been momentary saggings of proficiencies, but Masonic
industry and enthusiasm have triumphed, and I am able to report that as yet
there has not been any recession in our degree work, and lodge operations are
going forward "according to plan" and within the bounds of Masonic law and
custom. Although Masonic affairs within the several lodges are in a satisfactory condition, yet this continuing flux of officers is a matter of material
concern. The situation as it develops further under war conditions must be
watched carefully in order that we maintain throughout the State of California our high standards of Masonic work.
· Much credit must ·be and is most cheerfully and graciously given to the
inspectors of the several Masonic districts-that large group of brethren who
continue to labor in the vineyard so industriously for the welfare of Masonry--:for the work this past year has been unusUJ\lly burdensome in the qualifying

534

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and requalifying of brethren for Masonic offices, oftentimes under "forced
draft" conditions. Much credit is also due to the numerous Past Masters of
the several lodges who have accepted election; and even appointment, to fill
vacancies occuring in the lodge offices. These Past Masters have picked up the
burdens of this work with willingness and enthusiasm and their rededication
of service to Masonry has been timely and most effective.

available and the Master of the lodge was compelled to read the service without any apparent familiarity with its language. This has happened all too frequently and to the detriment of Masonry. By requiring the Master to memorize the service, he can always perform the duty admirably should occasion
require, and · the interests of Masonry will be best served by his being so
qualified.
Second, we wish to emphasize a piece of advice given last year in my
report to the Grand Lodge and also touched upon by the Grand Master -in his
remarks this morning. If an officer of a lodge be called to the service of the
United States, the lodge should fill the position by the election or appointment
of a Past Master who will adequately perform the duties of his office and who,
on the return of the brother, will readily and willingly step aside that the line
officer who departed and returned may take up his advancement from where
he left off his Masonic work. It is inadvisable for a brother in the service,
even though he may be temporarily stationed within ·the jurisdiction of his
lodge, to attempt to continue in office, particularly if he happens to be the
Master of his lodge, because he certainly cannot adequately and fully perform
his Masonic duties. Further, from the standpoint of the brother himself, he
will not want to look hack upon his year as Master as one of attempted service to Masonry under these conditions. Honor him on his return when he can
have the privilege and pleasure of efficient performance and may then, ever
after, glory in the accomplishments of his lodge while he was its ac.tive Master.
Third, we wish to further urge the inspectors and the lodge Masters to
arrange for the appointment of an officers' coach in each and every lodge in
California, and to attend to this matter immediately, if they hav.e not already
done so. Restrictions which have been placed upon travel emphasize the
wisdom of our having last year urged that this progressive step in the teaching
of our ritual be taken. In view of the further impending travel limitations, it
is 'doubly important that these specialists in the ritual be appointed in order to
maintain our California proficiency.
Fourth, we wish to urge the inspectors, and also these officers' coaches in
all their schools of instruction to emphasize matters of deliifery, expression and
enunciation, as well as perfection of wording. We know the problems they are
having and will have due to the changing personnel of lodge officers heretofore referred to, hut results can he accomplished in these matters, and this type
of instruction has materially added to the interest in the work, both for the
officers of the lodge and for the brethren on the sidelines, as well as for the
candidates receiving the degrees.

I also want to commend to you the most excellent Masonic services rendered to the Masons of California and to this, their Grand Lodge, by Assistant
Grand Lecturers Sidney K. Lehman, Obed W. Carr, Arthur M. Warren and
Charles A. Schwartz. They have borne well these additional burdens of
their offices.
During the past year the Ritual Committee has held its usual and regular
meetings, its members each time checking with one another the full work of
all three degrees and the candidates' lectures, studying matters of diction, delivery, enunciation and emphasis, as well as accuracy of wording. Problems oi
lodge administration also hav,e been discussed to the end that all might have
an· understanding of problems arising and also that a statewide viewpoint be
applied to the solution of the matters at hand.
Your Assistant Grand Lecturers, in addition to regular attendance at meetings of the Ritual Committee, have been assiduously conducting schools of instruction for the inspectors of their several divisions, holding group meetings
at various convenient points within their respective territories. At these
schools of instruction this year emphasis was put upon matters of enunciation,
style of delivery and inflection to the end that agreed "style of work" would
be passed on to the lodge officers. In addition to all this, serious and strenuous
effort has been made by your Grand Lecturer and by his assistants to see that
schools of instruction for lodge officers were available throughout the year on
several occasions for each lodge in this jurisdiction. Full and complete coverage in this respect has not been attained, but we are watching the records of
schools held and are endeavoring to get instruction to the individual lodges that
have been overlooked. Fortunately, their number is but few. However, if any
Master of a lodge in this jurisdiction feels .that his officers are not receiving
adequate instruction from brethren proficient in the ritual, either from the
district inspector or from one of his approved officers' coaches, your Grand
Lecturer will appreciate a direct communication upon the subject. Corrective
measures will be immediately undertaken and the instruction supplied.
Your Grand LectUTer, even under restricted travel, has attended many of
the important Masonic group gatherings held during the past year in the
several parts of the State. After such meetings he has held informal conferences with many of the inspectors in attendance to learn from them, at first
hand, their problems and how their work was progressing. In addition to this,
he has attended a few schools of instruction held by the inspectors to observe
the instr~ction given and the quality of the officers' work. I beg to report that
these observations indicated a high performance both by the instructors and
the instructed.
Looking to next year, permit me to make a few suggestions and issue a
warning: First, we wish to notify you and all the brethren of the fraternity
that the Ritual Committee has definitely decided that Masters-elect who are
to be installed after December 1, 1944, that is, Oll_e year and two months from
now, will be required,- as a part of their qualifying examinations, to deliver
from memory the Masonic funeral service. We do not imply that we intend
to suppress or supplant the present admirable system in use by many lodges,
that of having some particularly qualified Past Master act as Master of the
lodge in conducting funerals. This plan is working out quite satisfactorily in
many places, but many occasions have arisen when such a brother was not

Recommendations as to the Amendment of the Ritual:
Within the several degrees of Masonry and in the candidates' lectures,
there are many ·places where particular ideas are reiterated, but where the
language in one part differs slightly from the language used in the other portion of the work. Sometimes there are niceties of distinction brought out in
these slight variations of wording. However, the similarities of the wordings
are causing confusion, interpolations and recurring errors, making the memory
work and accuracy of delivery mm:h more difficult, with only a few of the
brethren appreciating the fine points attempted to be brought out by · the variations in the language. In my opinion, the effort of maintaining perfection and
the shades of meaning is not worth the results attempted to be attained. For
these reasons the Ritual Committee, through me as its chairman, is recommending a few amendments to our ritual. In one or two places, there are corrective
reasons for suggesting the particular amendment which will be noted in my
comments.
For the purpose of consideration, I am listing each group of related amendments as a single item. Inasmuch as all the items refer to the esoteric work, I

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNT:\

request the reporter to omit the following from. his notes, except to record the
number of the items discussed.
·
Item 1 to item 17, both included.
The adoption of these suggested amendments will result temporarily in
some confusion. The amendments will, however, lessen the labor of lodge
officers, eliminate errors of interpolation, improve our ritual and facilitate its
rendition. These amendments have the unanimous approval of the Ritual Committee and we recommend their adoption by formal action of Grand Lodge at
this communication.
Modification of Flag Ceremony:

In my report to the Grand Lodge oJ California at its ninety-second annual
communication, the Ritual Committee, speaking through me, recommend a
change in the form of flag ceremony then in use in our lodges (1941 Proceedings of Grand Lodge, Vol. XLVII, page 4SO). That recommendation was not
adopted, but an acceptable form was included in the revised Monitor and
Officers' Manual which was adopted in that communication of the Grand. Lodge
(1941 Proceedings, pages 6S9 and 674, and 1941 Monitor and Officers' Manual,
pages S3 to SS). On December 22, 1942, the Congress of the United States of
America by joint resolution (Public Law 829-77th Congress, Chapter 806,
House Joint Resolution 3S9) established a form of pledge to the flag which
is at variance with our adopted form. The Ritual Committee recommends that
our flag ceremony be· revised to comply with the form prescribed by the congressional resolution. The required amendments of wording .in the Monitor
and Officers' Manual will be submitted in detail to Grand Lodge when this
recommendation is called for i:onsideration.
,

In conclusion, I again want to thank those who have so materially as.sisted
in · the work of this department of Masonry, especially the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the inspectors of the several Masonic districts. Ritualistic perfec~
tion and smoothness of lodge operations are not the purpose and goal of
Masonry. There are greater and finer things being done and to be done by our
beloved order, yet these matters, falling within the particular province of the
Grand Lecturer's office, are a necessary and proper part of Masonry. To me
they are the very cement and support of our society, holding us together in
the bonds of brotherly love and uniting us in a common purpose, thus, through
unity of thought and action, enabling us to accompiish the greater and finer
things for which Masonry really exists.

Especially am I grateful to you for the privilege of serving as your
Grand Lecturer with Leslie E. Wood as Grand Master and Lloyd E. Wilson
as Grand Secretary. We three have labored long and closely together throughout the years. Therefore this year has been particularly interesting and pleasant, bringing the solution of many arising problems resolved in unanimity and
culminating ten years of service in understanding and companionship that ever
will .remain a beautiful remembrance.
Again I thank you for the privilege of serving.
Respectfully submitted,
CHESTER H. WARLOW, Grand Lecturer.

are loyal and patriotic citizens of the United States of America, united for
altruistic and non-political purposes, and desiring to contribute their efforts
in the promotion of truth; honor, justice and toleration for the benefit of the
public generally, and with no thought of obtaining special privileges for the
Fraternity, the members thereof, or any other individual or group of individuals ; and
·WHEREAS, The constituent Lodges of the Grand Lodge of Masons of
California, and the members thereof are vitally interested in the numerous
plans now being presented and discussed by the Congress of the United
States, public leaders of this nation and private citizens, for the formulation
of policies affecting the post-war period; and
WHEREAS, It is an obligation of such an institution as the Masonic Fraternity, and all American citizens to study such post-war plans in order t,o

participate in the establishment and maintenance of a just and lasting peace
among the nations of the world and insure the continuance of democratic,
constitutional processes in the United States;

Proposed Amendment to Section 218 of the Constitution and Ordinance
of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California.
An amendment to Section 218 is proposed by striking therefrom the
word "ten" as it appears in the fourth line of Section 218 and inserting
in lieu thereof the word "twenty-five."
The reason for the proposed amendment is that a perspn desiring
to file an application_ for degrees in a given Lodge should be permitted
a wider scope of choice than is offered by restricting the applicant to
choose a Lodge located within a radius of ten miles of his place of
'residence. Improved methods of transportation and communication existing at the present time make a distance of twenty-five miles a very short
distance as compared with ten mile.s twenty-five or thirty years ago. An
applicant may file a petition for membership in a Lodge located any place
within a large city such as the city of Los Angeles, where applicant may
live, in a place which is more than ten miles from the Lodgeroom of
the Lodge he desires to join. Many people who formerly resided in the
City and County of San Francisco have moved to suburban areas, retaining their former place of business · in the city and maintaining close
contacts with friends and relatives in the City of San Francisco. It is
clear that many of such persons now living in suburban areas would
prefer to join a Masonic Lodge in the City of San Francisco, for instance,
than in some of the suburban areas located within a radius of twenty-five

l

miles from the Masonic Temple at Oak and Van Ness Avenue, San
Francisco.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CREDENTIALS

ANNUAL ORATION
(B~,i ARTHUR PAULSEN,

Grand Orator}

Most Worshipful Grand Mast.er, Distingi1ished Past Grand Masters, My
Fellow Grand Lodge Officers and B~ethren:
Since . men first raised their eyes to behold the vision of a nobler
life beyond the sordid things of earth the gifted tongues of able men
have sounded the praises of this great institution, praises which no feeble
words of mine can embellish or enrich. I come to you today with no
panegyric upon Masonry, but as a blunt and lowly member of the craft,
impelled by the tragic current of events to use plain words and deal with
simple truths. I am not here to seek the plaudits of the crowd but to
bring to you the message of a troubled heart, hoping that some word or
thought.. of.mine might help, in some small way, dispel the clouds that
now obscure the light.
For more than thirty years I have labored in the quarries of Masonry
as did my father before me and I yield to no man in devotion to this
cause. And if I l~ved it less, I might now proceed to paint a glowing
picture of a brilliant past and then sit down content. Because the fervor
of my love has not abated with the lapse of time, and because I still
believe that the divine attribute of Truth is the foundation of every
virtue and that sincerity and plain dealing should distinguish us, I cannot
hold my tongue while all about a troubled world is crying for relief.
For years I have watched our workmen ply their trade and for
years I have pondered the meaning of it all. I have seen the march of
those who passed and in the fullness of their hearts embraced the wisdom
of our art; of those who came to see, and having seen passed on. I have
seen the faithful of the craft work on unsung, without the urge for rank
or praise. I have seen others by a patient and unselfish toil climb to
the heights of fame and then, when its delusive light .no longer cast its
luster on their names, still work on, giving to Masonry the last full

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

measure of devotion. I see them now, at home and here, sincere and
noble men, performing their allotted tasks, pondering, even as I have
done, the aim and object of it all.
/
. But the picture is not yet complete. I haye also seen divergent
schools of thought arise concerning the purpose of our work; one that
sometimes made a fetish of ritualism, forgetting the message that it
brought; the other so impressed by the lessons we impart that it some•
times sought to belittle the means employed to impart it.

And into such a world Masonry was born. Starting from the Middle
East, where man first grasped the concept of a God of Love, these craftsmen spread across the earth. Their paths were marked by stately temples
whose beauty and design have set a pattern rarely equaled since. Free
men were they, who knew that character and self-control were all that
kept them free. But gradually the plan was changed. The beauty then
took on symbolic mold and men of rank and wisdom came to lend their
talent and to build in newer forms. The trowel passed to other hands
that hoped to build a mighty temple of the soul where men, at last,
might be secure and free.

544

I have seen times when our lodges were full to overflowing; but
more often, night after night, mere handfuls of our total strength h.ave
met to work while in the neighboring block service clubs were flourishing with " ev~ry member in his place.
·
I have seen earnest, able and dynamic men lost to the craft because
be lacked a plan to utilize their skills without delay. I have seen some
stand in line for years waiting for their chance to serve and then, disheartened, turn away to use their talents in other fields; while others
have worked their way to win distinction in the Master's Chair, only
to find when that was done, that they could spend their time in small
assignments or could sit quietly and listen while other men conferred
degrees.
·
Brethren, what is wrong? Is there some defect in the design upon
the trestle-board? Or have we, perhaps, misread the plan?
What can our mission be? What means may we employ to make
our power felt? Is ritual the end? Or do all men, and we, need something more?
Let us turn back the swiftly moving pages of the past and see if we
can find some answer to these questions that now cause us such concern.
From tropic isles to frozen seas, from east and west, from all the
corners of the earth, we see the slow and painful struggle of ancestral
man. With head bowed down, his great concern is food, and shelter,
protection from wild beasts and wilder men, and freedom from the fears
of a mysterious universe he can not understand. He knows one law,
and only one: the law that might makes right. He hoards. his food, only
to have it taken by some neighbor with a longer spear. In time, he sees
a ray of hope, and, out of his. longing for a better life there slowly comes
the knowledge that a code of higher laws exists which teaches Love
and Truth and Justice for mankind. With greater hope he struggles on
and builds and hoards again, and with a stronger zest for life he plans
his future course in the belief that lip-service to these higher laws has
brought security at last; only to find that some neighboring group still
rules by sword and fire, and in the end his plans for peace and happiness
are cast aside and all his goods and liberty are lost.
So on and on through centuries we see this battle ebb and flow
between the peaceful toiler and the· tyrant with a lust for power, between
the law of jungle and the law of God.
From time to time new groups are formed which seek to solve the
troubles of this tragic world. Philosophies and creeds are born, each
in its turn offering to man its cure. Some are good, and some are bad.
Some strive with open minds to search for Truth; while others, equally
sincere, are sure that they, and they alone, have found the magic formula
of liberty and peace. Some carry on with noble and unselfish zeal;
while others, in pursuit of power, themselves succumb to the base traits
their founders sought to crush.

545

It was no accident that Speculative Masonry blossomed forth in
the land of Magna Charta and the Bill of Rights. For let us not forget
that Masonry and Freedom must go hand in hand. Where Freedom
fails, no Masonry exists;. and those who love its truth must ever fight
and work in Freedom's cause. It was the recognition of these facts
that caused the members of our craft one hundred tifty-six years ago to
help bring forth a new charter of liberty and human rights, a new landmark for the guidance of all men, the Constitution of the United States .•

And what happened since those days The ancient feuds went madly
on. The charter we had helped to build had recognized a thing that
free men could not tolerate. We fought, and Freedom won. And then
for years the right of men to go their way was paramount. But is it
now?
Compare our times with those just thirty years ago. Then we were
free. But when the ugly head of tyranny again was raised across the
sea, we sallied forth to do our part-a righteous war, I still believeproclaiming to the defenders of our faith that we were fighting tb make
the world safe for democracy. We bad a foe who taxed our courage
and our skill. Rich and fertile lands were plundered and defiled. The
arts of peace were crippled or destroyed. Huge debts piled up: \Ve ·
struggled on. In time we won that war. And then we lost the peace
because men were not yet prepared to adopt the principles we teach.
And in the wake of that great war, depression came to test our claim
that we were free. The wheels of industr·y were stilled. Trade languished
while men stood in line to beg for food. The terror and the fear of
those tragic days made us cry out for help from any source, at any
price, and for a time the cherished right to think arid write and speak
was almost lost.
Because men had rejected the stones that should have become the
head of the corner, the improvised temple of peace that was to have
brought liberty artd happiness to the oppressed of the world crumbled
and decayed. Because we ·and other peoples of the earth were determined
to believe that by mere repetition of the higher laws we could somehow
circumvent the Supreme Grand Master's plan; escape the consequences
of our acts and thus avoid the work that men must do if they expect
to climb, we helped prepare the way for greater crimes than men before
had ever seen.
The ancient doctrine of divine right of kings and rule by warrior
clans gave way to vicious creeds that now proclaimed the divine right
of blood and race, and ruthlessly set forth to murder or enslave all
those who, by the standards of those perverted minds, were of some
lesser breed. Fire and sword were used to torture and destroy the
helpless victims of that mad campaign. Masonry was first to go, as
was everything that dared to stand for what was right. Our brethren

547

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

were thrown into concentration camps or slain, and such an orgy of
spite and hate and murder was indulged in that even beasts of prey
were put to shame.
And now in almost every corner of this troubled earth our brethren
and other fearless and unselfish men who will not yield their right to
live as free men should, are giving up their lives that those they love,
and we, and other members of our craft, may be secure. Yes, be secure.
Secure how long? Until some other war reduces men to slavery and
despair?
In less than thirty years we have witnessed the greatest and most
savage wars that men have ever known. The first world war .derived
its name because it had eclipsed in power the most titanic struggles of
the past. The suffering, the loss of life, the staggering debts, the disaster
in its wake left men aghast. The aftermath of troubles that it brought
had not been solved when this new war arrived to dwarf the first in
pain and grief and cost of every kind.
And when this war is won, what then? Are we again to lose the
·peace? Are we to jeopardize the things for which we sacrificed and
fought by a selfish and short-sighted course that in the end will ·bring
destruction to the very things it was intended to preserve? Can we
then pursue our usual course in a world that will lie prostrate at our
feet? Where men are crazed by hatred and a longing for revenge?
Where someone must restore the values it has lost? Will ordinary
means suffice? Whose business will it be to teach disillusioned men
that Justice must prevail : that Truth is mightier than the sword, aµd
that we still believe that brotherly love can prevail and rule the destinies
of men?
What, then, must Masons do? Our first duty is to win this war
and to that end we must devote our time, our wealth and every energy
that we can muster to support this cause. For the time being, we must
give to our high command the power to fulfill the trying tasks we have
imposed. Let us be patient and resigned. The small privations here
at home are trivial when compared to hardships that must be born by
those who represent us at the front. Yes, we must carry on. We started
as free men and as free men we must continue to the bitter end. We
can not and we will not fail.
When the perverted and trea<;herous leaders of the Axis gangs have
been punished for their crimes, we must play our part by helping to
devise some just plan to see that they, or men like them, shall not return
again to plague the world. But can we find a way to prevent some
other race or power from repeating the attempt to rule the earth? Will
Masons in high places, who were taught the lessons of Brotherly Love
and Justice that we learned, stand by and lend their aid in execution
of the plan?
Whatever way we look, . new problems will arise to tax our ingenuity
and faith. Those whom we have thwarted will try to rise again. Throughout the world self-conscious, backward races will be on the march with
claims that must be reconciled.
·
And what are we to do about affairs at home? Are we prepared
when peace has come to make an effort to regain the powers we have
lent to prosecute the war? Or will depression stalk across the earth
again? And if it does, will free men, living in a land which has the
means to meet omr needs, produce the things we want, and still stay
free? Or shall we, the sovereigns here, abdicate again so we may eat?

Is there some easy way? ' Some short cut to our goal? We have
seen science lift the burdens from men's backs and give them happiness
and time to play. And we have often found that men with too mu~h
leisure time cannot stand the stress of modern life; that the things that
science brings to our relief are seized themselves to thrust us back into
the abyss from which we climbed.

546

Can not the great religions of the world unite mankind i' Not while
their partisans follow a thousand separate and divergent paths. Too
many still pursue some sacred cow.
Does some one say, "Then let us have a law to curb the gangsters
of this earth; that is our favorite cure"? Yes, let us have a law to do
that very thing but let us always know that laws do not enforce themselves. Our Constitution has guaranteed. the rights of men and stood
the test of time, but it has worked because the freedom-loving people
of this land determined that they could not let it fail. When we have
law, good or bad, the sanction of that law is force: good when the men
who gave it life, are good; bad when the men who gave it life, are bad.
No plan that rests on . force can long succeed unless the character
of men is raised to that high plain where the need for such a law has
almost ceased. We justify the use of force by us because we know, or
think we know, that we are just, but it has a rightful place only when
used to bring control until the day when men themselves are qualified
to carry on without injury to their fellow men; when Truth and Justice
are the guiding lights by which . the:y work.
What can we do? For years the grand design has been spread
upon our trestle-board where all who wished to look might see. The
broad outlines laid down may be approved by any honest man and they
present. the only plan that ever can succeed. Yet it is a plan that men
have shunned for ages because they thought it tiresome and slow. It is
no easy scheme for men who are afraid to work or those who wish to
build and hide behind a front. Its materials are common men. If they
are rough, it seeks to fit them to The Builder's use, and if the work is
carried forward to the end the time
come when free men may take
their place in a spacious and resplendent temple of enduring peace.

will

How are we to carry out this plan? The same as we have always
done? Brethren, when I began I said that I would use plain words,
and deal with simple truths. I would be remiss if I took your time to
paint word pictures of our glorious past when the picture of the future
is so stark and grim. What we need now is not more words, but facts;
yes facts that we can face and analyze so we can chart our course. The
picture of the years ahead does not reveal a rosy path that we can follow
blindly without heed to the lessons we have learned, or should have
learned, from the history of the past. The things that are to come are
written in an open book. The theme is just the same and the i~sues
have not . changed.
Brethren, more than a quarter of a century ago we reached the
end of a great era and embarked upon a new, but we did not recognize
the fact. Since the time the Pilgrims first landed on our shores we have
regarded this great land as a haven where men oppressed abroad might
come and be secure. And we have gone on in that belief, holding ourselves aloof from the problems of the outside world, maintaining that
we had no part to play in the wicked schemes of men in other lands
-lands that had long since passed the simple problems of this new
world. We found great, virgin forests, unlimited supplies of every kind,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and broad, fertile plains where men could take . the things they need.
We had no life line to maintain, no shortages to force us out into the
violent currents and tempestuous seas where other men were struggling
for their very lives.

more blocs appear to claim some special privilege, often forgetting in
their zeal that other men have rights.

548

And then, to our dismay, the myth of isolation exploded in our
face. Through the advance of science, men whose hearts were filled
with envy for our riches and our power, became our neighbors overnight and the problems that for centuries had tortured other men became
our problems too.
War came, and more than two million of our men sailed across the
sea to battle for a cause. Under the stimulus of that great conflict we
talked of Justice and proclaimed to all the world that men were free.
We planned a better world, with peace for all. The German fleet and
army were destroyed-or so we thought-and by our mandate they
could never rise _again. And we w ent home, we and our allies, tired
and disillusioned, to forget. But we forgot too much ; forgot that force
alone has never in · the long history of th,e human race lifted men above
the savage beasts, or changed the basic pattern of their being; forgot
that he who makes a plan must also make it work.
·
. Some years elapsed, and because we had neglected to prepare the
soil in which the cause of freedom thrives, new tyrants of a more malignant growth rose up and told us in no uncertain terms that everything
we cherished was outworn. Their purposes were not concealed. Their
leaders carefully announced the plan. But we had troubles of our own
and so we let them go to _c arry out their plot. The army that was
not to be, began to grow and in the course of time, small though it was,
it crossed into the forbidden valley of the Rhine. Did our old allies,
or we, who talked so much, take action then? One good division could
have turned them back. We still believed in miracles and shibboleths
and lost our chance by easy means thus -to avert the war that rrow is
shaking the whole earth.
Have we learned anything from this? We talk of Justice and make
plans, but when our men are back, tired and disillusioned as before, who
will provide the aircraft, garrisons and fleets for years to come and
promise never to forget? When taxes weigh us down from debts so
big we cannot even comprehend their size, shall we then remember the
things that now seem clear?
And let us not forget that freedom is not always lost to forces from
without. Wars pave the way for . greater evils from within.
The logi~ of events has justified our help to Russia, for by doing
so w e help ourselves and millions who are now oppressed. But do we
know what she will do when she is free to exercise her will ?
For six long years China has waged a battle for its life and yet
today a great communist army of Chinese stands by in idleness. What
is it waiting for? What vision has it seen?
When the present restraints have been removed from Europe and
new forces are unleashed, can any man be sure that communism will
not take command? And let no man delude himself into the belief that
this tyrant can be r econciled with the democratic principles that· we
hold dear.
What of conditions then at home? The same forces that have contended for ten thousand years are still contending here. Blocs and

549

Whatever progress we have made in the long years since life commenced upon this earth, has come from the slow development of character in man. Each starts from scratch, and each in turn must learn his
lessons in the treadmill that is life. This generation cannot do the work
of those who are to come. No magic formula can lift this burden from
their backs or save them from the course they must pursue. But if
enough are taught and learn their lessons well, then, and then only, will
mankind be free.
And if America has reached the time when it must play a more
important role, is it not possible, at least, that Masonry has reached a
turning point? Eternal principles will never change. The things we
treasure most will still endure. R elief will always be a work of love
with us, if we have caught the spirit of it all. And as the teacher must
provide a means to make the pupil see the beauty of the lesson he
imparts, so must perfection in our ritual be our constant care and a
great and lasting source of pride for every member of the craft.
But will our missions be fulfilled if we stop there? It has been
said "Talent is built in solitude ; character in the stream of life." Men
must be taught; and men must learn to live. Mere repetition has never
been enough. The noble concepts of Truth and Love and Justice may
take form, but in the haze that comes with time, they fade away, unless
by practice they are woven into the very fabric of our souls.
Within the recent history of our times, wise and discerning leaders
here have seen the light, and we have thus arrayed the ranks of Masonry
behind our public schools; and we have rallied to support that master
plan, once fashioned partly by Masonic hands, that now proclaims the
right to freedom in this land.
But I arri not convinced that we have yet exhausted all the means
that Masonry or Masons could employ to give our straying brothers
work or make our power felt. I am not unmindful of the fact that
Masonry in other lands has sometimes gone astray and suffered loss.
But in view of all the things that I have seen in this chaotic world, I
cannot now believe· that we have sketched in all the minor details of
the plan, or have built the character in men that we must have to reach
the last and highest goal: the Fatherhood of God, and the Brotherhood
of Man.
And never will this goal be reache~ while men in every land must
live in terror of the god of war and sacrifice their right to love, and
think, and grow, and search for Truth.
I am not here to urge some innovation in our work. I only hope
that we may catch the spirit of it all. Whatever landmarks might appear
to bar our way, we never can be lacking in the power to save ourselves
or carry through until we reach the height toward which we climb.
I am not here to recommend procedures ot techniques; for well I know
if we but have the will, the mea ns will soon be found.
Whatever rule or regulations may appear to hold us down, I know
there is a higher law that cannot be ignored: growth is the law of life,
and every living thing must grow or waste away and die.
And if we hesitate, then let us see the truth. Let us first ask what
every man must ask: "What_ is our allegiance to this cause? Are we
free men prepared to do the things that must be done if we stay free?

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In Justice something real that makes us want to render unto every man
his just due, without distinction? Do we believe in brotherly love that
regards the whole human species as one family? Do we want Truth.
itself, when it suddenly confronts us with some fact we do not dare to
face? And if we answer "No," let us forget the things that we profess
and join the countless miJ!ions who believe that men may have their
way no matter where it leads. And if we answer "Yes,'' let us as men
who have the faith and courage to support the right, stand up and tell
the world we will defend the cause we represent.

In the report made to you at the last communication of Grand Lodge
I mentioned that Past Grand Master Stafford and Mrs. Stafford were
interned near Bagino, and that Past lJrand Master Youngberg and Mrs.
Youngberg were confined in the camp at Santo Tomas University. We
have had no further information concerning them.

550

Brethren, we have work to do. Let us build men who will be adequate
to the performance of these great and glorious undertakings.
Our fathers' God! from out whose hand
The centuries fall like grains of sand,
We meet today, united, free,
And loyal to our land and Thee,
To thank Thee for the era done,
And trust Thee for the opening one.

.o make Thou us, through centuries long,
In peace secure, in justice strong;
Around our fight of freedom draw
The safeguards of thy righteous law:
And, cast in some diviner mould
Let the new cycle shame the old.

REPORT ON PHILIPPINE ISLANDS LODGES
Most W orshipf1tl Grand Master a11d Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Suffering and tragedy continue to be the lot of mankind; destru~tion
of life and property continue with unabated fury; the Four Horsemen
of the Apocalypse ride with an abandon unequalled in recorded history;
and the sick, the wounded, and the helpless call upon a loving God for
succor.
In the presence of such conditions it is fitting and proper that we
of the Grand Lodge of California should pause in our deliberations to
consider our brethren in the Philippine Islands who have been so unfortunate as to fall under the heel Df a cruel and inhuman conqueror.

551

We now learn that John R. McFie, Jr., Grand Master 1941 and
Mrs. McFie are interned at Santo Tomas. Brother McFie was' bor"n
at Las Cruces, New Mexico, April 25, 1889. Married Dorothy Podmore
1928, in Kobe, Japan.
'
Educated in the public schools of Las Cruces, graduated Ann' Arbor
Michigan, High School, 1905 ; Santa Fe, New Mexico, High School 1908'.
University of New Mexico, 1909; received the degree LL.B. at th~ Uni~
versity of Michigan in 1914. Admitted to the Bar Association of the
State of Michigan, 1914 and State of New Mexico, 1915; admitted to
the bar of the Philippines, May 1, 1922; President of American Bar
Association of the Philippines 1934.
Brother McFie became a Lieutenant Commander, U. S. N. R., 1938;
was called to service in November, 1941. He served through the siege
of Cavite and after the fall of ' that naval base was, with other. naval
reservists, returned by the Government of the United States to civilian
status. As a civilian he was interned. Later the Japanese, contending
that these reservists were spies, removed several from the concentration
camp, submitted them to severe cruelties, trying to force a confession of
their guilt. Whether Brother McFie was one of those submitted to
torture we do not know.
Shortly before the outbreak of hostilities, Mrs. McFie sailed from
the United States for the Islands. The ship upon which she was traveling took a circuitous route and was 45 days in' reaching Manila. At one
port of call Mrs. McFie found it necessary to cable to the United States
for funds. Brother McFie's youngest son is now residing with his
paternal grandmother in Honolulu:
One of the most interesting incidents in the history of the Grand
of the Philippines concerns Manuel Louis Quezon, Grand Master,
m 1918-19. Quezon was born in 1878 at Baler, on the Island of Luzon.
He took his law training at Santo Tomas University in Manila. In his
early twenties he was a major on the staff of Emilio Aguinaldo, insurrectionist leader against ·the United States, but he made his peace with
the territorial authorities and became a provincial prosecutor in 1903.
From 1907 to 1909 he was a member of the Philippine Assembly, and
from 1909 to 1916 resident commissioner to the United States Congress.
He returned to Manila in 1916 and was elected president of the Senate,
a strategic political post which he held until his election as president
of the new commonwealth on September 17, 1935.
~odge

No direct commtinieation can be had with the Islands, but from
various sources we have obtained the information that many of our
brethren ate confined to the internment camp at Santo Tomas University
in the city of Manila. Reports received indicate that the internees of this
camp fare .better than those of any other administered by the Japanese.

In the campaign for the presidency of the Philippines; Quezon's
two· opponents for that office were General Emilio Aguinaldo, his former
commander, and Bishop .Aglipay, formerly a prelate in the Roman
Catholic Church, and now head of the Independent Catholic Church of
the Philippine Islands. Both General Aguinaldo and Bishop Aglipay are
members of the Masonic Fraternity.

.Since the establishment of the Grand Lodge of the Philippine ISlan!is
on December 19, 1912, twenty-eight men have served as Grand Masters.
Seven died prior to the invasion,; one. died this year; one is now residing
in the United States; three ar.e Interned at Santo Tomas University; and
one is .interned in a c~mp .near Bagino; ·leaving fifteen unaccounted. for.·

Frederick' H. Stevens was Grand Master in 1923-24. We know
little of his life except that he was in the United States in 1941, at
which time he visited his mother in Chicago, Illinois. He returned to
Manila in September of that y'ear.
Of his Masonic career we know that he was a 33rd degree Mason;
was Deputy in the Philippines of the Supreme Council, Southern Jurisdiction of the Scottish Rite· Bodies. In the · York Rite Bodies he was
Past High Priest, Luzon Chapter No. 1, Royal Arch Masons; Past
Illustrious Master, Oriental Council No. 1, Royal and Select Masters;
Past Commander, Far East Commandery No. 1, Knights Templar.
Information obtained from a sister of a former Secretary of the
Scottish Rite Bodies in Manila declares that Brother Stevens is a prisoner
at Santo Tomas Camp. This information has been confirmed by our
State Department.
Milton Earle Springer served as Grand Master for the years 1919-20.
Brother Springer was born August 27, 1875, at Lewisburg, Pennsylvania;
died April 5, 1943, at Mechanicsburg, Penrisylvania. Wh~n Brother
Springer went to the Islands we do not know. We are adVlsed by the
Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite Bodies i!1 \Yashingtqn, D .. C., ~hat
he received the Scottish Rite degrees at Manila 1h 1911, at which time
his occupatiol). was given as merchant. He was elected a Knight Co~­
mander of the Court of Honor on October 22, 1913, elected to receive
the 33rd degree . on October 20, 1915, and received the latter on May 26,
1917. The recommendations for these honors speak most complementary
as to his executive ability, his industry, and his devotion to Masonry.
In the York Rite Bodies he was Past High Priest, Luzon Chapter
No. 1, Royal Arch Masons; Past Illustrious Master, Oriental Council
No. 1, Royal and Select Masters; Past Commander, Far East Commandery No. 1, Knights Templar.
Such honors received in other bodies and the fact that he was elevated to the highest office in the gift of his brethren of the Grand Lodge
of the Philippine Islands clearly indicate that his zeal and industry were
applied with equal enthusil!-sm to Blue Lodge Masonry. From the dates
given above it is evident he was in the Islands at least 10 years.

REPORT OF MASONIC WAR RELIEF FUND
COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

I have t?e· pleasur~ to report the results of activities of your War
F.und Committee. It 1s a good report which reflects credit upon the
discernment of Grand Master Smith who appointed the committee and
upon Grand Master Wood, who continued it, as well as upon yo~ and
the brethren. of t~; Lo?s:es for your support of this great Masonic charity.
Y ~ur. committee ts. pnv1l~ged in the opportunity to be the medium for
bringmg these mamfestahons of Masonic responsibilities into focus upon
our problems of the war.
When the committee was appointed hy Grand Master Smith a few
~onths af~er Pearl Ha~bor, America was in the darkest hour 'of her
history. With a substantial number of our capital ships on the bottom of
~ear~ Harbor, a large yart of our Navy i'n the Atlantic guarding the
hfe-lme bet"."'een America . and Britain, and with the full fury of the
Japanese poised for the . kill, we were indeed in peril. Everything that
Masonry s.tands for was m danger of destruction at that time. Even this
state was m danger of actual invasion.
. In making the report of the committee at our last communication, I
pomted out that the Grand Architect of the Universe had been good to
us here. During the first ten months of war, He and He alone restrained
the hands of our enemi~s while
were salvaging and rebuilding our
su?ken. fleet and otherwise preparing for a war of survival. Thanks to
Hts gmdance and to the responses of a nation united in adversity we
have this past year been able to help ourselves. We have whittled ~way
at the outer defenses of our enemies in the Atlantic, Mediterranean and
Pacific areas until now it is we who are poised for swift powerful attack
on ~he very home lands of our enemies. No longer are we on the defens1':'e; everywh~re we are ~m the offensive; and God willing, we shall
remam there until our enemies are driven under the ground or into the
sea and with the~ their dream of world domination and oppression. Then,
and only then, will the world become a place safe for the free and unrestricted practices of the principles of free Masonry. Then and only
then, can the word "peace" come to mean more than the word ''armistice."
The progress that we have made in the war duri~g the !~st year
might, to the unthinking, indicate that necessity for the War Relief Fund
has ended. On the other hand, to · those who are realistic it indicates
that we m1;1st still look .forward to the maximum demands upon such a
fun.d. Un~1l recently we ~ave been merely holding the line, fighting de~
laymg act10ns, and octas1onally lopping off one of the tentacles of the
octopus. Such military and naval action, particularly when successful·
involves a great number of casualties. But when we meet the enemy he.ad
on-when we chase him into his lair and still pursue him-the casualties
~re often appalling in their number, even though the · military oper:atio~
1s successful..
··

v:e

556

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

And so, my brothers, while we may confidently expect . successive
victories from this day on, it will be at a price-a terrible price.
I believe it is being only realistic to say that from this time on, our
casualties each month will probably be greater than for the entire first
eighteen months of the war. This jurisdiction alone has 8,866 of our
brethren in the armed forces. God alone knows how many· of them will
be called on to make the supreme sacrifice, and what the needs of their
families will be.
Yes, we will need our War Relief Fund from this time on, in increasing proportions.
It was the aim of Grand Master Smith to establish a fund equal in
dollars to the number of our brethren as of July 31, 1941. That number
was 125,843. When the committee was continued in existence by Grand
Master Wood, he set a similar goal, based upon the maximum m~mber­
ship in his year. That number was 126,313. That number today ts 129,509. I have the honor to report that the goal has been exceeded and your
committee has collected the sum of $131,220. This represents contributions
from approximately half of our membership. It was our hope that every
Mason in the jurisdiction might contribute and earn a feeling of duty well
performed in this great charity.
However, we have 8,866 members in service, who should not be called
upon; we have others who are scattered throughout the world and who
may not have full knowledge of our program; and there are others who
because of adversity are unable to contribute.
The full quota has been reached by 354 of our Lodges. It would be
fine if the others would do the same thing. It would give them one more
source of satisfaction-one more of those joys which will forever strengthen
and comfort those who have done their best in this supreme war effort
of the American nation to make Peace not only the ambition but also
the destiny of the people of the world.

Chairman
For the Committee.

EARL WARREN,

RESOLUTION
Resolved, That all constituent Lodges of this Grand Jurisdiction be
required to keep their books and records in the uniform system at present
available in the office of the Grand Secretary and presently required to
be used by newly constituted Lodges, or as may be hereafter prescribed
by Grand Lodge.
RALPH K. PIERSON'
FREDERICK WIED,
MILES McCLELLAND,
NIJ-ES 0 . MILLER,
CLARENCE FRASER,
HERBERT R. HARGRAVE,

Past Masters.

Referred to Committee on Policy and·General Purposes.

· Resolution
Whereas, It is the opinion of many members of Grand Lodge that
the Office of Secretary of the constituent Lodges is an important administrative office; and that a correct and efficient discharge of its duties
is essential to the welfare, harmony, and progress of the Lodge ;
And Whereas, It is their further opinion that a thorough knowledge
by the Secretary of the sections of the Constitution and General Regulations of the Grand Lodge as relate to the duties of a Secretary of a

568

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge, as well as a general knowledge of those portions of the Constitution and General Regulations which relate to the government of a Lodge,
is necessary for the efficient discharge of his duties;
Now, Therefore, Be It Resolved, That the Grand Lecturer be directed
by Grand Lodge to require of Inspectors due certification of the proficiency
of brethren elected to the office of Secretary of the constituent Lodges,
such certification to be based upon the proficiency of the Secretary-elect
in those portions of the Constitution and General Regulations of the
Grand Lodge relating to the duties of Secretary of a Lodge, and also
upon his general knowledge of those portions of the Constitution and
General Regulations of the Grand Lodge relating to the government of
a Lodge.
FRANK HARWELL, JR.,
RALPH K. PIERSON'
OWEN R. CRAGHEAD,
HERBERT R. HARGRAVE,

Past Masters.

Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes . .

afternoon.
