AFTERNOON SESSION
Tuesday, October 12, 1943.
Grand Lodge was called on at 2 :00 o'clock, the Grand Master
presiding.
The Invocation was given by the V. Rev. Grand Chaplain.

REPORT OF WAR SERVICE COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodyl' of California:
At the last communication of this Grand Lodge, the War Service
Committee, appointed in 1942 by M. W. Frank M. Smith, Grand Master,
for the purpose of formulating a War Service Program, submitted its
recommendations, which were adopted by this Grand Lodge.
The Committee recommended a program of service and relief for our
members who are in the Armed Forces and their families; a program
of service relief for all Masons who have returned from foreign service
and are confined in the Army and Navy hospitals in this state; a dock
information and assistance program for all Masons returning from sea
duty or foreign service; and the stimulation. of Lodge meetings for the
benefit of Masons in the service.
Today, Brethren, we are pleased to present a progress report of what
has been accomplished this past year.
Service to Our Members in the Armed Forces and Their Families
With great satisfaction, this Committee has observed the efforts of
the Lodge Committees on behalf of their members in the Service and
their families. Considering the Lodges of the State as a whole, we are
of the opinion that the work has been well done. Many lodges have
had very active Committees, who have made special efforts to regularly
keep in touch with their members by writin~ cheerful letters, giving •
interesting items about families and friends and the local news. Some
districts have joined together in the preparation of special news bulletins,
which have been sent to all their service members and those districts
have had the satisfaction of receiving many interesting and instructive
letters in reply.
I mention cheerful letters, Brethren, because that is ·important. In
our hospitals today are many men, classified as "Mental Cases." They
are from over-seas, yet they have not been in actual combat. They
cracked up before they had a chance to get in combat. On reliable
authority, I have been told one of the main causes has been worry over
conditions at home. Recently, I met a British Colonel, just retired from
an Indian Regiment. He was astounded at some of the letters American
boys 'in India had received from home. They told all the difficulties on
the Home Front-of the hardships of food and gas rationing and the
shortages of meat-the severity of taxes. It is easy to understand the
effect of letters like this have, so make yours CHEERFUL, Brethren, to
build a high morale among our boys.
Calling on families, some of the Lodge committees have done an
excellent job. They have made it an item of first importance to call on

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

every family and to those residing at distant places they have written.
The letters received in reply showed the effort has been worth while.
These calls and letters have brought cheer and comfort to the families
and men alike. We are appreciative of this effort and feel that the Lodges
who have done this work, will be well rewarded.
The number of cases where relief has been needed among those
families has been relatively few. We are aware that some Lodges have
felt it a personal responsibility and have taken care of that relief without
calling on the War Relief Fund and we commend this action by those
Lodges. Where ever relief has been needed, it has been taken care of,
as the individual cases required. The Committee wants to take this opportunity to thank the various Boards of Relief throughout the State for
their splendid efforts and cooperation in this direction. They have done
a good job, Brethren, ·and are to be congratulated.
For one reason or another a few Lodges have not been as active
keeping in touch with their service members and their families as they
might have been, and to the Masters and Wardens of those Lodges who
are present, we earnestly appeal that you give serious thought over ways
and means to get started. It is not near as difficult as you might think.
One very ~uccessful method ·I heard about was the placing of a bulletin
board in the Lodge Room, with the names and latest addresses of their
members in service. During the course of the evening, the Master
called attention to the board and asked the members to make
point to
write to one member each week. Paper and pencil were handy so that
names could be written down. In another .Lodge, with a large percentage
aw~y, lists were prepared and distributed to the members in open meeting. Each list contained four names and members were requested to
write to one a week and report at the next Stated Meeting that he had
done so. Don't forget, Brethren, that you and your Lodge will be remembered by those men, for what you have done. They will judge the whole
Masonic fraternity's war effort, by what they personally have received
and you are missing a golden opportunity to really put brotherly love
and affection into action.

To encourage those who need ideas, a display has be~n arranged in
the Black Room showing_ a few of the posters that are being used. This
is by no means all of them. Especially outstanding has been San Diego,
Long Beach, Fresno and the East Bay districts.

a

Announcing Lodge Meetings in Camps, Cantonments and Hospitals
We have had many requests this past year to furnish entertainment.
Frankly, Brethren, neither this committee nor this Grand Lodge is in
the entertainment business. If we were to provide all the entertainment
r~quested our funds would not last very long.
There is, however, a place where we can provide entertainment th~t
is uniquely Masonic and that is in our Lodges. Encouraging the men m
uniform to attend Lodge Meetings and making it easy for him to attend
is an important part of our program. Many districts have joined together
in the preparation of posters, showing location of Lodges and scheduled
meetings and extending an invitation to all Masons to attend. They have
seen to it that these posters have been placed where the men can see
them. This has attracted many service men to Lodge meetings. Individual Lodges have also been active in this direction. Particularly has
this been true of small Lodges adjacent to large camps. These Lodges
have conferred many courtesy degrees which have been well attended by
service men . One such meeting came to my attention . Thirty civilians
including the officers were present, and over one hundred service men
were in attendance seeing the degree conferred on one of their buddies.
Many successful parties and special meetings have been arranged and
we commend all the Lodges for their work in this direction.

Dock Information and Assistance
This Section was started as a ~mall group to work on the docks in
San Francisco and it was the intention, as the need arose, this work
would be expanded and additional groups formed. During the year, a
man was selected to head this work and plans were underway for expansion in line with our original ideas.
At the request of military authorities, who desired fewer people on
the docks when men were returning, expansion of this part of our work
has been temporarily laid aside. We are closely cooperating with those
in charge and as soon as it is feasible, t_his work will again be undertaken.
Army and Navy Base Hospitals
Expansion of Army and Navy hospitals . in this State is almost
beyond comprehension. Not very long ago, we had two Army and
two Navy Base hospitals. There are now seven · for the Navy and eight
for the Army with additional units under consideration. Many of these
units .have expanded froip an original fifteen or eighteen hundred beds
to three thousand beds and one unit is in excess of thirty-five hundred
beds.
Besides the Base Hospitals there are many Station Hospitals, Camp
Hospitals and Convalescent Hospitals, which are assuming more importance all the time. As an example, take the hospital at Camp Callen,
near San Diego. It has been expanded to a 1,500-bed unit-five hundred
of these beds are held in reserve for overseas veterans.
During this past year, the Chairman of this Committee has personally
contacted the commanding officers of the fifteen Army and Navy Hospitals already referred to, from the Army's Tomey General Hospital at
Palm Springs to their new DeWitt Hospital at Auburn, and for the Navy
from San Diego to Mare Island.
The set up between the Army and Navy is quite different. Headquarters for the Navy is in San Francisco, while the Army is at Salt
Lake. We are able to sit in with the Admiral in Command for the Navy
and discuss our work, which has been very helpful in our contacts with
the Navy commanding officers. With the Army it has been a situation
of contacting the different commanding officers without having ;my official
. recognition of our program.
As stated in our last report, there are no visiting committees going
through the hospitals, but rather .to have a member of the staff who is
a Mason, appointed by the Commanding Officer as our represent~tive.
Through this representative, we are able to keep in touch with the Masons.
This Committee stands ready to do for those Brethren, those things
that are pecularly Masonic and which only his Masonic Brethren can do
for him, be it relief, personal service or contacts with his family and
Lodge. If it is deemed necessary by those in charge, that a Mason's wife
o~ mother should come to him and funds are not available for her to
make the trip, on recommendation of the Masonic Representative, we
will immediately see she is brought here, taken care of while here and
returned to her home.
We are • at present encouraging the local Lodges to arrange special
meetings and to get posters into the hospitals so that men who are

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

allowed to leave, will know about them. Where a man requests it,
local Lodges are asked to have a brother call on him. Recent directives
has indicated a definite tightening up on visitors and it is possible that
special passes will have to be arranged through our representative.
. Captain Jensen, Commanding Officer at Corona, called my attentio~
to the fact that where a man has been injured, the Navy will do everything possible to replace lost arms or legs with some kind of a wooden
arn~ or ~ wooden leg. But if his eyesight or hearing has been damaged
or 1mpa1red, they do not supply glasses or hearing aids. He felt that if
we could provide needed glasses or hearing aids for Masons who could
not afford to pay for them, we would be· doing an invaluable service to
those men, as it was his experience that once they were out of the
service, many of these men failed to provide for themselves and their
servi<;:e to themselves and to the Community was not what it should
have been.
This matter was refer;ed to the Grand Master, and I am happy to
report Brethren, that with his wholehearted approval we will pay for
g~asses and hearing aids, from the War Relief Fund, for Masons being
discharged who are unable . to provide them for themselves. A simple
plan has been worked out to put this into operation.
The Grand Secretary's Office is receiving about 1,200 letters ·a month
requesting information about men in the service. Many of these men
are in the hospitals and through our representative we have been able
to keep in touch with these men and to advise their home Lodges of
their condition or progress.
To give you an idea of how efficiently this works, in some instances,
a few days ago, the Grand Secretary received a wire from the Grand
Secretary of South Dakota, advising that one of their members, in the
Navy, had been seriously injured in San Francisco. Could he find out
anything about him? The Grand Secretary knew he would be taken to
either Oak Knoll or Treasure Island, so he called our representative at
Treasure Island first. He knew all about the man, and within ten minutes
from the time of the receiJ?t of the telegram, a reply was on its way
giving full information on the injured man.
'
While our activities so far have been confined to the Base Hospitals
we are aware of the need of expanding this portion of our work to include
Station Hospitals and Camp Hospitals where overseas veterans are assigned to. This is being undertaken at the present time.
We want to take this opportunity to thank the Inspectors, Masters
and Secretaries whom we have called on this year to handle special cases
that have arisen. Their response has been generous and their efforts are
greatly appreciated.
As already stated, Brethren, the -number of relief cases has been
comparatively few, however, as we have traveled over the State seeing
military installations from one end to the other and have noted the increasing installations of hospitals, we are convinced that the road ahead
will bring many instances when the Relief Fund will be sorely needed
and at that time, this Grand Lodge will be thankful for the foresight ·of
those Grand Masters who conceived the fund and to the members who
have so generously contributed to it.
I was deeply impressed, Brethren, by the words of Winston Churchill, in a recent speech in Boston--his words "the price of greatness is
responsibility." The Masonic Fraternity, Brethren, is great-great for
its precepts and its teachings-great for its leaders-and great for what
its members have contributed to the welfare of Man.

Yet that greatness, Brethren, has its responsibilities-responsibilities
which are on the shoulders of your leaders-of the Masters and Wardens
of the Lodges. and on every individual member.
Some of the great problems facing us today are the Post-War Problems. Your leaders are aware of their responsibility and are planning to
meet those problems.
We are confident that when those boys return home, California
Masonry will not have failed them.
Respectfully submitted,

\V. Alexander Douglas Potts, Inspector of the 103rd District, presented the following report of the activities of our
Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands.

REPORT ON MASONRY IN THE HAWAIIAN ISLANDS
Presented at the 94th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
California by Alexander Douglas Potts, Grand Standard Bearer..

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethrer..:
One year ago it was my good fortune and privilege to address this
Grand Lodge on matters appertaining to Masonry in the Hawaiian
Islands. I am sure that all of you here in California are deeply concerned
and naturally interested over · the future of these eight Lodges located in
what was once known as the Paradise of the Pacific, and now more
appropriately termed the front line of defense of our Western Coast
line.
·
While it is true that .the restrictions placed on both Military and
Civilian personnel alike through the Martial Law, has in a great measure
created a complete change in our mode of living and particularly in the
hours of refreshment, this drastic change has materially effected the
smooth operations of our Masonic Lodges, yet, we are still able to carry
on our Masonic duties in as normal a manner as is humanly pos.sible.
While the effects of war have in many instances robbed many of
our communities of potential Masonic timber, it has acted just the opposite in other localities, and more especially in the Hawaiian Islands
today. I believe that it is safe to say without divulging any Military
secrets, that we have more Masons and prospective candidates for the
Degrees of Masonry assembled in the Hawaiian Islands than . we have
in any other part of our fighting fronts of equal area. This situation,
of course, is only natural, that our Government should take such necessary precautions as they have in utilizing this outpost of the Pacific as
a great arsenal of defense against our Western hemisphere, for it is
from this great reservoir of supplies that both men and material are
drawn to replace our ever expanding lines of attack in the South Pacific.
Those of you who have known Hawaii in the past as the Paradise
of the Pacific and have been privileged to visit it under normal conditions, .
admire its beautiful green hills and valleys, its abundance of flowers,
would, I am sure, find an entirely different kind of Hawaii today. Every

574

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

available space on that tiny Island is being utilized by Military installations and some oL the .most beautiful spots on the Island are now occupie<l by instruments of defense against our common enemy who so
treacherously attacked .u s at a time when they were talking peace terms.
It was then, and· only then, that the people of Hawaii were really faced
with the grim realities of war.
•
Little did any of us fully realize at the time, what the happenings of
that Sunday morning would mean to the future of .these Islands and
more particularly to the easy way of living of the people of these
Islands. Tremendous . changes have been made not only in our mode of
living but in the daily operations of our businesses. No one at the time
folly realized, prior · to· the December 7th attack, the hardships which the
war would place upon us. I, for one, had no conception of what effect it
would have on our Lodges.
·
I am sure that many of you will recall my remarks last year, relative
to our Black-out restrictions and the operation of our businesses, which
governed by Martial law, placed on us certain· restricted hours for opening
our places of business and the hours that we close, this, of course, being
made mandatory in order to clear everyone off the streets by. a certain
hour. While there have been some changes made in Black-out restrictions and an attempt on the part of the Military authorities to return
to the civil government .many Junctions of government not directly
effecting the war effort, it has in no way improved our situation so far
as the Masonic Lodges are coricern~d; whereby we are- enabled to hold our
meetings in the evenings. Last year, and more particularly during the
latter part of the year, we were confronted wi~h a situation never heretofore witnessed in the Hawaiian Islands even under peace time conditions. Many of these Lodges were receiving 40 to 50 applications for
the degrees of Masonry at each stated meeting. This condition would
lead one to believe that it was brought about by the unusually large
number of men being poured into the Hawaiian Islands. This, of course,
is not entirely true. We found among this large number of applications
the names of men who had lived practically all their lives in the Hawaiian
Islands, yet under peace times they never thought of applying for the
degrees of Masonry and now that the very existence of the Islands hung
in balance, their thoughts turned to Masonry. One would be prompted
to believe that this was brought about by the fact that these men were
either just plain joiners or were curiosity seekers, however, in going
over these applications I think you will find that this is not the case. I
am convinced that the grim realities of war brought them face to fa.c e
with something they felt they needed and that the Masonic Fraternity
was the place they could find the genuine fellowship so essential during
these times.
The question of receiving applications and the conferring of degrees
has not been the only problems that we have been confronted with
during the past year. Let us view the records of some of these Lodges,
and in so doing I refer more particularly to the Lodges in the 103td
District, not because this happens to be my District, but because these
Lodges are all located in and around Honolulu which is the hub of
activities and can be considered the distribution center for the entire
Hawaiian Area. It this District we have five Lodges, four of which
are all within close proximity of each other and the other Lodge, namely,
Schofield, is some thirty miles from Honolulu.
Due to the conjested conditions in and around Honolulu, and the
lack of proper recreational facilities, which was and still is today one of
our major problems, we found a condition existing especially among the

service men, which was beyond the control of the Authorities to cope
with. This is evidenced by the fact that it is a common sight to s.ee
lines two blocks long, mostly service men, on furlough trying to get into
a ·picture show, saloon or places of amusement where they could pe
privileged to sit down and rest for awhile, write letters, play a game of
cards and be away from the general grind of the life of a soldier. Many
complaints came to us from various sources that there was a large
number of Masons in the Armed Forces who were unable to visit a
Masonic Lodge during the time the Lodges were able to hold meetings
and that some sort of Masonic contact was necessary, and a place supplied
where these Masons could go and enjoy the atmosphere of a Masonic
Lodge. Here was a condition that the Masters of the Lodges especially
around Honolulu felt should be taken care of in a manner comparable to
the conditions that we were faced with and with the limited time we had
on hand. Several meetings were held and it was agreed that the proposition of asking the 0. C. D. who had occupied the ground floor of our
Temple to seek other quarters and that the space occupied by them be
put to use as a Masonic Service Bureau for the benefit of Masons in the
Armed Forces and defense workers. At considerable effort and expense
on the part of the Officers of these Lodges, this ground floor was redecorated and given a homelike atmosphere. The Eastern Star Chapters,
of which there are four, offered their services and together a committee
was formed and worked out plans whereby writing desks, card tables,
game tables, such as table tennis, were secured. The Eastern Star
Chapter furnished two hostesses who are · on duty six days of the week
to serve the bbys who drop in with hot coffee, cold drinks and supply
them. with all the ~riting material they want so that a boy away from
home can sit down and write his letters in a homelike surrounding and
get his mind off the every day grind of his military duties. This is our
small contribution in helping to support the morale of our fighting forces
· in the outpost of the Pacific.

575

Elections and Installations
Whl'le those '" !n our Government · are charged with the responsibility of replllcements and supplies, we too have had our problems, which
again all ties in with ·the . black-out restrictions. We have attempted to hold
such meetings as installations, etc., as joint affairs. Last December after
all the officers of the four Lodges had been elected and plans put into
action for a joint installation, thereby conserving time for both the officers
and members, we were confronted with a situation in Pearl Harbor Lodge
where the W. M. elect had been transferred to another job which rendered
it impossible to hold the position of W. M. for the year. This necessitated a change in our plans and special dispensation had to be given for
a special election. Taking into consideration that the membership of
this Lodge is composed almost in its entirety of brethren who are engaged with the furthering of the war effort by being connected either
with the armed services or employed at naval establishments,. it was a
difficult problem to secure a Master, who could put his time to the
position of that office. The Lodge elected one of its old Past Masters
and we felt that our problem so far as officers were concerned was taken
care of.
Immediately following the installation of officers it was brought to
our attention that the present owners of the building that Pearl Harbor
Lodge was renting from "as tennants at will" decided to increase the
revenue of their building and the ground floor was rented to a group
who had applied for and secured a liquor license and the place was to be

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

turned into a saloon. This, of course, made it undesirable as a proper
place to hold Lodge meetings especially during the daytime when the
members had to enter the Lodge room through the saloon, and the
members were forced to seek another meeting place. Through the kindness of the Trustees of the Oddfellows Temple, Pearl Harbor Lodge
was given permission to rent their Lodge room. I examined the building
and with but few minor changes I approved of its use as a proper place
to hold Masonic meetings, hence special dispensation was granted Pearl
Harbor Lodge to change its place of meeting and is now housed in the
Odd Fellows Temple for the duration.

the past year it has not to any great extent benefited the Lodges so far
as meetings are concerned. We are allowed what is known as a dimout, between the hours of 7:1.5 p. m. and 10:00 p. m. with the proviso
however, that no lights can be shown from any window or opening that
is exposed to the ocean. At the hour of 10 :00 p. m. all persons military
and civilian alike must be off the streets. While this dimout has its
advantages so far as it enables some of the people who are fortunate
enough to have windows or doors not facing the ocean some relief
from the hot weather has been a comfort to them. Those of you having
been to Hawaii know that practically all windows in any desirable part
of the houses, face the ocean. On the other hand can you imagine anyone
in Honolulu who would be foolish enough to build a home that did not
command an ocean view of some sort?
While we have had our hardships to contend with in Hawaii due to
the black-out restrictions and so-called Martial Law "a blessing in disguise" we should not overlook the fact that high tribute should be paid
to our Military Governor and members of his staff, many of them members of our craft, for their cooperation and the assistance that they have
extended to us in an endeavor to make living conditions as pleasant as
possible ever keeping in mind that the safety and security of these Islands
depends to a great measure of their good judgment and discretion in all
matters and the welfare and protection of our, businesses. To General
Delos C. Emmons, whom all of you know, and his successor General
Richardson, Jr., a member of our craft, I say on behalf of the fraternity
in the Hawaiian Islands that they have done a splendid job and we are
behind them 100 per cent. They have established for themselves an
enviable record· which shall go down in history when the final chapter
of this great conflict is written.
While we have gained both financially and numerjcally during the
past year we also have had our losses . to contend with, and seldom do
we attend a stated meeting of some Lodge but we ·he.ar these words so
commonly used these days "Missing in Action" to the memory of these
brave men who gave their lives for what Masonry stands for today.

sufficient number of officers to fill the chairs during a degree meeting,
which as I have already pointed out were all held during the daytime
when it was necessary for these officers to take time off from their work'
resulting in deductions in pay and criticism from some of their superiors.

Post-War Masonry
I am sure that many of you are familiar with the oft repeated term
appearing in our local papers concerning post-war conditions in this
country after the successful conclusion of the present confiict. I sometimes wonder if any thought has been given to post-war Masonry. When
we look at the many applications which are constantly pouring into our
Lodges, one sometimes wonders if these members who are now applying
for the Degrees of Masonry will continue in good standing, say ten years

578

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

from now. Our Grand Master has often repeated that we cannot make
Masons, we can only confer the degrees. I have always felt that too
muoh. care could not be exercised' over the reception of petitions when they
are :pfaced in the hands of the investigating committee and am convinced
that it is on this basis, the future membership of our Lodges ·should be
detet-mined, not after the .· candidate has been elected and received for
degrees.
Masonic War Relief
While :it is · gratifying to note that during the past year most of our
Lodges have realized the necessity of maintaining the Masonic War
Relief Fund and while it is true that no great demand may be placed upon
us during the present time, I am sure that all of you will agree with me ·
that when this conflict is over, our country is going to be faced with
conditions never · recorded in history.
.
We know that statements have been made by certain heads of our
government that the returning soldier will be given jobs, an opportunity
to return to universities and finish their education. But I note that there
is no mention made of where the funds are coming from to take care
of these men. I should think that all of us as Masons fully realize that
this tremendous program, which certain individuals in our government,
have taken upon themselves in the form of promises to the returning veterans
have made no mention of who was going to pay· for it. While we have
no intentions of making any reflection on any particular individual, such
a promise as has been made would be comparable to a statement made
by our present Grand Master from the ·floor of this Grand Lodge that if
you would reelect him to the office he now holds, he would promise to
reduce the dues in our constituent Lodges to 50 per cent of what they
now are.
Much has been said and credit given to young men and women of
this country who have so cheerfully and voluntarily offered their services
in the' defense of our liberties. I feel, however, that I cannot close these
remarks without paying some tribute to the fathers, mothers, wives,
brothers and sisters of these young men and women, who, keeping the
home fires burning, are still shouldering their share of responsibilities on
the home fronts. To many of our brethren who have knelt at the altar
of Masonry with us in the past and who have answered . the .suNeme sacrifice,
let us hope that the buildings of their Masonry and the · thought that all
is well with them now will soften the grief of their beloved ones at home
and that the knowledge of their loved one's high ability and sterling worth
will inspire the future generation to carry the banner of loyalty and virtue
high up the ramparts their fathers fearlessly scaled.

The committee originally was appointed for the purpose of promoting the observance of Constitution Day in our Lodges during the month
of September. With the' advent of the war, its functions were extended
to include the promotion of war activities pursuant to the order of the
Grand Master, including, for example, such objects as the purchase of
government bonds, contributions to the bl,ood bank, Red Cross and other
activities conducive to the successful prosecution of the war and the
alleviation of suffering in connection with it. During the war the attention
of the committee necessarily has been given primarily to war efforts.
On the other hand, the committee has not overlooked the importance
of the ultimate restoration of the normal rights of American citizens as
defined in the . Constitution. In some respects, the restoration of these
rights: follo'\Ving abnormal war conditions is a subject matter which is
more important for the consideration of Masonry than the prosecution
of the war itself. Sooner or later the war will end. There are many
organizations contributing to its prosecution. The maintenance of personal
rights and liberties exemplified in the Constitution are the result of cen-

581

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

turies of effort and sacrifice; if those privileges are not maintained through
centuries to come, the war, even if successful, will have been fought fn
vain.

It is impossible for any Lodge to obtain complete information. T.he remammg statistics are relatively accurate, excep.t for the assumption of
corresponding ·activity on the part of non-reporting Lodges.
In . any event, it is obvious that substantial results have been obtained
at a relatively small investment by Grand Lodge.
The results are due to the activity of both the Northern and the
Southern membership of the committee. The chairman cannot pay too
high tribute to these men, and to the officers and members of the Lod!§~S
throughout the jurisdiction who have so loyally suppo:ted ~he ;wa~ activities of our country, and the desire to perpetuate American mshtuhons.

580

The results throughout the Lodges of this jurisdiction have been substantial; the expenses incurred have been nominal. The total expenses
of the committee, including printing, postage and other items, have been
less than $300.00 ~or the year.
Reports
Reports have been received from 212 Lodges of a total .of 581, being
approximately 40 per cent. The statistics are taken. from these reports
from less than half the Lodges. It is a reasonable assumption that the
accomplishments for an average of the Lodges in the State should be
increased by approximately 60 per cent.
In some instances the i.-Uggestion has been made that the request
for reports should have been issued at an earlier date. The difficulty
which the committee encountered in issuing an earlier request is that
the observance of Constitution month occurs throughout the month of
September, and it was desired to bring the reports of all activities as
nearly as possible to the date of this communication of Grand Lodge.
Statistics
One hundred and seventy-seven meetings were held for the observance
of Constitution month; fifty open meetings, with an attendance of 4,214;
127 closed meetings, with an attendance of 6,901. Applying the above
mentioned percentage to Lodges which have not yet reported, the assumption is that a total of approximately 440 meetings were held, with
an attendance at open meetings of over 10,000, and an attendance at
closed meetings of over 17,000.
The total number of war activities meetings reported is approximately
the same, being 174 meetings held, with an attendance of 5,000 at public
meetings, and an attendance of 6,700 at closed meetings. If these figures
are increased by 60 per cent, they will roughly correspond to the estimated totals above listed for meetings for the observance of Constitution
Month.
Government bonds held by reporting Lodges on September I, 1942,
aggregated $655,000, and on September 1, 1943, the bond holdings aggregated $934,000, or an increase of $279,000. Applying the above percentage, this indicates an increase of bond holdings throughout the jurisdiction of approximately $700,000.
During the year there has been an increase in Lodge attendance in
73 Lodges, and a decreased attendance in 54 Lodges.
Initiations have increased in 167 Lodges, and have decreased in seven
Lodges.
These computations of Lodge attendance and initiations must be respectively increased by 60 per cent, as above indicated.
Reports show 6,500 members engaged in civilian war activities, and
2,000 members who have contributed to the· blood bank. Using the same
percentage, this indicates that of the Lodge membership in this jurisdiction, over 16,000 are engaged in civilian war activities, and 5,000 h4ve
contributed to the blood bank.
Necessarily figures as to war activities and contributions to the blood
bank are inadequate even as applied to the Lodges which have reported.

The report of this committee refers only to Lodges and Lodge members as such, but cannot include the personal efforts of the ~reth~e? . of
the jurisdiction which do not come within the scope of Masonic act1v1t1es.
For example, according to our last repo~ts, ove: 8,900. members of our
Lodges are in military service. Another illustration which deserves note
is that the Inspector for the Hawaiian Islands reports that over 80 per cent
of the membership are engaged either in defense "'.or~, or are ~embers
of the military forces. He apologizes for the om1ss10n of detailed attempts by the Island Lodges to observe Constitution month; the apology
was unnecessary.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE
MASONIC HOMES
I

To the Most Worshipfi'l Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith present
the fifty··first annual report, for the year ending July 31, 1943, together
with the reports of the Superintendents of our Homes, and the financial
reports of. the Secretary and Treasurer.
The Board of Trustees met on October 16, 1942, after the adjournment
of Grand Lodge with the following members present:
Charles M. Woilenberg (term expires 1946).
James B. Gist ·(term expires 1943).
Samuel E. Burke (term expires 1944).
Chas:· Albert Adams (term expires 1945).
Claude H. Morrison, Deputy Grand Master.
Gilbert C. DeForest, Senior Grand Warden.
Lawrence C. Kelley, Junior Grand Warden.
The reappointment of Past Grand Master, Charles M. Wollenberg, to
the Board of Trustees for a four-year term commencing October 16, 1942,
and the election of Claude H. Morrison, Deputy Grand Master; Gilbert
C. ·DeForest, Senior Grand Warden; Lawrence C. Kelley, Junior Grand
Warden, were formally reported to the board.
The board then organized for the ensuing year by electing the following officers:
Charles M. Wollenberg,, president.
James B. Gist, vice president.
By virtue of his reelection as Treasurer of th~ Grand Lodge, F. & A.
M. of California, William P. Filmer remained Treasurer of the Masonic
·Homes of California; until his death November 22, 1942, ·and was succeeded by Francis V. Keesling as of that date.
By virtue of· his reelection as Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge,
· F; & A. M. of California, Lloyd E. Wilson remains Secretary of the
. Masonic Homes of California.

583

On November 22, 1942, scarcely more than a month after the close
·Of Grand Lodge the Board of Trustees suffered a great loss in the passing
of Most 'Vorshipful William P. Filmer, Grand Treasurer, who. since his
election to that office on October 17, 1913, had served as the Treasurer
of the Masonic Homes.
The Homes have experienced their greatest growth duri:ng these years
both in properties and in funds, and the sound financial condition which
we enjoy today is largely attributable to the great interest which Brother
Filmer took in the conduct of our financial affairs. Th.e ability which
Brother Filmer brought to the consideration of our problems helped lift
the entire standard of the Board and we shall never be able. adequately
to express our appreciation of the splendid service which he rendered.
Commendation
Under the superv1s10n of our able Superintendents, Brother Eubanks
at Decoto, and Brother Downen at Covina, our Homes have met the
various problems that arise in institutions such as these. At all times in
homes for the aged there are some disgruntled members of the family
and small grievances are magnified. With little complaint our families
have adjusted themselves to the food restrictions entailed by War Time
shortages and regulations, and both the aged at Decoto and the children
at Covina have responded in meeting the labor shortage.
Population
At Decoto we find our population has decreased. This is largely due
to the fact that a number of our aged have secured war time work, and
applications for admission have decreased due to the fact that those who
might have applied are now engaged in war activities. With higher
costs of food, clothing and, in fact, everything that goes for comfort and
health, the increase of the State pension to $50.00 is not sufficient to enable an aged person to live in comfort unless there are immediate relatives who can afford shelter and care, and with the return to normal
conditions we anticipate a large increase in the population of the Decoto
Home.
·
At Covina our population shows a decline from 99 children as reported
one year ago to 81 today. This is reflecte!I by a reduction in operating
costs of 11.3 per cent.
The increased demands made upon us for child care following the
last World War will in all probability be repeated in the post war
period ahead and i~ such proves to be the case, our Home at Co'vina will
be well prepared to meet the situation.

The maintenance cost includes general maintenance, hospital, farm,

Summer Camp
The Masonic Homes has for years maintained a summer camp for our
children on Balboa Island in Newport Bay. For obvious reasons, the
camp has not been opened since Pearl Harbor.
This year we allowed the use of part of the buildings at Camp Tucker,
Balboa, to the Marine Division of the Girl Scouts of Ame~ica for the
summer. The leadership of this group consisted of responsible people;
their occupancy of the camp was beneficial rather than otherwise, and it
brought about the cleaning up and putting in order that part of the
premises which they are using.
We have leased four of the dormitory buildings at the camp to the
Newport Beach Grammar School for the duration of the war. They are
paying $50.00 a month· rental, plus any extra charges which the Homes
may sustain by reason of their occupancy.
Alumni in the Armed Forces
One hundred twenty-six alumni of the Covina Home are in the Armed
Forces of the United States.
Four of our young women graduates are in the Armed Forces:
Georgiana Davis, Tujunga Lodge No. 592, left the Home in 1935 and is
a private in the Women's Army Corps. Rosetta Lewin," Los Angeles
Lodge No. 42, left the Home in 1938, and Marian Hass, San Francisco
Lodge No. 360, who left in 1940, are both privates in the U. S. Marines.
Helen Schulte, Hermann Lodge No. 127, left the Home in 1936, is a
Second Lieutenant in the U. S. Army Nursing Corps and is at present
on . foreign service.

585

Twenty of the Masonic Home Alumni have received commissions as
of!icers:. one Colonel, one Lieutenant-Commander, one Captain, eight
First Lieutenants, seven Second Lieutenants, and two Ensigns. These
commissioned officers constitute 16 per cent of their whole number
whereas in the armed services generally the proportion of commissioned
officers is only 7 per cent; in other words our alumni have more than
twice as many commissioned officers as might be normally expected.
this st:iking fact we find evidence that the mode of life, training and
influence m the Home, while in no wise military, do tend to develop
qualities of initiative and leadership.

!n

Of the many· cases that have come to our attention of boys who brought
honor to the Home in the service of their country, we will recite several
for your information:
·
First Lieutenant Clarence Boyer (Alhambra Lodge No. 322) U. S.
Army Air Corps : We have received information that Lieutenant Boyer
has piloted one of the Spitfires that escorted large formations of Fortresses
in their devastating bombing of the German Naval Base at Kiel. These
Spitfires were praised for their aid by Colonel Herbert T . Thatcher,
Bomber Group Commander.
Boyer graduated from the flying school at Lake Charles Louisiana
in August, _1942, and was rai9Cd to the rank of First Lieutenant' in January'.
1943. He left for England in May of this year.
Harold Lounsbury (Yosemite Lodge No. 99) Machinist's Mate, 2/c,
U. S .. Navy: Saw combat service in the Pacific Ocean during 1942. At
one time was at sea 72 days without sighting land. Was in the Stewart
Island action, also battles of Midway and Coral Sea and was on the
Hornet when it was sunk.
·
Excerpts from Letters
James E . Rowland, Seaman, 2/c, U. S. Navy, training at University
of Chicago, writes: "I have never thanked you for what you did ·for
me while I was in the Home. I never realized then how lucky I was.
Tell the boys and girls that they are the luckiest kids on earth. They
may not think so now, but I never thought so either-until I left the
Home. I was taught one of the most important things I know, and that
was to respect my elders. . . . I want to thank you for the, shall I say,
'basic training' I received at the Home. I believe I owe most of my
success in the Navy to the faculty of the. Home."
Cadet J, D . Colvin (Bell Lodge- No. 483) U. S. Navy Pre-Flight
School, Del Monte, Calif., writes: "During my time here my body has
gone through some things I never thought possible before. But I know
now! I can say that I have thanked the Home a million times for all
you did to help me, even though we were probably just a little bit backward when it came to accepting your administration. Getting along with
other men is one of the main factors that help a fellow so much in
accepting. the discipline of the caliber we get here, (and like it)."

.Alfred Chetham (Sequoia Lodge No. 349), who left the Home ten
years ago, writes from the Advanced Flying School, La Junta, Colorado.
After recounting the good times he. had while a boy at the Home, and
his subsequent life after leaving it, he says that he is getting Masonic
Degrees from San Francisco Lodge No. 360, and adds: "The main
reason I wanted to join the Masons is that they were directly responsible
for the happiest years of my life, excepting the time in which I have been
married. . . . I now know that it was those years at the Home which
formed my life. I want to pass on to someone else the chances for
character-building, education and happiness which were so generously
given to me, even though I did not realize it at the time."
Ben Helwig
One more alumnus of the Home should be mentioned, not in a uniform
of the Armed Forces but working for the war in jeans and jumper.
A number of years ago Ben Helwig, a ward of Orange Grove· Lodge
No. 293, was playing a game at the Home in which a crooked stick was
knocked in the air. Through mischance he was hit in the eye, infection
set in, and although the best physicians available were consulted lie lost
the sight of both eyes. He was sent to the Blind School at Berkeley,
spending his vacations at the Home each year. On graduation a "Seeing
Eye" dog was provided and, having been trained as a wood worker and
mechanic, he was provided with an electrically driven saw, planer and
lathe which were installed in the rear of his mother's home.
After Pearl Harbor; he endeavored to get employment in the Air
Plane Industry and did succeed in securing a job wherein he became an
inspector aluminum castings. Through sensitiveness of his hands and
hearing he was able to detect flaws. This reached the- newspapers, and
recently Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer produced a film in which he was the
hero, the name of it being "Seeing Hands." If any of you have seen it we
know. you would be interested in knowing that the hero of this picture
was one of our boys. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer set aside part of the income
from this film for the purpose of sending Ben to New York to consult
the best oculists in the country. A few weeks ago Superintendent Downen
received a letter from Ben in which he stated that after examinations it
had been determined that the restoration of his sight was hopeless. He
closed his letter by saying: "I am having a grand time seeing New
York." I am sure you all join me in saying we are proud of Ben. In
spite of his handicap, he has adjusted himself to life and is a useful
citizen doing his bit for his country.
Byron Athan
In 1936, Byron D . Athan, Petaluma Lodge No. 180, left the Covina
Home. On his arrival in San Francisco, he was employed for a short
time in the office of ·the Grand Secretary. He then, with the assistance
of his mother, entered college with the hope of becoming a lawyer. In
1941, he called on the reader of this report asking for advice. He was a
member of the National Guard with the rank of Second Lieutenant. The
Guard was being called into Federal Service. Inasmuch as he was attending law school, he had an opportunity to withdraw. After some discussion
he desired to follow his inclination in what he conceived to be a patriotic
duty and remained with the Guard.
In January, of this year, he was promoted to First Lieutenant. Celebrating that promotion his wife called on me, presenting a $100 War Bond,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNtA

Health at the Decoto Home

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home
Brethren: As Superintendent, I herewith submit for your consideration, my third annual report of the Masonic Home at Decoto, for the
year ending August 31, 1943. This being the forty-fourth annual report
filed by its superintendents during the existence of the Home. ·
At the beginning of the fiscal year there were 305 residents enjoying
the comfort and protection of the Home. During the year there were
admitted eleven men, at an average age of 65.91 years, and twenty
women, at an average age of 77.9 years. During the same period we
lost by death 27 men, at an average age of 77.41 years and 17 women,
at an average age of 77 years. By withdrawal 8 men and 1 woman.
The end of the year leaves us with 131 men and 152 women, a total
of 283 residents. This includes fourteen married couples.
The age groups of the residents are as follows:

From the report of Dr. W. L. Whirter, Home Physician and Surgeon,
we give the following excerpts:
The Home Hospital, under the direct supervision of Miss Esther G.
Payne, R. N., who has served the Home Residents long and faithfully,
consists of accommodations for fifty patients. In an emergency, sixty
beds can be provided for patients. The average number of patients cared
for in the hospital is forty-five per day.
Regular Clinic hours are ·maintained five days per week. The average
number visiting the Clinic daily are six. Daily visits to hospital patients
and evening calls upon those who are seriously ill are made throughout
the year. Emergency visits, day or night, are made when necessary.
The physio-therapy department is equipped with a short wave Diathermy machine, Infra-red lamps, ultra violet cold quartz lamp and other
modalities for heat and cold therapy. Average daily treatments are four,
with Miss Payne acting technician.
X-rays are made by the Home Physician for the diagnosis of fractures.
Minor surgery is done at the Home Hospital. Those requiring major or
special surgery are promptly transported to hospitals in San Frandsco,
Oakland or San Jose, in the Home Station wagon ambulance.
Special diets · for the Home Residents are prescribed when deemed
necessary, and are faithfully carried out by the dietitian. Inspections of
the kitchens and food are made at least once weekly by the medical department and uniformly sanitary conditions and well balanced meals are
always found.
Finances
This year we come to Grand Lodge reporting a surplus of $141,658.39.
Several factors are responsible for this. One factor is the $25.00.contribution from initiates who, as you have been informed, have this year increased in large numbers and second that war time restrictions and
rationing have curtailed our expenditures.
For three years we have been unable to secure material for repairs,
replacement and modernization of our properties. At such time as peace
permits, we face large expenditures for painting, carpentry, plumbing,
rebuilding and · modernization of elevators; laundry equipment, carpets
and furnishings, a new roof on the ramp from dining room to hospital,
and a multitude of minor items.
With' the realization that from five to seven years may pass during
which time replacements and rehabilitation or proper modernization of our
Homes will be prevented by war activities, we deemed it advisable to set
up a reserve of $100,000 out of the surplus, to be used for Post War
building, equipment, and modernization, leaving available for general maintenance purposes the sum of $41,658.39. This will enable us to make a
material reduction in our per capita, and, we therefore, recommend that
the per capita assessment for the support of the Hom~s be reduced 50
per cent and thus fixed at 20 cents for the ensuing year.
CHARLES M. WOLLENBERG,
JAMES B. GIST,
CHAS. ALBERT ADAMS,
SAMUEL E. BURKE,
CLAUDE H. MORRISON,
GILBERT
DEFOREST,
LAWRENCE C. KELLEY, Trustees.

The average age at this time is 75.86 years for the women and 76.11
for men.
In addition to the wonderful climatic conditions which exist in this
locality, the regular habits, proper diet, contentment and careful medical
supervision which the residents enjoy, I am sure helps much in permitting the elder folk to attain the additional years which the above table
indicates have been added to the proverbial three score and ten.
Generally speaking, the health condition at the Home during the
year has been very good. However, advancing years bring with them
the inevitable infirmities. Therefore we shall always find it necessary
to care for the infirm, blind and crippled in the hospital. At present
43 residents are being cared for in that department.
We are fortunate indeed in having Miss Esther Gill Payne to supervise the work in the hospital, where kind, faithful and considerate
servic~ is her constant watchword. Then, too, we are fortunate in having
Dr. W. L. McWhirter as our physician. He is one of the busiest men
in the community, due to the absence of so many of the doctors, who
have been called into service. However, Dr. McWhirter finds time to
visit the Home every day, and ne'v er hesitates to come when .called in
emergencies.
The policy of creating a home-like atmosphere in the Home, and
harmony and contentment among the residents, which Mrs. Virginia
Meek Lord, our Matron, and myself adopted when we took over the
management, is being diligently pursued.
The labor problem, with which everyone is confronted today, has
had its effect on our Home. For the past six months ·we have been
unable to maintain a full staff in all departments, and at times it has
been very critical. The residents are helping in every way possible.
However, there is a limit to their ability. For several months we have
been without, and unable to secure, a painter or a fireman, and during
the month of August our food has been prepared by our chef, who has
as his assistant, one of the residents. As a result certain services have
been curtailed, but I am confident our standard has not been lowered.
With all this shortage of help we feel that the Home and the grounds
still present a very clean and attractive appearance.

592

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Along with the labor situation we also have our food problems. With
the help of the Almighty and the Washington Township Ration Board
our Home is still functioning, and I want to say here that we are fortunate in having a Ration. Board who are capable and very understanding
of our situation. The food allowed us by the local Ration Board has
been ample for our needs so far without in any manner lessening the
quality or quantity of food served. We, of course, do not have the
variety to select from. However, in most cases we are able to find
satisfactory substitutes.
'
In the past twelve months we have served 310,119 meals at an average
cost of $0.1605 per meal.
Most of the farm land is leased on a cash basis, the small portion
retained for Home use furnishes a goodly amount of the fruit, vegetables
and berries. The poultry department has not done so well this year.
We have plans for the future which we hope will improve this department.
We acquired 14 head of hogs the early part of the year. Apparently
this acquisition is going to prove profitable. To date this department
has supplied the Home with about 1000 lbs. of meat and we still have
on hand 21 feeders for future use, in addition to two brood sows and
a boar.
A list of the programs presented by the Lodges will be found in
another part of the report. To those Lodges go our grateful thanks
and appreciation. We only wish we could have more.
On August 21st the East Bay Past Matrons' Association visited the
Home. In their usual generous manner they presented the Home with a
very generous supply of cakes, jellies and jams. Also a supply of pajamas,
night gowns and table covers and comforters. We want to assure this
fine organization that the family fully appreciate the interest shown in
their behalf.
After lunch, provided by the Association, which was served in the
basement banquet room, they adjourned to the auditorium and introduced the Grand Matron and the Grand Patron of the 0 . E. S. with their
official family and all the past a~d present officers of the Association. A
very fine program, consisting of recitations, instrumental and vocal numbers was presented.
A report of the devotional services will be found elsewhere in the
report. We feel very much indebted to these Reverend gentlemen for
the fine message they bring to us each Sunday.
Our Thursday evening program which is s~pplied by the R K 0,
Columbia Pictures Corporation, United Artists Corporation, Warner
Bros. Pictures, Twentieth Century-Fox, Film Distributing Companies of
Sa n Francisco, is greatly appreciated by the family and to these fine
organizations go our grateful thanks. We were almost robbed of these
programs due to the fact that the Union is unable to furnish an operator.
We have soh,ed this difficulty by operating the picture machines ourselves; therefore, the show goes on just the same.
Our many friends and members of the fraternity keep the Home
well supplied with magazines, books and periodicals, which the members
enjoy reading and appreciate very much.
During the year, Grand Master Leslie Wood and his family honored
us with a visit, and made a careful inspection of the Home.
The Trustees, Grand Secretary, and other Grand Lodge officers have
made periodical visits to the Home, during the year.

593

We appreciate these visits and urge their continuance, knowing that
we are going to be greatly benefited by your kindly advice.
The past year has been a very unusual one. We have met our problems continuously and have attempted to dispose of them with sensible
judgment, and trust our judgment has met with your approval.
In conclusion, Mrs. Lord and myself wish to extend our appreciation
of the loyal service rendered by our employees. To the members of the
Home who are so ably assisting go our grateful thanks, and··to express
to the members of the Board of Trustees our sincere gratitude for their
counsel and advice.
:•
Respectfully submitted,
J. R. EuaANKS, Superintendent.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina Home
To the Trustees of the Masonic Hom es of California:
In my report of a year ago, I said: "The last year in the Covina Home
has been marked by decreasing enrollment, many changes in the personnel of our employed staff, necessity to increase salaries, rise in p'r ices
of all commodities, inevitable increase in our per capita cost of operation."
All the conditions indicated in the paragraph above have continued
during the year 1942-43.
Enrollment and Expense for Past Year-Our enrollment as of Ju1y
31st; 1943, was 82 children; one year earlier the enrollment was 99. In
other words, our number of children has decreased 17 per cent during the
past year.
Comparison of our expense for "Care of Children" for the two years
in shown in the following table:
1943
1942
$23,543
Food ................................................................................$26,312
Other Subsistence Expense...................................... 7,081

Operating expense for the year was 11.3 per cent less than for the year
before.
Adjustment to Decreasing Enrollment-We have adjusted our operation to decreasing enrollment by vacating one and one-half to our four
residence buildings for children; or three-eighths of our dormitory building space. We have vacated one of our two dining rooms. We have

609

reduced our staff of employees by one secretary, three houseparents, one
dining room woman, and one seamstress.
Certain services and maintenance cannot be reduced in proportion to
the reduction of the number of children in our· care. T h e same acreage
of grounds, and as many square feet of buildings, must continue to be
cared for and kept in order; the engineer's department and the laundry
must be kept going with the same number of employees; the farm work
must go. on; the hospital must be kept staffed and ready to serve. U n der
these conditions per capita figures have little significance.
Employees--The past year has been one of unprecedented difficulty
in obtaining and holding satisfactory epiployees, especially men. At the
present time we have only three men under sixty years old. During th e
summer vacation our children have had behavior difficulties which would
not have occurred if we had been able to secure the recreational leadership
which they needed, and which we tried without success to employ.
Mechanical Work and Repairs--Owing to limitations of help and supplies, this type of work has been kept at a minimum. W e have, however,
painted the exterior wood work on most of the buildings in order to
prevent weather, damage.
Inspection by the Los Angeles County Fire Prevention department
called for quite a program of improvement in electrical wiring, which had
to be done before our operating license could be renewed; and, was done.
Our mechanical plant is on the whole in good condition now.
Rationing-The amount of difficulty in connection with the rationing
of food, shoes and gasoline, has been on the whole less than might have
been exp~cted. Mrs. Flynn, head of our subsistence department, has
bought for this department and done it well. Food cost was 31 per cent
of our operating cost for each of the last two years. In 1943 food cost
per meal was 30 per cent higher than in 1941 ; for last two months has
averaged 16.7c per meal.
To meet present conditions we planted nearly two acres in garden
vegetables, which have yielded well and have kept us sufficiently supplied.
A considerable quantity of vegetables have been canned. Our canning
operations have been limited by inability to get the desired amount of jars.
Physical Care of Children-Health of the children during the year
has been excellent, with no case of serious illness .. In view of the reduced
availability of medical service, the competent preventive work of our
nurse has taken on new importance. T h e daily average number of patients
in the hospLtal during the year has been only 2.25.
Donations, Visitations and Entertainments--Appended herewith is a
list of donations, visitations and entertainments. During th e past year the
number of visitors to the Home has been curtailed by reason of prevailing
conditions in transportation. Considering current limitations of travel, the
numb~r of visitors has been surprising and gratifying.
We wish to acknowledge again the continued special interest of Mount
Olive Lodge No. 506, as indicated by their maintenance of the Mount
Olive Lodge Recreation Fund, from which we draw from time to time
as needed for special recreational purposes. Amollg the nice things which

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this Lodge has done for us was to bring to us on one memorable occasion
Gloria Jean of the motion pictures, a thrilling event for our children.

A strong and real basis of religious inculcation is found in the religious
foundation of Masonry. Being children of Masons, our boys and girls
inherit a respect for Masonry and its ideals. They learn that the Home
itself 'is a concrete expression of those ideals, that the Masons founded
and support this Home voluntarily, as an expression of their ethical and
religious principles. They learn that the letter "G" symbolizes · the Diety
as the central thing in Masonry. They have considerable personal contact
with Masons and get to know the kind of people they are. The existence
of Masonry as the children witness its expression here is an impressive
religious influence in their lives.

610

It has been the custom of Monrovia Lodge No. 308 for many years
to take our children to Monrovia for a Christmas party. This year it
was impossible to make the trip, but the Lodge put the party on at the
Home, with all its unusual features, including a gift for every child.
Our Christmas observance was also greatly aided by the continuance,
as in many years past, of the custom of a contribution for a present for
every child by the Westerners Club, of the Twentieth Century-Fox
Studios.
A good friend of the Home, Brother Carl Peters, has contrbuted from
time to time throughout the year generous lots of cartons of candy bars,
which were very welcome in view of the present curtailment of the candy
supply.
We had several children who were in need of orthodontia treatment,
which is expensive. We are indebted to the Supreme Pyramid, Ancient
Egyptian Order of Sciots, James A. Lynch, Pharaoh, for a special donation for this purpose. Another special donation for this purpose came
from Wilshire Lodge No. 445.
Wilshire Lodge also made inquiry as to what they could do in a
material way to add to the comfort of the children; and, after consideration, the refurnishing of the living room in the Girls' Building was decided upon. A committee of the Lodge was appointed under the chairmanship of Brother W. G. Lane. Brother Lane and his good wife took
a keen interest and spent much time in personal supervision of this improvement. When they had finished, the room was indeed a beautiful
addition to our facilities, and will do much through the ye~rs to add to
the happiness and elevate the tastes of the girls of the Home.
Moral and Religious Training-An inquiry recently made concerning
moral and religious training in the Home suggests the inclusion here of
some information on that subject. We do not place much reliance upon
moral instruction in the abstract. It is the concrete situations of daily
living that furnish the best opportunities for the inculcation of ethical
principles. Within the institutional group more situations arise involving
questions of right and equity than are found in a pi:ivate home. If a boy
invades the property rights of another, we have an opportunity to teach
him about honesty, with the help of the boy whose rights have been disregarded-and both are learning. Childre~ living in groups teach each
other a great deal in the processes of social contacts. Because of the
variety of their social experiences in the Home, our children go forth
better prepared than the average to deal rightly with those among whom
they are to live and worlc.
In the Home grace is said before each meal. Our smallest children
receive Sunday school instruction from their housemothers; the others
are required to attend regularly some church or Sunday school in Covina.
There they make beneficial acquaintances, by which they are broadened
and improved. We do not urge them to take on church memberships,
though in some cases they do so of their own accord.

611

Alumni in Military Service-A year ago the panel in the hallway of
the Administration Building at the Covina Home contained the names of
63 of its alumni who were in their country's service. Now this number
has been exactly doubled to 126.
Letters-Letters from alumni are coming in much greater volume than
before the war. They reflect the yearning of the young soldier for home;
we are always glad when that longing expresses itself in a letter to us.
These letters are often read to the children now in the Home, for whom
they have great interest as well as character-training value.
Due to the war, our activity in issuing newsletters to the alumni has
increased. Formerly we issued one Newsletter per year; .but because of
the great demand from those in military service we have already issued
five newsletters during 1943. We have received many expressions indicating how great a need these are filling; the one thing that soldiers overseas
seem to want above all is letters from home
·
A letter just received from Edward Bounds (Pharmacist's Mate 3/c),
in the Navy, now in the Southwest Pacific, says: "All of us kids keep in
touch with at least a few of the others, and I notice that we all seem to
say something like this 'Remember the good old carefree days in the M.
H.?' 'What do you hear from any of the Home kids?' It seems for sure
that wherever we go we always think back on the Home and kids; we
really realize how lucky we were, not only for our bringing-up but for the
friends we made."
Alumni Evaluations-We often say to the boy or girl who may express
dissatisfaction with some of our procedures or decisions, "We are not so
much concerned with what you think about this now as we are about
what you will think of it five years from now. When you are one of our
alumni, come back and advise us how to run the Home and we will listen
to you."
And we are in fact influenced by the opinions and comments of the
boys and girls and men and women who have lived here, when they come
back to see us or write to us after they have had experience in the outside
world. This is one reason why we are . so much interested in keeping in
contact with them.
We have abundant evidence that .our alumni do not feel that the regime
of the Home was too severe or too strict. They often say, "When we

612

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

were there we didn't realize what it was all about; we had to try living
in the outside world to find what the Masonic Home was. No, you
weren't too strict 'fith us; if anything, you were too easy."
We think their success after they leave .us is evidence that w~atever
indulgence we showed them did not unfit them to meet the tests of adult
life.
JOHN M. DOWNEN,
Superintendent.

The report was 'adopted except that portion . dealing with
fi'nances, which was referred to the Finance Committee.
At this point Grand Lodge was called from labor to refreshment and President Wollenberg of the Board of Trustees presented and introduced Miss Helen Schulte, a graduate of our
Masonic Home at Covina, who had just returned from the Aleutian
Islands where she served at a 2nd lieutenant in the U. S. Army
N ursin'g Corps.
· For financial reports, see Spec'.i al Ap~endix.

.:~/

' Grand Lodge was then called from refreshme~t to labor.

623

Following in the footsteps of your previous boards, and in an effort to
measure up to the splendid records achieved in past years, we have carried forward the work of stimulating interest in our two Homes, among the lodges and
membership within the jurisdic'tion.
This has included a general educational campaign, having for its purposes
not only the securing of voluntary contributions to the Endowment Fund, but
also a better understanding on the part of the craft, of this magnificent program-which has now become one of California Masonry's most important
undertakings.
·
' . In bringing this phase of our activities to the attention of the brothers, we
have emphasized the permanency of the fund and have stressed the fact that
contributions become part of the fund itself and that income only is used foi:.operational and maintenance expenses.
. We have tried to implant in the minds o f our members the ·privilege that
is theirs of participating in this great benevolent activity and to bring home to
them the real and lasting good being accomplished by our Homes at Decoto
and Covina.
·
·
It is perhaps unnecessary to. point out that the impact of war has had a
,
somewhat demoralizing effect upon all of our activities, and particularly upon
our Endowment Fund program. :) Demands upon our members, resulting from
war-time conditions, have ·seriously affected many and placed a heavy strain
upon others. Our own War Relief Fund efforts, which may well be considered
as highly necessary if not paramount, have added to some extent, at least, to
the individual responsibilities of our membership.
In the face of all of these conflicting conditions, your board ·is happy to
report to the Grand Lodge that our members have responded to our appeal with
generous hearts. The following figures tell their own story-a story that proves
again that California Masonry is not only aware of its responsibilities and duty
to our unfortunates, but me.ets those responsibilities with genuine Masonic
solicitude and interest, an interest that wells from the heart and overflows with
brotherly love and a sincere desire to g ive help where help is needed.
Total Assets of Fund

Appreciation

In this connection, your board desires to ·express its sincere thanks and appreciation to the Masters, secretaries, endowment chairmen, inspectors, and
all others who have given of their time and effort in the carrying out of this
vital program, and withotllt whose co-operation little could have been accomplished.
Our special thanks and appreciation go to the Grand Master for the
magnificent support he has given our efforts throughout the entire year. Particular reference is made to his official proclamation designating the month of
May as Homes Endowment Fund Month-a declaration of Masonic precepts
and principles that brought inspiration and thoughtful consideration to the
members of the Craft throughout the entire jurisdiction.
In no less a degree, we likewise express our appreciation of the splendid
support given your board by all of the officers of. the Grand Lodge, a support
which gave added pleasure to our efforts.
Indicative of the interest which has manifested itself during the past
twelve months, is the great amount of correspondence which your board has
handled, numbering many hundreds of incoming and outgoing communications.
To this activity should be added the distribution of many thousands of pieces of
literature dealing with the subject, as well as receipts and letters of acknowledgment sent to all donors. Printing, postage, and clerical assistance, necessary
to the proper carrying on of our activities, were of considerable magnitude.

Although accrument to the Endowment Fund through the medium of wills
and bequests represents a substantial portion of its gradual increase, it is our
belief that the opportunity along this particular line of endeavor is in fact a
virgin field. In line with that belief we have continued to keep the subject
before the proper individuals and like our predecessors, have continued to sow
seeds which will bear fruit in the years to come.
War Savings Stamps and Bonds
Successfully initiated by last year's board, the plan of performing a double
duty through the purchase of War Savings Stamps and Bonds, and in turn
donating them t o the Endowment Fund, has been given our every encouragement and has produced most satisfactory results, as reflected in the foregoing
financial statements. Too much credit for the success of this particular phase
of our activities cannot be given to the secretaries and endowment chairmen
for their untiring efforts in this matter. War Stavings Stamps in the amount
of $1,622.85 was received from the individual lodges.

In order that your board may function during the ensuing y~r, we offer
the following resolution and recommend its adoption: "Resolved, that the sum
of six thousand dollars be and is hereby appropriated from the funds of this
Grand Lodge to be paid to the Masonic Homes Endowment Board for its
expenses for the year ending July 31, 1944."
The healthy condition of your Endowment Fund at this time, and its gradual growth from year to year, are concrete evidence of its value to the fraternity and the lasting benefits made possible by its operation. Because its
activities are cumulative and thus make possible a gradual enlargement of its
accomplishments, your board urges active continuance, in the hope that some
day its shall have reached such proportions as will make it unnecessary to call
upon our members, as individuals, for further assistance.
Conclusion
The individual members of your board are deeply grateful for having had
the honor and opportunity of serving so worthy a cause during the year now
ending; a cause that has received the generous approval of the members of the
Craft, as shown by their sympathetic interest in the welfare of our guests at
the homes at Decoto and Covina.
Although the war has brought its dislocations, its sorrows and its grief to
many of us, the history of the past year, as particularly applied to the activities
of this board, has proved' that the spirit of democracy g.till lives. We still have
our freedoms and our ability to carry out the traditional programs of charity,
brotherly love and . inutual assistance-the foundation and cardinal principles
of our great fraternity.
Fraternally submitted,
