REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TWENTY-FOURTH
ANNUAL OBSERVANCE OF PUBLIC
SCHOOLS WEEK
To the Most Worshipful Grand iodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Master of one of the lodges in a city which ·had held an especially
successful observance this year stated in his report that the success was
"spotty.'' It developed that what he meant was that while the observ:~n<:e
was otherwise very successful, there were ' two night meetings at which
the· attendance had not been as large as it should have been. Well, a
somewhat similar situation prevailed throughout the state generally.
The twenty-fourth annual observance of Public Schools Week was
one of the most successful ever held. Indeed there were many communities, it appears from the reports, in which in spite of war conditions,
or perhaps because of them, the observance aroused more public interest
and received more support than ever before.
The success reported was especially gr_a.tifying in that it appears it
was not generally expected. Attached to the report from one of our
lodges was a letter from the District Superintendent of Schools to the
lodge from which we quote because it expresses what we have in mind :
"I am 'happy to submit this annual report on Public Schools Week in.
the - - - School District. It has been made up by the Principals of the
various schools in the District and is a complete summary of the week's
program. . . .
"I had considerable misgiving that Public Schools Week this year
would receive less attention from the patrons of the school district because of the many requirements of the war effort. However, now that
the week is over I am happy to report that regardless of the emergency,
Public Schools Week was an outstanding success .. ..
"We believe that there were fully as many people that visited their
public schools during the observance, as in any year in the past. . . .
"The members of the governing board, the administrative council
and the teachers of the district share with me the enthusiasm that we
have because of the support given us by - - - Masonic Lodge.. . . Thank
you for your splendid cooperation.''
Although, as we have said, our latest observance was as a whole, one
of the most successful ever held, there were some black spot's. There
were some lodges (fortunately not many) which made no effort whatever to overcome the obstacles presented by war time conditioni<. They
did not measure up to the opportunity presented. There were others

628

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

where the difficulties were virtually unsurmountable; and in one community an outbreak of measles, and in another of whooping cough, made
it necessary to cancel the arrangements which had been made for an
observance. Blame should not therefore attach to every lodge which
failed to comply with the proclamation of the Grand Master to join in
the observance of Public Schools Week.
In justice to some of the lodges which made no effort to join in the
observance it should be stated that in some places this was due to the
fact that the school authorities discouraged the holding of an observance
this year. The reason given was that because of war conditions, the
schools, and the teachers, were already burdened with an extremely
heavy load and that with their other duties, the teachers could not
devote the necessary time to an observance. Of course, it is a fact that
there are communities in which the school population has more than
doubled; and the schools like other war industries, are being operated
in "shifts"-and with the same teacher taking two shifts.
It was obvious at the outset that the prevailing conditions made a
successful observance more difficult than it otherwise would have been;
and, therefore, in the first notice from our committee to the Masters
they were reminded that to overcome the handicap it would be necessary
to make extraordinary efforts this year.
The dim-out regulations, gas rationing and other transportation difficulties would naturally affect the attendance. But in addition to this,
many of the Masters and other officers and members of the lodge were
engaged in war work of some sort, or were having additional demands
made upon their time by the manpower shortage; and the deer.e ased
number of teachers made it difficult for some of the school people to
give as full cooperation as would be ordinarily expected.
It must be remembered, too, that among those who would ordinarily
join in the observance there will be found · some who, for one reason or
another have failed to realize the relationship between public education
and th~ momentous world affairs which now engage our attention. To
them the observance of PubHc Schools Week is dwarfed by what are
obviously war time duties and obligations.
The situation presented was a challenge not only to the loyalty of
the craft, but to the intelligence as well as the zeal of those charged
with the responsibility of making the arrangements. And marvelously
did they respond to it.
There were some communities where in spite of war conditions no
change whatever was made in the form of the observance ; and the success was the result of the extraordinary effort which was made. In
others the form was changed to meet the local conditions. For th_e
most part the change simply meant holding no night meetings a!ld
featuring visits to the schools with classroom exhibits and demonstrations.
It will be remembered that because of the interference of the Easter
vacation the time of our observance was changed from the regular date
-the fo~rth Monday in April to the second Monday. This made possible
a form of observance of which mention will be made later.
Whatever the form of the observance, the program was in one way
or another predicated on the theme "Education for Victory"; and was
designed to call attention to the part the schools are playing in the
national emergency.
Probably the most amazing thing in connection with the observance
was the response of the public. It would seem as though there were
more than one community like that bf which the Master said in his

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

629

report "Public Schools Week in - - - is always looked forward to and
attended with much pleasure and enthusiasm. This year seemed better
than ever before."
But, hardly less amazing is the fact that there are still people in
California who apparently "don't know what it's all about." In a report
from one of our lodges the Master wrote: "Most people, particularly
those without children, wonder why they are asked to attend. They
believe that like all the other great American institutions and privileges,
public schools are to be expected ; and as long as no one is trying to
close them or take them away why should they bother ?"
Why bother ? Because as was pointed out this year in an admirable
address by a County Superintendent of Schools "Probably the thing to
guard against most is the too common practice of taking things for
granted. Well conducted institutions do not function properly in an
automatic way. Good schools come as a direct result of live interest
in them on the part of our people and from careful efficient planning
by those whose duty it is to direct our schools."
Why bother? Why do we observe Public Schools Week? Well
perhaps as good an answer as could be given appears in the following
excerpts from a splendid newspaper editorial published in a metropolitan
daily at the beginning of this year's observance:
"We take the free public school too much for grant ed. We forget
it is -something men have fought and died for. We shut our eyes to the
evidence all about us that it can be taken away from us over night if
we do not exert ourselves to protect and preserve it. •. ."
"How can we then as American citizens take our schools so casually?
Why are we not moved to such high appreciation of them as to give
them our constant, unremitting encouragement and support? Not just
financial support through our payment of taxes, but moral and spiritual
support as well. . . ."
and then followed this ringiRg appeal to mo~hers and fathers:
"Will you mothers and fathers of children now in school or of
children who were once in school and are now offering their lives in
t heir country's service-will you honor them by taking the trouble this
week to visit your neighborhood school, take an interest in what is being
done there and speak a word of encouragement to the teachers to whose
trust you have committed your children."
Of course, there are always a lot of people who would visit the
schools if they were not so busy. That was the sort the students of a
junior high school must have have had in mind when they commenced
t he invitation they sent out with these words:
"Good afternoon I Busy ? We h ope so. For only busy people find
time to do worthwhile things, and we think this is t ruly worthwhile.
"For we are busy too, buying jeeps, picking and packing citrus fruit,
replacing service men and women in downtown stores and on the ranches
and trying to keep up our school work at the same time."
With this invitation was one sent out by the Senior High School
which commenced as follows:
"We realize, of course, that in this battle-torn world of today you .
have little time to study the effect the war is having on our system of
education; but we think you ought to know" ;
and then followed the story of their "Victory Corps" and the description
of the "first-class corpsmen" who in six weeks had either worked 150

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAN:D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

hours on an outside job or given 30 hours of their time to such activities
as OP duty, real "service" without pay.

In t~e "long ago" there was one community, a comparatively large
one, which never seemed able to hold a successful observance, although
there was no apparent reason for the failures. But for ·many years now
the arran~ements h~ve been made, with outstanding success, by a school
man appomted by the Masters and Wardens and who is described as the
"liaison officer" between the schools and the lodges. He evidently "has
what it takes," because in referring to the success this year one of the
Masters in his report says. ~ "Public Schools Week in - - - is probably
one of the best in the state."
Mention has been repeatedly made in these r eports of the cooperation
of the school aut}iorities in arranging for our annual ol:>servance, and of
the participation of the pupils in the program. But this year in one community, not only · was the evening program at the high school which
P?rtrayed the activity of the schools in the war effort entirely written,
directed and enacted by the students, but the full responsibility for the
organization of the whole week's observance was taken by the Victory
C:orps. And they apparently did a first class job. A particularly impressive feature of the program was the presentation of gifts, consisting of
lap boards, robes and books to the -hospital of a nearby Army camp.
The editorial from which we have quoted was only one of a great
many which constituted a part of the fine publicity so generously given
us by the newspapers and over the radio. Typical of many was one on
"Public Education, Constant and Vital Source of True Americanism"
which was concluded with these paragraphs:
"The observance of Public Schools Week has contributed a great
deal to the maintenance of American standards of education. It serves
as a vehicle of resistance to disparagement and diminishment of those
standards.
"Let us indeed observe it with renewed interest and vigilance now
when our American principles and our American concept give u~
strength for the great struggle in which we are engaged."
There were many communities where the local newspapers carried
if not in full, ample digests of, addresses which had been delivered ·at
meetings held for the observance of Public Schools Week; and in one
place where there was no public meeting, an entire program was broadcast from a local station.
One of the reasons for a change in the form of the observance in
some communities was the fact that the teachers and pupils were engaged
in work made necessary by the shortage in farm labor. The letter from
one of our Masters explaining the situation in his community is so very
interesting that we fee l impelled to quote at some length from it (but, ·o f
course, omitting names and identifying features):
"As you will notice by the enclosed report no special program w_as
arranged. When the Grand Master's proclamation was received we discussed the advisability of presenting our usual program and on the
advice of our Senior Deacon who is also principal of th~ high school
decided it would not be quite proper.
"As you probably have read the farmers are having difficulty in
harvesting their crops. This is a farming community, and each night
after school and on Saturdays and Sundays bus loads of students, teachers
and other townspeople would go out into the fie lds and harvest the
cotton, almonds and grapes. In fact, · the greater part of the cotton in
· this dis_trict was harvested by students. We felt that since. the pupils
of the local schools have been actually showing the people what they
could do, a special program was unnecessary. Each evening the bus

630

The invitations must have been effective because the Master of the
lodge reported "best attendance in several years"-and this in spite of
bad weather and "transportation difficulties." Incidentally this was only
one of many reports of "unusually heavy attendance at all events this
year."
In connection with the question of attendance at events featured
during the week it is amusing to note that one Master reported that the
reason the attendance at the public meeting was so small was that the
people were entirely satisfied with the way the schools in that community were being conducted; while another Master gave practically
the same reason to account for the overflow attendance they always had
at their observance.
One of the most interesting reports with respect to attendance came
from a city where a meti'culous tally is kept of the visitors to each school
with a "break down" of elementary, junior high, and senior high schools
and the junior college; and a comparison in each case with the preceding
year. From this report it appears that despite the pressure of many war
time duties, the public responded very generously to the invitations sent
out by the schools. As was anticipated, the elementary schools had the
most visitors. T.he total number visiting the elementary and junior high
.schools for 1943 exceeded the number visiting during the 1942 observance.However, the number of visitors at the senior high schools and junior
college was very much smaller than last year.
This year for the first time there appeared in one of the reports an
account of a visit made to an Extended Day Care School for childreh
of employed mothers. As its contribution to the observance of Public
Schools Week it held "open house" on one day during the week. Visitors
were conducted through the play room, sleeping quarters, play yard and
kitchen; and had an opportunity of becoming acquainted with the methods
of entertaining and educating these pre-school age children.' Entertainment was provided by group singing and rhythm play with musicial
accompaniment. And it apparently proved to be an extremely interesting
feature of a fine observance.
In a newspaper clipping accompanying a report, the account of a local
observance noted as extremely significant the fact that visitors had appeared at the very first classes of the day and had arrived with the
pupils at the opening of the school. It was indeed indicative of an admirable public interest in that community and which no doubt .a ccounted
for a very successful observance.
In addition to a display of th e ordinary products of class room
activities there were this year exhibits of war time work. From the
domestic science classes there came displays of fresh, dehydrated and
home canned fruits and vegetables, and of appliances including home
dehydrators and pressure cookers; and the shop work in some schools
included completed parts that would be incorporated in industrially
produced machines and implements of war.
Generally speaking, this year, as every year, the success of the local
observance was proportionate to the zeal, industry and intelligence of
those charged with the responsibility of preparing for it. And as usual
the prime factor was the cooperation received from the schoolpeople
and from the newspapers and broadca&ting systems.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

loads of cotton pickers went to a different farm and so covered the entire
community. The great majority of the students' parents live on farms.
If we had arranged a special program for them in town, •they would
have felt obligated to attend yet they must watch their tires and
gasoline.
"So it was decided that open house be declared at the schools. Patrons
invited to attend whenever they came to town on business. There were
exhibits in the class rooms and visitors were shown the various projects
now in progress-most of them in some way connected with the war
effort. It was a great success·. There were many visitors-mostly people
who had come to town for groceries or to have their machinery repaired.

and of which it was said: "It was not merely another 'big town meeting'
all fl.ash and no substance. It was a real Public Schools Celebration."

632

"We felt we have done our part in helping to preserve rubber and
gas, and yet not fail to observe Public Schools Week."
That lodge did indeed do its part. And incidentally the letter (aft of
which was not quoted) was handwritten by the Master-which of itself
must have been some "bother."
This was only one of numerous instances in which school children
were reported as rendering a conspicuous and valuable service in connection with the manpower shortage; and, of course, school children
everywhere have engaged in the various campaigns and "drives" for ·
salvage, Junior Red Cross, War Saving Stamps and Victory Gardens.
It is now well known, of course, that drastic changes have been
made in the school curriculum to adjust it to war time needs~ Not so
well known, however, is the fact that not only have curricula been
changed, but in some school systems a form of cooperative education
has been introduced which is similar in some respects to that which
has long distinguished Antioch College.
At a joint meeting of service clubs held in observance of Public
Schools Week, the Superintendent of Schools in a city in the southern
part of the state, in detailing just what the schools are doing, and in
mentioning changes made in the curriculum, called attention to the fact
that 200 high school boys were working four hours every day in a
neighboring airplane factory and spending four hours in school.
While the public meetings held at night are no longer the feat~re
they once were, important addresses continue to be given-frequently
at the noonday meetings of service clubs and of other organizations. In
one city this year every service club held a special meeting for the
observance of Public Schools Week. There we're addresses by school
men, and in some instances by students, with vocal and instrumel\tal
music furnished by the members of the school glee clubs and orchestras.
In one form or another "The Place of the High School in War Time"
was the theme of many addresses. It seemed to be the consensus ~h_at
while additional courses in mechanics, mathematics, mechanical drawing
and kindred subjects have been properly added to the curriculum, this
did not mean that this solved the problem of what constituted sound
educational procedure in ordinary times.
One speaker pointed out that if school administrators had insisted
ten years ago on all the mathematics for which the Navy is now asking
there would have been an immediate and vociferous protest by the, parents
against a curriculum of that sort.
Many of the meetings this year might be described as was one
where an address on "The Future of Our Public Schools" was an outstanding feature of an interesting, instructive and inspirational program;

633

Pageants were again this year featured in many of the programs. The
motif in almost every case was a patriotic one, and in most instances
was either directly or indirectly related to the war. We cannot, of course,
even briefly mention every one deserving of notice; but typical of many
more or less elaborate was one in which each character represented one
of the allied nations. He was garbed in the costume of the land he
represented and carried that nation's flag. The characters made their
entry in the sequence in which that country joined the allies in the war
for freedom. With the appearance of each character the narrator gave a
short history of the country he represented and either the glee club or
the school orchestra rendered a selection typical of the nation. With the
conclusion of the pageant the participants and the audience join:ed in
singing the first verse of our national anthem.

In recognition of the fact that a particularly important phase of
public education today is the development of a friendly understanding
between this country and our neighbors to the south of us, and because
with the changed time of our observance the dates coincided, Public
Schools Week was observed in some communities in conjunction with PanAmerican Week. At one school there was an elaborate program on each
of four days during the week. One of the features was a "Pageant of
the Americas" with the representation of a street in Mexico and the
introduction of music and dances typical of Latin-America. One of the
addresses was delivered by the Vice Consul of Honduras; and there
was what was reported as an extremely interesting address on "What
Our Pan-American Neighbors Mean to U. S." The subject of the
only other formal address was "The Meaning and Purpose of Public
Schools Week." The remainder of the program consisted of appropriate
vocal and instrumental music furnished by the pupils.
.
Another "tie in" of our observance reported this year was with the
celebration of Thomas Jefferson's birthday. Nothing could be more appropriate in view of his attitude toward public education. It was Jefferson
who said: "I think by far the most important bill in our whole code is
that for diffusion of knowledge among the people. No other sure foundation can be devised for the preservation of freedom and happiness."
"Preach a crusade against ignorance, establish and improve the law
for educating the common people. Let our countrymen know that the
people alone can protect us against these evils ; and the tax which will be
paid for the purpose is not more than the thousandth part of what will
be paid to kings, priests and nobles who will rise among us if we
leave the people in ignorance."
As is known, and for reasons which have been repeatedly explained,
we never mention by name, or otherwise identify, any lodge in either
praise or censure. The only exception we ever make is with respect to
our Island Lodges. And this year it is again Maui which held its observance on the usual date to "tie in" to Lei Day-or May Day. This
year it was also "Stamp and Bond Day" with a carnival which was· a
great success in spite of a rainstorm. Every school on the island held
some sort of observance. At a m eeting of the Rotary Club held for the
observance of Public Schools Week the Principal of the West Maui
School is reported to have said in the course of his address that the
problem of dealing with school children became pressing with the start
of hostilities "in the Hawaiian area, and that the military authorities

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

decided that the best policy would be to keep the schools open so that the
children would be occupied and under control. He also said that the
teachers were able during those first few months of war to put over
a certain amount of propaganda that was desired by the military authorities which helped to keep the community calm and allow the military
units to fully perform their duties.
In Honolulu the conditions this year were no more favorable for
holding an observance than they were last year. But again this year
the Masters joined in a letter to our Committee reminding us of the
situation and expressing regret at their inability to join in our annual
observance.
Here, as elsewhere, the school children are contributing to the war
effort. From the letter it appears that the schools in turn send out
several hundred children each day of the week to work on the pineapple
plantations to relieve labor for other war work. In this way they are
fulfilling a very important role in this all-out war effort, and it is proving
very satisfactory to the industry involved.

634

We are all more or less familiar with the three R's, the three C's
·and the four H's. This year the four S's-studies, skills, safety and
service---made their appearance. They keynoted an observance in a
community which also observed "Safety Week." And because these
four S's so clearly indicate just what is being done today in the high
schools of California we give this brief description of them.
The first " S"--studies-refers to the study methods that are now being
stressed with the change in the school turriculum. History, mathematics,
civics and political science are being taught to equip pupils to aid the
war effort and so that they may better understand what is taking place
in the world around them.
The second "S"-skills-covers the work being done to qualify men
and women to operate the machinery which turns out guns, planes, ships
and ammunition. The old manual training class of a decade ago has
been supplanted by modern and fully equipped shops in which qualified
instructors teach students how to work with the lathe, the acetylene
torch and all the precision instruments of an industrial war worker's
tool kit.
The third "S"-safety-refers to the methods that are being stressed
to inculcate in the pupils those habits which are not only conducive to
their own well being, but affect the health and safety of thos.e with whom
they live and play and work. Emphasis is laid on the menace of careless
driving on the highway and the careless handling of tools in the factory
and on the farm.
·
The last "S"--service-features the activities of the high school "Victory Corps" work to prepare students for wartime, civilian and military
activity after they have been graduated.
Although the three C's, the four H's and the four S's very properly
c.onstitute a part of the work of the modern school, visitors during
Public Schools Week were made aware of the fact that the three R's are
by no means being neglected.
"Spelling Bees" were featured in many programs. And a recognition
of the importance of spelling appeared in the awards given by a lodge
for the best speller in each of two groups of elementary grades. Incidentally a splendid report from. that lodge shows that there were also
awards for the winners of debates and essays on current topics. One .of
the prizes was a silver trophy bearing the name of the . ·winning pupil

635

It is more than likely that there will be few, if any, among the thousands who availed themselves of the opportunity presented by the observance of Public Schools Week who will ever again give heed to that
uninformed criticism to which our public schools always have been, and
probably always will be, subjected.
If there were more people who knew what our schools are really
doing, and understood why it is being done, there would be fewer to
grow hysterical over what they think should be done--<>r left undone.
They would know that notwithstanding what they might have read, or
heard, the "fundamentals" are not being neglected. They would al.so
know that teachers and school administrators everywhere, especially in
the high schools and colleges, have unhesitatingly, and willingly and
cheerfully, 'subordinated everything to such activities as will best enable
us to win the war. And they should have . learned by this time that · no
one has any right to question the loyalty and patriotism of the product
of our public schools:

And finally: It should never be forgotten that the purpose of public
education in a democracy is to teach children, and particularly adolescents,
to think-and not merely to think what some one else wants them to
think.
It is the direct opposite of what it is in the totalitarian countries
where children are developed into "little robots-automatons who think,
and act ·and ·live (or die) as slaves of the state."
Our schools are not perfect, of course. What human institution is?
But in spite of all its defects and shortcomings, real or only fancied, now,
no less than it always has been, our system of public education is the
backbone of our democracy. It is not merely conducive to, it is our
American way of life.
All of which is respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Pursuant to the requirements of our Grand Lodge Constitution .the
committee has' audited all bills, claims and demands against this Grand ,
Lodge which were presented to the Grand Secretary, and have approved
those which in our opinion were proper to be paid.
The committee, in a regular meeting held at the Grand Secretary's
office February 27, 1943, devised and put into operation a change in the
method of approving these bills, claims and demands whereby the Grand
Secretary must personally affix his approval to each and every invoice
parable rather than to the vouchers and or recaps representing groups
of such invoices . ·An exception to this rule is allowed during the absence
of the Grand Secretary when it will be the duty of the Assistant Grand
Secretary to so affix his approval. The committee feels that this method
will assure a closer scrutiny of all bills paid through the Grand Secretary's
office and presents a more complete and acceptable audit of these accounts.

Second: Owing to war time conditions the usual required records,
namely, the dispensation, the minutes, attested copy of By-Laws, together with a comprehensive report, financial and otherwise, pertaining
to the activities of this Lodge, have not been returned, and therefore
have not been made available for examination by your committee.
However, we feel that the personnel of charter members, some of
whose names have been above noted, is sufficient assurance that our Masonic Laws will be fully observed in the _spirit, if not in the letter.
Third : The correspondence file in the matter of this dispensation
contains many items of personal interest, and your particular attention
is directed to the following:
(1) Telegram.
(2) Translation of telegram.
(3) See Wood letter, 4-3-43, first and last paragraph.
(4) See DePass letter of 4-7-43, as marked.
The formal report now follows.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CLANDE.STINE
MASONRY

Whereas, The Masons of California have contributed to the War
Relief Fund with the assurance that the purpose of such fund was to
assist Lodges financially unable to meet needs occasioned by war conditions; to aid worthy service members and their families; and help visiting
brethren in our midst; and
Whereas, There has been expended from that fund the sum of $10,000.00 which was foreign to the purposes for which the fund was created,
as follows:
$5,000.00 to United Service Organizations.
$2,500.00 to the American Red Cross.
$2,500.00 for distressed Masons -in China.
Be It Resolved, That the War Relief Fund be reimbursed in the
sum of $10,000.00 for these expenditures and that the said sum be drawn
from the funds of Grand Lodge which are available for charity and outside agencies upon the order of the Grand Master.
MARK A. SAWRIE.

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report 8S .
follows:
Since the last report its activities have been varied and its correspondence heavier than ever before. This activity has been in the line
of giving out correct information as to the character of these spurious
.a ctivities and awakening true Masonry to the existence of the false and
to some of the methods to be employed in its suppression.
As to the status of the Clandestine Lodges, the movement is no different than has been previously reported excepting that there is a little
more prosperity in the Lodges than was th(! case last year. This may lead
to a growth in membership, but if it continues to be among the classes
heretofore appealed to, Masonry has nothing to be disturbed over. So far
as reported to the co~mittee, to date, no new Lodges have been started.
The example cited in last year's report of a Masonic publication
carrying an article on Clandestine Filipino Masonry extended itself in
two more directions during the ·year. Substantially the same article appeared in the official organ of the Grand Lodge of Washington. No
information could be obtained as to where the article originated or who
furnished it to the editor. Our Grand Secretary promptly informed the
Grand Lodge of Washington that this kind of Masonry was not recognized
and we were assured that it would not be repeated. The committee asked
the editor of the 'publication for a correction but to date has received no
information concerning such a correction.
The article was later reproduced in a Masonic paper published in
Los Angeles. The editor was contacted, admitted his mistake and has
agreed to publish an article to be prepared by the committee.
The editor of the paper which first published the article .w as then
contacted and in the issue of that publication for June, 1943, there
appeared in its editorial comment the statement that the material in this
article did "not square with the facts concerning matters which the
craft in California is endeavoring to stamp out concerning spu.rious
activity."
Not being able to trace the ongm or source of this activity in the
Masonic press, and because the headquarters of this seemingly current
activity was stated to be in the Masonic Temple at West Los Angeles,
your chairman visited our Lodge meeting in that Temple. The Master
informed him that there were no such Filipino Lodges meeting in that
Temple and never had been. When told of the reason for the inquiry,
the Master said that the only incident connected with the Temple which
'could possibly give credence to the statement made in the article of a
large gathering of so-called Masons there was that about two years ago
some Filipinos had rented the dance hall on the ground floor and had
held a dance there. This was apparently the Masonic activity claimed
by the Filipinos and is a typical example of many of the will-o-the-wisps
this committee had . to chase to earth. We trust this will furnish the
period to this incident and its much publicised much-ado-about-nothing.
Another subject mentioned in last year's report was the possibility
of chartering some Lodges to work in the Spanish language in order to
combat any substantial growth in the Mexican clandestine activity. This

643

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

suggestion was based upon the action of the Grand Lodge of Texas in
authorizing its Lodges to confer degrees in the Spanish language when
certain requirements of the constitution were complied with. During
the year correspondence with the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of
Texas has developed that this legislation in Texas has been repealed
because of the fact that apparently it was not taken advantage of by the
Lodges. In this connection no information could be gleaned as to
whether the power to confer degrees in the Spanish had in any way
curbed this clandestine activity in Texas.
The Grand Lodge of Texas some years ago appointed a committee
headed by one of their Past Grand Masters to stamp out this activity in
Texas. Attempts to obtain details of the work of such committee for
the guidance of this committee has to date not been successful. So far
as can be ascertained, the one thing apparently accomplished by that
committee- was to cause the removal of the headquarters of one of the
spurious grand lodges from Texas to New York. As to the effect of
that committee's work on subordinate bodies and individuals nothing has
been obtained for the guidance of this committee.
Another line of investigation carried out during the past year has
been to ascertain if these spurious organizations have been in any way
connected with subversive activities. The Federal Bureau of Investigation has from time to time contacted the committee in this regard but
so far no connection has been uncovered. The Bureau has cooperated
willingly in this work and the committee has furnished information concerning the location and personnel of some of these so-called lodges.
The balance of the activities of the committee during the past year
has been educational in uncovering these activities to individuals. No
fraud upon our members or others has developed during the year.
The membership of Grand Lodge is again reminded that no regular
Mason shall have Masonic intercourse with a clandestine body or a member thereof either by recognizing such Lodge or admitting any of its
members to his own Lodge. The most effective suppression of this
activity is by not acknowledging its existence.
A card file of the information gathered by this committee is being
prepared for the Grand Secretary. Additional information secured at a
late date has prevented the completion of this file at the time of this
report. However, it will be completed and furnished to the Grand Secretary at an early date.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand_ Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report of its activities during the past year, together with its recommendations.
Last year your committee came into possesion of the Roster, ByLaws, and Minutes of the Midway Island Square and Compass Club, and
have also recently received a copy of the By-Laws and roster of members
of the Wake Island Square and Compass Club. During the year we
have endeavored to contact each member of these clubs who is affiliated
in this jurisdiction, and hope eventually to have a f~ll and .comple~e
story of their personal and fraternal experiences while serving their
country on these two outposts of the United States. The Midway Island
Club had a total recorded membership of 132, and of that number 47
were from California Lodges. Wake Island Club had a membership of
53, with 16 of them from California Lodges.
Our correspondence with the members and their Lodges has disclosed
the fact that a relatively high percentage of the members enrolled on
both rosters had been suspended by their Lodges in years past for non-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

payment of dues. The very nature of their work, in places far removed
from the mainland, has resulted in their more or less losing touch with
their home community, and as a natural consequence, they have failed
or neglected to keep in good standing with their Lodges.

L. A. Woolley, who became a life member of Mt. Moriah Lodge No.
44 of San Francisco. was one of California's most energetic and useful
citizens. He was a member of the Society of California Pioneers, and an
active member of the San Francisco Vigilante Committee of 1856. In
1913, at the age of 84 years, he wrote and published his experiences in
California. From this publication we learn many interesting facts connected with the formation of the Vigilantes of 1856, and his work throws
some highly informative side lights upon the activities of that organization
during its stormy career. His entire life history is too long to be included
in this report.
The only member of the famous "Jay Hawker Party" who. was a
Mason, was John Gollar, who afterwards became a citizen of Los Angeles, and engag·ed in the blacksmith business. He was a member of
Los Angeles Lodge No. 42.
For many years your committee has endeavored to obtain a good
photograph of Chief Winnemucca, without success. But just before completing this report, we learn that we will soon receive an authentic picture
of the old Chief, dressed in his usual spectacular regalia, part Indian .:i:i:id
part white man clothes, with a high hat, feathers, and a miscellaneous <;ollection of "tinsel show and a' that."
You will remember that the old Chief frequented Susanville in the
very early days, and had learned from someone a number of our signs,
including our· signal of distress. And it is related that he greatly embarrassed the Masons of that vicinity on many occasions when he would
give these signs in the presence of non-Masons.
·
Some of the descendants of our first Grand Master, Jonathan D.
Stevenson, are preparing a rather extensive family hist~ry of .our distinguished brother, and we feel sure we shall learn many mterestmg facts
having to do with his long, and at times, stormy career; facts which have
never before been published. We are looking forward with much interest
to the completion of this history of our colorful first Grand Master.
During the year we have received much valuable information relative to
his early Masonic career in the state of New York
Nat Vise was a member of at least four California Lodges. He was
well-known in the latter part of 1849 and the beginning of 1850 to the
residents of San Francisco. He ran a fashionable eating house on
Kearny street, and in his advertisements he always signed his name "Nat
Vise, alias Bear Hunter." He did not make a success of his San
Francisco business.
Giving up his business, he left on a hunting expedition in the region
of Four Creeks, in 1852, and was caught in the flood waters and forced
to remain until the waters receded. He built a log cabin in the vicinity
of what is now Visalia, and remained there during the winter. It is said
that Visalia was named for him. Later he kept a restaurant in San
Diego, in partnership with one, Jerry Pond ; and, there got "religion"
and became an exhorter of the most rabid variety. He was an excellent
marksman, well liked by all who knew' him, being warm hearted and
open-handed. He left his mark on many locations in this State.
We are indebted to Brother James B. Murray, a member of Westwood Lodge No. 501, for a most exhaustive and detailed history of
Brother Saschel Woods, the first Master of Western Star Lodge No. 2.
Among other things, he relates the circumstances attending the surrender
of the Mormon commander in a town .called Far West, in the State of

One member on Wake Island had been suspended for non-payment
of dues, and just before the fall of the Island had written his Lodge inquiring as to the amount of money necessary to.put him in good standing,
expressing his desire to be reinstated, and that upon receipt of word from
the Secretary as to the. proper amount demanded by the Lodge, he would
immediately remit. Before the Secretary could communicate with him
he was a prisoner of war in the hands of the Japs. His Lodge, recognizing his earnest desire for reinstatement, and his inability to communicate
with the Lodge immediately reinstated him-a fraternal ad which will
'ultimately be fully appreciated by the brother in question.
In the letters thus far received from the members of both clubs, are
found many expressions of appreciation to those responsible for the
establishment and maintenance of the clubs. There being practically no
means of entertainment on the Islands, the clubs afforded a convenient
and congenial place to meet, engage-in games, and to mak;e friends with
members of the craft from so many sections of the Union. It enabled
them to keep the Masonic touch. Thus did the clubs fill a very definite
need on the part of these men so far from home and acquaintances.
·
During the past year we have earnestly endeavored· to complete the
life history of many of our veteran members. We have divided that
work among the seve_ral members of the committee, and some are still
engaged in an effort to bring this part of our work to a close. We have
also carried on a rather extensiye series of correspondence with Lodges
and committees of foreign jurisdictions throughout the United States and
Canada. Many Grand Lodge history committees have greatly assisted us
in obtaining much valuable information in regard to our early day Masons.
We have also received numerous inquiries from other Grand Lodge committees, soliciting our assistance in tracing the Masonic and personal experiences of some of their early day members who were for a time residents of California. In some instances the research involved persons and
events as early as 1849. We have been pleased to render this assistance to
other jurisdictions.
Briefly, we have included in this report some additional information
with respect to early day Masons and others. Dr. Obed Macy, a Mason
from Indiana, had a rather hectic experience in crossing the plains en
route to California, with his wife and eight children. They left Indiana
in April 1850. After being on the trail some time, a daughter was stricken
with cholera one morning, and passed away that night. They stopped in
Salt Lake City two months, to rest and recuperate their stock as well
as themselves. On resuming their trip to the west, disaster strucJ.c again.
For some reason, not ascertained, they lost all their animals, which necessitated them walking the last 400 miles to El Monte, California, where
they settled. Macy's first venture in El Monte was a crop of onions,
raised and shipped to the San Francisco market, from which he received
a handsome profit. He afterwards moved to Los Angeles and became the
owner of the Bella Union Hotel, which, for years was the gathering place
for members of the craft in that southern Pueblo. He was an ardent
Mason, and his acts of Masonic charity were many and varied. He died
in Los Angeles, July 9th, 1857.

Today, as motorists speed along the new highway, between Los
Gatos and Santa Cruz, they may see near the half way point, a trail
leading to Glenwood and McKiernan's Resort on the old highway. The
latter place was once some of Mountain Charley's property.
In 1859, five years after his bear fight, he joined Santa Cruz Lodge
No. 38, later becoming a member of San Jose Lodge No. 10, which
affiliation he maintained for the rest of his life. In 1878 Mountain
Charley built his famous mansion on San Augustine street, San Jose. He
died in 1892. It is interesting to note• that all of Mountain Charley's
relatives, with the exception of his two sons, were Roman Catholics. His
two sons followed their father's way of thinking, and were members of
the fraternity.
When he was on his death bed, strong persuasion and pressure were
exerted to induce Charley to foreswear Masonry, and return to the
church. He steadfastly maintained that he had lived as a Mason, and
intended to die as one. He was buried in San Jose Oak Hill Cemetery,
under the auspices of San Jose Lodge No. 10.
John Judson Ames, who in maturity stood six feet, six and ohe half
inches tall, and weighed 240 pounds, was born in the State of Maine. Bis
father sent him as second mate, on a trip to Europe in the early '40's.
On the return trip, a rather tough set of characters gained possession
of the boat, and started trouble. Ames struck one of the ringleaders on
the chest, the blow felling him dead at his feet. Ames was tried for
manslaughter, and because of his size and strength, was found guilty.
President Tyler later became interested in the case and pardoned Ames.

When Wakenda Lodge No. 52 was organized at Carrollton, Missouri, Brother VI/ oods presented the Hinkle sword to the Lodge, and it
has since been used by the tylers guarding the outer door.
The first two rules adopted by that Lodge give some inkling of the
community and the times, at least in that part of the country. They were:
Rule 1. "That no brother shall be present in the Lodge and remain
in a state of intoxication, under penalty of expulsion."
Rule 2. "No profane swearing shall be allowed in the Lodge room
at any time, under penalty of expulsion."
The Santa Cruz Mountain country has produced more than its share
of pioneer "characters," a few of whom even became involved in international difficulties. Among them were Captain Isaac Graham, uncle of
Billy Ware; Joe Majors and Henry Naile; all of whom are today relegated
to the a\most forgotten pages of history, and the public remembers only
one of the venturesome souls who, in the early days, engaged in logging
and sawmill activities in 'the redwood section of the county: Charles McKiernan, popularly known as "Mountain Charley."
He was born in Ireland in the year 1825, and like so many of his
countrymen, was brought up in the Roman Cathlolic faith. As he grew
up and began to shift for himself, he abandoned the faith of his fathers,
intent upon doing his own thinking on all matters spiritual, social and
political. As a very young man he joined the British army and went to
Australia as a Quartermaster. Upon hearing of the discovery of gold in
California, he abandoned his army career and headed for America, arriving in San Francisco on the El Dorado in the year 1849.
He did some mining, but soon came to the conclusion that California, with its tremendou·s wealth of natural resources, offered a much
better and quicker way to acquire a financial competency. He therefore
went into the lumbering business in Santa Cruz and Santa Clara counties.
His fair dealings in business, his sympathetic helpfulness and high integrity,
won for him many friends, and insured for him a lasting place in the affections of all who came in contact with him.
The event that brought Mountain Charley to the attention of the
entire State took place in the year 1854. Charley and a friend named Taylor,
were walking through the forest, presumably on a hunting trip. Suddenly,
and without warning, they found themselves confronted with a huge
grizzly bear, in no mood to be trifled with. According to one story, a
shot was fired, and the bear, wounded, made for Charley, who was compelled to use his empty gun as a club. The bear flicked it out of his
·hands as · though it were a toothpick, at the same time making another
pass that opened a great hole in his skull. He hit the ground, presumably
dead, while Taylor made for safer ground, and the bear disappeared.
Later on help arrived, and Charley was taken to a hospital in. San
Jose. The physician in charge patched the hole in his skull with a plate
fashioned from two silver dollars. From that time on, to people who did
not know his proper name, he was known as "the man with the silver
skull." Charley was further immortalized when a giant redwood tree
and a winding, tortuous road through the mountains were named after
him-Mountain Charley Tree, an? Mountain Charley Road.

Following the gold rush to California, he arrived in San Francisco
penniless. Being a man of energy, he · borrowed a push cart and em- .
barked in the transporation business, moving baggage from the boats.
His first fee was 25 cents, a coin which he kept until his death. He was
sent to San Diego to advocate the division of the State, and Senator
Gwinn backed him financially in the operating of a newspaper in that
town. During this time he made a trip to San Francisc;o, leaving the
paper in the hands of Lieut. George Derby, the latter changed the entire
political policy of the paper, and Derby facetiously described an imaginary
encounter with Ames, when he returned to San Diego. •
Soon after the death of his wife, a storm destroyed his home. Following this calamity, the marker on his wife's grave was mutilated by
some vandal. These events seemed to make him lose his grip on life,
and he turned to the inordinate use of intoxicating liquor. He afterwards
established the San Bernardino Herald, which venture was not a success.
The press, one of the first to come to California, is now owned and
operated by the Inyo Independent. His was a rather tempestuous and
stormy career. He was truly a product of times. He was a member of
San Diego Lodge No. 35.
Here is the story, wherein a blackball in a California Masonic
Lodge played a very important part in a murder case. John H. Boyle,
a lawyer in the town of Quincy, in 1913, petitioned Plumas Lodge No.
60 for the degrees ' of Masonry. His petition was rejected by black ball.
This action by the Lodge provoked intense hostility and resentment on
the part of Boyle against all members of the Lodge, and particularly
against F. G. Hail, whom he suspected of blackballing him.
Shortly after his rejection he asked Hail, in the presence of others
if he was present at the Lodge when his petition 'was rejected. Hail
replied that he was, whereupon Boyle denounced him as the one who
had blackballed him, angrily applying approbrious epithets, and threat-

. He took a course in assaying and mining engineering in San Francisco. In 1887 he was appointed Assistant Adjutant General for Nevada.
His powder-smoke days were over. He died April 20th, 1920, while in

This is the only case of record in California, wherein a Masonic blackball
was the cause leading to so unfortunate an encounter.
This is a sketch of a man; who, if his lot had been cast in more
conspicuotts surroundings, would· probably have ra·n ked with Bat Masterson, the Earp Brothers, and a few others of equal note· for fearless courage.
This man was Oliver Roberts, and remained throughout his career
a consistent supporter of law and order. Before he was 21 he had lived
a whole life of adventure and violence, but to his dying day his record
was not marred by crime for crime's sake. His most hectic experiences
took olace in Darwin, in Inyo County, California, and also at Looko1;1t,
located fourteen miles from Darwin. The principle period involved was
during the seventies, following the decline of that rather short lived
rollicking camp called Panamint.
Before he reached Darwin, he had worked as a fireman on the rai~­
road between Winnemucca and Wadsworth , Nevada. Later he had his
wages stolen from him by a friend whom he trusted. He finally b~at
his way south and started on the long trek across the desert to Darwm,
which place he reached more dead than alive. Being of slight stature
·the trip was too much for his endurance, and he wa_s forced _to .go to
bed where he was in a delirious condition for several days, and 1t was
a n'ionth before · he could hobble around. He then decided to see the
town and to rest his weary body he entered a saloon to sit down. A
would-be bad man while under the influence of liquor saw him, and
fancied h.e had a grievance against the boy, whom he had never seen in
his life nevertheless he knocked him down with his sixshooter and
kicked him viciously while he was down. Covered with blood young
Roberts crawled· back to his room. A number of men who had witnessed
the brutal assault visited him, to ascertain his condition after the brutal
assault. Finding him in no immediate danger, they departed, and shor~ly
afterwards a shot was heard, and his assailant, Mott, became the chief
figure at a funeral.
Roberts met an old friend, Ned Reddy, whom he had known in
Rhode Island. In order to protect himself he soon learned to handle a
pistol, in which he became adept. He was shot at and wou~de~ many
times during his career in Darwin, and was com~elled to kill m . s~lf­
defense. · Roberts engaged in several gun fights m defense of mmmg
property during the union troubles in Darwin, and at times seemed to ~e
leading a charmed life. No task appeared to be too dangerous for this
boy, who had running gun fights _with claim jumpers, w_a s ambushed by
hostile Indians, one of whom he killed. He was shot at m the _dark by a
Mexican the bullet burning his neck. He squared accounts with a man
who ref~sed him food on the remembered walk from Mojave. At one
time he chased a Mexican h e tried to arrest, jumped on the man in a
hole while a knife menaced him, and brought him in a prisoner. He
worked for the Wells Fargo Company as shot gun messenger, but his
reputation as a crack shot and a fearless defender of his employers property saved that company many hold-ups.

Here is a detailed account of the experiences of one of our California
Masons, taken from "Behind the Rising Sun," by James R. Young 1941
p. 203-"This is the spy story to stop all spy stories."
'
'
M~rk A. Pierce, a prominent Los Angeles, California, business man
was seized at Kobe, Japan, and held for investigation eleven days. His
original detention was based on taking photographs as the Japanese
boat on which he was a passenger was sailing down the river from
Shanghai. He was a movie camera fan, and even his shots of the ship's
captain playing deck tennis with passengers were interpreted by the
police as violating Military Secrets Law.
His Rotary pin placed him .under suspicicion, since Japanese police
believe · that Rotary- which is known to them as Rotary Internationale·
is a part of the Third Internationale, operating out of Russia.
. His Shrine pin made matters worse. Japanese police claim the Masonic
and Shrine movements originate in Paris, and are Jewish revolutionary
movements . or organizations designed to overthrow established governments.
. Further search of Pierce' s baggage, of which he had a great deal,
since he was on a world tour, revealed a small black notebook with
cryptic designations such as, G. M., U. S. S., A. T . & · T., G. E ., etc.
Police charged it was a secret code book he was carrying. An explanation
that they were designations of his stock broker in Los Angeles was not
sufficient to remove their deep suspicion that they had caught the mastermind of a world-wide espionage ring. They also found among his effects
a gold police badge, an honorary shield presented him by the Governor
of California after he had served a term as one of the City of Los
Angeles police commissioners. This only gave them the idea that they
had caught a state-police spy, officially accredited to the California government. They questioned him at length as to his Kentucky Colonelship,
evidence of which they found in his papers.
That he was a naval spy was a charge leveled against him when
it was discovered that he was a Commodore of the San Pedro Yacht
Club. His position was not helped when it was discovered 'that he was
an ex-member of the California Legislature.
After eleven days and nights of quizzing by eight officials, they released him with a fine e>f 30 Yen-about $7.00. He had violated 30 yen's
worth of military secrets by filming the banks of the Yangtze - River,
already long familiar to any r eade_r of the National Geographic or any
other illustrated magazine.
The Pierce case finally became an issue with the Imperial household
and Foreign .Minister. High officials were somewhat abashed and cha-

grined when they learned that Pierce's uncle had once been decorated by
the Jap.anese Emperor for his religious work, and for his helpfulness to

We again respectfully urge all Lodge secretaries to become more
history conscious, and to more fully record current Masonic events,
whether at the time considered of any real significance or not. Our
acts of today become the history of tomorrow. Remember there isn't
such a thing as an isolated historic event. Events of only apparent local
significance may be either directly or indirectly presently, or remotely
related to or connected with events of far greater moment. It is highly
desirable that the Lodge minutes contain in some detail Masonic events
and the part played by individual members of the Lodges in those events.
The future student of our history must, of necessity in the main,
depend upon the official records as contained in our minute books.
Therefore reasonable detailed recording will greatly aid in the proper
interpretation of local Masonic activities.

Again permit us to urge the Lodges, particularly those in the mountain districts, where the fire hazards are great, to immediately take steps
to provide vaults or other adequate fire-proof repositories for their precious records. It only takes one fire to forever destroy your records. Some
of the Mother Lode Lodges have provided vaults, where their books and
documents are safely kept, thus insuring to posterity their records, which
cannot othewise be duplicated.
A very constructive suggestion has been advanced by our Junior
Grand Warden, Laurence C. Kelley, with respect to the older charters
and Lodge records, including the original by-laws containing the signatures of members .. He cites the fact that Pentalpha Lodge No. 202 of
Los Angeles, has recently photostated the original charter and by-laws.
He · proposed that Grand Lodge, enact legislation permitting a Lodge ·to
operate under a photostated copy of the charter or some other certified or
authenticated copy, and allow the Lodges to carefully preserve in a safe or
fireproof place the original charter, with the further provision that such
charter must be produced at the time of the annual meeting, and afso
at the installation of officers.
From my own experiences in visiting practically every Lodge in the
State during the past fifteen years, and realizing the great fire hazards
existing in the vast majority of the Lodges, your committee heartily
endorses this recommendation of the Junior Grand Warden.
Move that this be referred to the Committee on Charters with instructions to consider the same report their finding at the next annual
communication of Grand Lodge.

record of every member of this Grand Jurisdiction serving in the armed

country in a worthwhile or outstanding manner, either at home or
abroad, we are again asking the constituent Lodges, or their Masters, to
appoint a competent and enthusiastic member to keep up-to-date until
they arc all discharged, a full and complete report on each individual so

REPORT OF TH E TRUSTEE S O F THE MASONIC
CLUBHOUSE OF THE UNIVERSITY OF
CALIF ORNIA AT BERKELEY
To the Most W orshipf11l Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Directors of the Masonic Clubhouse of the University
of California presents this annual report covering the past Masonic year.
P roperty Main tenance
The building qnd its furnishings are in excellent condition. More
permanent repairs to the roof were made during this past year together
with miscellaneous maintenance work. The total cost was $1,002:53.
The certified public accountant's statement has been submitted to
your Finance Committee.
T he U niversity Gear ed to the W ar E ffor t
As a direct result of the war your Board of Trustees has been and
is confronted with an entirely new and different set of circumstances
than has existed in any other year. The university student life has been
completely changed with the switch from the semester system to the
quarter system.
The summer quarter ends October 28th. This quarter, from the
standpoint of the clubhouse activity, has been a trying one. The . aggre-

654

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

gate number of students on the campus has been substantially reducedthe greatest decline being in the number of men students in regular
attendance. It was found necessary for the men's and women's Masonic
clubs to consolidate into one club for the summer quarter with an active
membership of forty-five st~dents. They contemplate operating as a
single ·club for the duration. It is expected their membership for the
fall quarter will reach between 75 to 150 students.
A check with university authorities indicates an expected increase
from approximately 6,300 students to 8,500 for the fall quarter. It i~
further expected that of the 8,500 students approximately 2,000 will be
service men. Many GJf these service men are college graduates and some
are members of the fraternity. They are on the campus for a period of
approximately sixteen weeks.
Your Board of Directors has held several meetings and has gone
into the matter of clubhouse activities very thoroughly. At the last
meeting of the board it was the unanimous opinion that:
1. There is a definite need on the campus for clubhouse activity
since many of the other organizations have actually been taken over
by the armed services.
2. Social life on the campus of necessity is presently limited to
Saturday nights and a few free hours during the daytime.
3. The .Purpose for which the clubhouse was built can best be
carried out by gearing the club activities to the present circumstances.
From its inception the clubhouse activities have been supported by
the student membership. The 1941 report to Grand Lodge shows that
students have raised and spent between $2,500 to $3,000 each of the last
few years in support of their activities. These funds were raised through
tnembership fees. Since the membership has been substantially reduced,
your Board fee.ls that in view of the fact that many of the service men
on the canwus are Masons or sons of Masons tl:iat the student budget
should be supplemented by Grand Lodge and has appealed to the Committee on Finance accordingly for $1 ,500 toward supporting this program.
The remaining students who" are members of the clubhouse are willing
and able to sponsor appropriate programs. The record shows there ar e
many club alumni living in the vicinity of the clubhouse who could and
would lend a hand in helping the club members in planning and arranging
worth while activities. Financially they must receive outside s upport.
Your board feels that by making the clubhouse available to affiliated
Masonic service men and Masons on th e campus we will be carrying
out the ultimate objective of the Masonic Clubhouse to its fullest extent. It will tend to make better Masons by keeping those from numerous distant Lodges in touch with Masonic activities during their
stay on the campus; it will maintain the high position of Masonry among
college students and service men from whom Masonic Lodges are glad
to receive petitions; it will provide a Masonic home where the numerous
members of our "Masonic family" can come together and get acquainted,
thus developing worthwhile friendships. The University Clubhouse occupies a strategic place in university life. Making continued use of these
facilities· available to our men in the service is a real contribution to the
war effort. To this end at a special meeting of the Board of Directors
held October 1, 1943, the followin g resolution was unanimously adopted:
" It was" moved seconded and unanimously carried, that the trustees
request the usual 'budget of $7,500 at the Annual Communication of
Grand Lodge, and that an additional amount of $1 ,500 be requested to
enable the trustees to enlarge the program at the clubhouse to take care

GRAN D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

655

of entertainment of Masonic affiliates now in the service and enrolled at
the university."
Fraternally submitted by order of the Board of Directors.
EDWARD H. SIEMS.

The report was adopted and referred to the Finance Committee.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE MASONIC
CLUBHOUSE OF U. C. L.A.
To the Most Worshipfi1l Grand Lodge of California :
As the representative of the Board of Directors of the clubhouse at
the University of California at Los Angeles, I bring you our annual
report.
The expected has happened; on April 1st of this year th e university
took over the major part of our building to u se as a mess hall for Army
cadets. It did not take long to learn that, with an increasing number of
serVice men arriving at the university, the entire building would be required. On May 1st, all of our furnishings went into storage and we
moved our club activities to space rented in the Y. W. C. A. building at
574 Hilgard avenue.
Our very efficient hostess, Mrs. Faith C. Sheldon, having resigned
to go into U. S. 0 . work in Honolulu, we secured the part-time services
of a graduate student, Miss Frances Shanks. She maintains office hours
from 1 to 5 p. m., keeps all records and generally stimulates and coordinates
all club activities. Our members have the same privileges in the building
as do the Y. W. C. A. members themselves.
It is interesting to note that of th e nine persons comprising the
Masonic Affiliate Council which is directly charged with the operation
of club affairs, four are men and three of these, including the president,
are in Navy uniforms.
A letter received from Earl J. Miller, dean of undergraduates, commending the work of the club, is evidence of its effectiveness, and ours
is the strongest and best organized group on the campus today.
For a number of months, nine hundred uniformed men have been
served three hot meals · each day in our building. This requires every
foot of space including the stage, which accommodates one hundred men.
It was necessary for the caterer to spend $18,000.00 and the Army
$10,700.00 for additional ranges, refrigerators, dish washing machines,
etc., to do the job.
A check of these service men indicat es that at least 35 per cent of
them are members of our fraternity or come from Masonic families, and
we are advised that many have expressed their appredation of the fine
facilities afforded them.
Under our agreement with the university, they paid for moving and
storing our person;i.1 property and are to return it to place when the
building is vacated. They pay us a monthly r ental of $800.00. At the
time this rental began, we had on hand $3,096.99 of the $7,500.00 appropriated by Grand Lodge last October for our operations this year. This
amount we immediately impounded and have been paying and will continue
to pay our expenses out of rentals.
Our Board of Directors has adopted a budget for the year 1943-44
a copy of which is attached and made a part hereof. It will be noted that
the budget divides itself into two parts, the expense of carrying on the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

656

657

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

activities of the club itself, an amount of $1,825.00 for the year, and the
expense of the clubhouse property itself, an amount of $4,020.00, depreciation, taxes, gardening, building maintenance, etc.
No one 'knows how long the university will continue to use the property because no one knows when the war will end. If the occupancy
should run through to October 1, 1944, our income from rentals will be
$9,600.00. The difference between our expected expenses and this amount,
i. e., $3,755.00, we propose to place in a contingent reserve to be used
toward restoring the building and furnishings when the property is returned to us. A complete statement of our financial condition is reflected by Brother Reynold E. Blight's report which is attached ;uid made
a part hereof.
Our normal operating budget is $7,500.00. Since we do not know
when the occupancy of the property by the university will terminate and
knowing that we will immediately resume full activities there whenever
it is vacated, we respectfully ~equest that this Grand Lodge appropriate
for our use for the year 1943-44 the sum of $7,500.00 less the amount of
$3,096.99 which we have now impounded. The money appropriated to
be held in a contingent fund by Grand Lodge and only drawn on by us
if necessity requires, which would only be occasioned by the sudden
ending of the war.
Fraternally submitted by order of the Board of Directors,
BEN

G. WRIGHT.

The report was adopted and referred to the Committee on
Finance.

REPORT OF SPECIALTAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipf11l G·ran.d Lodge of California:

The special Taxation Committee has functioned continuously since
its appointment pursuant to resolution of the 89th Annual Communication
in 1938, and during 1943, the. membership of the committee has not been
changed.
Our recornrnendatiOns are that the subordinate Lodges continue to
pay Social Security and Unemployment taxes in accordance with our
report of 1941, to be found in the proceedings of that year, page 669.
The Committee has held many meetings during the year and have
conferred with your officers of Grand Lodge on many questions. In
addition many queries from subordinate Lodges have been answered by
letter.
On January 15th, 1943, the Committee made a special report to
the Grand Master holding that the Service Men's Moratorium Act had

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

no application to the payment of dues to Masonic Lodges, and also
holding that all Masonic Lodges should pay the Victory Tax. This
report was sent to all Lodges under date of January 20th, 1943, by order
of the Grand Master, and a copy is attached hereto as an exhibit.
Similarly our opiniion is that Grand Lodge and all subordinate
Lodges are subject to the withholding income tax insofar as the wages
of employees are concerned. The Grand Lodge and subordinate Lodges
are themselves exempt from income tax but their employees are subject
to the tax.
In our r'eport for 1942 we called attention to the fact that recent
employment of additional clerical help by Grand Lodge might make it
subject to the State Unemployment Reserves Tax. A ruling has bee~
obtained that the Grand Lecturer is not subject to either the Federal or
State Social Security taxes. The California Department of Employment
has tentatively ruled that the Grand Tiler and Grand Organist will also
not be taxed.
It has been further tentatively ruled by that department that the
Grand Treasurer and his assistant, th.e Chairman of the Correspondence
Committee, the parties who do the clerical work for the Masonic Homes
Endowment Boar'CI, and all persons who receive in excess of $45.00 a
calendar quarter for services in the· boards of relief and employment
bureaus, are to be counted as employees of Grand Lodge and subject
to a tax since January 1st, 1940. The department holds that payment
of an unallocated expense account shall be treated as payment of a wage.
The committee prepared and filed an extended brief with the Department
of Employment, but so far wi.thout beneficial results. These tentative
rulings are of great importance to Grand Lodge in many aspects other
than taxation. On the same line of reasoning the State Employment
Department may next hold that all subordinate Lodges must report
through Grand Lodge and pay taxes accordingly. A complete examination of the relationship of Grand Lodge to various committees and organizations in which it has a deep interest should be made. From a
standpoint of taxation, however, the rulings already made will result in
an assessment of delinquent taxes amounting to approximately $2,500.00.
The Committee recommends to Grand Lodge that it be empowered,
by and with the consent of the Grand Master, to engage as an attorney,
a tax specialist, to present the legal aspects of this matter to the California Department of Employment, and to take such other action legally
as may be necessary to protect the interests of Grand Lodge.
·
Last year the committee recommended, and there was allocated, the
sum of $1,200.00 against a possible assessment for past unemployment
reserves. This fund has not been used. The committee now recommends,
in view of the recent tentative holding of the California Department of
Unemployment, that a new appropriation be made so that a total fund
of $3,500.00 will be available to· meet the threatened assessment for back
. taxes, and any legal expenses that may become necessary.
Because of these pressing matters it is recommended that the committee be continued for the ensuing year.
Respectfully submitted,

GEORGE STODDARD, Grand Bible Bearer
On January 30th, 1943, this Grand Lodge suffered a severe loss in
the death of our beloved Grand Bible Bearer, Worshipful George Sto·d dard. In the words of our most Worshipful Grand Master, "Masonry
lost one of its grand old men with the passing of Worshipful George
Stoddard, Grand Bible Bearer, member and Past Master of Stanislaus
Lodge No. 260 of Modesto."
He was born March 20th 1861; initiated April 27th, 1889; passed
May 23rd, 1889, and raised June 29, 1889. The Secretary of his Lodge
informs me that he had served his Lodge as Master seven times, a marvelous record.
He was born in San Francisco, and attended the public schools there
until he was seventeen years of age. Leaving school at this early age,
he entered the employ of the Southern Pacific Railroad Company. He
came to Modesto as Station Agent in 1888. Leaving the employ of the
railroad company in November of that year, he entered upon a life-long
career as a banker. He retired from active service in 1938, at which
time he was as·s istant vice president, and a member of the advisory board
of the Bank of America.
His funeral services were held in the Shannon Chapel in Modesto,
with Rev. Homer K. Pitman, of San Francisco, and Stanislaus Lodge
No. 206 F. & A. M., officiating.
He was a member of Stanislaus Lodge No. 206 for fifty-four years.
He was a life member and Past High Priest of Modesto Chapter of
R. A. M. and Prelate Emeritus of Modesto Commandery of K. T. No.
57, for fifty-four years he was an active member of Electa Chapter No.

boys sang for him, as they preceded him down the aisle 'Hark Hark
My Soul.' His ashes now rest in the grave of his fath~r, Dr. 'Georg~
Wright, in Redlands, California." As I read the many beautiful things
said about him at the time of his death, one thought kept ringing through
my very soul, "He is not dead! He lives! He lives!"
May his life be a benediction and an inspiration to each one of us.

REV. GEORGE HENRY BURWELL WRIGHT,
Past Grand Chaplain
On December 12, 1942, many of our brethren were saddened by the
death of our Rev. Brother George Henry Burwell Wright, who passed
away suddenly at his home in Berkeley. He was a member of Ingleside
Lodge No. 630, F. & A. M. He was a charter member of Ingleside
having demitted from Forest Hill Lodge No. 534; initiated January 31st,
1923, passed May 9th 1923, and raised November 28, 1923. He was appointed Grand Chaplain by Past Grand Master Charles M. Wallenberg
in 1929. Canon Wright, as he was known in the Episcopal Church, was
an outstanding man in social work, having been active in Boy Scout Tro()P
No. 16, the Travelers' Aid, the Indian Association, and St. Dorothis
Rest.
He was also a very active member' of the California Historical Society
and in their "Quarterly," following his death, they gave him a very fine
obituary. · From his bereaved wife, Aimee De Turbeville Wright, I .have
received many beautiful tributes and personal touches, a few of which I
shall incorporate in this eulogy.
He was born in Toronto, Canada, April 14, 1875, and with his
parents he moved to Redlands, California, in his early teens. Quoting
from the California Historical Society, "The Canon received his early
scholastic training at the Modell School, Toronto. From Stanford U11iversity, wh~re he graduated in 1898 with an A. B. degree, he entered
