JUDGE WILLIAM J. MOSSHOLDER, 1852-1943,
Past Master San Diego Lodge
Brother vVilliam J. Mossholder, Past Master of San Diego Lodge
No. 35 F. & A. M., during the years of 1892 and 1893, passed to the Great
Beyond on April 10th, 1943. Masonic funeral services were held April
13th, 1943. Right Worshipful Claude H. Morrison, Deputy Grand Master
of Masons in California, and Rev. John B. Osborn, officiating.
Judge, as he was affectionately known to his many friends and brothers,
received his title by serving as judge of Polk county, Nebraska, as a
young man. He was made a Master Mason, June 29th, 1883, at Osceola,
Nebraska, affiliated with San Diego Lodge No. 35, November 26th, 1887.
Judge Mossholder ,was a Mason for 60 years. He was born August 27th.
1852, the year before the granting of our Charter, in Martinsburg, Ohio.
He attained his law degree at the University of Iowa and a bachelor of
philosophy degree at Nebraska Wesleyan University.
Judge came to San Diego for his health, in December, 1885, and
practiced law here up until two weeks of his passing.
A leader in public, civic and fraternal activities in this community,
Brother Mossholder will be greatly missed for his wise counsel to all
who loved him and respected his truth and sincerity.
He was an upright citizen and a zealous Mason, but our loss is
heaven's gain.
There comes a time in the lives of men, and of Masons, that we
feel the need of a sure and safe anchorage, a haven of rest, a mountain
top of faith. Such a time confronts us now. In the year that has just
ended, we have laid away the mortal bodies of two hundred and three
members of this Grand Lodge. The roster of these brethren will not
be read at this time, but will become a part of the minutes of Grand
~~

.

In addition to this, the roll of our honored dead in this war of
survival is becoming larger every day. It is then very natural for us
to inquire, "Where are they now?" This is the burning question uppermost in the minds and hearts of all our sorrowing loved ones.
For answer to this question let us delve deep into the eternal truths
in the great Light of Masonry. Let us not place our hope in the pihosophy of the ancients and in the man-made doctrines of the sages. Let us
ask the question with the Psalmist of old, "What is man that Thou art
mindful of him? And the son of man, that Thou visitest him?" The
answer comes back to us strong with comfort, "Thou hast made him a

little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and
honour."

Let us read again those matchless words, "He that believeth in me,
though he were dead, yet shall he live and whosoever, livetl:i and believeth
in me, shall never die." "And I heard a voice from Heavert saying unto
me, 'Write, blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth:
Yea saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their

Benicia Lodge No. 5·:
Harry Bodine Carr, died April, 1943. ·

This is an expression of that age old conflict waged between life
and death. Life always wins in this struggle, for through death we attain
life. Listen to the victorious proclamation from God's holy Word. "That
which Thou sowest is not quickened, except it die." This is the victory
of life over death. This is the answer to the aching hearts of our loved
ones.
As we drop again the curtain separating time and eternity, we bid a
loving farewell to our brethren whom death has stricken in the last year.
Death! No, but rather eternal life has called them into that "house not
made with hands eternal in the heavens."
IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE
By Dr. Rohert Freeman
"In my Father's House are many rooms."

John 14:2.

No, not cold beneath the grasses,
Not close-walled within th e tomb;
Ratner, in my Father's mansion,
Living in another room.
Living, like the one who loves me,
Like my child with cheeks abloom,
Out of sight, at desk or school book,
Busy in another room.
Nearer than my son whom fortune
Beckons where the strange lands loom;
Just behind the hanging curtain,
Serving in another room.
Shall I doubt my Father's mercy?
Shall I think of death as doom?
Or the stepping o'er the threshold
To a bigger, brighter room?
Shall I blame my Father's wisdom?
Shall I sit enswathed in gloom
When I know my loves are happy,
Waiting in the other room?

WILLIAM PARKER FILMER
Past Grand Master and Grand Treasurer
To the Most Worshipf11l Grand Lodge, F. &. A. M. of California:

William Parker Filmer, Past Grand Master and Grand Treasurer of
this Grand Lodge, passed beyond the veil on the 22nd day of November,
1942, after a lingering illness. He endured the sufferings which attended
his fatal illness with fortitude ·that manifested his courage. The person
of our brother and friend has been removed from us. The Scottish Rite
and the York Rite suffer very much in the passing of this real man.
As I review my personal association, I may say that one of ~he best
friends I ever had has been removed. From the beginnings of a frie ndship in the misty past of more than forty years, there is only fondest
recollection of continuous and ever-increasing frie ndly relations between
my friend and me. Not a cross word had broken a serene understanding.
we mourn and yet we should be comforted in the fact that our
friend and brother has lived a full and a very useful life. It may not be
said of him" ! look behind me, and I see no mark
Beside my road of time, no fruit, no flowers,
No indicated lasting good thing done
To build Thee praise, or help my fellow men
Along the way I will not tread again."
Mourning is essentially self-sympathy. We sorrow for ourselves in
that we are deprived of the benign presence of the one we love.
Fortunately I recall with considerable sati.sfaction that the bouquet
which my feeble effort may gather and offer in appreciation of our friend
and brother today is just another of the many tributes I have paid him
on every opportunity during the time he lived.
Brother Filmer was born March 22nd, 1866, in New York City. He
came to San Francisco as a young child where he attended grammar

674

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

school from 1872 to 1875, when he moved to New Haven, Connecticµt,
where he continued his grammar school education. Upon returning to
San Francisco, he resumed attendance at Valencia Grammar Schoo~,
. graduating in 1880. Following that he became associated with his father
in the Filmer, Stiller Electrotype Company. In 1884, he went to New
York City, complet'ing his training as an electrotyper with the then
well-known electrotype firm of Ringler & Co. He returned to San Francisco in 1885 and continued his association with his father in the electrotype business.

but that's the way it was-he was 'Billy' Filmer to us. He was president .
of the Golden Gate Bridge Board and I was a director and I could riot
begin to count the number of times he ruled against me in controversies
which at times prevailed, but, even as he ruled me wrong, I knew
'Billy' F~lmer would not do so unless he felt he was right-and to myself I confessed he was."

In 1886, he married Matilda Sproul and from this marriage there
was an only child, Marian, now Mrs. Friedman. From 1886 to 1890, he·
lived on a ranch in Lake County primarily for his health. Incidentally,
he planted the first olive grove in that county. He then returned to
San Francisco and continued in business with his father, which business
eventuated in Filmer Bros. Electrotype Co., of which he was president
from 1900 until his death. The company is well-known in the field of
law book and court record printing and binding.
An early manifestation of his civic interest was enlistment in Company "B," First Regiment, National Guard of California in 1888. This
company was originally known as the "City Guard," organized in 1854,
the first company of National Guard Infantry to exist in this state.
His interest in Masonry no doubt had its inception in the Masonic
activities of his father, William Filmer, who became a 33rd Degree
Mason of the Northern Jurisdiction on the 28th day of August in 1861.
He was a Past Master of King Solomon's Lodge No. 260 and, in April,
1898, conferred the First Degree on his two sons, William and George.
William Parker Filmer was the eldest of three brothers, the two
others being Colonel George Filmer, well known in Masonic, Shri~e,
Kiwanis and civic activities, and John, who devoted his entire time and
attention to operation of the electrotyping department of the business.
As we consider our brother's life, we are aware of a home of
abundance, of love and appreciation, and then a g·reat void when he was
deprived of his beloved life companion. We are aware of affection for
his brothers, demonstrated by marked loyalty; an honorable and a successful business career; a willingness to serve and a frequent response
to call for public service. His greatest attainment in public service no
doubt was the successful administration of the affairs of the Golden
Gate Bridge and Highway District in its formulative period, through the
construction of the Bridge, and into the early period of operation, until
he voluntarily laid aside further responsibility. That he was an officer
of that Bridge and Highway District lent great confidence in the integrity
of construction and operation, which might have suffered from political
manipulation.
ln all these relationships, there is a preeminent manifestation of
human understanding in the friendships which existed. He was ever
modest, kindly, just and thoroughly courageous. Of him one of his
fellow directors on the Golden Gate Bridge commented :
"To my way of rating men I had never met a finer personality than
William Parker Filmer. He was intensely human. We called him
'Billy,' because he was so lovable a character and we knew when we
did so, the designation, although it was an endearing one, was grotesque
because William Parker Filmer was one who reflected all the graces,
the polish, tact and respect-commanding attributes deference should be
paid and it always appeared out of place to refer to Mr. Filmer as 'Bi11'y,'

675

This wi:iter referred to one of Billy Filmer's outstanding characteristics, namely, his love of flowers. He continued:
"I, a Roman Catholic, sta·n ding by his ~Jeeping place, am going to
pray to 'Billy' Filmer's God-his God and my God-he be dealt with
kindly for here on earth 'Billy' Filmer saw no difference between a Mason
and a Catholic-his broad tolerance would not permit him to--and, in
Heaven, he will find there is none."
·
The man who wrote this is a fighting, yet gentle, Irish editor, A. R.
O'Brien.
Another editor, Edward F. O'Day, also a Catholic, said of him:
"Masonry was 'Billy' Filmer's religion, and civic helpful~ess was his
self-imposed, life-long obligation." ·
Notwithstanding other accomplishments, William Filmer's greatest
achievement lies in his Masonic service. He was a member of all Masonic bodies. It is unnecessary to dwell on detail-it will suffice to relate
that 4e progressively served as Master of King Solomon's Lodge, (1903),
and treasurer thereof for many years, High Priest of King Solomon's
Chapter, Royal Arch Masons, (1906), and Grand High Priest of the
Royal Arch Masons of California, (1918), Grand Master of Masons in
the Jurisdiction of California, (1912), and Grand Treasurer of the Grand
Lodge since 1913, Master of the Lodge of Perfection and Commanderin-Chief of the Consistory in the Scottish Rite, being successively elevat.ed
to become Knight Commander of the Court of Honor, 33rd . Degree
Honorary, ultimately 33rd Degree active member of the Supreme Council
of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite for the Southern Jurisdiction
of the United States; serving as Lieutenant Grand Commander and
Sovereign Grand Inspector General in California at the time of his
death. These honors are sufficient unto themselves but in his life they
are indicative of only a part of the very great service he rendered as
a member of the fraternity. Perhaps more than any other individual m
recent years, he is responsible for the great dignity and attainment of
the Grand Lodge of California, which we of this Jurisdiction believe to
be the greatest Grand Lodge in America.
What does this mean? It means that he devoted his life to a great
agency for the develop~ent of character, such as is being done in
similar institutions. All who think fundamentally of the causes of war
realize that peace in the world will be impossible until ultim<1tely there
shall be in the nations of the world individual character and dignity
sufficient to outlaw human conflicts.
"Peace has its victories
No less renowned than war-"
But our brother was no pacifist-he was e~er a realist.
Of him it may be said his monument is builded " in the hearts and
memories" of his brethren and friends and his name will be remembered
because "he has lived" and "The fruits of his labor live after him."

FROM A GARDEN WALL

tories and ' the dirges of transitory defeats, may be read these ancient
character, "It is later than :1101t think."

G. Er.LSWORTH MEYER
Swiftly, silently the annual tides bear brethren "from out our bourne
of time and place," tides "too full for sound or foam." As they sail beyond the far horizon, we who remain endeavor by these services and our
humble words to bid a fond adieu. Scarce one of us but has lost a
particular frien·d, whom we had grappled to our hearts with enduring
bonds. His name upon the roll makes these services very personal as
we jointly mourn the loss of all, but it is not fitting and proper, nor our
desire, to vex Providence with lamentations or ostentatious grief; rather,
·we pay tribute to virtue and kindly deed, console ourselves with the firm
conviction of the immortality of the soul and the realization that human
influences live beyond the grave.
We honor the memory of our departed brethren not to gratify them,
for they are lifted above earthly hqnors, but as a fit reward for their
endeavor to. exemplify in their daily lives those exalted concepts which
Freemasonry inculcates in the hearts and minds of men. Our brethren
were human and therefore prone to err, but any particular in which they
may have exhibited human frailty, we have forgotten. The good, the
true, the just in their lives far outweighed the ill and the memory of
these we preserve as evidence of our appreciation and our desire to emulate, so that when we too shall have turned again home, it may be said
that our lives were fruitful of all good works.
The going of our brethren is enshrouded by the great mystery of
life and death, the enigma of every age, but death is the portion of every
man who ever drew the J?reath of life. We cannot question it, for death
is as much a part of the Divine Plan as life, but we need never face it
stricken dumb ; rather, we may inquire:
Shall we question our Father's wisdom?
Shall we sit enswathed in gloom,
When we know our friends are happyLiving in some other room?
(Robt. ·Freeman)
Did we not believe in the existence of that other room, somewhere
beyond our sight, truly would we mourn our brethren ''.beneath the
grasses, close-walled within the tomb." But when we lift our eyes upward, not to a God of Wrath, but to an omnipotent, wise, loving Father,
then are we persuaded that though man measureth time by things which
fall away and die, these are but tiny flutterings in the hand of the
Eternal.
·
The abode for which our brethren have departed is not to be beheld
by mortal eyes, nor are its sounds caught by mortal ear. It must be
seen through the eyes of faith with which the soul is endowed, its echoes
must be heard in the throb of human breasts and in the words of the
great teachers of every faith, one of whom said, "In my Father's mansion,
there are many rooms. If it were not so, I would have told you."
As we perform these final offices of brotherly affec.t ion, as we voice
our earnest desire to personify exemplary conduct and exalted virtue,
there comes to mind an inscription upon an ancient bronze plaque set
in a certain Chinese garden wall. All record of the hand which placed
it is lost, the name of the sage who spoke its lines is not preserved even
by family tradition, but there in the fragrance of a spacious garden, evidencing worldly wealth, there cloistered from the accolades of petty vie-

677

Yes, it is later than we sometimes think and the departure of brother
after br·o ther so reminds us.
It is later than you think.
Yes, it is too late in the life of the youngest within this room to
live basely, act unworthily or decide unjustly. It is too late to continue
withholding any reserved hand of friendship. It is too late to further
procrastinate doing that which needs .to be done. It is too late to leave
to tomorrow · the undoing of any wrong committed against friend or
brother.
.
·
These reflect.ions, italicized i~ the bit of Chinese philosophy are not
too somber, they are not too funereal for the man who can bear success
with humility, the affection of his friends without pride and his final
earthly day with befitting courage.
Their negatives whisper that time is fleeting, but their positives
shout that, "Today is the day. Today is the day to live radiantly. Today
is the day to firmly grasp the hand of friend and brother. T oday is the
day to slide a shoulder beneath his burden, to go on foot and out of the
way. Tomorrow never comes.
Verily, it was later in the lives of our brethren than we thought.
They have crossed the sea to take up their abode in those other rooms,
though they will not pass again this way, though we are seemingly
separated by a barrier yet impassable, we bid them farewell with the
consolation and promise of a borrowed aphorism-"Those whom virtue
hath joined, death cannot separate." '

No. 1026.
To the ·Most Worshipf1,1 Gra.nd Lodge of California:
To your Committee on Appeals and Grievances there have been referred the eight trial records and the five petitions for restoration which
have arisen during the current Masonic year. One of the petitions for
restoration has been withdrawn by the petitioner and therefore requires
no further consideration. The remaining four will be separately reported
for your consideration.
•
We look with favor on the practice now followed by most Lodges
of appointing investigating committees when notice of a petition for
restoration is received; particularly is this true in those cases where the
committee makes a real investigation and files a written report of its
findings. The action taken by the interested Lodges may be most helpful
to your committee and fo Grand Lodge. But this is only true when we
are advised as to the facts before the Lodge at the time it votes on the
m,atter. Of course, action by the Lodge is not required but we feel it is
quite desirable. If the facts relative to the rehabilitation of the petitioner
are not sent on to Grand Lodge then we are left in the dark as to 'whether
the Lodge action was an advised action or not.
Letters relative to the rehabilitation of a petitioner are also helpful
but particularly so when they set out facts in addition to the opinion of
the writer. In these matters, your committee is interested in knowing
where petitioner has resided, his occupation, position held, family reiations, his various activities, and any other facts which may throw light
on whetlier reh'abilitation has in fact occurred. In cases of embezzlement
or theft of funds, we like to know if restitution has been made and, if
not, why. Letters which fail to disclose the extent of the acquaintance of
the wdter and which express only his opinion, as to whether the petitioner
should or should not be restored are not very helpful. Let us have the
facts-good or bad.
The trial records before your committee this year show, for the most
part, the various cases to have been intelligently and fairly handled. We
are not unmindful of the difficulty of a non-lawyer Master in ruling on the
admissibility of evidence. They do surprisingly well and it is only in the
exceptional instance where an error is made which affects the substantial
rights of the accused. Masonic trials should be kept on a basis of giving
the accused a fair, impartial and thorough hearing. The fairness and impartiality of such hearings rest primarily with 'the Master and the Trial
Commission. The thoroughness depends largely in the diligence of the
accuser. Masonic charges should not be preferred unless they are to
be diligently handled and it is the duty of the accuser to see that available evidence is gathered and presented.
In one case covered by this
report, no evidence at all was presented to the Trial Commission and,
of course, an acquittal r esulted. Your committee was inclined to recommend reversal and send the matter back for trial. However, correspo.n-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

dence developed the fact that no witnesses were available and no evidence
could be produced on a rehearing. In such a situation, charges should not
be preferred in the first instance. But where there is a failure to produce
evidence that would appear to be available, a showing should be made
in the record as to the reason for such failure.
Your committee has carefully reviewed the records in the following
cases:
Case No. 1019-A member of San Bernardino Lodge No. 348. Expelled September 3, 1942.
Case No. 1020--A member of Oakland Lodge No. 188. Acquitted
October 7, 1942.
Case No. 1021-A member of Occidental Lodge No. 22. Expelled
November 2, 1942.
· Case No. 1022-A member of Union Lodge No. 58. · Expelled January
6, 1943.
Case No. 1023-A member of Russian River Lodge No. 181. Acquitted
November 3, 1942.
Case No. .1026-A member of Palestine Lodge No. 351. Expelled
August 2, 1943.
We find in these records no errors affecting the substantial rights of
the accused, that substantial justice has been accomplished. We recommend affirmance ·in all of these cases, and, therefore, offer the following
resolution.
.
Be it Resolved, That the action of the Trial Commission and Lodges
in each of the above cases, together with the penalties imposed, be and
they hereby are ratified, affirmed and approved.
·

The Grand Lodge at the present time limits and prescribes the
character of investments than can be made of the endowment funds of
the Masonic Homes and of Life Membership funds but does not make
apy limitation on the investment of the general funds except to the extent of twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000.00) which are required to
be held in sound banking institutions or invested in seasoned interest
bearing bonds as provided in Section 655 of the Edicts and Resolutions.
The matter of the investment of endowment funds which are of considerable magnitude has been given careful attention and the rule therefor would be properly applied to the investment of the general funds.
Your committee therefor recommends that Section 655 of the Edicts and
Resolutions be repealed and further recommends the adoption of the
following resolution:

680

655 Recognition as to the handling and investment of Grand Lodge

this Grand Lodge in the general fund shall at all times be held in sound
banking institutions or the same invested in Federal, State, County or
municipal bonds legal for investment of savings banks.

LODGE CONTRIBUTIONS TO ORGANIZATIONS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the
proposed amendment to Section 159 of the Constitution and Ordinances
of Grand Lodge providing that a . Lodge may expend in its discretion
not to exceed twenty per cent (20%) of its total revenues for the purpose of refreshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse and that
during the continuance of the present war a Lodge may contribute t)le
unexpended balance in its refreshment fund to the American Red Cross,
the National War Fund or any other purpose designed to promote the
National Defense and approved by the Grand Master. Our law wisely
provides that the funds of the Lodges, from whatever source derived,
are trust funds for the payment of the necessary expenses of the Lodge
and for the special calls of charity and prohibits the use of its funds
for any other thing whatsoever except the payment of its officers or
representatives attending the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge
and for the purpose of a testimonial for a retiring Master and for floral
pieces for an ill or deceased brother or his family and not to exceed
twenty per cent (20%) of its total revenues for purpose of refreshment and
the promotion of fraternal intercourse. Your committee is of the opinion
that the restrictions on the expenditures of Lodge funds should not be
reduced and therefor recommends that the proposed amendment be not
adopted.

Adopted.

WAR FUNDS
To the Most WorshiPful Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand ~aster referred in his message to three payments heretofore made by him from the. War Relief Fund, first in the sum of twentyfive hundred dollars to Fortitude Lodge, U. D., in Chungking, China, to
feed and care for the starving and unfortunate Masons in the South of
China.; and, then in the sums of twenty-five hundred dollars to the
American Red Cross, and five t)10usand dollars to the United Service
Organization on behalf of the Lodges and brethren:· of the jurisdiction of
California.
Your committee agrees with his statement that there is no question
about the urgent need of the Masons in China and agrees that it was
proper. to _make some contribution from Masonic funds for that purpose.
Also, m view of· the fact that about ten thousand California Masons are
serving in_ the armed forces of the United. States, the contributions ·to
the American Red Cross and the United Service Organizations were de~
sirable and appropriate.
However, your committee questions the propriety of making these
payments .from the War Relief Fund. In this connection there has been
referred . to Y<:>~r committee the resolution introduced by Brother Mark
A. Sawri,e reciting that the Masons of California have contributed to the
War Relief F1.1nd with the assurance that the purpose of this fund was
tc:i _assist Lod.ges financially unable to meet needs occasioned by war cond~t~o.ns; to aid wc:irthy ser~ice members and their families, and to help
vis1ttng brethren m our midst; further reciting . the contribution of the
sum of ten thousand dollars ($10,000.00) as detailed in the message of the
Grand Master, and then resolving "that the War Relief Fund be reimbursed in the sum of ten thousand dollars ($10,000.00) for these expen_ditures and. that said sum. be drawn from the funds of Grand Lodge
which arc ava1lable for charity and outside agencies upon the order of
the Grand Master."
The re~itals in the resolution of Brother Sawrie, in the opinion of
your committee, correctly reflect the purposes of the War Relief Fund
as represented to the Masons of California who have contributed and
will hereafter contribute to the fund; and that the integrity of the fund
for the purposes so intended should be safeguarded.
·
Although the contributions made by the Grand Master were for a
proper Masonic purpose, it appears that they were made from a fund not
properly expendable therefor.
Your committee recommends that the . resolution of Brother Sawrie
be approved and that the sum of ten thousand dollars ($10,000.00) be
transferred from the general funsJs of Grand Lodge to the War Relief
Funds as reimbursement.

Adopted.

.PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
A resolution is presented jointly by Brothers James W. ·c rosby,
Master of Hollywood Lodge No. 355, John H . Hargreaves, Master of
Henry Knox Lodge No. 662 and Alford L. Foster, Master of Glassell
Park Lodge No. 605, proposing to amend sections 208 and. 209 of the
Constitution and Ordinances of the Grand Lodge relating to physical
qualifications of applicants for the degrees· of Masonry.
·
By the amendment of section 208 it is propose<;! to substitute the
word "figuratively" for the vvord "substantially" in the present sentence
of the section which provides that the applicant must have "no maim or
defect in his body that may render him incapable. o.f learning the Art"
and must be "physically able to conform substantially to what the several
degrees respectively require of him." The proponents of the resolution
stated frankly to your committee that the purpose of the substitution of
the word "figuratively" for the word "substantially" was to so relax the
present rule as to qualify applicants with substituted m"embers in the
place of natural members of the body, such as artificial hands, arms and
legs.
·
·
It goes without saying that men who are so unfortunate as to be
without the natural members of the body may otherwise be well qualified
for membership in our order, but your committee questions the wisdqm
or desirability of departing from the time honored and universal requir:ement of physical · fitness to receive the degrees in due and ancient form.
The question of physical qualifications has been the subject of discussion
in years past and the problem of formulating a rule in such . ;i. way as to
preserve the traditional forms and ceremonies and still be fair to an
applicant with some physical defects has vexed the draftsmen of Masonic
law in most jurisdictions. A thorough consideration of the question by
this Grand Lodge in times past resulted in liberalizing the old rule of a
literal conformance to a substantial conformance with the requirements.
of the degrees. It is true that even with this liberalization the problem
of determining in a particular case whether an applicant can substantially
conform is often a difficult and delicate one. Under our present law that
question is left for decision to the sound discretion of the constituent
Lodge. There it should continue to reside, in the opinion of your
committee.
The proposal to amend section 209 is to strike out the provision
leaving the question of the physical fitness of the applicant to the sound
discretion of the Lodge and inserting a provision that if elected to receive the degrees, no degree shall be conferred on the candidate without
first obtaining the approval of the Inspector of the Masonic District _in
which the Lodge is located and the consent of the Grand Master.
Your committee is of the view that this proposed innovation would
result in an unnecessary and undesirable encroachment upon the powers
and functions of the constituent Lodge and would, in addition, impose a
further and undue burden on the Grand Master.
Your committee therefore recommtnds that the resolution be not
adopted.

Adopted.

There are many old Lodges in California In towns and villages which
for one reason or another have not grown as rapidly as other localitfes
and. still remain more or less of the size and character as existed when
the Lodge was chartered. Necessarily, in such small communities applicants are few and such Lodges, in the opinion of your committ'ee, ought
not be deprived of their exclusive jurisdiction over the members of their
own community.

HISTORY COMMITTEE
Past Grand Master Fischer presented a verbal report for the
committee, recommending that the History Committee be continued for another year and the recommendation was adopted.

Such Lodges are necessary and essential elements in the American
way of life and should be, and usually are, the center and rallying point
of community life in the smaller places. It is true that they may not
. have the. beautiful Lodge rooms and large memberships of the larger
communities, but like the Lodge over Simpson's store they often harbor
the truly Masonic spirit of brotherly love and devotion.
Your committee are of the opinion that to make any ·changes that
would tend to the extinction of these Lodges, many of which are among
the older Lodges of the jurisdiction, would be a distinct detriment to the
order and to the communities · where those Lodges exist.
We, therefore, recommend that the : proposal be not adopted.

Adopted.

NOTIFICATION TO MEMBERS TO ALL APPLICATIONS
To the Most Worshipful Grattd Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was referred the recommendation of the Grand Master that our Lodges be
required to notify their members of all applications for the degrees or
for affiliation within ten· days after their reception by the Lodge and
that the notice shall carry the full names, residence, and business addresses
and the age and occupation of the applicant, has had the same under
consideration.
Your committee, after a careful study of this subject and appreciating
the reasons for the recommendation, is unable to find itself in accord
with the same. The present law makes ample provision for handling
this matter . amon'g those {..odges having concurrent jurisdiction. The
adoption of . this recommendation could be the basis for re:vealing to the
profane Masonic information to which they are not entitled.
In a report to this Grand Lodge by the Jurisprudence Committee
·thereof in 1897 the restriction was added that the names of applicants
for the degrees must not be printed and dispersed in folders, and a
similar report by the same c.ommittee in 1913 applies a like restriction
.to the use of postal card~ for the same purpose. Both these reports were
. adopted by the Grand Lodge. The committee, therefore, offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON POLICY AND
. GENERAL PURPOSES
CONSTITUTION MONTH OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge:
Brethren:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had under
consideration the proposal of Southland Lodge No. 618 that "the annual
ce-Jebration of the adoption of our Constitution in the month of September
be extended to the public schools to the end that our youth may be taught
that all of the great blessings of liberty they now enjoy were secured
to them by the noble patriots who framed and handed down to us that
greatest of charters ever composed by man."
·
Your committee points out that we now have Masonic observance of
public schools week and also observance of the constitution annually in
the month of September. This would appear to correspond fully to .our
obligation in these particular matters. We believe that our public schools
are teaching our youth with respect to the constitution. This is a matter
wholely with the province of the school authorities.
Your committee therefor recommends that no action be taken with
reference to the proposal of Southland Lodge.

Adopted.

POST-WAR PROGRAM
To the Most Worshipful ~rnnd Lodge of California:
Brethren:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the
following resolution submitted · by Pacific Lodge No. 136:
"Now, therefore, be it resolved, That the Grand Master set aside
sufficient time on the agenda of the Communication of the Grand Lodge
of Masons of California, commencing October 11, 1943, fot: discussion
of this subject, and if the representatives assembled determine that the
Grand Lodge and the constituent Lodges should contribute to post-war
planning programs, that the newly-elected Grand . Master be authorized
to appoint a committee properly instructed to study the subject and assist the constituent Lodges in the formulation of a program whereby the
members of the fraternity, as Ame.dean citizens as well as Masons, may
join in taking an active part in the accomplishment of sound post-war
policies, consistent with the democratic principles of the Government of
the United States."
With reference to the foregoing, your committee begs le.ay~ to report
as follows:
We believe that every citizen should inform himself to the best of
his ability with respect to post-war plans, both international and domestic,
aiid .give to those charged with resp~nsibi!ity for decisions the benefit of
his views. We do not, however, believe that it is practical fqr the Grand
Lodg.e to formulate or for constituent Lodges to adopt a post-war program.
Any post-war plan or program that can be devised is certain to propose
the adoption of economic and political P:Olicies and measures with respect
to which many and often bitter differences of opinion will arise.
The President of the United St11tes and his Cabinet, the Congress
of the United States and the several State Legislatures and hundreds of
economic, commercial, industrial, scientific, agricultural, educational, religious, social, and labor organizations are working on the subject of postwar plans. It is doubtful if there is any citizen of California who cannot
find a convenient forum in which to develop his views.
In the opinion of your committee, however, Masonry does not constitute such a forum and, we, therefore, recommend that the resolution
be not adopted.

Adopted.

TO REPEAL SECTION 218

will confront our fraternity in the near and post-war future. In accordance
therewith a special meeting was called for October 12th for the purpose
of conferring with representatives of the Boards of Relief and Employment Services, to consider the immediate and post-war problems. There
was a very laTge and deeply interested attendance. There was a general
exchange of information regarding the problems that have already confronted the different boards, and how they have been handled.

Past Grand Master Ogden of Policy Committee, reporting on proposal to repeal Section 218 of the Constitution and Ordinances, reported
as follows:
I ask leave to file written report of the proposal to repeal Section 218
at a later time. This is the section which we had in discussion this
morning, whereby the jurisdiction would be changed to twenty-five 11'.iles
instead of ten miles.
It is all very well to consider the merits of this one section, but unfortunately the repeal of this . section, my bi:ethren, would' necessitate a
number of other sections being repealed or changed. For instance, there
is a special provision for San Fernando Lodge. San Fernando Lodge,
operating under .Section 699 of the Ross Digest, · is granted jurisdiction
over all the ·territory which it had prior to its annexation to the City of
•Los Angeles.

My own personal opinion would be if we repeal section 218, Lankershim Lodge and others would be without any territory at all, and any
petition received from those Lodges would have to be upon waiver from
San Fernando Lodge. I, therefore, ask that this go over until next
communication of Grand Lodge as unfinished business, because our
committee is not prepared to give full consideration to the matter and the
time is too short for the Jurisprudence Committee to consider it. ·
I move the adoption of this report.

Adopted.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California :

Your Board of Control presents the following report of the activities
that came under its supervision during the past Masonic year. · I ti; work
has been benefited by the information and kind assistance given by the
Grand Master, the Grand Secretary ·a nd his assistants.
The board feels that all justified , relief has been freely extended as
usual in accordance with the policy of 01,1r Grand Lodge.
The Board of Control is convinced that the efficiency of the Boards
of Relief and Employment Services is now at its very highest level; that
they stand ready to meet the uncertain future with a large degree of
confidence in' their ability, to handle successfully the multitude of problems
with which they may be confronted.
The greatest degree of harmony and ~ooperatio.n continues between
the Boards of Relief and Employment Services and the Board of Control.
Commendation is due the Boards of Relief and Employment Services
for the excellence of their personnel.

1943 SUMMARY OF BOARDS OF RELIEF

692

· Employment Service
Notwithstanding the continually increasing . demand for .person.a l
services, 15,048 applications were received by ,9ur seven employment
bureaus from our brethren and their dependents during the fisc;al year
just closed. These applications plus 5,973 whieh were o'n hand at the
beginning of the year were converted into 13,016 ·jobs of which 10,519
pr 80 per cent were permanent. Last year we thought our employers'
requests for help totaling 30,303 would perhaps· stand for some time to
come, but this year the figure was 37,260, an increase of 22.9 .per cent.
It is quite obvious that we could. have filled many more jobs if we had
had qualified applicants available. The expense for the year was $31,286.70 of which Grand Lodge :appropriated $19,200.00 or 58.5 per cent.
The average cost per job secured was $2.52, and once more, a large sum
of money, over one-quarter of a million dollars, was saved to our brethren.
The war is not over, but we are already serving our brethren of the
armed forces. In one· month, one bureau found jobs for twenty returned
service men, not men over thirty-eight years of age but younger men
honorably discharged because of some disability.
This is Masopry in action.

REPORT OF GRIEVANCE COMMITTEE
Trial Record No, 502
To the Most Worshipful Grand 'Lodge of California :
Your committee on grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 502 (also No. 581), reports as· follows:
A charge of un-Masonic · conduct set forth in one specification of
embezzlement, was filed against petitioner in February, 1926. .
A trial was regularly had which resulted in the suspension of accused.
At the meeting of Grand Lodge the action was reversed and the
matter was remanded for a new trial. On the second trial, which was
Numbered 581, the result was a finding of guilt and a like sentence of
suspension. This action was -affirmed by Grand Lodge at its session
of 1927.
·
The conviction arose out of a grand jury audit of petitioner's books
who, at the time, was under-sheriff of the County of Tulare. The District
Attorney who prosecuted accused, is, according to ··a, letter appearing in
the files, a member of a near by Masonic Lodge. · ,:•
Dinuba Lodge No. 385, of which petitioner was a member before
his suspension, gave notice of the application for reinstatement to
the entire membership, as far as practical, stating. the meeting at which
the petition for reinstatement was received and giving notice that action
would be taken at the next stated meeting. There was but one dissenting
vote of the members present.
·
Petitioner has been employed from 1926 to 1929 as a linotype operator
on the Dinuba Sentinel; from 1929 to 1934 he was employed by a printing
cr,mcern in Los Angeles; frotn 1934 · to 1940 he was district manager for
a company operating out of San Jose, California, 'and from 1940 to the
present time has been owner of a printing shop in Dinuba. These facts
appear in a letter from the Secretary of the Lodge which further states
that the money involved was offered to be restored . but the offer was
rejected.
The file in this case contains several letters from responsible busin.e ss
and professional men all of which are favorable to applicant and endorsing
his petition but one from the former district attorney, to which reference
has been already made, is particularly convincing to your committee.
Among other things it contains the following language:
"I was a witness before the Lodge at Dinuba, and also being a member of an adjoining Lodge, I was very familiar with the trial, and concurred with the Lodge in the action it took at that time .
I now understand that the Dinuba Lodge has reelected him to membership, and I again concur with the Lodge, for I feel that Mr. H. is
now just as worthy of Masonic friendships as any other good and loyal

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

citizen, and I believe that he has earned the restoration to membership
in the Lodge, and were I a member of the Dinuba Lodge and present at
the time of the election for restoration to membership, I would certainly
have voted for it.
Under the circumstances, I hope that ·your Grievance Committee,
when called upon to review the action of the Dinuba Lodge,, will approve
it, and that I may again have the privilege of sitting in Lodge with Mr. H."
Your committee recommends that the petition of C. R. H. for restoration to all of the rights and privileges of Masonry be granted and offers
the following resolution:
Resolved, That the petition of said former member of Dinuba Lodge,
No. 385, F. & A. M., be and the same is hereby granted and he be
restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.

Trial Record No. 930
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee, to which was referred the application of J. S. T.
for restoration to all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be.gs leave
to report as follows:
The applicant was expelled by Rising Light Lodge No. · 397, on
December 7, 1937, pursuant to the provisions of Section 332 of Constitution and Ordinances, he having theretofore entered a plea of. guilty in
the Superior Court of the County of Los Angeles to a charge of Grand
Theft, and having been committed to State Prison.
The applicant was confined in San Quentin Prison for a period of approximately two years and five months and then returned to Los Angeles.
He has had practically continuous employment since his release, and is
now operating his own apparently successful office as a public accountant.
He was granted a pardon by the Governor of this State on September 9,
1942, restoring him to all his rights as a citizen.
The favorable recommendations presented in support of his application included a very impressive and persuasive letter from the Superior
Court Judge who had committed him to State Prison; and all strongly
indicate a complete rehabilitation of the applicant.
The Lodge which expelled the applicant has voted by a vote of
fifty to one to petition Grand Lodge to restore him to all the rights and
privileges of Masonry. Your committee believes that this application
should be granted, and offers the following resolution.
Resolved, That the petition of J. S. T. for restoration to all the
rights and privileges of Masonry, be, and the same is hereby granted.
Dated: October 11, 1943.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee to which has been referred the .application for resto all. the rights and privileges of Masonry of L. J. F., begs
leave to report as follows:
~oration

The applicant was expelled by Sequoia Lodge No. 349, on January 5,
1932, and that action was affirmed at the 1932 communication of Grand
Lodge.
The misconduct of which the applicant was convicted by the Lodge
consisted of the alienation by bim of the affections of the wife of a
. Master .Ma.son, resulting in the divorce of said Master Mason and his
wife; that the applicant thereafter married this woman, and abandoned
her about a year after their marriage; that the applicant exhibited to his
wife an unfavorable report he was making relative to a petitioner for the
degrees of Masonry. He was found guilty of the specifications and of unMasonic conduct by a vote of six to one.
After being divorced in 1933 by the woman involved in the charges
upon which he was tried before the Lodge, he remarried at Reno, Nevada,
on August 3, 1940, artd now lives with his wife and child in San Leandro.
Your committee is informed inforll]ally that Sequoia Lodge has
voted to oppose the restoration of this applicant. Your committee has
endeavored to determine whether or not this action by the Lodge is based
upon the conduct of the appl:.:ant since his expulsion, and after interviewing representatives of the Lodge have concluded that the Lodge was
not at the time of its action in possession of the information as to the
rehabilitation of the applicant which has been presented to your committee.

In support of his application the applicant has presented ;i number
of letters of recommendation from very responsible and prominent citizens
of Alameda County. All of these letters are highly commendatory of the
character and conduct of the applicant, during the past eleven years. They
indicate to your committee that the applicant has, during ' those 'eleven
years which have elapsed since his expulsion, pursued a course of honorable conduct, and · has become a respected citizen of the community in
which he lives.
Your committee believes that this application may well be granted,
restoring the applicant to Masonry as a member at large, in order that
he may apply for membership in a Lodge in the community where he
has rehabilitated himself, and your committee offers the following
resolution.
Resolved, That the application of L. J. F. for restoration to all the
rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same hereby is granted.
Dated: · October 11, 1943.

Trial Record No. 1025

But lurking in the background in. this case is apparently a much
more sinister situation.
We are fearful the episodes above described may have been the manifestation of a blight in this Masonic Lodge whereby individuals, in greater
or lesser number, have so far forgotten their duties and their obligations
as to blackball petitioners for the degrees for no other reason than to
satisfy some fancied slight or insult, or to further some perverted idea
of the person· or persons casting such ballots. And we are concerned that
perhaps there is · developing here some sort of racial antagonism which
has no place ever in Masonry. Perhaps such conditions, if they be true,
may be developed by a new trial in this case.
Moreover, in an interview with representatives of this Lodge, it
was the feeling of some of them that on the trial .under review all evidence
available was not secured or presented because the accuser did not have
the aid of a lawyer while the accused had the benefit of representation
by able counsel. Under the circumstances before us in this case your
committee is of the opinion that there is considerable merit to this
suggestion.
We express no opinion as to the truth or falsity of any charge or
specification here under review, or that may be hereafter added.
·
Your committee recommends the adoption of the following resolution:
Be it Resolved, in Trial Record No. 1025 that action of the trial commission in acquitting the accused of the first specification in the charges
against him be affirmed and that the action of the trial commission as to
the second specification in said charges in suspending the accused be
reversed and set aside, and the matter be remanded for a new trial in
some Lodge in the jurisdiction, to be designated by tr. e M. W. Grand
Master, other than the Lodge of the accuser and the accused; that the
Grand Master designate counsel to aid the accuser and that the accuser
be permitted, if he so desires, to add, change, or amend the specifications
and charges, so that any and all issues as against the accused may be
heard and determined.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
On October 6, 1942, a stated meeting was held of the Lodge of which
the accuser and the accused· were members. The accuser was.. then Master
of the Lodge. While the Lodge was in session, the M·astei;, announced
that the Investigating Committee had reported adversely upon the petition
of an individual to receive the degrees of Masonry in that ·L odge.
After the Lodge was closed the accused went to the Ma~ter's station
and asked to be permitted to see the petition which ha<,! been rejected. It
is a fair inference from this request that he desii;:ed to know who the
members of the committee were. Thereupon the ·Master said to him,
"Who in · the hell are you that you want to see., tbis?'~ To this remark,
the accused rejoined: "Wait a minute, pleai;e, I· am , a little older man
than you are, and you have no business talking to me in that tone of
voice."
In the following year, after the term of this ·Master had expired; he
filed charges against the accused, with two specifications : The first
specification was that the .accused demanded of him the names ~f the
Investigating Committee in a "loud and arrogant manner." . The second
specification was that the accused called the Secretary of the Lodge a
son-of-a-bitch. ·
·
The trial commission acquitted the · accused on the first 'Specification;
convicted him upon the second, and fixed the penalty at suspension.

.

.

.

.

The Secretary testified that' he called the accused on the . telephone,
and asked him to make a Past Master's jewel, as the accused had done
for many years gone by,. and that the accused then said to him. over the
telephone that he would not make up the jewel "for you or any other
son-of-a-bitch."
·
The use of this language was categorically denied by ·the accused.
He said he received a telephone call from the Secretary, who asked him_
to make the jewel, ·and that he declined to do so. That the telephone
over· which the conversation was ha,d. was out in an open jewelry store
in plain hearing of one of his women clerks and _of customers who w~re
there present. The woman clerk testified that she heard the conv:ersat10n
of her employer, and that he did not use the language complained of.
A careful reading of the record disclosed that there was evidently
very bitter personal feeling between the accuser and the accused, and
some of the witnesses against the accused. The Master who presided
at the trial would not permit counsel for the accused on cross-examinatibn
to inquire into this feeling. It is settled law that when a witness testifies
to a fact upon cross-examination, inquiry ·may be made to develop his
state of mind. Not to permit this is an undue limitation of the right which
every accused has of cress-examination of witnesses who testify_against
him, and a denial of due process of law, guaranteed to every Master
Mason before he may. be deprived of his Masonic rights and privileges.
For this reason alone, the findings and judgment of the trial commission
may not stand.
While it is highly regrettable if either the accuser or accused used
the language charged to him by the other, assuming they did, there have
been Masonic offenses brought to the attention of Grand Lodge more
serious in nature. Therefore, your committee has discussed the advis·ability of terminating the case now by presenting to this Grand Lodge a
resolution acquitting the accused.

Trial Record No. 1024
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California :
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1024, begs leave to report as follows :
On December 1, 1942, written charges of un-Masonic conduct were
filed against Brother M. D. J. of Los Cerritos Lodge No. 674 by the
Junior Warden thereof, upon the following. specifications, to-wit:
First: That for some time prior to the 11th day of July, 1940, and
at all times since, he has so openly and notoriously associated himself
with a certain woman, not his wife, known as J. S. P., as to bring himself
into contempt and the craft to shame and disrepute.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Second: That on or about the 10th day of November, 1941, at the
City of Long Beach, he . did conduct himself in a lewd and lascivious
manner with a woman known as J. S. P.

At the outset your committee is willing to concede that the commissioners were justified in exonerating the accused on Specifications "First"
and "Third" because no substantial proof was offered on either of these
specificatioris. Your committee has reviewed the entire transcript of testimony, covering llS typewritten pages, and the facts as we see them are as
follows :
On December 23rd, 1922, accused married his present wife, Mrs.
S. J. They have three children, aged 18, 17, and 15 years.
On July 10th, 1940, she instituted a suit for separate maintenance
against the accused, who is a physician and surgeon practicing his profession in the City of Long Beach. The accused subsequently countered
with a suit for divorce, which was later denied, but at the time of his
Masonic trial, in January, 1943, he had apparently instituted another suit
for divorce. Mrs. J . obtained a decree of separate maintenance and sup.port for ·,herself and the three children, as well as their custody.
· The accused had evidently become infatuated with the woman named
in specifications 1, 2, and 3, of the charges whom we shall hereafter refer
to as the "Affinity" and who was undoubtedly the direct cause of the
institution of divorce proceedings by the wife of accused. The affinity
was
divorcee and had been a supposed friend of Mrs. J . for about
fifteen years. It was not, however, until about a week before Decoration
Day; 1940, that she definitely had cause to suspect that all was not well.
Shortly. thereafter ~ ¥rs. J. employed a detective agency to shadow her
husband; the a.c cused, as a result of which on November ll, 1941, accused
was observ.ed from.' the street, with the affinity in 11- nude condition in
her apartment, , being No . .36, and upon the detectives knocking on the
door and being admitted after a few minutes, they found accused in the
bathroom without underwear,.:. and only with his trousers on, but attempting to put on his socks: ·The affinity was clad in a nightrobe and
she and he attempted to explain his presence in that condition on the
ground that he was· taking a bath. It should here be noted that accused
had apartment No. 33 in the. same apartment house and no valid reason
was given as, to why he was not taking a bath in his own apartment. The
bathroom was not wet, nor was there any evidence that his ·statement was
true. It should further be noted that the testimony of the wife, the head
of the detective agency, and the latt.er's two operatives indicated that
the roll-away bed in the apartment where accused was found on this

.
The accused called no witnesses whatsoever to refute the claims of
his wife and the detectives, but he and his counsel attempted to impeach

Your committee is at a loss to understand why these precautions
were so necessary if his conduct was above reproach.
The accused in his own testimony admitted that "some of the witnesses testified truthfully." He admitted that he was in his affinity's
apartment, but stated that he was washing (at 11 :15 p. m.) ?pd had Ii.is
shirt on. The above fairly represents the testimony supporting specification

A special meeting of the Lodge was held on December 10th, 1942,
for the election of trial commissioners, at which meeting nine commissioners, one of whom was the Senior Warden, were elected to hear and
determine the charges. The Master set Monday, the 4th day of January,
1943, at 8 :00 p. m .' in the .New Masonic Temple (Long Beach), as the time
and place for the first meeting of the commissioners. Proper notice of
proceeding~ was given to all interested parties. The trial was held at the
above time and place, with Brother Francis H. Gentry, Master of the
Lodge, presiding.
· ·
The accuser and accused ·were represented by c.iunsel and it was
stipulated that all proceedings were thus far J_"egular.
The accused entered a plea of "Not Guilty" as · to each separate
specification in the accusation. -.
At the c'o nclusion of the triaJ the comm1ss10ners balloted on each
separate specification, with the following results:
First specification: "Guilty, 2".; "Not guilty, 7."
Second specification: "Guilty; O"; " Not guilty, 9."
Third specification: "Guilty, 1'' ; "Not guilty, 8."
Fourth specificati.on: "Guilty, 1"; "Not guilty, 8."
The findings of "Not Guilty" by the Commissioners were submitted
to the Lodge on the next evening, being the stated meeting, of January
5th, 1943, as a result of which the accused stood acquitted and exonerated
of all charges.
No appeal from the decision of the commissioners was taken by the
accuser, and under circumstances where the testimony is so conflicting
that reasonable men might disagree concerning the same, your Committee
on Grievances would be precluded from disturbing their findings on question of fact. In the present case, however, there is no such conflict, and
a serious miscarriage of justice in the opinion of the committee has resulted. (See Section 341 of Constitution and Ordinances.)
The admissions of defendant, himself, as to specification No. 2 were
sufficient to convict him and certified court records definitely established
the truth of Count No. 4.
The line of questioning indulged in by some of the commissioners
also indicates to your committee that a majority of said commissioners
were prejudiced against the wife of the accused to such an extent as to
have rendered them unfit and unfair in the discharge of their sworn
duties as commissioners. Some of the questions put to a witness for the
accuser were furthermore insulting. The commissioners were apparently
more interested in acquitting the accused than they were to get at the
truth or falsity of the charge.

To the Most Worshipf11l Grand I.,odge of California:
Menorah Lodge No. 623, F. & A. M. has again. petitioned Grand
Lodge for the restoration of G. D. G. (Trial Record No. 990) an expelled Mason, to the rights and privileges of Masonry, un:der the provisions of Section 347 of the Constitution. This is the second application
by said Lodge on behalf of said expelled member.
The previous history of this case which we have taken very largely
from the latest petition filed by Menorah Lodge for the reinstatement of
this former brother, and which we found to be correct, is as follows:
G. D. G. was formerly a Mason in good standing of Menorah Lodge
No. 623. He was expelled by default, after he had been convicted of a
felony, to-wit, second degree murder. Notice of the conviction was formally served upon him as required by the Constitution, on July 7, 1940,
and on .his failure to demand a trial he was declared expelled by the Lodg e
on November 5, 1940.
Executive clemency was granted 'to him by the then Governor of
California on April 4, 1941, by commuting his sentence to time served
and on July 1, 1941, he requested Menorah Lodge to petition Grand
Lodge in his behalf as above stated. The Master of his Lodge in that year
thereupon appointed a committee to investigate and examine into the
matter and report to . the Lodge, ·This committee returned a favorable
report, and at the stated meeting of the Lodge held on August 5th, 1941,
a vote by secret ballot was taken on the question as to whether or no~
the Lodge should petition Grand Lodge for the restoration of this former
member to the rights and privileges of · Masonry. The ballot was 58 members favoring petitioning .Grand Lodge, and four against, being considerably mo:e than the requisite two-thirds vote of the members present.
Menorah Lodge thereupon petitioned Grand Lodge for the restoration of this former brother, whereupon the said petition was, at the 1941
Communication of Grand Lodge, referred to this committee, which recommended that said petition should be denied at that time, without prejudice,
for the reason that it felt that G. D . G. had not been released from in~ ·
carceration a sufficient period of time to clearly demonstrate that he
had been properly rehabilitated to justify his being restored to membership in the fraternity.
Since the filing of the first petition further executive clemency has
been granted to this former brother by the Governor of California, who,
on or about December 31st, 1942, granted him a full and unconditional
pardon and restoration to all civil rights under the law.
The petition now before Grand Lodge was filed with Menorah Lodge
No. 623 on August 2nd, 1943, under the provisions of Section 347 of the
Constitution. The Master of the Lodge thereupon appointed a committee,
consisting of two Past Masters who are lawyers and who had served on
the previous committee and three laymen who are prominent business
executives, two of whom did not know petitioner personally. A copy
of the committee's report and the exhibits attached to the report was
submitted to your committee.
At the stated meeting last m entioned, to-wit, Afig ust 2nd, 1943, t.h e
r equest of said G. D. G. was read to the Lodge and the motion was made
that a vote be taken at the next stated meeting, to-wit, September 7, 1943, ·
on the question as to whether or not the Lodge should petition Grand
Lodge for the restoration of this brother to all the rights and privileges of

710

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Masonry. A written notice that such vote would be taken was sent to
every member of the Lodge, on August 25th, 1943.
At the stated meeting of Septemb~r 7th, 1943, fifty members of the
Lodge being present (which we are advised is representative and an
average attendance at stated meetings) the committee theretofore appointed by the Master made its report to the Lodge and a secret ballot
was thereupon ordered, and as a result of said ballot 47 members were
in favor of the Lodge petitioning Grand Lodge for the restoration of
G. D.' G. and three members against--agaii:t being considerably mc:ire than
the requisite two-thirds vote of the members present.
In view of the fact that this case has been before your committee
of Grand Lodge on a previo.u s occasion, we do not deem it necessary to
go into the facts of the case at length; excepting to say that applicant
was convicted of second degree murder arising out of ·a conspiracy trial
involving several of the leaders of the deaning and dyeing business .in
Los Angeles at a time when there was considerable sabotage being
practiced in the cl~aning and dyeing business. The basis of the conspiracy
trial however was that seven and one-half (7~) years before the return
of the indict~ent and trial, a negro' porter had been ·found dead in one
of these establishments, under circumstances indicating murder. There
was no proof direct or otherwise that accused had anything to do with
the murder or had any part therein.
Applicant has lived in Los Angeles since 1912. He married his
present wife in 1914 and his family consists of his wife and two children,
a. son who is now serving in the United States Air Corps, and a daughter
who graduated from the University of California at Los Angeles, and
who is married to an officer in the United States Army.
He has continued in the same business practically during the past
thirty years. He owns his own home; is connected fraternally with
numerous · social and fraternal organizations, and was never involved in
any difficulties, least of all charges of moral turpitude prior to the time
he was indicted on the charge above referred to. He seems to have been
a man of good civil qualities, interested in public welfare, and 'was
honored by his Lodge in having been elected Master thereof about fifteen
years ago.
Your committee is therefore satisfied that G. D . G., being the subject of Trial Record No. 990, is fully rehabilitated and entitled to be
restored to the Lodge which has petitioned to that effect in his behalf.
Your committee therefore offers the following resolution and moves
its adoption.
That in the matter of Trial° Record No. 990, involving one G. D. G.,
a member of Menorah Lodge No. 623, . that the petition of said Lodge
on behalf of said member should be granted, and that said member should
be restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry, and your committee so recommends.
Dated: October 13, 1943.
ARTHUR W. BROUILLET,
FRANK B. BELCHER,

To the Most Worshipful Grand·Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which has be.en
referred the recommendation made by the Grand Treasurer that the m-

713

vestment of the general funds of Grand Lodge be limited to Federal,
State, County, or municipal bonds legal for savings banks.
The Grand Lodge at the present time limits and prescribes the character of investments that can be made of the endowment funds of the
Masonic Homes and of Life Membership funds but does not make any
limitation on the investment of the general funds except to the extent of
twenty~fi.ve thousand dollars ($25,000.00) which are required to be held
in sound banking institutions or invested in safe interest carrying bonds
as provided in Section 655 of the Edicts and Resolutions. The matter
of the investment of endowment funds which are• of considerable magnitude has been given careful attention and the rule therefore would be
properly applied to the investment of the general funds. Your committee
therefore recommends that Section 655 of the Edicts and Resolutions be
repealed and further recommends the adoption of the following resolution:
655. Regulation as to the handling and investm~nt of Grand Lodge
funds: Resolved that no appropriations of the funds of the Grand -Lodge
shall be made, except in times of great loss or great calamity, when the
moneys in the general fund do not exceed the sum of twenty-five thousand
dollars ($25,000.00); and, be it further resolved, that the funds of this
Grand Lodge in the general fund shall at all times be held in sound
banking institutions or the same invested in Federal, State, County or
Municipal bonds legal for investment of savings banks.
The Jurisprudence Committee has approved the foregoing resolution
in principle and as to sum.

Audit of Accounts
Your committee has again employed Brother Floyd F. Webb of the
firm of Ruckstell, Burrows and Webb, certified public accountants, to
examine the books and records of the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary, the Masonic Homes of California and the Endowment Fund. The
reports of Brother Webb's examination of these records have been filed
with your committee and have h·ad its consideration. These reports are
now on file with the records of Grand Lodge and will be published in the.
annual proceedings in the report of the Grand Secretary. They indicate
that all records are correct and in proper shape and all receipts properly
accounted for and all expenditures properly made.
The accountants now make a supplemental report on the cash r:e-·
ceived since the close of the fiscal year on July 31st. This supplement.al
report is most helpful to the committee in making calculations on the
income for the coming year.

sum the Homes paid $1,475.00 and the balance of $250.00. has been paid
out of Grand Lodge funds. This is an increase of .$1,025.00 over the

the need for a special audit at the time of the death of our Most Worshipful William P. Filmer, Grand Treasurer. This was essential as it was

Committee . on Correspondence
It has been the practice of this Grand Lodge for most of its existence
to have a Committee on Correspondence, the duties of the committee
being the reviewing of the proceedings of other Grand Lodges throughout the world and making a resume of the important activities and happenings in such jurisdictions and reporting the same to Grand Lodge,
which report has always been printed in the annual proceedings.
For this purpose the committee for a number of years appropriated
$500.00, coyering the · expenses o_f ,.compiling this report.
This past year, under the chairmanship of Worshipful Brother Henry
C. Clausen, this reviewing was partialed out among the membership of
the committee and the reviewing and compiling has largely been done
without expense to Grand Lodge. It was found necessary by the committee, however, to expend $100.00 in performing its work, which was the
total amount expended out of the $500.00 appropriated. For this work
and compiling, and it is very co"nsiderable and has been done with verly
little expense to Grand Lodge, the Committee on Finance wishes to express its gratitude.
·
This committee is of the opinion that the reviewing ·of annual pr:oceedings is a valuable work arid should be encouraged. After all, whatever Masonry is doing, wherever it may exist, is something in which we
are all interested. Such information is made available through the good
work of the Committee on Correspondence. The report of this committee
should have much more consideration than is ordinarily given it. We
commend to all, and particularly to the Masters of Lodges, the reading
of the report compiled by this Committee on Correspondence.
In discussing the work for the coming year with the present chairman
of the committee, he expresses the belief that $250.00 will fully · cover
all needs of the committee. This committee therefore offers the following
resolution and recommends its adoption: ,
Resolved, That the sum of $250.00· or as much thereof as may be
required, be appropriated from the funds of this Grand Lodge, for the
purpose of defraying the expenses of the Committee on Correspondence,
said bills to be paid in the usual manner on approval .of the Committee
on Accounts.

Report of Grand Treasurer
For the first time in more than thirty years this report is being made
by other than the Most Worshipful vVi!liam P. Filmer, due to the death
of this Grand Mason last November.
·
It is a loss deeply felt by this committee, as of necessity this ~om­
mittee was often in consultation with Most Worshipful Brother Filmer
and greatly valued his advice, but most of all his friendship, as there had
always been an intimate friendship between him and members of the
committee. His loss to this Grand Lodge and to Masonry in general is
genuinely great. His life was truly a benediction to all who came in contact with him.
In the opinion of the committee, no worthier Mason could have been
selected to succeed Brother Filmer than our present Grand Treasurer
Most \ .Vorshipful Francis V. Keesling. He, too, is a man or sound judg~
ment, of absolutely irreproachable integrity and of very high purpose.
It is certain that Grand Lodge will be well served by him.
·
His report has been reviewed with more than usual interest by this
committee. It displays a complete grasp of the finances of Grand Lodge.
There has also come to the attention of this committee the survey
which our Grand Treasurer has made of the securities of Grand Lodge
and of the Endowment Fund. It displays much research and is sure
to be of inestimable benefit in the years to come and we commend the
Grand Treasurer for his thoughtfulness in pteparing this report and upon
its thoroughness.
This committee again wants to call to the attention of Grand Lodge
the great responsibility which r ests upon the Gra nd Treasurer. While
the careful handling of Grand Lodge fund s is imperative and yet, the
greatest responsibility is the investment of and . continued analysis of the
securities held, not only by Grand Lodge but also the . Endowment Fund
and various other agencies of Grand Lodge.

Portraits of Preceding Past Grand Masters
It has been the thought of this committee for a number of years
that our gallery of portraits of those who have presided over the destinies
of Masonry, in this jurisdiction, should be complete. We are sure that all
who were familiar with our gallery of some years ago will admit that its
appea1:ance has been materially improved in the last few years. It is
again the thought of this committee that this improvement should be
continued and that the portraits of those Past Grand Masters which are
not yet in the gallery should be included.
It is to be noted, with regret, that there have been no additions to
our gallery of Past Grand Masters during the past year, which now makes
three, who have served this Grand Lodge in the Oriental East in recent
years, missing, among them being that of our present Governor Earl
Warren, who, as the craft will recall was Grand Master in 1935. It is
also noted, with regret, that the portraits of neither Past Grand Master
Wilson or Smith are in the gallery. This committee is sure this Grand
Lodge will want the portraits of these three illustrious Masons, who
have served this fraternity and society as a whole so well, included in
the gallery.
Your committee therefore repeats the request heretofore made, that
these three Most Worshipful Brothers have their portraits painted, the
bill for each to be in an amount not to exceed $250.00 and when presented
to the Grand Secretary, to be paid by him out of Grand Lodge funds and
the portraits to be hung in the gallery of our Past Grand Masters.

Traveling Expenses of Grand Master
Your committee has discussed with the incoming Grand Master his
plans for the year and particularly as to the extent of his visitations.
We have been greatly impressed with the apparent study he has
already made of his responsibilities and the very serious manner in which
he is approaching the duties of Grand Master. It is obvious that the
craft will be well served this coming year.
The incoming Grand Master expresses the intent of traveling throughout the jurisdiction as extensively as conditions will permit. · Your committee is in hearty accord with this intent. It has been the~ oft-repeated
statement of the committee that the visitations of the Grand Master are
of great benefit to the craft and should be encouraged. We are sure this
is doubly true this year.
It is, of course, difficult to determine just what the expenses of t}l.e
Grand .Master may be. Your committee is thoroughly of the opinion that
the Grand Master should not be circumscribed in any activities which he
considers of benefit' to the craft. Due to the increased cost of traveling
your committee is recommending an increase of the appropriation from
$4,500 to $5,'000, whh the understanding, however, that it is to be left to
his good judgment as to how much, if any, additional he considers it
necessary to expend and that should he be out more than the appropriation recommended such additional amount should be recommended for
allowance at the next session of Gra,nd Lodge. Your committee therefore
offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption:
. " Resolved, That the sum of $5,000.00 be appropriated fro~ the . funds
of Grand Lodge for the purpose of defraying the traveling expenses of
the Grand Master.

During the past two Grand Lodge years the Grand Masters have
found it necessary to pay for the services of stenographic help. It has
always been the thought of this committee that the Grand Master, in
properly caring for the duties of his office, is called upon· for much sacrifice in the way of time and personal effort and neglect of his· own personal
business, and that to . this sacrifice should not be added the cost to him
personally for any of the needs of efficiently carrying on his activities as
Grand Master. Stenographic service is definitely one of these needs, as
the amount of correspondence required of the Grand Master is extensive.
