Reimbursement of Expenses of Inspectors
Some years ago Grand Lodge changed the policy of reimbursement
of inspectors for expenses in attending to their .duties, by appropriating
the payment therefor from Grand Lodge funds. An estimate at that time
was made of the amount that would be required to care for the necessary

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

expenses of all inspectors in carrying out their duties of inspection.· The
estimate was in excess of $3,500.00.
Each year this committee has appropriated and .had budgeted an
amount approximating the total amount that would be paid out should
all inspectors ask for the reimbursement of the amounts to which they
would be entitled. It is noted and with high commendation to the spiti(
of the inspectors that, while this money has been available for these expenses only a small portion of it has ever been asked for. This important
body of Masonic workers is performing a real service for Masonry and
could, in complete propriety, ask for the return of expenses and yet most
of the Work is being done for the pure joy of the services rendered and
without the willingness to accept any return for any money out. This is
the spirit that makes Masonry what it is. This Grand Jurisdiction is indeed fortunate to have such a body of faithful workers . .
While it is the wish of this committee that all expenses incurted by
inspectors. should be reimbursed, and it is recognized 'that should all
ask for the amount to which they are justly entitled, it would require at
least $3,500 and yet, Jess than one-third of this amount has been asked
for. It is the belief of the committee, however, that the actual expenses
that will be asked for should be set up as nearly as possible and it is
therefore making an appropriation of $1,000 and setting this amount up in
the budget. However, the committee wishes it understood that should an
additional amount be required it recommends the payment thereof.
In the discussion with the Grand Lecturer it has appeared to all that·
$1,000 will be ample to cover all the reimbursements requested and this
committee is therefore budgeting that amount. It therefore offers the
following resolution and recommends its adoption.
Resolved, That the sum of $1,000 be appropriated from the funds of
Grand Lodge for the purpose of defraying expenses of inspectors, .in
performing their official duties, such repayment .to be made upon bills
duly presented to the Grand Secretary which said bills shall first be approved by the Grand Lecturer.

Two years interest has accumulated on the loan, amounting to
$200. While the Lodge has not made a request for the waiving of this
interest, the inspector of the district, Brother Ralph Hine, has suggested
that it would be of material help to the . Lodge and to the interest .of
Masonry in that community were this interest to be forgiven. Past Grand
Master Wilson also makes such a recommendation.
The Lodge is small, having a membership of only 71. It has always
carried the banner of Masonry high and has never once indicated it would
not completely meet all its obligations, both in a fraternal and in a
monetary way.
It is the belief of this committee that the forgiving of the accumulated
interest of $200 would be lifting from the Lodge a burden that may be
substantially heavy. The committee therefore offers the following resolution and recommends its adoption:
Resolved, That the $2,500 paid by Carpinteria Lodge No. 444, on its
note be accepted as full settlement of the obligation of this Lodge to
Grand Lodge.

Carpinteria Lodge
At the annual session of Grand Lodge in 1941, Grand Lodge approvecl the action taken by the then Grand Master, Lloyd E. Wilson, in
granting to Carpinteria Lodge a loan of $2,500, for the purpose of enabling
the Lodge to repair damages done by earthquake to its temple. ';I'he
granting of this loan also permitted the Lodge to refinance the then
existing obligation against its temple and secure a generous discount of
the debt. For the loan a note of the Lodge was given, bearing four
per cent interest.
Since that time the Lodge has been able to meet the payments on
the loan and care for the expenses . of all its ordinary functions. Due
to this record the loaning institution has recently made the Temple Association an. advance sufficient to enable the Lodge to pay off its obligation
to Grand Lodge.

and promotion of this worthy enterprise. Time, patience and perseverance
have been expended freely by him. Gratifying results have been attained.

be retained for the same purpose.

Grand Secretary's Report
You have read the Grand Secretary's annual repo'rt. It contains information of importance,' indicatit.;g a substantial gain" in members. and

increasing activities in the Lodges of this jurisdiction. Study the comparisons on page 526. · ·
Naturally so many gains, which, added to the extra work occasioned
by the war, mean increased duties and responsibilities for the Grand
Secretary and his efficient corps of assistants. Office rec9rds and reports
are up to date, and this year an audit has been made of the 1943 annual
returns (see Supplemental Audit of 1943 Annual Returns), as well as
the regular audit report by the public accountants.
Our compliments are extended to our able Grand Secretary and his
staff for the thoroughly capable manner in which the affairs of his imJ?Ortant office are conducted.

It should be borne in mind that the budget which is being set up is
for the current fiscal year and that the money is on hand to care for
the appropriations now being made and the expenses to be incurred for
the operation of affairs in Masonry in this jurisdiction. It should also
be borne in mind that the per capita levy is for the purpose of raising
funds for next fiscal year's operations and further, that many imponderable conditio~s and expenses may arise and therefore the estimated
deficit which the budget shows may be less than the am~unt given.
Your are already acquainted with the recommendation of the Trustees
of _the Homes, that instead of the per capita levy of forty (40c) cents,
which has been asked for several preceding years it is now reduced to
twenty (20c) cents as has been stated in the report 'which this committee
already made on the Homes. This committee accepts the recommendation
of the Board of Trustee~.
•
The need which has arisen to appropriate funds for the restoration
of expenditures from the War Relief Fund of $20,393.93 has, as will be
noted from the budget which will follow, required the committee to show
a deficit for this coming year. This deficit will of necessity have to be taken
from the previous surpluses built up in Grand 1Lodge. It might be called
to the attention of the members of Grand Lodge that this is one of the
purposes for a surplus.
·
The decision also that the expense of war service being performed
by Grand Lodge is not properly chargeable to the War Relief Fund,
has necessitated an aditional contribution of $10,000.00 to be used by the
Grand Master for that purpose and is also an additional drain upon the
reserve funds of Grand Lodge.
It is the opinion ot' the Finance Committee that an additional per
capita levy should be made to reimburse the reserve fund of Grand Lodge,
for the amount now being· appropriated from this reserve. In order to
provide for this return of expended surplus and for the per ·capita levy of
twenty (20c) cents, for the maintenance of the Homes, your committee
finds it necessary to ask for a per capita levy in addition to the constitutional requirements of seventy-five (75c) cents. While this committee is
reluctant to ··recommend any additional per capita levy, it is consoled 'by
the fact that the Lodges are now prospering and therefore the increase in
levy will probably not prove burdensome. It also means that by restoring
the reserves in times like the present, it will probably prevent the necesc
sity of increasing the per capita levy at a time when the Lodges may be
much less able to stand the increase.
It is worthy of comment that during the tough times of ten y~a.rs
ago the total per capita levy was $1.8~.
The levy for the corning year will be made up as follows:

726

Masonic Information
Your Committee on Finance has analyzed the report .of the Committee
on Masonic Information and has concluded that this committee is engaged
in important Masonic work and that the appropriation of last year to
carry on this work has been spent to good advantage and that this work
should be continued.
·
Your Committee on Finance is of the opinion that the quiz programs
prepared by this committee have proven very beneficial to the Lodges
of this jurisdiction by bringing before the brethren a program that is
not only entertaining, but also edur.ationat
Your committee is also of the opinion that the series of pamphlets
prepared by this comrriittee for the coaches' use, in instructing candidates,
have also proven their worth. For how well it is known the barrage of
questions new candidates have in mind and how well we know that upon
our coaches are these questions asked.'
We therefore submit the followirig resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That the sum of $750.00 be appropriated for the use of this
committee, that they may be able to continue this splendid work.
Grand Lodge Per Capita
The constitution provides for the. levying of a per capitil of fifty
(50c) cents, to pay for the expenses of Grand Lodge and its various
activities. In additiori ·to the St;1m provided for by this J?er capita levy,
there is additional revenue accruing to Grand Lodge from degrees conferred and income on investments and from some other sources of approximately $20,000.00. '
There is also some other revenue derived from the sale of supplies and
from surety bonds covering Lodge officers. This revenue, however, cannot be taken into consideration in the budget because it is offset by
corresponding items of disbursements, which are also eliminated from
the budget. It also should be borne in mind that there are always expenses which cannot be estimated-this ·is particularly true this year due
to war conditions and the probability that further emergencies will arise.
It is pleasing to note that, despite the emergencies and uncertain
conditions under which Grand Lodge operated this ·past year, the · budget
which was set up a year ago has been as closely followed as -conditions
would permit and that the year ended with a surplus of ineome over
expenses-this surplus is · being added to the general -reserve-. ·of Grand
Lodge.
·
As usual the committee has prepared a· budget which will be submitted illlµiesliately fo116wing this portion of . the committee's report.
The budget s°ets up the estimated income and expenses for the coming year;

JURISPRUDENCE COMMITTEE REPORT
Past Grand Master Well er, chairman, reported for the J urisprudence Committee on the legislation necessary to notify
all members of each Lodge of the applications for degrees and
affiliations and stated that so many provisions of the law would
be effected that it was impracticable to attempt to present legislation at this communication and asked that the matter be referred to the Jurisprudence Committee to present legislation at
the next Annual Communication. The request was appr~ved.

Friday morning.

AUDITOR'S REPORT
Grand Lodge Report
August 31, 1943.
Gentlemen:
We have audited the accounts 'and records of the Grand Lodge F. &
A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1943, and submit
herewith the following statements:

Exhibit A:

Grand Lodge Funds
Statement of all Grand Lodge cash received and disbursed
by the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer for the fiscal
year ended July 31, 1943.

Grand Secretary's Accounts
Resume of cash received and disbursed August l, 1942, to
July 31,' 1943.
Exhibit C-1: Statement of Grand Lodge per capita dues collected from
1942 annual returns.
Exhibit C-2: Statement of Masonic Homes per capita dues and $25 contributions collected during the year 1942-43.
Exhibit B:

· Grand Treasurer's Accounts
War relief and Philippine dues funds. Statement of cash
receipts and disbursements August 1, 1942, to July 31, 1943.
Exhibit E: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements August 1, 1942,
to July 31, 1943.
Exhibit F: Statement of assets and capital account as at July 31, 1943.
Exhibit G: List of investments, as at July 31, 1943.
Exhibit D:

Comments
As shown in the capital account of Exhibit F, the revenue from per
capita dues and other sources exceeded the total of expenses and appropriations by $9,259.31.
All per capita dues, as .reported on the 1942 annual returns from constituent Lodges, have been paid in full. Our Exhibits C-1 and C-2 show
proof of the revenue due from the Lodges in accordance with their 1942
annual returns and the $25.00 Homes Contribution reports for the first
three quarters of the fiscal year 1942-43. The total revenue due, as shown,
agrees with the total cash received from the Lodges by the Grand
Secretary.
Cash receipts were accounted for and traced to the proper depositaries.
Disbursements were made by checks and supported by properly approved
vouchers. · All bank balances were verified by correspondence with the
depositaries. Certified lists of the stocks and bonds were received from the
Anglo California National Bank which holds the securities for' safe
keeping. Securities as recorded in the books of account were verified to
these lists.
No payment of principal or interest has been received from Carpinteria
Lod~~ No. 444 on their loan of $2,500.00.

This leaves the very small amoun.t of $55.55 as uncollected from 1943
annual returns up to and including September 30, 1943: These small amounts
arise solely as suspense items pending the correction and revision of returns,
and not due to their uncollectibility.
The requiring of an audit 0f the 1943 annual returns, at this time, when
the major po~tion of the collections from such returns are received after the
close of the regular audit period, July 31, and by September 30th of each year,
is commendable indeed. Thus the responsibility for the interim receipt and
accountability of quite substantial sums of money is established and cleared
before the annual communication of the Grand Lodge, and before the customary audit of such funds a year later. This is the first time in many years of
experience that such an early audit has been made _possible. Much credit is
due the Grand Secretary for the organization of material, its availability in
summary form, the prompt review and correction of returns from lodges, all
of which made possible adequate proofs of revenue received. '

J,_ife insurance . policies, received mainly from residents of the Hom~s,
have been recorded at the amount recoverable at the death of the insured,
if determinable, otherwise at a nominal value of $1.00.
Originally, real estate was recorded at the assessed value as taken
from the tax bills. Due to the constant fluctuation in real estate values,
and to avoid reporting book losses resulting from such fluctuation when
as a . fact no actual loss had occurred, all real estate donated during the
.past several years has been recorded on the books for record purposes
at a nominal value of $1.00.
- ·
·
The stocks and bonds and some of the notes are held by the Anglo
California National Bank for safekeeping. These were verified by certification from the bank. The remainder of the notes and the insurance
policies are held at the office of the Homes Secretary and were inspected
by us.
Trust and Annuity Funds:
Under Schedules B-4, B-5, B-6, B-7 and B-8, are shown the details
of the vario'u·s.· trust and annuity funds. Payments due from the annuity
funds in :accordance with the contracts and agreements were made from
th~ Homes 'general fund. Reinbursements were later made to the general
fund from the various trust and annuity funds.
All Bank balances and securities of these funds were verified by cor.respondence with the depositaries.

ROBERT W. DAVIES,

To the Most W orshipf1{l Grand Lodge of. California:
The Report of the Correspondence Committee is being written this
year from Washington, D. C., where your chairman is presently stationed.
The assembling of important and readable items of interest culled from
the various Grand Lodge jurisdictions, has been made possibl~ by the help
of all members of the Committee. It is .hoped the brethren will pe charitable and patient in their opinion until the return of normalcy will assure
the type of review which is most desirable.

FREDERICK

In continental United States the Masonic Lodges and Masons, each in
their own and perhaps individual way, are contributing much to the welfare of our craft in the armed services. The problem as to how such help
should be given has been solved in a uniformly intelligent manner. The
over-all outlook from this vantage point bids fair to present a picture of
which we can be proud.
But against this background the leaders of our craft should now .pose
the critical question: And when the war is over, what then? The returning men will have been taught to fight or die. They will not be content
to lapse into mediocrity. They will ha~e learned the active, the realistic
life, the habit of doing things. They will have a new criterion with which
to measure "the same old routine." They will be in search of a new
code of life. Horace Mann wisely said, "One might as well ~ttempt to
steer his boat without a rudder as to live his life without a Code of
Living."
Here then, is a thought for those on the higher watchtowers of
Masonry to ponder: How to assure that the Masonic way of life will
prevail, a code which comes out of the experience of the centuries, rich in
moral and spiritual values.
One thing is certain: We who are 'away will be glad to return to
our homes, to greet our old co-laborers in the Masonic quarries, to pass
from · the field of war int~ our own temples of Masonic meditation. Perhaps, therefore, the Report for this year should be closed with this
significant prayer by Jam es A. Quincy :
"In this made hour,
When nations, petulant as children in the night,
Cry down appeal to reason, and resort
To arms; when men and ships
Come home to us from all the seven seas
As blood stained doves returning t~ the ark-

0. EATON,

FRANK HOBERG,
OSCAR' OLSON,
HARRY M. p ARKER,
CHARLES L. PIODA,

GRAND MASTERS
After a man has served his brethren as Grand Master of Masons in:
his state and on the eve of the annual communication writes his message
to the craft, born in sincerity and humiliation, there is issued an inspired
document. Even though the subjects are seemingly specific to his par'ticular jurisdiction, invariably the recommendations are common to air
humanity, and all the brethren, whithersoever dispersed, can learn much
and profit by their perusal.
Georgia, 1942 (Proceedings):
Yes, my brethren, we must carry our Masonry into our homes to
strengthen this citadel of civilization and safeguard it against the laxities
and unwholesome influences that always follow in the wake of economic,
social and political upheavals.·
From these homes have 'come the boys who are fighting and dying
to preserve our way of life. Unless we can maintain our American concept
of the home, their victories will be robberi of much of their glory. The
terrible experiences through which they are passing are giving them a
better understanding of spiritual values and a greater reliance upon a
Supreme Being. Reports trickling back from the fighting front solemnly
said: "'there were no atheists in the foxholes ... of Bataan."
We must carry our Masonry into our religious activities to make our
churches a more virile force in the spiritual life of the community; to
bulwark our communities against the moral let-down and disregard for
law that followed our last great war.
We must carry our Masonry into our business to bring harmony
between employer and employee so that the production and flow of es-

869

GRAND LODGE OF CALI.FORNIA

sential war materials may continue uninterruptedly. We must take it into
our business to end sharp practices which too often prevail in our commercial dealings.

under present interpretation of our law, may close the door of fellowship
to a man of the highest possible character and integrity, perhaps one a
leader in civil life, · whose contribution to Freemasonry might be incalculable. Nothing : could be more repugnant to the fundamentals of our
institution.
"Nor can this travesty be justified by the provision that the Grand
Master has the power to issue a dispensation permitting the initiation of
one under a physical handicap. Common justice and ordinary fairness
dictate that this theory of quality be affirmed or rejected as part of our
law, and not foisted, at considerable private sacrifice 'and expense in int.erviewing hundreds of applicants, upon the individual you honor by e1evation
to the exalted office of Grand Master.

868

We must carry our Masonry into our civic affairs to insure a higher
type· -of leadership in public office and keep a firm foundation under our
governmental structures. We need only to act as our conscience dictates
and not be influenced by prejudice and selfish interests.
Illinois, 1942 (Proceedings):
Because the ideals which it has embraced throughout the ages, and the
democratic form of government with which it has been coincident and
under· which it has flourished during that time, have peen the object .of
attack by savage and treacherous, yet withal, determined and powerful,
foes, all other events in our present day lives pale into insignificance
when compared with the events following the wilful and wanton attack on
Pearl Harbor. This country, and its allies, are engaged in a titanic
struggle to determine whether peoples are created to serve governments,
or, as we would have it, governments are created to serve peoples. This
war is waged against the democratic form of living, and in such a struggle,
involving an attack on its fundamental philosophy, Freemasonry itselt is
attacked. Modern eve.nts prove that this is not a figure of speech. As
the · dictators have invaded smaller and less resistant nations, many of
whom embraced the . doctrines of Freemasonry, our fraternity has been
scourged, its altars razed, its properties confiscated, its · members persecuted, and its leaders doomed. Never in the history of the world, not excepting 1828-32 when it became the butt of political campaigns, has our
institution been more the object of the concentrated fury of its enemies.
Since the inception of the Government of the United States, Freemasons have been concomitant with the success of this Republic. Across
the horizon of the ages march a galaxy of distinguished Americans who
were true Masons. That picture has not changed in this struggle. Lead
by the indomitable MacArthur, our fraternity is again offering to the
Nation which nourished it, a full measure of devotion.
Maine, 1943 (Proceedings):
At meetings beyond the state which I have attended, and in Masonic
writings which have come to my notice, I sense a trend of thought which
will undoubtedly crystallize into action within the next few years. I refer
to the generally accepted standards of physical qualifications required for
membership in the fraternity now in effect ~n the several Grand Jurisdictions of the United States. These qualifications, generally stated, are that
"every candidate applying for the degr ees in Masonry must . . . possess
. . . no maim or defect in, his body that may render him incapable of
conforming to what the seve~al degrees respectively require of him."
While our Grand Lodge Constitution does not use identical language, it
conveys practically the same meaning. One Grand Master, speaking on
this subject, says :
"Nothing in our constitutions so thoroughly indicates the antiquity
of our fraternity a s this law, which h earkens back to the Middle Ages,
when physical fitness had some justification in the regulations and administration of the operative Guilds of England, considered by many
the cornerstone of present Freemasonry. Whatever importance external

"Finally, and, in my humble opinion, conclusively, the dreaded, hatef~l,
and dreary consequence of this gigantic military struggle, undou~ted.ly; ·will
be the return to this. State and Nation, of too many men, constitutmg the
very flower of our manhood and citizenry, and precisely within the ran.ge
of age from which Freemasonry should draw its future enrollments, with
physical defects incurred in the defense of this democracy.
"Are we going to cheer their return, and pay homage to their courage
and stamina which kept this country safe for us, and then slam the doors
of our lodges in their faces, because their heroic defense ~f us brought
them the sacrifice of some physical member? Are we gomg to say to
these heroes 'You were good enough to protect me and mine, but you
are not ·fit to be ·a Mason because in that defense you lost an arm, or a
leg, or your sight?' Are we going to say to them and to the world at
large that the bonds of fraternity and r ecognition between Master Masons
is physical and not mental? Or are we going to. practice our c.reed, and
search a man's soul, and nothing else, to ascertain whether he is worthy
to be our brother!
"I submit, that to automatically eliminate an applicant from membership because of physical disqualification unassociated· with his mental,
moral and spiritual worth, is unworthy of an institution 'more ancient than
the Golden Fleece or Roman Eagle, more honorable than the ~tar and
Garter or any other order that can be conferred upon you at this or
any future period by prince, potentate, or any other person except he be a
Mason.' And I give it to you strictly in charge that the eyes of an otherwise friendly world gaze upon us with growing distrust because of such
a peurile and illogical fixation. Let us turn our backs on t~e darkness of
the past, and face a glorious future unashamed and unafraid. Abov.e all,
let us not confuse precedent with justice. Let us, rather, have the simple
courage to do what is right. May moral qualifications, alone and forever,
be the open sesame to the treasure house of Freemasonry!"
The foregoing has been presented ·solely as food for thought and as
matter for reflection, because the trend in this direction is growing ~ver
stronger, and may in the future come before this Grand Lodge· for serious
consideration.

Manitoba, 1942 (Proceedings):
There is today in some of our lodges a great force of enthusiastic en·
deavor, but there is in some of our lodges a lamentable amount of apathetic
i.nefficiency. I am reminded of the story in the 25th Chapter of St.
Matthew's gospel when I get around to the various places on my visits
-the story of the talents, and I think. we probably over-emphasize the
men who received the five talents and the two talents, and we forget altogether the man who just received the one talent because he is the
character we do not like very much. I ask you to consider the man of one
talent tonight because he is much akin to many of us; for there is a man
who had an opportunity to do a job, there is a man who was given something to do, there is a man who refused to do his task; there is · a man
who lapsed into inefficiency, into respectability, who s·a id "Everything will
get along all right whether I do this job or not." He didn't do it and
he became one of the crowd of inefficient people who clutter up the work
of such a great fraternity as ours. He refused the conditions of successful
effort which seems to be too hard for us today. This man declined the
constant and persevering ventures of faith. To refuse to do our job in
the lodge is to forfeit the right to call God our Father. To say that what
is required of us is too hard for us, is too much for. us ; to say that we
have been given so little and we have been asked for so much, is to
acquiesce in inefficiency. To do such a thing as that is to be content with
respectability. The one talent man, I suggest to you tonight, was cast
out into darkness not because he didn't have opportunity but because he
preferred to be respectable, to be at his ease, and to get away with as
little as he could possibly do.
We need not remind you that Masonry, in many countries of the
world, has come under the ban of the totalitarian powers. What is the
offense committed by this noble fraternity, that it should be summarily
abolished? It is largely because of its ideals of education, of · right and
honorable living, and of democracy. Freemasonry has built its program
u~on the foundation rock of truth, justice, tolerance, understanding, goodwill and brotherly love. True enough it is, that if these principles were
made the dynamic of the relationship between men and nations, there
would, indeed, be "peace on earth and goodwill towards all men." The
mission of Masonry is still, and has always been, the building of the ideal
human temple.
·
The design of Freemasonry is not a destructive force. It is always
constructive and progressive. We are builders, and to that program
Masons are committed by voluntary choice and solemn obligation. We
stand foi: peace and progress. War and progress are incompatible, and
so as Masons, we can never accept war as an effective instrument nor as
the ultimate in carrying out the Masonic design. War will fail to achieve
the ends we have in view. Dictators now, as heretofore, may do their
worst, but the end of all their nefarious activities will result only in leaving
all their countries smaller and poorer.
Maryland, 1942 (Proceedings):
Immediately upon the declaration of war your Grand Master wrote
to the Governor of the State of Maryland and to the Mayor of Baltimore
City, in charge of the war activities in their respective jurisdictions, and
assured them of the wholehearted support of the craft and its anxiety and
desire to be of service wherever possible.
An order was also issued at once, directing the Masters of all Lodges
to make appropriate changes in the ceremonies by presenting the colors
at the altar, giving the Pledge of Allegiance and singing one verse of the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

871

What are the principles to which we ought now to rededicate, to reconsecrate. ourselves? They are as old as Freemasonry itself. They arc
found m the charge to the Entered · Appr.e ntice candidate. "There arc
three great duties which, as a Mason, you a.re charged to inculcate-to
G?d, to ~our n.eighbor, and to yourself." They are repeated, for emphasis,
with a smgle important addition, in the obligation of each of the three
degrees wherein we are told there in nothing contained therein which will
conflict with the duties you owe to God, your country, your neighbor or
yourself. Along that path is the road to the right.
The duty you owe to God-The Mason who forgets. God in his daily
life faces extinction as a man. He. is bound for hell and is dragging the
fraternity then;: with him. Such a man is no better than our Axis enemies
who are the lowest form of men of which I can conceive. Faith in and
allegiance to God is the only Salvation for Masons as .it is for souls. Let
us here, now, return to a God-like life H we would save America; save
Freemasonry.
·
The duty you owe to country-It is second only to God. Ameri~a's
perils are almost as great from within as from without. Last night I
saw a revelation. This morning it seems almost like a dream, yet I know
'tis true.. I saw the. spirit of Freemas<;mry in action, alive, throbbing with
power, with love, with the humanness of which R. W. Brother Lathwood,
Pennsylvania's Grand Master, spoke yes.terd;i.y. I saw it in our Masonic
Temple, in t~e real job being done by The Ma?onic Service Association
for our boys in the Armed Forces. Masonry was justifying itself there
as it did its part to make happier the lot of Amedca's boys in uniform'.
There I saw 250 boys in The Masonic Servi<;e Association Center as our
guests. There I saw Masonry doing duty to eountry in that service. I
spoke to 62 of them in separate conversations and from 62 lips came the .
same expression. "This is great, this is tops. It is wonderful. Almost
I think I'm home again."

Intelligent interest in the fraternity must start with a familiar knowledge of our Ritual. We have all heard the man who objects to the
repetition of the Ritual as a deadly monotony. I suppose the Lord's
Prayer might be droned to monotony, but in moments of agony and need
what reality is revealed in the words "Our Father!" When men first read
the Declaration of Independence they thrilled at the words ·as revealing
a new concept of human rights and the function of government. For a
century and a half thereafter we accepted as our rights the enjoyment
of the great principles which those words disclose. The words cooled
in our ears because our lives were lived without contradiction of their
meaning. Then came Poland and Czechoslovakia and Holland and Belgium
and France and Denmark and Norway and Yugoslavia and Greece and
Dunkirk and Pearl Harbor, and again the words leap to life: "Men are
endowed by their. Creator with certain inalienable rights; * * * that to
secure these rights, governments are instituted among men, deriving
their just powers from the consent of the governed." Words again became
vital because they revealed the only reality which really counted, hecause
they were a revelation of the soql of America and the aspiratipn of all
men who strive for human liberty.
The ideals of human integrity and of human brotherhood which our
Ritual exemplifies are today principles for which men and nations are
prepared to make the utmost sacrifice. The other day I received an elo. quent letter in which a brother said that he wished the four walls of our
Lodge rooms would fall down and reveal to the eyes and ears of the
world the Ritual and the teachings of our fraternity, that the influences
of the Lodge room might extend to all mankind for the perpetuation of
those principles which are basic in our civilization. For such is the fidelity
of our precepts and of our Ritual that they underlie the expression of
the democratic principles. These are realities for which men can live and ·
die; these are the realities by which Masonry must live: Let us repeat
and repeat the words so that they may become the familiar com.p anions
of our lives, and then indeed shall there be intelligent interest and understanding of the purpose and the meaning of our fraternity.

I have declined to permit balloting on petitions except at regular communications and have declined to shorten the time specified in the code

Prince Edward Island, 1942 (Proceedings):
The Masonic craft, like every other institution among us, has felt the
impact of the war. In some cases, as has been mentioned, it has been
necessary to speed the conferring of degrees in order that candidates In
the services might be raised before being sent away with their units. Our
Lodges have been delighted to welcome sailors, soldiers and airmen from
other places as visiting brethren. Some· members of the forces from
abroad, having sojourned amongst us for the required time, have been
elected to receive our mysteries and become members of our Lodgee.
Many of our brethren have enlisted in the armed forces and ar.e on active
service in Canada or overseas.
The men of the Canadian navy, army and air force are writing as
brilliant a page in Canadian annals as did their predecessors in World
War I.
·
But this is total war. The civil population have their duty to do, their
sacrifices to make, even as the armed forces. It is the duty of all of us,
whether Masons. or non-Masons, v.hether in uniform or in mufti, to wage
this war. Let us civilians with fortitude and cheerfulness bear our burdens
of taxation, obey the regulations of our Government, cooperate in every
war effort, and dedicate our resources and our energies, as the· men in
uniform are dedicating their lives, to the winning of the ·war. Loyalty in
this crisis is the supreme virtue~loyalty to our men in arms, loyalty to
· this good country we call home, loyalty to our noble King. Struggle
and bitter · sorrow lie before us, but fortitude and faith will sustain us
to the end, and glorious peace will be our reward.
But though the war must for the present be our chief preoccupation,
it is not the only menace to our welfare.
My brethrtn, we are living in a terrible age. Gr~at nations have passed
under the rule of dictators whereby the rights and dignity of the individual
man are set at naught. In all countries there seem to be a weakening of
moral restraint, a loss of reverence for those things which from of old
were held sacred, confusion of thought, bewildered groping amongst conflicting ideals and contrary views of life's purposes; and now the war,
with its bitter enmities, its destruction, sorrow and privation, its agonies
of pain and its terrific harvest of death. But amid the confusion and
horror of our distracted and stricken world, our Order stands for stability,
brotherhood, faith, and life. Here, the ancient landmarks stand. The
plumb, level and square abide, not only as the tests of behavior but as the
sanctions of man's worth and dignity. Human kindness stretches forth
a hand to aid and save a brother. From the Book upon our altars speak
the oracles of the eternal, and through faith in God all the energies and
interests of life are focused to a common purpose and a· common glory.
So all life is enriched and flourishes like the acacia sprig which had no
root in earth but still grew green because it was rooted in the unending
life.
Masonry has a great mission to our age. We are united in a splendid
work. The· contribution which each one makes to the common effort may
be small but not insignificant. The great end is to be achieved by practic-

ing in our individual lives the principles inculcated in our Lodges and
by ~rawing ever closer the ties that bind us together in fellowship and
service.

South Carolina, 1943 (Proceedings):
Strive for a correct rendering of the work. Have rehearsals with thl
officers. Keep on trying to do the thing right. Every candidate has a
right to expect and to receive the degrees given in an effective and
helpful manner. It is not honest to content ourselves to fOnfer the

.
Throw yours.e lves into this national emergency. Masonry cannot
afford to go less than "all out" for the winning of this war. Some people
have said and are saying that "this is not Masonry's war." I want to say
to you that if there was ever a war which was Masonry's, it is this one,
in my opinion. For it seems to me that Masonry has ev:erything at stake
in this war. Wherever our enemies have gone they have trampled Masonry
under foot; they have confiscated our property, persecuted our brethren,
banned our meetings and, in many instances executed our brethren for
no other crime than that of being Masons. So, it appears to me that
Masonry as an organized ·functioning power in the world has its very
life at stake in this conflict. Cooperate with all worthy local agencies in
their efforts .to strengthen and keep strong the home front. Support our
Government in every way possible. Don't spread rumors. While we wish
to insist upon the right of free speech we feel that this is no time for
too much criticism unless it is clear that it has some very constructive
purpose. Therefore, avoid undue criticism. Invest all the money you can
afford in war bonds and stamps. If your Lodges have money lying idle
put that into war bonds. Thus you will be helping your Government,
Masonry and yourselves in so doing. This is not only patriotic, it is simple
common sense and good business as well.

This Eighty-fifth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Washington brings forcefully to mind the. serious situatiop now facing our
government. Many of our Masters· and Wardens are in the service of
our Country; many of our sons and near kin are serving in the ranks.

good citizen has rallied to the support and preservation of our Country,
its institutions and our American way of life.
Notwithstanding, Freemasonry in Washington and Alaska continues
to carry on with undiminished activity. It has not faltered, nor are we
dismayed. For eighty-eight and one-half years, since the chartering of
Olympia Lddge, No. 1, it has not faltered. It has continued to be a vital
moral force in the lives of our people. For nearly eighty-four years the
Grand Lodge of Washington has continued the ·preservation of the Ancient
Landmarks and the precious traditions of our craft.
The hour has arrived for this Grand Lodge to resume its labor. The
craftsmen are in their places; the working tools have been committed to
th'eir care. I trust that rough ashlars will become perfect ashlars, and
that each stone placed in this structure _w ill be plumb, square and level.

exercised here, be tried by the working tools of our profession, thereby

It is difficult to speak of these appalling and shameful atrocities before men who can have no better ambition than to be missionaries of the
Golden Rule, but the curse of the Dark Ages is upon the world and free

Tasmania, 1942 (Proceedings):
Now, it has long been the custom on such an occasion as is this, to
dwell on the nature and purpose of our institution. What, then, is Freemasonry? In simple terms, it is a divinely constituted society of just, upright, and free men, bound together by a common allegiance to the one
true God, and united to uphold the principles of brotherly love, relief, and
truth. Its history shows that in all ages and among a-ll peoples, this belief
in the Fatherhood of God, and the Brotherhood of Man, has had a
strengthening yet refining influence. We know, too, that Freemasonry is
founded on the purest principles of piety and virtue. It stands four-square
on the cardinal virtues of Temperance, Fortitude, Prt\dence, and Justice.

FOREIGN MASONRY
The ruthless hand of ignorance and the devastations of war have laid
waste and destroyed many valuable monuments of antiquity...• Masonry
:has not escaped the unsparing ravages of barbarous force . • . but notwithstanding has still survived. And will continue to survive.
Manitoba, 1941 (Correspondence Chairman):
During the past hundred and fifty years, Masonry has not been countenanced in Russia, and the former Russian provinces of Latvia, L ithuania
and · Estonia, now under Russian influence.
In Hungary, another dictator country, Freemasonry w as abolished
some fifteen years ago on the excuse that some of the Lodges had been
active politically. The fine Grand Lodge building in Budapest was converted into a Labor Temple.

884

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In Turkey, Freemasonry was suppressed five or six years ago by the
late Kernel Ataturk, and no Masonic organizations exi~t there of which
we have any knowledge.
In Italy, both the Grand Orient of Italy and the Grand Lodge of
Italy were dissolved by Mussolini, with ruthlessness. A number of distinguished brethren were murdered in cold blood for no reason except their
connection with the Order. The Grand Master of the Grand Lodge was
exiled, became blind, and later died in prison.
In the recently seized Kingdom of Albania, Masonry has never been
organized, and of course does not exist under Italian rule.
In Spain also Freemasonry has been suppressed by Dictator Franco.
During the civil war there was much testimony to the effect that when·
ever the insurgents occupied a town they shot or murdered in the most
diabolical way, all Masons whom they could identify; and even those
related to them. Masonry was classed along' with communism and all
its property confiscated. Members of the Order were required to file a
statement with · the government within two months, explaining why they
joined the Order and why they left it. If their excuse was not acceptable
to the government, they were made liable to six years imprisonment, or
twelve years if they had received higher degrees, or held a position of
special trust, or attended international meetings.
In Germany, where Masonry once flourished under seven Grand
Lodges, Hitler ordered the dissolution of all Masonic Lodges shortly
after he came into power in 1934. Some of these bodies tried to continue
their existence under other names, but they were compelled to dissolve
and all properties were confiscated.
·
Turning now to the rest of Europe, we find that in Austria, whose.
Grand Lodge of Vienna was fraternally recognized by us, the Germans
seized the Headquarters on the first day of their occupation, placed the
Grand Master in an ·internment camp, where he died as the result of an
operation, and confiscated all property and effects belonging to the Order.

other r~gular Grand Lodges. While isolated by reason of the German
occupation and because of religious reasons as well, this Grand __ Lodge
which faced a similar catastrophe, will undoubtedly some day regai!i its
freedom and be re-established.
In France, there are three· Grand Lodges, the Grand Orient of France,
the Grand Lodge of France and the National Grand Lodge of France and
its dependencies. The last was formed about 1918 and was sponsored by
,the Grand Lodge of England.
The· Grand Orient, because it has been active politically, has not been
considered regular and does not adhere to the fundamentals of Freemasonry, such as belief in God, the presence in the lodge of the V. s.. L.,
etc.· it has been involved in several unsavory scandals such as the Stav1sky
atialr. Against all three bodies there is considerable anti-Mason ic agitation, but the probability is that all three will survive and be stronger
when France has purged itself of the Hun influence.
Switzerland with its Grand Lodge Alpina, recognized by the Grand
Lodge, is a bright spot in European Masonry. Here strong anti-Masonic,
Fascist and Communistic action forced the government to take a referendum on the continuance of the institution. The scandalous charges
against the Order were completely answered by the Masonic authorities,
and the result of referendum was the emergence of the Order stronger
than ever Switzerland may go down in the maelstrom of the present
war, but Europe without Switzerland is not probable, and Masonry will
again flourish when the conflict is over.
In Greece, Bulgaria, Jugo-Slavia, and the Balkans the situation obscures
the light and we must await developments.

When Czecho-Slovakia was seized the two Grand Lodges voluntarily
agreed to dissolve; these were the Grand Lodge of Czecho-Slovakia and
the Grand Lodge Lessing of the Three Rings.
In Denmark, with whose Grand Lodge-headed by the King as Grand
Master-we have enjoyed fraternal relations, we very much doubt whether
the. Grand Lodge of Denmark dare function as such during the present
German "protective occupation" so-called.
The same statement must be made respecting Norway and the Grand
Lodge of Norway, and respecting Holland and the Grand Lodge of
Nether lands. In spite of much insoleqt and annoying underground agitation before the occupation of these countries and outright opposition
since, we have no doubt that in Denmark, Norway and Holland, Masonry
will live again.
In Sweden, in spite of the fact that the King is Grand Master and
the Crown Prince and other members of the Royal family are officers of
the Grand Lodge, Masonry has had to face sharp and malicious antiMasonic influences.
In Finland, the small Grand Lodge of Finland has had a struggle for
an existence against communistic and Nazi attacks; · but here, too,· we
believe that when victory is achieved over the evil forces which seem
now to dominate the world, Masonry will be restored to favor.
In Belgium, the Grand Orient of Belgium, because c;>f its removal some
years ago of the Holy Bible from its altars, has cut itself off from all

On February 4, 1942, I received the following request from Lafayette
Lodge No. 14: In order that the Charter of the said Lodge, which is
115 years old and which has the signatures of Lafayette, his son and

Committees, commissions, and boards have worked on this subject and

Canada, 1942 (Grand Master):
Under the able chairmanship of R. W . Brother C. W. Robb, the
Committee on Masonic Education have continued to supervise and encourage this important part of our Masonic work. In many districts. and
lodges regular instruction is an accepted and acceptable part .of fre9uent
program and much of value is accomplished. There is, however, _in
some lodges a tendency to relax and to neglect this phase of Masonry.
Possibly in some lodges this is accentuated by the increasing number of ·
candidates, but yet it would seem that there is the very best opportunity
to inculcate Masonic lore and practise. In too many lodges it seems apparent from the monthly summonses that no attempt is being made to
continue this work by having the members prepare short interesting talks.
Frequently one hears the cry that the Mason, not an officer, is given
nothing to do. If there is merit in this contention then, surely, here is
a phase of . Masonic endeavor in which many should be asked and encouraged to take part.
If lodges find that for the moment their own members .are not ready or
are reluctant to prepare and deliver instructional addresses then at least

some effort should be expended to secure, preferably several times a year,
interesting speakers from nearby lodges and thus increase the interest
of their program. In so doing the willing Mason should not be overworked nor should lodges forget, as many frequently do, that travel
costs money and, while we fortunately have ·many enthusiastic talented
Masons who gladly give of their best and travel often many miles to
deliver Masonic addresses or conduct Masonic ceremonies, yet . it is

Georgia, 1942 (Proceedings):
Every truly American institution must re-think its program in terms
of the national need. Our Lodges, our. schools, our· churches and our
homes have an unparalleled responsibility resting upon them. Our schools
are democracy's most distinctive institution; they must enlist "for the
duration and for the long future." Therefore, we should pronouncedly
dramatize the Bill of Rights a~d its significant meaning to the free and
untrammeled people of America.
We should also make our subordinate Lodge meetings tremendously
inviting, interesting and constructive. Our meetings should be objective
in their planning, program and procedure.
Suggestions-That the public school citizenship program be definitely
and decidedly emphasized.
That every Masonic Lodge hold a public &chool artd citizenship week
in its jurisdiction sometime during the spring. That this suggestion include not · only the high schools ..but also the elementary schools and
colleges.
That each Lodge prepare and keep a service flag on which to honor
the number of its members who are in the Armed Forces.
Maryland, 1942 · (Proceedings):
Masonry is said to be a speculative science; that is, one having to do
with ideas artd theories, rather than with facts. Its ideology forms the
basis for finer thinking and better living. But how many of us have progressed beyond the primary stage of our education in the basic concepts of
Masonry? How many of us have advanced· beyond the point which we
reached when we were raised? How much independent investigation have
we made by reading the works of Masonic masters? How much thinking
have we done as to the possibility of rounding out life's values by .the
application of Masonic ideals to our daily problems? Until we divert the
rich essence of the Masonic philosophy from library shelves into the
channels of everyday life, Masonry cannot hope to have the high place
among the contributing factors to human advancement which is its just
heritage.
With this object in mind it is my purpose to enlist the cooperation of
some of our outstanding Masonic students in this jurisdiction, in the establishment of a course of lectures or discussions upon the history of Masonry, its traditions, its landmarks, its basic philosophy and its application
to the problems of everyday life. It is my hope that such presentations
will commend themselves sufficiently to the thoughtful members of the
fraternity to warrant the establishment of such a feature as part of our
Masonic activities, standing side by side with the Schools of Instruction
and the Schools of Law, thus giving emphasis not only to the ritual and
the law, but also to the philosophy of Masonry as well.

Minnesota, 1943 (Grand Master):
It is my conce9tion of the fundamental, underlying and everlasting
purpose of our institution to so firmly establish the light of Free Masonry
in the hearts and minds of those who subscribe to our Order that it will
illuminate the pathway of their lives to the highest possible peaks of
moral attainment. William Preston, to whom the craft is so much indebted, believed it to be the chief end of Masonry to instil wisdom and
convey knowledge. A wise man desires truth and seeks knowledge, not
in order to pose as a scholar or a learned man but in order that he may
live happily. Enlightenment is a thing every Mason stands pledged to
seek, and seek it he must if he is to be a Mason in fact as well as in
name. But truth must be sought for. It is not an entity lying outside
us, like a boulder on the path, but a living and changing thing, which
must evermore be possessed anew. For each one of us men the truth is a
word that is lost, and each of us must himself go in search of it.
Nebraska, 1943 (Grand Master):
The petitioner who knocks at the portals of Freemasonry possesses
li.t tle knowledge of what lies within. He may have observed the influence
of Masonry in the lives of other men. At some time he may have heard
that Freemasonry's mission in the world is the building of character in
men. If he has thought about it at all his conception of Freemasonry
probably is that it is a secret society, composed of men of character and
standing. But he really knows little or nothing about the basic ideals, the
essential principles or the significant teachings of our fraternity.
The new brother cannot become enthusiastic about Masonry until he
knows something· about it. The more a brother learns about Masonry the
more interested he will be, and it is only by showing our interest that
we can hope to interest a new brother. What is said of the needs of the
new brother may also be said of many who have been members for years.
Too frequently in the years gone by, and also in many lodges in this day,
the brother is conducted to a seat among the brethren immediately after
signing · the by-laws of the lodge, and that is the last he hears about
Masonry or Masonic instruction. Compliance with Section 66 of ' the law
is not sufficient to teach even the fundamentals of Masonry. True, the
lectures should inspire a brother to think for himself and to cultivate a
knowledge of the mystic art, but in the last analysis it is our interest
in him that must inspire the desire to know mort!' about the Brotherhood
of which he is now a part.
The true Mason labors to help his Order reach its noble ends. But
do we teach him what its noble ends are? If we fail to , do our duty by
providing proper Masonic instruction, we will have only ourselves to
blame if our new brother loses interest and drops out when the first
financial pinch comes.
Ev.e ry man carries his purse close to his heart. Only the things that
are first there freely untie the strings. As evidence of that go to any
football game, any baseball game, or to a sporting event of a~y k~nd
and observe the thousands who place such things first. Can you 1magme
any suspensions for non-payment of dues if Masonry occupied first place
in every brother's heart?
North Carolina, 1942 (Proceedings):
The Committee on Masonic Education reports the following recommendations:

890

PROCEEDINGS ·OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In these troubled times, the fraternal and the spiritual message of
Masonry has become more than ever of importance. This message is
implicit in the Masonic ritual and it is of the greatest importance, therefore, that all Masons should learn the ritual. We urge upon the lodges
that the officers be required to learn their work so that they can open and
close the Lodge efficiently, and can put on the degree work with credit
to themselves and their lodges. We further suggest occasional meetings
when the whole membership can review the catechisms. In this connection
we find it desirable that Master Masons should be taught the catechism
of the third degree. Competitions between teams in meeting will add
pleasure to this work.
Knowledge of the words of the ritual is not sufficient. They must be
understood. That the candidate may be properly instructed. the attention
of the Lodge officers is directed to the pamphlet entitled "The Lodge
System of Masonic Education" prepared by this committee some years
ago. Copies are available in the office of the Grand Secretary. The subordinate lodges are requested to consider its use.

MASONIC HOMES

Ohio, 1942 (Correspondence Reports):
First: The ceremonies of the several degrees are not alone for · the
benefit of the candidate of the particular occasion, but are intended to
contribute to the enlightenment of the members of the craft in attendance.
No portion of the work should be performed in complete darkness, or in
a light so dim that the brethren cannot see and appreciate the dramtic expression of movement as well as hear the inflection of the spoken word.
Second: Never, at any time, should the brethren lose sight of the
serious formality of the entire ceremony. A portion of our Third Degree
includes a form which alludes to one of the oldest-known initiatory rites
and also symbolizes a very important ·e vent in the history of the human
race. Any lightness of atmosphere within the Lodge room during that
portion of the degree is sure to defeat the purpose we have in mind, to
detract from the impression which we seek to make upon the candidate,
and to affect adversely his attitude toward the fraternity and the basic
teachings which we seek to inculcate into his very existence.
Utah, 1943 (Proceedings):
· This r eport deals principally with the calendar year 1942, although for
comparative purposes, some of the data are arranged to include the entire
Grand Lodge Year, from September, 1941, to December, 1942, inclusive.
A sharp decline is to be noted in most cases, in both educational and
attendance data. This is due to several causes, but the ones most noticeable are, a decline in the resident memberships of most Lodges, the rapid
rise of industrial activity, the loss of many regular Lodge attendants due
to their induction into military service and the extra burden which has
been placed upon many Lodge officers in respect to civilian defense activities. Most of the declining figures can therefore be traced directly to war
conditions.
Another interesting item on attendance is gasoline rationing. I will
quote briefly from one of several Lodges which have written on this
subject. Basin Lodge reports "every officer except the Treasurer living
out from Myton." Each must drive an average of 40 miles to attend
Lodge. The Junior Deacon drives 110 miles, the Junior Warden 50 miles.
They now confine all degree 'work to regular business meetings and education programs will suffer thereby.

891

This is a subject well worth serious study by the lay members of the
fraternity. It would be well if they took a keen interest and when they
learn of successful innovations in other jurisdictions, insist on their adoption locally.

Minnesota, 1943 (Grand Master):
This Grand Lodge, in 1942, adopted a resolution which was aimed at
final liquidation of outstanding, delinquent Masonic Home assessments.
It looked like a drastic step. There were those who honestly and sincerely
counseled that in the stress of war it was inadvisable to proceed. All of
the pros and cons were given consideration. Were any of the prospective
future officers o.f this Grand Lodge better equipped to undertake the
task? What would you have thought of me if I had sidetracked the matter
and dodged the issue? In what light would I have stood before you today?
We determined to go through with it.
The approximate number of delinquent accounts, after making allowances for deceased members and discr<;pancies between Lodge records and
Masonic Home records, was 6,874 one year ago. The approximate aggregate
unpaid assessments at that time was $66,000.00. That was our starting
point. We are pleased to report accomplishments of the year. Many of
you may take just pride in your contributions to those accomplishmen~s.
You have been on the firing line and have done yeoman service. The
Committee on Masonic Home Assessments and the Committe'e on Lodges
will give you the breakdown on figures. It is sufficient for me to state at
this point that during the year the sum of $40,741.29 has been paid on
delinquent assessments; $2,278.92 has been cancelled by the committee
upon recommendation of Lodges on account of inability to p~y; approximately $7,660.00 is represented by promises to pay in regular installments;
$800.00 was unpaid by members who have passed away. The aggregate
amount of foregoing is approximately $51,480.21, which, deducted from
$66,000.00 leaves $14,519.79 for other consideration and action. This balance represents less than 3 per cent o:P the membership of this Grand
Jurisdiction. In other words more than 97 per cent of our members hav~
discharged their obligation to the Home.

Prince Edward Island, 1942 (Grand Master):
The examination of the records disclosed a variety of conditions, but
on. the whole one can say that the Order in this Jurisdiction is in a healthy
state. All the Lodges held meetings during the preceding year in numb.er
from seven to nineteen; about half of them conferred degrees, one as many
as 19, and although the tendency toward net loss of membership in the
Jurisdiction as a whole was not arrested, the falling off was very small
and I have hopes that by now the worst is past and that we may look
forward to a · gradual growth in numbers. In all the Lodges there were
dues in arrear; the amounts averaging from 37c per member in one Lodge
to $3.33 in another, A Lodge having arrears of 44c per member had recently achieved this low figure by a special effort whereby overdue sums
amounting to $132.00 were got in. Where arrears have accumulated, a
determined drive to recover past due amounts is greatly to be commended;
but even more to be commended would be the steady and efficient action
of Lodge Officers in getting in each year's dues as they become payab)e,
thus preventing .the accumulation of arrears. When a member fails to
make his payments r egularly he not only deprives his Lodge of the use
of money rightly due, but his default gives rise to a state of mind on his
own part towards the Lodge, and on the part of his Brethren towards
him, which chills the fraternal spirit and weakens the Lodge. Cases
sometimes occur in which a Brother finds it impossible to keep up his
payments. When investigation has shown that a wo.rthy Brother _is so
situated, he should be helped by the remission of his indebtedne.s s in

PATRIOTISM
The following might well be a hint to committees on Masonic education--5timulate an interest on the part of the membership.
Mirinesota, 1943 (Grand Orator):
I~ you will study the theories advanced by Washington, Hamilton,
Madison and others among our apostles of freedom who erected the
most faultless and enduring temple to the liberties of mankind, you will
find that the fountain, th<! source of all authority, was the citizen. The
individual was surrounded by the township, the county, the state, the
nation, like so many concentric circles, each serving a double purpose,
each invested with the greatest possible Jurisdiction. Citizens were thereby
prevented from encroaching upon one anothers rights. Barriers were
erected between all of the citizens and the ambitious tyrant, which must
be demolished before the liberties of the people could be swallowed up in
a federal despotism. Then and now between the tyranny of centralization
· and the freedom of the citizen stands the integrity of the state. Thus
were established inherent and inalienable rights, enjoyed not by the grace
of governments, but of God. Thus was drawn the sacred circle which
circumscribes the independence of the individual and the sanctity of his
person and his property. This constitutes our American legacy. Thus
was established an ism, a way of life, which has on the whole been more
successful and more revolutionary than all others: Americanism. As the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

897

purpose and -the strength of America begins to unfold increasingly in this
conflict our perception becomes clearer of what the contribution of America
to the trend of civilization has been in the past, and what it can and
must be tomorrow. That contribution must help to shape a better world
order.
In that great objective Masonry can and will lend a helping hand. It
had a silent but mighty part in the making of America, and in fashioning
its fundamental life and law. The . future of Masonry in America and in
the world depends upon the part they now take in establishing the wider
freedoms and how they continue to be held together by the peculiar tie
which Masons spin and weave between men.

Oregon, 1942 (Correspondence Chairman):
If memory serves this scribe aright, this plan of having the Masonic
Service Association act as a central organization through which welfare
work would be carried on among the personnel of the Armed Forces,
resulted from our having been pushed around a bit during World War
No. 1. We had been denied the privilege that had been accorded the
Y. M. C. A., Knights of Columbus, Salvation Army and others, because
the officials of the army and navy were loath to deal with forty-nine
Grand Bodies, lacking a central organization.
Piqued? Yes, possibly, Chagrined? ·Most assuredly. Determined that
it should not occur again? Yes! And to insure this, plans were prepared
and the organization designated that would take the field in cas.e _of
eventualities, so that Masonry would be represented on an equal footing
with any other organization.
Such was the picture as viewed in 1918 and such was · the picture
Masonry continued to see all during the years intervening between the
close of World War No. 1 and the opening of the present hostilities.
Like the French who having built their Maginot Line, could not see any
other plan of battle other than that which they had seen in 1914 to 1918,
so Masonry having made its plan of action could not see the possibility
of any other.
Plans made in 1917 were as obsolete when applied to the welfare
problems · of 1941 as were the plans of war drawn in 1917, when confronted with the needs of the present rapid mechanized form of warfare.
We did not recognize the changing set-up and the result is that the
U. S. 0., born of the necessity for unity, the reduction of overhead and
the need for service to all men in uniform rather than our own particular
group, came into being, with new plans, a trained personnel, a broader
conception of welfare service and a financial backing based on a nationwide appeal.
This writer has no quarrel with the Masonic Service Association or its
supporting Masonic Jurisdictions over their desire to be of service, for
that is putting into practice the teachings of the craft, but he does take
issue with them over the manner and form in which the service is being
rendered.
In appearing on the present scene with Huts, Hospitality Houses, Recreation Centers, or whatever term you may prefer to designate them, the
Masonic Service Association places Maso.nry'in an unenviable position regardless of what plan of action they may pursue in conducting these
establishments.
Either they will serve all comers, both Masonic or profane, and in
so doing introduce competition and a bidding for the patronage of the
men, an intensely objectionable feature that marred the welfare work of
World \:Var No. 1, or they will confine their efforts to serving Masons

Montana, 1942 (D. G. M., District of Columbia):
Only Masonry can carry Masonry · to the Armed Forces and our sons
and relatives. It is that which we are doing at your behest . . . The
Masonic Service Association has not asked for money from anybody but
Masons. There has never yet been erected a Masonic Service center
where anything is sold. Everything is given free. Your money is not
used to buy and then to sell again. The hungry lad who comes in is
fed. The worried lad uses the long distance phone, and we pay the' bills.
He has writing paper free'. We have trained field agents who are Master
Masons in good standing; old enough to get the boys' respect, and young
enough to understand their problems, to whom they can bring their
problems and talk as Mason to Mason.

South Australia, 1942 (Proceedings):
The exercise and management of Freemasonry in this time of National peril are subject to special directions called for by the circumstances,
and the M.W. Grand Master has accordingly approved the following recommendations of the Board:
Lo.dges should continue to hold meetings as usual, so long as Commonwealth and State War Regulations are observed in their entirety.
Any particular Lodge or Lodges may be permitted to meet at such
time, place, and at such intervals as may be approved by the Grand Master.
The practice of Grand Officers conducting Installation Ceremoni.es
will be continued, subject to transport facilities being available. The attention of Lodges is drawn to Constitution 64, which deals with the position where they are unable to hold their usual meetings for the election
and installation of officers. In such event, Lodges are asked to communicate immediately with the Grand Secretary, who will report the circumstances to the Grand Master for his decision. This procedure is also
to be followed in regard to other Lodge meetings.
Whilst recognizing that evening .dress is the accepted dress for Masonic functions under normal conditions, the wearing of street clothes,
with the apron outside the coat, is recommended for general adoption
by the brethren at ordinary Lodge meetings, installations, and Grand
Lodge Communications ·during the present emergency.
·
Lodges are urged to open not later than 7 :30 p. m., and to insure that
all brethren shall retire from Lodge premises not later than 10 :30 p. m.
Festive Boards should be continued, but expenditures thereon shall be
reduced to il minimum.
The brethren are exhorted to use public conveyances wherever possible to get to Lodge functions. This applies more especially to the
metropolitan area.
On the sounding of an air-raid warning, the presiding officer shall
declare the Lodge "called off" summarily. The Director of Ceremonies,
or Marshal to be appointed ·for the purpose, shall supervise the prompt
evacuation of the brethren from the Lodge Room to the nearest shelter.
These directions will operate during the present emergency and/or until
varied by authority of the Grand Master.

Washington, 1942 (Grand Master) :
I have been in close touch with the work of the Committee on Masons
in the Armed Forces. This Committee has submitted its report to me _in
advance of the convening of Grand Lodge, and I am in accord with its
recommendations.
When this Committee was appointed we were not at war; tlie problems
with which it has to deal have been multiplied and intensified by our
entry into the conflict. While I agree heartily with the viewpoint of the
Committee that we should not join the Masonic Service Association in its
program of establishing Welfare Centers, we must make sure that we
adequately carry out the program that we have outlined for ourselves,
to-wit :
l. Encouraging Lodges to keep in touch with their own members.
2. Informing Masons in the service of all Masonic meetings held in
proximity to the places where they may be stationed; and keeping them
in contact with things Masonic.
Washington, 1943 (Committee):
This committee was appointed by the Grand M aster on November 12,
1941. It was clearly the sentiment of .the last Grand Lodge, and we believe it reflected the feeling of the great majority · of the Masons of this
jurisdiction then and now, that we should not engage in any program iµvolving the establishment of huts or "welfare" centers for our brethren
in the Armed Forces. Our feeling was and is that the cost would be prohibitive and that it would be merely a duplication of the work of agencies
such as those in the U. S. 0., which are better equipped to do that type
of work.
The committee has therefore attempted J,:o develop a twofold program:
l. Encouraging Lodges to keep in contact with their own members in
the service.
2. Informing Masons in the service of all Masonic meetings held in
proximity to the places where they may be stationed; and keeping them
in contact with things Masonic.
No one plan or program can be univ(!rsally applicable, but we have
encouraged each community to work out something which meets its
particular problems.
Outstanding meetings honoring our brethren in the service have been
held by a number of our Lodges, and there has been a very real effort tO
make them feel that no matter in what part of the United States their
family home might be, their ·Masonic home was no farther away than
our nearest Lodge Dances and entertainments of various kinds have been
sponsored.
Of the two hundred fifty· dollars appropriated for our work only $50.22
has been expended. This does not mean that there should be any reduction
in the amount budgeted for the work of this committee; as a matter of
fact, that amount should be substantially increased if the work of the
committee is to be continued.
While it has been a source of satisfaction to the committee to receive
letters of commendation and expressions of approval of what is being

of the men in the service, particularly our· Brethren and our sons. This
is an obligation not only of the individual but it is an obligation of the

fraternity; it is because such cooperation is important and necessary in the
common effort to preserve those principles of liberty and democracy which
are the outgrowth of and predicated upon our system of Masonic philosophy. The preservation of our way of life and the maintena~ce of our
ideals as potent factors . in the shaping of human relationships require that
Freemasonry be not lacking in its utmost endeavor.
·
To this end, I have called upqn every Mason in the State of New
York to contribute at least one dollar a year for the duration of the emergency to the Masonic War-Chest.
It ·may be that as Mas.o ns, as A.merlcans, we have taken our obligations lightly; tha_t confident of our privileges we have forgotten to secure
their protection ; that in· the comfort of our own estate we have ignored
our neighbor's needs, not heeding that if his house burns our own home
and possessions are in danger of the conflagration. Perhaps we too have ·
gathered into barns as in the parable of old and said, "Soul, thou hast
much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease"-forgetting that
"where the treasure ·is there will the heart be also."
If so, then it is also true that slowly and in travail we are learning that
the real treasures lie not in the tangibles but in the intangibles and that
the great values of life are revealed to us "not in moments of happiness
but are taught to us in moments of sorrow.'"
May I repeat to you what was said twenty-five years ago by our late
Senior Grand Chaplain, R.W. Samuel Parkes Cadman:
"We are here to redeem .ourselves and to maintain that we do not
gather simply to blow our trumpets in t he new moon and cry out what
profitable servants we are, but rather to try and serve a stricken and bleeding world, in which there are millions of broken hearts ·t~day, and many,
many more tomorrow. For there are men sitting in my presence who
have given up their flesh and blood, who will have to sacrifice .the com. petences with which they had hoped to cheer and relieve the infirmity of
age, who will see their backgrounds shattered and their projects laid in
the dust, and the homes which were built up by the love of family, by labor
and devotion, either robed in grief or slipping beyond their pecuniary care.
To help these is the real task of Masonry. These are the things to which
we stand pledg'e d by all that ther.e is in us, and this is why we are leaving
the comparative obscurity in which we rather love to linger that we may
do something for the great want and woe of mankind."

Wyoming, 1942 (Proceedings):
Since the convening of the Grand Lodge last August, we have become
engaged in another World War. Masonry is ably represented by thousands of brethren in the Armed Forces. They are demonstrating the same
determination and the same loyalty to patriotism that have characterized
Masons from the beginning of this nation. We owe them every consideration that we can give them. From my information, the Masonic Service
Association is doing a splendid work in behalf of these brethren.
At our last session, we set up a per capita q~ota -0f ten cents per
member. This proved inadequate in the light of the emergency. With
the assistance of the Grand Secretary, I issued a letter to the subordinate
Lodges, urging each member to contribute one dollar to this· service. The
response was excellent, and to date we have received $2,648.20. Masonic
centers have been established. This association is the only medium through
which we can adequately serve our brethren in the Armed Forces.
I have ,"given this problem serious consideration and urge this Grand
Lodge to take affirmative action in setting the per capita quota in such
an amount as may be deemed adequate in the light of all the circumstances. There seems to be only one of two alternatives we cah follow:
A. Voluntary contributions.
B. Raise the per capita assessment.
It occurs to me that the per capita assessment is the better of the two
methods.

Canada, 1942 (Grand Master):
Following the action of Grand Lodge of a year ago the committee has
been continued in office and throughout the year they have done most excellent work. The committee continued to arrange for the comfort of
those relatives of British Masons who came to Canada but found unexpectedly that exchange regulations would not permit them to receive
money from the home land. The . major work of the committee lay in
the prosecution of the continuance of the appeal for the fund known as
the Grand Lodge British War Relief Fund. This original appeal was
made about Marsh 1st, 1941, and when Grand Lodge met a year ago the
report was made that the members of the craft had contributed in the
short space of a little ove.r four months, $115,000. This year our effo~ts
on behalf of this fund have spread over a period beginning last September
and I am happy to report that another $115,000 and more has been contributed . and that contributions are still coming in. This splendid result'
has .b~en achieved under the energetic efforts and leadership of this
committee.
