GOOD AND WELFARE
A new heading in these reports. Many interesting and instructive suggestions will be found in these notes.
District of Columbia, 1942 (Grand Master):
From innumerable sources there have come to me proofs that our
brethren desire strongly to have an individual part in contributing to the
comfort and well-being of those near and dear to us who are actively engaged in the war effort, to give them positive assurance of our determination that, so far as lies in our power, and at any sacrifice, we shall give
them that loving aid and comfort which Freemasonry knows so well how
to bestow. I feel ·strongly that our individual brethren should be afforded
the opportunity, which they so earnestly desire, to contribute of their
means to this noble purpose.
In conformity with this belief, and by virtue of the power and authority
vested in me as Grand Master of Masons of the District of Columbia, I do
hereby create and establish a District of Columbia Masonic Welfare Fund.
I further decree and direct: ·
·
1. That every Master Mason of our District of Columbia Lodges be requested to contribute not less than one dollar to the said Masonic Welfare
Fund for the present year.
Maine, 1943 (Committee on Jurisprudence):
We believe our Grand Lodge has gone as far as possible in a liberal
interpretation of the ancient landmarks and the last and crowning landmark of all, is that the landmarks can never be changed, but were received
from our predecessors under a soleinn obligation and duty to transmit
them to our successors.
·
·
The question therefore involves more than a denial of the privileges
of Masonry to those who under the ancient landmarks through no fault
of their own are unable to meet its 'requirements. There are many other
institutions where they can be of service to their fellow men, and no man,
however worthy, has an inherent right to become a Mason. It is a
privilege that he may secure only under the ancient landmarks and
customs of the fraternity. If he cannot meet these requirements, and the
ancient landmarks are changed for his accommodation, he may be a
member of an organization, but it will not be Masonry. As honorable men
and Masons intrusted with the care and management of our ancient and
honorable institution, we are under solemn oath to strictly comply with
all ancient Masonic. usages and transmit them unimpaired to our successors. It is not within our power to change them even were we convinced
that it is advisable so to do.

Minnesota, 1943 (Grand Master):
lt is customary to give briefly a recapitulation of the gains and losses
in membership during the year. When I sat on this platform one year
ago listening to the proposed legislation relating to liquidation of the
Masonic Home assessment, I had a sinking sensation from which I did not
recover for weeks. There were approximately six thousand eight hundred
delinquent Masonic Home accounts. I had visions of thousands of members being stricken because of failure to respond. I said to myself, as
Grand Master you are going to take the greatest licking in membership
losses of any Grand Master in the history of this Grand Lodge. It is,
therefore, with much pride of accomplishment for you and for me that
I tell you that in spite of the liquidation of more than seventy-five per
cent of the $66,000.00 of delinquent Masonic Home assessments existing
one year ago, this Grand Lodge has suffered the lowest net loss in membership during 1942 of any year since 1929. I know you will rejoice with
me as a result. May I express the hope that my successor will be able to
throw away the red ink and actually establish us on the increase again.
During 1942, 1,033 were raised, 382 joined, and 222 were restored.
Four hundred ninety-nine withdrew, 717 were stricken and 815 died,
suspended and expelled 5, making a net loss of 399, as compared with 583
in 1941, 653 in 1940, and 715 in 1939.
Nova Scotia, 1942 (Grand Secretary):
We are able to report a general improvement all along the line, for the
year ending December 31st, 1941.
The number of candidates raised tota.led 266 against 171 for the previous year, 137 were suspended against 212 in 1940; the riet loss in membership was 11, while in 1940 it was 137; gross amount of dues exceeded the
previous year by $657.30.
We have good reason to be proud of the response received from the
members, both towards the Sprinkler Fund, and the Queen's Canadian
Fund. These · amounts were collected at a minimum of cost, and most
cheerfully subscribed by . a very large majority of the craft.
A very large number of members, are actively engaged, not only in
the services, but in various other war activities. Let us remember there is
a place for all to do something, of one kind or another.
1942 has opened well, and we have every reason to believe, that we will
have turned the corner by the end of this year.

Washington, 1942 (Grand Master):
The general condition of Masonry in Washington and Alaska appears
to be sound and progressive. Many of our Lodges are experiencing a ·
marked increase in degree work, and many are exercising a great effort
to render good and faithful service to their brethren who are in the
Armed Forces of our Country. The war, unquestionably, is showing its
effect in the government of ou.r Lodges, for many now have one or more
of their three principal officers in the service. I am, however, happy to
report that no serious emergencies have yet arisen demanding the attention
of the Grand Master. The work of the Lodges has been carried on uninterrupted, by the officers next in rank. I am a-lso pleased to report' that

GRAND LODGE OF CAJ.IFORNIA

907

we have not yet .experienced any great or unusual influx of war-time
applications such as we did some twenty-five years ago. We will remember what effect this condition wrought upon .our fraternity, a nd the many
warnings we have since received to guard against such a recurrence. Our
leaders in the past have sounded this warning, so let us heed th e words of
one of our illustrious Past Grand Masters, who once said : "Our design
is not to put more m~n into Masonry but to put more Masonry into men."
In a bulletin ac;ldressed to all our Lodges I pointed out the five common weaknesses of a Lodge and suggested, under five paragraphs, how
these weaknesses might be partially corrected or at least strengthened. In
determining the common ailments of a Lodge I used the analogy of a
doctor examining a patient; how he would first test the pulse, temperature,
heart and blood, and if it was then necessary he would use every other
test known to medical scienc·e. He would determine the cause, locate the
weak or affected parts, after which the treatment would be prescribed or
the remedy administered. In like manner we should x-ray our own case.
By a careful study we would find many of our Lodges with five weaknesses-five weak spots needing examination and attention. Space will not
permit me to go into any lengthy detail, so here they are in brief form:
1. Lack of leadership in our Lodges-Worshipful Masters and Officers
have not the ability, or have not the inspiration to plan and work.
2. Lack of proper Lodge management-Meetings are poorly conducted,
not interesting, too slow, and draggy- too late at night. M any Lodge
rooms are too big and barny for the average attendance. I m proper ventilation and poor acoustics.
3. Lack of well planned programs-No preliminary arrangements made
to organize good programs.
4. Lack of a genuine spirit of fellowship-Officers are cold and
unfriendly.
5. Lack of inter-Lodge visitations-No inspiration ·to emulate the
good work and fellowship of other Lodges.
1. Endeavor by every means at your command to inspire your Worshipful Masters to be leaders. Inspire them with the idea that the Masonic
Lodge room is offering them the opportunity, material, and equipment
. fOr their own self-training and self-improvement, enjoyed by only a few
men and profited only by those who study, work and plan.
2. Emphasize better Lodge management. Open an d close on time;
better and shorter meetings is the solution to this problem. Open
promptly, carry on uninterruptedly, and close early to insure interesting
and well-attended meetings. It is my opinion that we should have no such
practice as "calling at ease" or "free from restraint until the sound of the
G. in the E." This should be the time to have a word from visitors, the
report of the sick committee, or other matters. All Lodges should be
dark at 10 :30 o'clock, the brethren on their way home or at the refreshment table.
3. Encourage well planned programs. Our most successful Lodges
have regular monthly officers' meetings and issue a bulletin or trestle
board thirty days in advance. Lodge notices published in the local papers
have brought resu,lts and have had a good effect upon the general public.
Many of our Lodges are overlooking the opportunity to have at least three
outstanding meetings a year.
4. Every Lodge should make an effort to improve the spirit of friendship and fellowship. I like to meet with a group of good fellows who
really show it by the warmth of their welcome and the smile on their
faces, and who always maintain that proper regard for the dignity of

Masonry. Officers and members should be friendly, kind and considerate
to one another, especially the timid brother, young or old, who has trouble
getting to his feet and expressing his thoughts or convictions. A Lodge
cannot expect to have regular visitors if the officers and members are un·
friendly, quarrelsome, critical and ridicule the mistakes of others. The
Master who has a "run the Lodge" attitude, usually runs the Lodge alone.
5. In.ter-Lodge visitations widens our acquaintance, enlarges our conception of brotherhood, and inspires our officers and members to a greater
degree of proficiency in the work. Therefore, may I ask that every Lodge
in your district set aside a night and invite the officers and members of
some other Lodge outside of your district, or at least from another town,
to visit the Lodge. The visiting Lodge should confer a degree or furnish
a speaker or a program of music, or "what have you." This should create
greater interest and activity in your district these coming winter months.
Utah, 1943 (Grarid Master):
The most important committees a Master of a Lodge is called upon
to appoint are the committees to .which · he entrusts the work of investigating the qualifications of those who seek admission into the fraternity.
The committee personnel being different in each case, it follows that the
character of investigations will likewise differ.
For the purpose of improving upon present practice and for the government of Committees on Investigation of petitioners for the degrees, I
recommend that a new form of petition blank be drafted, along with a
questionnaire to be signed by the committees, cove\'ing those points upon
which information is necessary to the determination of the fitness of the
petitioner to become a Mason.

South Dakota, 1942 (Committee Report):
This report is taken from all the Grand Lodges of the United States
and the District of Columbia, with the exception of six : Alabama, Michigan, New York, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Uta~ and Washington,
none of which have come to.my desk. In addition, I have received fifteen
Foreign Grand Lodge proceedings: thirteen reviewed and two (being in
foreign language) I was unable to read.
In the minds of some, the Reviewer's services are very limited, and
that the cost of printing , exceeds the services rendered. This view is
caused by lack of Masonic Education with some, and lack of interest with
·others. Until such time as the local Lodges find time and have the interest
to seek a broader view of universal Masonry, there will undoubtedly be
that tendency. The Grand Lodge night, as adopted in our Educational
Program, is intended to fill this needed want. Without a good report
through the Foreign Correspondent, little opportunity is offered to local
Lodges to know what is happening even in a Sister Jurisdiction, to say
nothing of those more distant, and especially those outside our own
country.
There is no greater opportunity for the individual Mason to broaden
his knowledge than through the proceedings of other Jurisdictions. Those
engaged in Ritualistic work demonstrate a variety of reasons fqr their
activities; some to be conspicuous, some to acquire title and others for
various reasons. The largest group represents those eagerly searching for
more Masonic light. Even within this group too few give proper attention
to the Annual Report of the Grand Lodge.

RELIEF
Relief of the needy brethren, and the distressed, is the first duty o~
Masonry. The following reports indicate that some jurisdictions do not
rest at that.
•Canada, 1942 (Grand Master):
In the larger cities the practical operation of Freemasonry presents
problems that are not encountered in those centers where there is but
one Lodge or even two or three. Much valuable work is accomplished
by Masonic Boards of Relief but the work of the Toronto Board calls for
special mention and high praise. The valuable' work that this Board doe~
is of benefit not only to the Lodges and Masons of Toronto but also to
the craft throughout the jurisdiction and even beyond, in looking after
the needs of transient Masons and those in distress who seek its able and
sympathetic aid.
Colorado, 1942 (Co.mmittee):
The fund was established in 1901, the fund at that time being $1,501.45. It has grown so that in this report we are accounting for $362,430.21. During the year we have paid out $9,995.00 to 38 beneficiaries,
hailing from 29 different Lodges.
The board of trustees consists of five members, each serving five years,
appointed by the Grand Master, the term of one member expiring each
year. The work of the board is divided into five departments, the first
being general relief, the second Colorado Soldier Masons War Relief, the
third, finances, the fourth , real estate and the fifth the Jacobson Memorial
Scholarship fund.

911

The first important function of the Trustees is to take care of the
beneficiaries. In each instance when relief is required application forms
prepared by the Board have to be signed by the Master. and Secretary of
the Lodge requesting help in the taking care of its member or the dependents of a member. With the information disclosed on the written
application, together with such data as can be accumulated, the Trustees
give careful consideration to the actual requirements of the applicant for
whom relief is sought. Occasionally the Trustees do not agree with the
recommendations of the Lodge. In some instances they believe more
money will be required than the Lodge recommends. In other instances
they have reduced the amount asked for. It is the fixed opinion of t):i.e
Trustees that the applicant should feel that the relief comes directly from
the Lodge, or at least that the Lodge is the instrumentality through which
it comes, therefore, wherever it is practical, the benefit checks are sent
directly to the Secretary of the Lodge, it being hoped that the Secretary
will deposit the checks and draw the Lodge's check in favor of the beneficiary for like amount.
It is intended and expected, where a Lodge can afford to carry the
relief of a brother, it will do so. There are many instances, however,
where the Lodge is unable to do so and appeal to the Trustees of the
Benevolent Fund for assistance. However, in nearly every instance the
Trustees desire that the Lodge pay a portion of the benefit allotted, no
matter how small. This is done for two purposes : first, that the Lodge
may feel its responsibility to care for the distressed brother, widow or ,
orphans, and second, to keep the matter continually before the Lodge, so
that the Lodge will realize, as we all do, that financial help thus rendered
is only a .discharge of a part of our Masonic obligation, and we may say,
a small part, the larger part being that of personal s ervice and friendship.
In 1918, I. Ernest Newsom, the then Grand Master of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Colorado, and others sponsored the raising · of a fund known as Colorado
Soldier. Masons War Relief Fund for the purpose of affording relief and
rehabilitation of soldier Masons, who were maimed or wounded while in
any of the Armed Forces of the first World War. Considerable effort
was made in raising this money and much zeal and fervor put into it. The
sum of $40,000 was collected in small amounts from many members of the
craft. The fund was placed in the hands of a Board of Control consisting
of seven members, each one resident of different parts of the State.
While the fund was not intended to be invested, but utilized for the
purposes for which it was raised, very shortly the Board of Control
found that, because of activities of the Veterans Bureau, adequate relief,
far in excess of what this Fund had contemplated, was granted to the
veterans returning from the World War. After ten years the Board of
Control paid out slightly over $10,000, which was $5,396.38 less than the
interest derived from the investment of the Fund.
North Carolina, 1943 (Proceedings):
The . Masonic Educational Loan Fund Committee reviewed in detail
the reports submitted by the several Educational Institutions administering the Masonic Educational Loan Fund and from these reports have
condensed the following pertinent data:
To the question as to whether more money could be used to advantage
with safety, 14 report "No," 10 report "Yes," four give no reply.
To the question as to whether it is burden~ome to select really worthy
students for these loans, 24 answer "No," two answer "Yes," two make
no reply.

912

As to preference being accorded to students of Masonic kinship, 20
answer "No," six answer "Yes," two make no reply.
In view of the above, the committee deemed it advisable to make a
study of the amounts of unloaned funds at each institution for eight
preceding years-thereby securing a clear picture 6f the trend of available
unused funds at each college over that time period.
It was learned that the unloaned balances · in all the institutions in
1935 was $11,849.06, which increased to $41,040.02 in 1943. This gradually
increasing " Cash on Hand" seems to be caused largely by the fact that
funds are available from both government and other sources at interest
rates much lower than the 6 per cent rate charged on our loans, in fact
the Federal Director of Student War Loan Funds states that North
Carolina institutions have already · taken advantage of such federal funds
to the extent of $137,000.00 and the Congress has appropriated $5,000,000.00
for such loans over the United States at interest rates of 2Y, per cent and
obtainable under other far more favorable conditions than afforded under
our regulatio?s, all these facts greatly lessening the demand for our funds.
